News.title: At least 11 dead and 17 injured as huge inferno erupts and rips through shop on popular resort island in Thailand
News.content:
Next

AT LEAST eleven people have died and 17 others are injured after a massive fire ripped through a building in Thailand.

Firefighters and emergency crews raced to the scene in the southern resort island of Phuket in the early hours this morning.



The blaze broke out in a four-storey building housing flats, a restaurant and a motorcycle rental shop at around 2am.

Flames tore through the building before spreading at a terrifying pace into neighbouring homes.



Harrowing details have emerged of victims desperately trying to flee to higher floors.

One body was found on the third floor and 10 others were found on the fifth floor, authorities said.

Footage shows firefighters battling the blaze with hoses as fierce flames raged from the ground floor to the roof.

It took crews about an hour to bring the blaze under control.



Phuket police commander Surachai Sooksai said officers are still investigating the cause of the fire.

But initial investigations found an electrical transformer near the building had exploded just before the fire started.

Phuket Govenor Chodnarin Koedsom said the rental shop had about 100 motorcycles, along with stored gas, engine oil, plastic materials and tires.

The materials could have contributed to the rapid spread of the fire.

Images from the scene show the building torn open and burnt black by the inferno.



The motorbike shop on the ground floor completely collapsed with the metal roof melted into singed vehicles.

News.title: Urgent hunt to find missing schoolgirl, 14, who vanished from fire station in UK town
News.content:
FIND HER Urgent hunt to find missing schoolgirl, 14, who vanished from fire station in UK town







Next

A SCHOOLGIRL has disappeared, with police launching an urgent search.

Phoebe, 14, was last seen at a fire station in Bolton on Sunday afternoon.

Officers are becoming increasingly concerned for the teenager’s welfare and are urging anyone who’s seen her to get in touch.

Phoebe was last seen at around 12pm on November 15 at Horwich fire station on Chorley New Road.





She is described as white, around 5ft 5in tall, of medium build and with long dark hair worn down.

She was last seen wearing dark grey loose-fitting joggers, a light grey Adanola hoodie, a black fitted puffer jacket and cream, purple and silver Asics trainers.

In an appeal, police said: “Officers are becoming increasingly concerned about Phoebe and want to make sure they are safe and well.”

News.title: Burnham’s plans to end Freeview risks a communications blackout during a crisis, warns probe
News.content:
Next

LABOUR plans to end Freeview telly risks a communications blackout during a crisis, a Parliamentary probe has warned.

A cross-party group of peers has urged Andy Burnham to abandon the switch-off “which risks weakening national resilience by reducing universal access to communication”.



Ministers are proposing to scrap free-to-air TV as soon as 2034 and move all services online instead.

The controversial bid could clobber an estimated eight million households that do not have their TV hooked up to the internet.



But the Lords National Resilience Committee has warned that this would expose the country in times of emergency and present “a significant resilience weakness”.

It says: “We recommend that the Government should abandon its plan to switch off Digital Terrestrial Television, which risks weakening national resilience by reducing universal access to communication.”

A spokesperson for campaign group Broadcast 2040+ said: “We welcome this clear recommendation from the committee, which further highlights the importance of protecting terrestrial television.

“At a time of growing threats, switching it off would be a mistake we cannot fix.

“Ministers should take this recommendation seriously and commit to a long-term future for terrestrial TV until at least 2044.”

Mr Burnham has previously said he is “concerned” by the plans and will review them following pressure from The Sun’s Save Our Sets campaign.

News.title: Kemi Badenoch vows to cut screentime in schools with return to pen-and-paper learning under Tory plan
News.content:
Next

SCHOOLS would be forced to ditch laptops and bring back textbooks under a Tory plan to drastically cut screentime during lessons.

Kemi Badenoch will today outline proposals to do away with electronic devices in most classrooms and return to pen-and-paper learning.



She will warn that Britain has “sleepwalked” into an unhealthy situation where the majority of pupils use screens during lessons.

The Tory leader is pledging to axe devices altogether for under-5s amid concerns of the impact in their cognitive development.



Primary schools would be told to only give kids screens when absolutely necessary – like computer class – while secondary pupils would be limited to two hours each day.

Health experts have warned of the impact on excessive screen use for youngsters, including weakening their attention spans.



Ms Badenoch is also concerned that pupils are becoming overly reliant on artificial intelligence which is “lowering educational standards”.

She will today pledge to divert part of an existing £950million government “EdTech” budget for laptops and instead commit £250million for physical textbooks.

Shadow Education Secretary Laura Trott said last night: “We have sleepwalked into a situation where nearly a million children spend almost every lesson on a screen, while medical professionals warn of the damage excessive screen time can do to children’s health, development and learning.

“I want to slash screen use in classrooms and set a new norm where screens are no longer the default.



“Everything in schools must be safe for children and improve standards.”

Most kids are already compelled to hand their mobile phones into schools during the day.

Some headteachers are already shunning laptops in favour of traditional methods.

This year top fee-paying school Winchester scrapped screens entirely from their lessons amid fears they were too distracting for the pupils.

Dr Rebecca Foljambe, founder of Health Professionals for Safer Screens, said last night: “We have become excessively preoccupied with why children are on screens.



“Although content is important, this distracts from the fact that daily screen time can profoundly affect a child’s health, whatever they are watching or doing.”

News.title: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies in hospital aged 80 after notorious reign as Guadalajara Cartel boss
News.content:
Next

A NOTORIOUS Mexican drug lord who founded the Guadalajara Cartel has died aged 80.

Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, dubbed “The Boss of Bosses”, died in hospital on Sunday after reportedly suffering multiple organ failures.



He was rushed to a medical centre from his Puente Grande prison cell alongside a heavy security team including air support.

Authorities have not disclosed his official cause of death yet.



The narcotics kingpin was widely considered one of the biggest smugglers in the world and is considered among the most well known traffickers in history.

He was credited with building alliances between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel.



Gallardo was convicted of killing a US drug-enforcement agent in 1985 – solidifying his name in history as one of the country’s most dangerous traffickers.

His Guadalajara Cartel swept over the Mexican drug scene in the 1980s at the peak of the cocaine boom.

The foundations of the illegal drug network he helped pioneer still endure to this day.

He has been in jail since 1989.



The security ministry in Jalisco, where he was being held, said: “After remaining under observation with a guarded prognosis, he died on November 15 at the medical facility.”

His health had spiralled in recent years – blighted by issues including high blood pressure, diabetes and deafness.

In 2022, then-Mexican president Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador said he was “in very poor health”.



A judge granted him house arrest, but technical problems with electronic ankle monitoring prevented his transfer.

Gallardo was from Sinaloa, where he was born on January 8, 1946.

His 1985 conviction came after he murdered US narcotics agent Camarena Salazar, who was kidnapped and tortured.

Gallardo was arrested in April 1989 but continued to run the criminal enterprise from behind bars.

News.title: Burnham set to insist his Brexit reversal plot will be welcomed by his constituents in Makerfield
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham will tonight insist his Brexit reversal plot will be welcomed by his constituents in Makerfield who overwhelmingly voted Leave.

The PM has previously sparked anger with claims nobody believed in the current “hard” deal with Europe during the 2016 referendum.



This week, he will use a summit to lock in EU deals set to increase youth immigration and to make Britain contribute more cash.

In a speech at Mansion House tonight, the PM will say: “It’s like the Emperor’s new clothes — where no-one is prepared to say the obvious truth.



“The Brexit we were given has not worked.

“We have lost more than we gained.”



He will say his new terms will bring the Brexit deal “closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016”.

He also stressed the deal will have to pass the “Makerfield test” and improve people’s lives.

But Makerfield voted to leave the EU by 65 per cent in 2016.

Pro-Brexit group Stay Out said: “He won that seat promising not to undo Brexit and has since said his ultimate goal is to take Britain back in.”



Mr Burnham will rule out rejoining the single market, customs union, or reviving freedom of movement this Parliament.

News.title: Labour’s benefits overhaul under fire as it’s revealed welfare bill will still be surging after next election
News.content:
Next

LABOUR’S benefits overhaul was under fire last night as ministers admitted the bill would still be surging beyond the next election.

Welfare Secretary Pat McFadden refused to guarantee reductions in this parliamentary term – while government czar Alan Milburn said it could take 10 years for spending to start falling.



Mr Milburn will tomorrow present his long-awaited plan to get a near-million jobless youngsters off the dole and into work.

He yesterday said he would recommend slashing benefits for some younger claimants to pay for employment support.



The ex-Health Secretary also urged ministers to scrap the system of GPs signing people off sick and to slow down hikes to the youth minimum wage.

Andy Burnham is expected to adopt his demands, teeing up a showdown with left-wing Labour MPs who oppose benefit cuts and are threatening rebellion.

But even with the changes, Mr Milburn warned they would not deliver spending reductions for at least a decade.

Taxpayers are currently footing an annual £145billion working age welfare bill that is projected to keep rising every year.

Asked if he would make progress reducing this before the next election, Mr McFadden said: “Look I can’t say that, we upgrade benefits every year and I think that’s important to keep people up with the cost of living.

“These are some of the poorest people in the country and the best way to get the benefits bill down is exactly with the long term reset that we are talking about.”



Reform’s Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick told The Sun: “We can’t afford to waste 10 years before we fix the youth jobs crisis.

“Radical action is needed now to cut taxes on jobs, end poor quality university courses and boost apprenticeships. Burnham doesn’t have any time to waste.”

Mr McFadden also drew criticism from bosses who said that Labour’s tax hikes have made it harder to hire youngsters.

The London Chamber of Commerce said: “The Government will not tackle the NEET crisis while continuing to make it more difficult and more expensive for businesses to employ people.

“The fundamental reset Pat McFadden has described must include reducing hiring costs and ensuring our education system gives young people the skills businesses need, rather than tweaks to the edges of the welfare system.”

News.title: How a harmonious start to Burnham’s time in No10 could start to shift as three rebellions are brewing
News.content:
POLITICS FIX How a harmonious start to Burnham’s time in No10 could start to shift as three rebellions are brewing







Next

ANDY Burnham is about to discover that those Labour MPs who installed him in No10 are a hard group to please.

While they have largely behaved themselves during his first few months in power, this could be the week where discord starts to break out.



There are three potential rebellions brewing that the PM will be looking to head off.

The first could blow tomorrow when the long-awaited welfare report by Alan Milburn is finally published.



Ministers are due to adopt recommendations to cut benefits for jobless young people and use that money to fund more employment support.

While this sounds sensible to many voters, Labour left-wingers have already vowed to reject any kind of reductions.



Downing Street has spent months rolling the pitch for tomorrow’s moment and will be hoping to dampen the flames of mutiny as much as possible.

Lessons from Sir Keir Starmer‘s doomed welfare overhaul have been learned and Mr Burnham will be hoping to weather the inevitable row.

A second crunch is looming over the Rosebank oil field, which the party’s eco-minded MPs are dead against.

After ministers approved the Jackdaw gas field that begins piping energy into homes today, more than 75 rebels are telling the PM any further North Sea drilling would be a line crossed.



But the party is divided on the issue, and many MPs are ferociously in favour of extracting more homegrown resources to power British industry.

Take Henry Tufnell, who told me last night: “We cannot and should not turn our backs on those industrial communities that have powered this country for generations.”

Finally, Mr Burnham is flying into the mother-of-all spats on Friday when he heads to Brussels to meet EU leaders.

He is seeking closer ties with the bloc to smooth trade frictions, but will fire the starting gun on a massive watering down of Brexit.

The PM will give us more of a hint of his plan in a speech tonight, but we know he is keen on freedom of movement and even rejoining entirely at some point.



While this is music to the ears of many left-wingers, his MPs in Leave-voting seats are less than impressed.

After a relatively harmonious start to his time in No10, things could be about to get a whole lot more restless.

News.title: Cut National Insurance for under-25s to create jobs, Milburn report to say
News.content:
National Insurance (NI) paid by businesses on workers aged under 25 should be gradually lowered to encourage companies to create jobs for young people, a major review of youth unemployment will say.

A report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn will suggest the government should reduce NI costs over five years for people aged between 21 and 24 years old, starting in retail and hospitality.

Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms. Milburn will say the number of young people not in employment, education or training - known as Neets - was not started by the NI rise.

But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing".

The independent report, which has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday, will also make recommendations on reducing the UK's benefits bill.

Milburn has said the government spends Â£22bn a year supporting young people who are economically inactive. There are nearly one million so-called Neets aged between 16 and 24 in the UK, according to data from the Office for National Statistics.

He will recommend that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Milburn wants the government to provide a legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support. Those who refuse to take up help could lose their benefits.

Milburn is also expected to say that helping young people develop skills is pointless if there are no jobs available for them.

The former health secretary will recommend doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from Â£5,000 to Â£10,000.

But he will say this should only be done "when fiscal conditions allow".

Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost Â£5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank.

Milburn is set to say that given the UK's fiscal position, an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money.

News.title: UK lost more than it gained from Brexit, Burnham to say ahead of EU summit
News.content:
The prime minister is expected to argue that the UK has lost more than it has gained from leaving the European Union in a speech ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels later this week.

Speaking at the Lord Mayor's Banquet on Monday, Andy Burnham will compare the UK's Brexit deal to the "emperor's new clothes" - saying "a needlessly hard Brexit" created barriers for businesses and the promise to "take back control" was not delivered.

He is seeking to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility with the bloc at Friday's summit, where he has said a "win-win" deal can be struck.

The Conservatives have said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset".

Burnham is expected to say on Monday: "It's like the emperor's new clothes â where no-one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on.

"The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we have gained."

The prime minister says he wants to reset Britain's relationship with the EU - and his argument is not that Brexit was wrong, but the way it happened was.

He will say any deal must pass the "Makerfield test" of providing tangible improvements to everyday lives, and deliver an arrangement which is closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.

Burnham is also expected to restate his commitment to Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledge that there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement".

He will say the prospect of a new deal is a "win-win" and illustrates a "new approach".

"Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges. But being constructive and positive - showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges."

News.title: Prince and Princess of Wales arrive in India ahead of meeting with Modi
News.content:
The Prince and Princess of Wales have arrived in India for a three-day visit that will include a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The visit is the first time William and Catherine have been on an official overseas trip together in four years.

Her cancer treatment has limited the amount of international travel she has undertaken but she will be with her husband for several engagements this week.

Most are related to the Earthshot Prize, founded by Prince William, which awards five Â£1m prizes for the best solutions to the biggest climate challenges.

"The princess is enormously proud of what the prince has achieved with Earthshot and is really looking forward to being alongside him for what is one of the most important moments in his year," said a spokesperson for the royals.

"She's seen it develop into something truly remarkable and is excited to experience first-hand just how far it has come."

News.title: Trident submarine returns home after record-breaking undersea patrol
News.content:
A Royal Navy submarine carrying Trident nuclear missiles has returned to its Scottish base after a record-breaking 217 days spent submerged on patrol.

The 140-strong crew of HMS Vengeance have spent the tour in almost total isolation beneath the surface after setting out from Faslane, near Helensburgh, Argyll and Bute, on 12 April.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting was at HM Naval Base Clyde to welcome them home after the longest undersea deployment at sea for a British vessel.

The typical patrol length for the UK's Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines has more than doubled in recent years, with six-month durations now routine due to a shortage of seaworthy vessels.

Crew members could be seen standing on HMS Vengeance as it travelled up Gare Loch earlier, accompanied by some smaller Naval support vessels and tug boats.

The vessel was encrusted in marine growth and some of its sound-absorbing tiles were missing.

HMS Vengeance was expected back at Faslane last weekend, but that was reported to have been delayed, external when the submarine replacing it on patrol had to return to base to fix a technical fault.

The head of the navy, First Sea Lord Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, praised the dedication of submariners in keeping Nato safe at a conference last week in Oslo, but said the UK must do better at maintaining the fleet.

News.title: 'I'd throw up in the car park': How school anxiety is harming children's futures
News.content:
Total school absence numbers have fallen since their peak during the pandemic but they're yet to return to pre-Covid levels.

In the autumn and spring terms of the 2025/26 academic year, the overall absence rate was 6.6%, down from 7.38% in 2021/2022 but much higher than pre-pandemic levels, which were below 5%.

The latest figures published in October show that 168,000 pupils (2.32%) were classed as severely absent - missing more than half of their classes - in the 2025/2026 autumn and spring terms. Back in spring 2019, this figure was under 60,000.

Experts are concerned that this absence will translate into worse outcomes for thousands of young people.

New analysis from the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ) shows that 133,000 of today's persistently absent GCSE pupils (those missing more than 10% of school) are on course to spend a year or more being Neet. Similar research from the National Centre for Social Research linked persistent absence to much higher rates of not being in work, education or training between the ages of 16 and 24.

"Ministers must recognise that getting children back into school is the first step to getting young people into work," says Dan Lilley, head of youth at the Centre for Social Justice.

"That means restoring the expectation that children are in school every day."

Research suggests many parents may be comfortable with regular school absences. CSJ polling found that 44% of parents think it reasonable for a child to miss one in every 10 school days â the threshold for persistent absence.

In response to the CSJ research, the Department for Education said it was "helping tackle the barriers that stop children attending school, through free breakfast clubs in every primary school, better mental health support and earlier help for pupils with special educational needs".

Autism and ADHD can contribute to children avoiding school, says Sheila Griffiths, who co-founded the charity Hope4More in Crewe after her own son struggled to attend school.

"The classroom environment doesn't suit [those children], so we support them here," she explains.

Hope4More runs art classes that combine creativity and business skills, and it also supports parents to ask for the help they need from schools or their local authority to get their child back into education.

"We've got families here who have already had to give up work. They're struggling. It's so stressful the situations they end up in."

Sheila also runs a programme at Cheshire College South & West to help young people with the transition into further education.

She says: "With our older ones, so perhaps the ones that should be in year 10 or 11, we work with them at college and then they get used to being in that environment which is different to school, but it's also still quite busy."

Paul Browne, who is one of the assistant principals there, says: "Especially since Covid, there's a lot of learners who are not engaging in education. The thought of coming into a mainstream college is quite a big step for them.

News.title: 'It felt like I was dying': Why some teenagers don't go to school
News.content:
Thousands of school pupils in England miss more than half the academic year, which experts say puts them more at risk of becoming Neet - not in employment, education or training.

A government-commissioned review into how to solve the problem of nearly one million young people being Neet is due to be published on Tuesday.

Two teenagers who experience school anxiety have spoken to the BBC about what led them to stop attending classes.

Mali, 18, is autistic and stopped going to school three years ago after experiencing panic attacks. She said leaving her bedroom would make her legs go numb.

"It felt like I was dying," she told the BBC.

Thirteen-year-old Eva, who is also autistic, stopped going to school after struggling with the transition to secondary education.

"It's like a physical barrier that you can't cross and you can't move," she said.

Read more on this story.

News.title: Brand moved from Wandsworth to category C prison, his wife confirms on podcast
News.content:
Russell Brand has been transferred to a category C prison, his wife Laura has confirmed, in her first public comments since he was jailed.

On Monday, the comedian was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Over the weekend, Brand was transferred from category B HMP Wandsworth in London to HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, which houses men convicted of sexual offences.

Laura Brand returned to the couple's podcast on Sunday, saying that she had spoken to her husband in prison and he "is OK and is praying". Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following among believers, including in the US.

HMP Littlehey, a category C training prison, is one of the largest prisons in Europe for men convicted of sexual offences.

It held more than 1,200 prisoners as of January 2025, according to data from the Independent Monitoring Board.

Before Brand's move to the prison, a source close to the disgraced comedian said he was doing "remarkably well considering the circumstances" at HMP Wandsworth and that he had been moved from isolation to a main wing.

A member of staff at Wandsworth said there had been "much excitement" among the inmates about Brand's arrival, with some slamming on cell doors and shouting out his name. They added that there had also been some anger displayed about his crimes.

Staff at other prisons told the BBC Brand's fame, combined with the nature of his crimes, could make him a target for other inmates.

In the couple's podcast, released on Sunday, Laura Brand can seen sitting on a sofa in what looks like a conservatory. She is holding a Bible with a candle burning in front of her.

The couple had continued their YouTube podcast during Brand's trial. They often read snippets of the Bible and discussed religion.

On Sunday, Laura told their followers: "We trust his [God's] plan and everything he is doing just now, even though it's painful and obviously will take some getting used to."

During the show, Laura played an episode she said had been recorded before her husband was jailed.

It featured the couple singing to the American folk singer Woody Guthrie before praying together.

Towards the end of the podcast, Laura returned on her own to read a message from her husband, in which he said he was not guilty for the offences he had been jailed for.

He called staff at HMP Littlehey "strong", "kind" and "dedicated", and he asked people to support his "treasured wife and family".

News.title: Cancer 'sponge' tests could be offered to more people with bad indigestion
News.content:
It's thought between one and two adults in every 100 has Barrett's oesophagus, where cells have started to change. Most won't go on to develop cancer, but demand for NHS endoscopy is high, meaning some with the condition aren't checked as often as recommended.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) says the sponge tests, already offered in some places, could help give more patients peace of mind.

For the test, patients swallow a small dissolving capsule attached to a thread. Once in the stomach, it releases a tiny sponge. This collect cells from the lining of the gullet as it's gently pulled back out of the patient's mouth by the doctor.

The cells can then be analysed.

Prof Jonathan Benger, chief executive of NICE, says sponge tests offer a "quick and less invasive" way to detect concerning changes, helping to identify people who should go on to have further tests and treatment.

Prof Peter Johnson, national clinical director for cancer at NHS England, said: "The NHS is always looking for better ways to get to the bottom of people's symptoms, and thousands have already benefited from this incredibly efficient test through pilots we have been running, so it's fantastic it is now being considered for roll out across the country.

"Many people have acid reflux, and having an easier way to check for changes in the lining of the oesophagus can make a big difference for patients, reducing the need for more complicated endoscopy tests and helping the NHS free up resources to find cancers at an earlier stage."

However, no diagnostic test, including endoscopy, identifies every case and people who receive an all-clear sponge test result should still be monitored in the long term, NICE adds.

The sponge tests can help detect oesophageal cancer and Barrett's oesophagus in people with reflux disease.

Final recommendations by NICE will be made in the new year.

News.title: Workers should get paid time off to train for crises, say peers
News.content:
Workers should be able to take paid time off to prepare for national emergencies, a House of Lords committee has recommended.

In a report, the peers said a new "civic resilience leave" would enable employees to undertake training and emergency volunteering without losing income.

It is one of a slew of recommendations from a 12-strong committee that has been examining how to make the UK better able to respond to crises including war, power cuts, cyber-attacks and natural disasters.

It comes after the government launched a campaign calling on the British public to stock up on tinned food and bottled water to be prepared for emergencies.

In a report published on Monday, peers on the national resilience committee will say the government's campaign, launched last month, was a "welcome step".

But it will argue that Britain is still underprepared for potential disruption, adding that the public did not have the "full picture" about potential threats from Russia, China and Iran, including cyber attacks.

It will recommend that all local councils should draw up registers of volunteers with "relevant skills and capabilities" to help out during crises, as well as lists of buildings in their area that could be used as emergency shelters.

The government should also launch a national campaign for registered volunteers and civil reservists, it added, modelled on the programme launched by the NHS for "volunteer responders" during the Covid pandemic.

News.title: Gas starts flowing from Jackdaw after government green light
News.content:
Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter.

Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case.

It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura.

The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.

News.title: Families of the Disappeared to meet the Pope
News.content:
Some families of the Disappeared will meet Pope Leo XIV on Wednesday in what is hoped will be a "spiritual boost" for the relatives.

The Disappeared are those who were abducted, murdered and secretly buried by republicans during Northern Ireland's Troubles.

Despite extensive and painstaking searches, the bodies have never been found of four out of 17 people listed by the commission set up to locate victims' remains.

The trip has been organised by the WAVE Trauma Centre which has supported the families since 1995.

Speaking before the group departed from Dublin Airport on Monday morning, Sandra Peake CEO of WAVE said the trip was "many months in the making and we are all very grateful for those who have made it possible".

Alongside the families travelling to Rome are the head of the Catholic Church in Ireland, Archbishop of Armagh Eamon Martin, and Fr Joe Gormley.

It is thought that the Pope will read the 'Prayer for the return of The Disappeared' which was written by Gormley.

News.title: UK will have 'voice' but no vote on EU food rules in Brexit reset
News.content:
The UK will have a "voice in the room" but no vote on European Union food policies as part of a so-called "Brexit reset" to reduce red tape, EU relations minister Hamish Falconer has told the BBC.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham hopes to agree a deal at a summit on Friday but critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker" but not a rule maker.

Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules and said the deal could help bring down prices for shoppers.

The reset would not involve any upfront payments, Falconer added, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment.

Falconer said it was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements.

"The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said.

The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit.

The reset means they will be dismantled.

In September, the Conservative Party said it was "raising the alarm" over the government's planned reset, saying it would leave British consumers and businesses "dangerously exposed, with no input on how regulations are made or power to reject them".

Both the Conservatives and Reform have said they would undo the planned reset if they were in power.

News.title: Hidden tongue movement found in 'strong R' study
News.content:
Scientists have observed "hidden" tongue movements in one of the last places in England still using a distinctive pronunciation of the letter R and they also witnessed a decline in the historical sound.

By using ultrasound technology, Lancaster University researchers have been able to watch how the tongue moves during speech.

The rhoticity study focused on people in Blackburn, as its older residents still pronounce a "strong R" sound after vowels in words like star and heart.

Dr Danielle Turton, who led the research, said the findings were "fascinating" as she witnessed the centuries-old sound "gradually disappearing" as the younger generations who took part had much weaker tongue movement.

Dr Turton told BBC Radio Lancashire: "East Lancashire is one of the last places in England where people are [distinctively] pronouncing the 'R' sounds.

"But that distinctive sound we found was gradually disappearing so we went to Blackburn with an ultrasound machine - the same technology we would use to look at babies in the womb - and we used it to monitor people's tongues moving as they spoke."

News.title: Staggered age of consent to be discussed after Brand case, minister says
News.content:
A discussion over a staggered age of consent is to take place, the work and pensions secretary has said, as the government faces calls to change the law following the case against Russell Brand.

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Pat McFadden said that "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men" have emerged this week.

A woman who alleges she was raped by jailed comedian Brand when she was 16 is now campaigning to see the law changed so that relationships between 16 and 17-year-olds and adults would be illegal.

Questions over a staggered age of consent have "been raised and will be discussed" McFadden said, adding: "[I] can't tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights."

Adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds, under UK law.

Mia Latter, who has waived her right to anonymity, told the Sunday Times that she wants the age of consent to be staggered.

Latter is one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.

Brand denied the allegations at the time and none of the six women were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.

At Southwark Crown Court on Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half-years imprisonment after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, involving four women between 2004 and 2009. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

Latter said she was 16 when she met the comedian, then 30. She told the Sunday Times: "I think people were so struck by my story because of the age difference and the clear imbalance [in power].

"I don't want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other.

"If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to.

"But...if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence."

Latter told the Sunday Times the CPS decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but police wanted her to be part of "subsequent" proceedings.

She told the paper she was "devastated" by the decision and that police had said they didn't want the trial "to become 'the Alice show'", a reference to her pseudonym in the stories published in 2023.

It is understood the Met Police has apologised for the language officers used in a meeting with Latter about her case.

A Met spokesperson said: "This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence."

Layla Stone, founder of the campaign group Close the Consent Gap, said bringing in a staggered age of consent was about addressing a "power imbalance" in relationships involving 16 and 17 year-olds and adults. She urged ministers to commit to such a change.

Stone, a child protection social worker, told the BBC that 16 and 17 year-olds were seen as children in "every single framework of the law" and "we don't believe [they are] old enough to consent to having sex with much older adults".

Close the Consent Gap is proposing that 16 year-olds would not be able to have a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and that someone aged 17 would be prohibited from a relationship with anyone older than 20.

Further allegations of sexual misconduct in the entertainment industry came in the same week Brand was convicted.

ITV News and the Guardian published a story alleging that comedian David Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

One woman said she now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour when he was a judge at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.

Walliams said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

The Metropolitan Police said on Friday it has launched an investigation into Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences", after the ITV News and the Guardian story. The Met said that the allegations it is investigating are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian but that it was "also proactively reviewing that reporting".

Speaking to Sky News, the work and pensions secretary said: "I do think that between Russell Brand, David Walliams, what's been put out there, people are looking at these issues in a new light."

News.title: Man and woman die and four arrested after police pursuit crash in Leeds
News.content:
Two people have been killed after their car was hit by a vehicle fleeing from police in Leeds.

West Yorkshire Police said it happened at 00:44 GMT, when a blue BMW 123D failed to stop for officers in Gelderd Road and then crashed into a white Volkswagen Scirocco.

The driver of the Volkswagen, a 22-year-old man, died at the scene. His passenger, a woman, 23, died later in hospital. Both were from York.

The occupants of the BMW, a 39-year-old man from Harrogate, two boys aged 16 and 17 and a 16-year-old girl, have been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.

The 39-year-old is also being held on suspicion of driving while over the prescribed limit for cannabis, the force confirmed.

The teenagers in the BMW were taken to hospital for treatment to injuries that were not considered life-threatening.

A spokesperson for West Yorkshire Police said a referral had been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which confirmed it had started an investigation.

News.title: Tories pledge to halt screen-based school exams and cut coursework
News.content:
The Conservatives have promised to halt screen-based exams and cut coursework in a bid to limit the use of AI by schoolchildren in England if the party returns to power.

The party has also pledged to develop new guidelines so that laptops and tablets are not the "default in classrooms".

Shadow education secretary Laura Trott cited recent warnings from clinicians that excessive screen time could be damaging children's health, adding that "everything in schools must be safe for children and improve standards".

The government is currently developing new screen-time guidance for children and has previously said it would consult on the safety of AI in schools.

The vast majority of school exams in the UK are pen and paper based. Under the previous government led by Sir Keir Starmer, exam regulator Ofqual launched a consultation last year, external on the introduction of on-screen exams.

But it emphasised that pen and paper would "remain central" and that the most widely taken subjects would not be moving to digital assessments for the "foreseeable future".

In their announcement on Sunday, the Tories said they would "put a stop" to the introduction of screen-based exams, and require screen time for secondary pupils to be limited to no more than two hours a day.

The party said it would also minimise the amount of coursework in school assessments to avoid lowering educational standards "by allowing children to become overly reliant on the use of generative AI platforms".

Under the plans, primary schools would be required to keep screen use to a minimum and only use screens where necessary, such as in computing lessons.

News.title: How England found a new edge to beat Spain and exorcise agony of Argentina defeat
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

England hold out, for a raucous win that will rightly be held up. Sure, it might not have been what it could have been as Ben White surged in for a sensational third in Madrid… but that last word remains key.

England beat the world and European champions 3-2 in their own capital, to end the longest unbeaten run in international history, that stretched back to March 2024.

Spain couldn’t make it 44 games, as England just about made it to 94 minutes. That was ultimately down to a brilliant double save from James Trafford, who was one of many positives on another Nations League night of enjoyably entertaining drama. Might Jordan Pickford’s first place have gone with Spain’s unbeaten run?

open image in gallery James Trafford made a crucial double save in injury time ( Reuters )

Trafford had to show his best. This was never going to be easy, no matter how Thomas Tuchel’s side made it look for 63 minutes - until Elliot Anderson’s red card. That will be the manager’s main takeaway from the game, the “proof of concept” as he put it the night before. With 11 against 11, England were denying this Spanish team the ball and creating some swift chances that the world champions were struggling to live with.

That was what the game-opening goal came from. Even if there was also debate about Anderson’s follow-through in that instance, England had opened another gap in the Spanish structure while looking so more cohesive and coruscating themselves.

This is a team that can sustain attacking waves much better than the one who mostly forced their way through the summer on individual impact. White’s supreme goal, that had the world champions looking at each other and pointing fingers, was the grand exhibition of that.

open image in gallery England celebrate a famous victory (Adam Davy/PA) ( PA Wire )

Just as crucially, it was so different to what Spain do. It was something of England's own. In between, Ezri Konsa scored the plundered set-piece header that his recent performances have deserved. Jude Bellingham was at that point bossing the Spanish midfield, in the kind of way people have long imagined as his career has only escalated.

This, and the very confidence from such a marker of a win, are what England have to take through to finally win that trophy at Euro 2028.

So many positives, so many solutions… until Spain asked the most severe questions, and Tuchel didn’t always have the answers. That is where there is obvious context to a win that should still inspire confidence.

It clearly meant much more to England given the fact Spain are the world champions who had won at Wembley. They're the ones who have done it, the benchmark. Tuchel and all the players were aware they had to do something more, to close this year with a performance that offered more for the future; that they had to stand up.

open image in gallery Harry Kane put England ahead from the spot (Adam Davy/PA) ( PA Wire )

They had admittedly felt frustration from that Wembley defeat; that they could have won. As a consequence, England just looked sharper for pretty much all of the first hour. Spain didn’t even have a shot on target in the first half, as Unai Simon immediately had to withstand an England flurry.

The world champions weren’t counter-pressing in the way they were in the summer. England were starting to overrun them. The ultimate expression of that, in White’s goal, did seem to spark something in response.

It is possible that England themselves even got a bit overconfident. In what has been a theme in this double of games - that ended 3-2 apiece but see England top the group on goal difference - Tuchel’s side gave the ball away for a Spanish goal.

This time it was Anthony Gordon, who seemed to forget what Lamine Yamal can do. Even the Barcelona playmaker took a poor touch from there, leading to what felt like a needless challenge from Anderson. He was sent off, and Spain were set off.

open image in gallery Anderson was sent off and conceded a penalty for hauling down Yamal ( Getty )

It was immediately a different game. Spain were doing everything they weren’t in the first half. A change of midfield helped, with Fermin Lopez offering the impetus that Luis De La Fuente’s midfield had been missing. Nico Williams’s brilliant finish from an utterly sensational Yamal pass was then a goal to match White’s.

And so, in what was almost humorous irony, England ended 2026 in the way they’d ended its defining games: backs to the wall, a backline of nine, Tuchel hauling off his best attackers, and questions about the subs.

Spain really pressed. Yamal was at the heart of every move, creating almost every chance. The game then seemed to just constantly be the ball being fired across the England box. England were probably one bad bounce away from another inquest about Tuchel’s substitutions, and how he manages these matches.

But that bounce didn’t come. The equaliser didn't come. England stood up.

open image in gallery Ben White scored the third before the game was flipped on its head ( Getty )

And that might be because of a decision Tuchel doesn’t even have to make. Trafford made his claim. England made their mark.

Tuchel has ultimately overseen their most significant win for some time, at least as regards what it means for finally winning that trophy. That’s what all this is about, after all.

Spain can fairly say that what really matters is what happens in tournaments, but it didn’t feel meaningless as they toiled to keep that unbeaten record and the Madrid crowd willed them on. That run is now over. Might that finally signal that this could be England’s time?

It is far too early to say, but this was the end to the year Tuchel wanted. It was the performance England needed.

News.title: A home for older residents eagerly awaits Pope Leo XIV's return to Peruvian port city
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The walls of the home for older people run by Catholic religious sisters in the Peruvian port city of Callao were recently painted. The courtyard was spruced up. More importantly, its residents were filled with a renewed sense of hope. Everyone and everything is ready for the moment they have been waiting for: a visit by Pope Leo XIV.

“It’s hard to believe that he is coming to this tiny little place — a place that is small, but full of heart,” said Silvia del Castillo, 84, who has lived at the home of the Little Sisters of the Destitute Elderly for three years.

The pontiff will visit the home Monday before presiding over a Mass expected to draw more than a million people to Las Palmas Air Base in Lima.

Leo’s visit to Peru marked the final leg of his three-nation tour of South America and its emotional highlight, given the more than two decades that the former Robert Prevost spent there as a missionary priest and later bishop. Leo has said it was where he learned “what it means to be a shepherd.”

The pope was in Peru during the coronavirus pandemic and helped the older persons' home at the time.

Peruvians know him as Father Roberto

The humble home in Callao provides 60 residents with food, medicine and occasional recreational activities to keep up their spirits.

“For me, this home has meant a new life,” said Del Castillo, whose only daughter is unable to care for her due to an autoimmune disease. “When you’re old and have nowhere else to go, and people open their hearts to you, even before they open the doors of their home, you find happiness. That is what these dear sisters have given me.”

The Little Sisters of the Destitute Elderly are a congregation founded in Spain in 1873 by the priest Saturnino López Novoa and Saint Teresa Jornet, who was canonized a century later for her love and service to those most in need.

During his time as bishop, Leo focused much of his effort on supporting the poorest residents in the area, including those in the Callao province community of Pachacutec, distributing water, medicine and thousands of chickens and pigs.

Callao Mayor César Pérez told The Associated Press that Father Roberto, as he is known to the Peruvian people, would drive approximately 12 hours from Chiclayo in northern Peru to Callao during the pandemic because he wanted to ensure the well-being of older residents.

Leo delivered food and other supplies to the home but did not enter the facility in order to protect the residents from the virus, Pérez said.

Callao home has limited resources

Renovations ahead of the Pope’s visit to the home were carried out and paid for by the Callao municipal government. The nursing home is funded through donations from some of the residents’ families when they are able. That leaves limited resources to care for all the residents.

“We truly value and are deeply grateful for the help in renovating the space and improving the quality of life for our elderly residents,” Sister María Agripina Garrido said Friday during a ceremony marking the completion of the project.

While some residents are confined to their beds or must use wheelchairs, Delia Chávez, 82, moves with a slow but steady gait and is able to climb stairs.

“The sisters are kind. They help us with everything they can,” she said. “When they have medicine to give us, they do, but it’s a modest home with limited funds. So, if a medication is very expensive, the family has to buy it.”

Chávez moved to the nursing facility following the death of her husband. She misses her home but living alone was not a viable option and her three children are unable to provide full-time care.

In Peru, 32% of impoverished households as of 2025 included at least one adult over the age of 65, according to the National Institute of Statistics and Informatics.

“Sometimes, when my son is on vacation, he takes me out of the home for a while, but this time I told him, ‘No! I’m going to see the pope,'” Chávez said, beaming with joy.

News.title: Arsenal make no sense – and defiant Mary Earps proves why
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Alone in an empty penalty box, Mary Earps dropped to her knees and yelled into the cold night air. With an eight-save, player-of-the-match display, the ‘Queen of Stops’ properly marked the end of her exile and return to the Women’s Super League with an outstanding performance between the posts for the London City Lionesses in their 1-1 draw with Arsenal, a reminder to anyone who needed it that the former England No 1 is not done yet.

“Tiring,” Earps exhaled when asked to sum up a night where she did it all, including a sensational late stop to tip Frida Maanum’s dipping strike onto the bar and earn her side a point. There was agility, presence, bravery, but how about the timing, as well, to produce such a performance in front of the biggest crowd of the season at the Emirates and keep the disrupters London City above Arsenal in the race for the Champions League positions. In front of Sarina Wiegman, too.

But Earps and London City also managed to ensure that Arsenal’s miserable wait without a home win this season continued, with five successive draws at the Emirates to begin their campaign. It will be little consolation to Renee Slegers that her side showed more intent and direction that in their previous draws against Crystal Palace, Manchester United, Birmingham City and Aston Villa this season: this was billed as a must-win for Arsenal and the sight of the goalkeeper Misa Rodriguez going forward for a corner in the final seconds of stoppage time, at 1-1, revealed as much.

open image in gallery Renee Slegers watched on as her side dropped points at home for the fifth game in a row ( PA )

That Arsenal’s corner failed to even reach the box, with Smilla Holmberg’s outswinging delivery instead drifting out of play, summed up how perplexing their season has become. A team who started the season with title aspirations, to go along with the club’s wider ambitions, are left sitting sixth in the WSL after 10 games, 12 points off leaders Chelsea and six points off London City, the holders of the final Champions League place. Arsenal are simultaneously a team capable of going to Barcelona and the Camp Nou on Wednesday and drawing 1-1, while also failing to register a victory in front of the biggest women’s football crowd in the country in the last six months.

In a way, London City were the sort of opponents Arsenal should have enjoyed facing. The plucky upstarts, with the billionaire owner and Ballon d’Or holder in midfield, are expansive in possession and have interesting ideas about what to do on the ball. They arrived at the Emirates with a plan and ambition to do more than just nullify their opponents and it was a measure of their ability to dictate that Arsenal, at times, did not even attempt to press. London City had more possession and more passes, which for Arsenal at least allowed them to break out of the sterile, side-to-side patterns of play that had defined their previous stalemates here.

And there was a reminder, too, that Arsenal can be dangerous when they are presented with space, to attack in a way where they can move up the pitch and have a shot within seconds. Earps was kept busy, after all, and a lot of Arsenal managed to find made sense, at last: using Alessia Russo’s ability to work the channels and her awareness to bring others into play, looking to release Lisa Baum on the right and instructing her to be direct when she had a clear line to goal.

open image in gallery Maanum converted Russo’s cut-back to give Arsenal the lead ( Getty )

open image in gallery But Goodwin evaded Williamson to level for London City ( PA )

Maanum’s goal, after just 10 minutes, was an example of that. Emily Fox was invited to drive forwards and was directed to find Russo’s bending run off the shoulder of the last defender. There was a synchronisation to the way Russo didn’t even need to look up to know that Maanum would be arriving on the edge of the box, if she could find the right angle on the pull-back. There was a sense to Slegers leaving Olivia Smith and many of her summer signings on the bench and trusting the understanding between players like Russo and Maanum.

But then Arsenal this season have usually displayed a way of shooting themselves in the foot, too. As Maanum celebrated and her team-mates huddled around her, Leah Williamson was pointing to her head and telling them they still needed to stay switched on. Yet within 98 seconds London City were level due to a moment, a glitch in the system. It came from Williamson, failing to match Izzy Goodwin’s run, stepping in at the wrong time in the box. The England captain was horribly bypassed by a centre-forward who offered a sharp contrast by simply being in total control of what she was doing.

The frustration from Arsenal is their errors keep piling on top of each other, the scrutiny too. It is now just three wins from 10 in the WSL. Earps, in her defiance, sensed her opportunity to ensure there would be no respite.

News.title: I’m a Celebrity’s Sharky: From YouTube and Beta Squad to the ITV show’s jungle camp
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

After last year’s I’m a Celebrity… Get Me Out Of Here! saw AngryGinge crowned King of the Jungle, another YouTuber is going mainstream.

Football-obsessed Sharky is one of the 11 celebrities on the ITV show’s initial 2026 line-up, alongside the likes of Big Brother host AJ Odudu, Kaiser Chiefs frontman Ricky Wilson and former Love Islander Chloe Burrows.

But what do we know about the YouTube star?

Sharky – real name Shamarke Mohamud – was born in Utrecht, the Netherlands and is the eldest of seven siblings. His family relocated to north London when he was a child and one of the sports-loving star’s first jobs was as a steward at Arsenal’s Emirates Stadium.

In 2015, he launched his YouTube channel with the username ‘afcsharky’ in a nod to the club. His videos initially focused on football, gaming and challenges – a winning formula he’s largely stuck to, resulting in 1.5 million subscribers. Some of his most popular videos include ‘Tasting the Weirdest Japanese Candy’, which has so far been viewed an impressive 1.3m times, and ‘I Gave My Best Friend One Hour To Spend £1,000’, which has a view count of 1.2m.

Sharky has pulled off his best and biggest YouTube stunts with a little help from some friends, though: his fellow Beta Squad members. In 2019, a group of British YouTubers announced that they’d be moving in together and creating content in their (predictably chaotic) house share.

Even if you haven’t heard of Beta Squad, it’s likely you will recognise at least one of its members: Celebrity Traitors star King Kenny, who came incredibly close to stealing the prize pot in last month’s series, after being recruited as a Traitor. The group’s other co-founders were Sharky, Chunkz, AJ Shabeel and Niko Omilana, the last of whom was the first person banished in last year’s Celebrity Traitors. “There are five of us in the Beta Squad and we all have different personalities,” Sharky said ahead of entering the jungle. “It will be great for people to get to know me as an individual.”

On their joint YouTube channel, Beta Squad have an impressive 12m followers and the group has pulled off some seriously ambitious stunts and games, with a ‘Last to Leave The Box’ game racking up an incredible 43m views, while ‘Guess the Footballer’ featuring England star Trent Alexander-Arnold has been watched 38m times.

Unsurprisingly, he reckons the rest of the squad will be voting for him to do trials. “They will be leading the charge online,” he said. “They are all really excited for me to go on this show. But I am actually looking forward to doing a trial. They are the funniest moments on the programme.”

Of course, he’s not the first YouTuber to enter the camp – and AngryGinge set the bar high when he walked away as King of the Jungle last year. “It is big boots to follow,” he said. “But Ginge is a great guy and he was made for something like this. I am not surprised he won, but I don't feel any pressure. I want to do my own thing and be myself.”

open image in gallery This year’s ‘I’m A Celebrity’ line-up ( ITV )

As well as continuing to rack up millions of views on YouTube, Sharky fronts his own podcast SDS , which stands for ‘Sharky Does Sports’, and welcomes various guests to chat all things football. He also manages a six-a-side team of the same name.

When it comes to meeting his fellow campmates, there’s one in particular who Sharky will have been very excited about – England legend Wayne Rooney. Before the series began, Sharky was asked who he’d move to see the jungle and replied: “I’m an Arsenal fan, so any ex-player would be great or an ex-England player.

“I’d love to hear their stories and what goes on behind the scenes. When you’re having conversations with the lads, you are always talking about football.”

News.title: UK ‘seriously underprepared’ for emergencies and threats, peers warn
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Britain is “seriously underprepared” for emergencies and threats, including cyberattacks and extreme weather, an influential group of peers has warned.

In a report published on Monday, the Lords National Resilience Committee told the government to stop being “squeamish” and be blunt with the public about the nature of threats.

The Lords group called on the government to appoint a Cabinet minister responsible solely for resilience within the next six months, arguing that current arrangements lack the “seniority” needed for the task at hand.

The peers said more needs to be done “at a greater pace” to prepare for the way modern risks can intensify one another, with limited stockpiles of food and medicine leaving the country “dangerously exposed” to disruption in global supply chains.

“A cyber-attack can quickly morph into a power cut, then a shutdown of transport, then empty food shelves in the shops,” crossbench peer and chairwoman of the committee Baroness Jean Coussins said.

open image in gallery Limited stockpiles of food and medicine are leaving the country ’dangerously exposed’ ( AFP/Getty )

In a report published on Monday, the committee also recommended:

Expanding eligibility for the armed forces “gap year” scheme to include Neets – 16 to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training – as part of efforts to increase enrolment of civilian volunteers and reservists.

Scrapping the plan to switch off digital terrestrial television, which it argues would weaken universal access to communication in an emergency.

A statutory duty on private and public sector companies and services to conduct “routine stress-testing exercises.”

Requirements for water companies to demonstrate that they can maintain emergency supplies and distribution during prolonged outages.

Teaching resilience skills, critical thinking and information literacy in schools, further education and workplaces as part of efforts to foster a “whole of society” approach to national emergencies.

Alongside extreme weather and flooding, the committee has warned of “grey zone” hostility from Russia, China and Iran in the form of possible cyberattacks, proxy acts of violence and sabotage of critical undersea cables and pipelines.

The UK also no longer has any domestic manufacturers of antibiotics, leaving the country highly dependent on Chinese imports, the committee warned.

The peers acknowledged arrangements such as an eight-week “buffer stock” requirement for certain medicines mandated by the Department of Health offered “important” protections.

But they said ministers should look at whether this provides “sufficient coverage” of products “critical to national resilience, including during prolonged disruption.”

“The UK’s national resilience is seriously undermined by its limited domestic production and stockpiles of vital products, including food and medicines,” the committee said.

“This leaves the country dangerously exposed to disruption in global supply chains.

“The government should also invest in domestic production capacity for essential medicines and pharmaceutical ingredients.”

open image in gallery A Cabinet Office spokesperson said: “This was top of the Security Minister’s agenda when he met some of the UK’s closest allies aboard HMS Prince of Wales in Oslo last week.” ( AFP/Getty )

Elsewhere, the report welcomed the government’s “Be Ready” campaign that recently saw ministers urge Britons to stockpile days’ worth of food and water for crisis situations.

But it urged politicians and officials to “trust the public and take them into their confidence as much as security will allow” by sharing more information about challenges the country could face.

“Evidence shows that the public would be reassured, not alarmed, by candid information. People are more than willing to step up in an emergency but less clear why and how,” Baroness Coussins said.

A Cabinet Office spokesperson said: “We thank the committee for their report, which we will carefully review.

“It highlights the need for action across government and society to boost our collective resilience – closely involving local, regional and national bodies.

“That is exactly what this government is doing.

“From launching a national campaign to raise awareness of the simple steps households can take to stay safe in everyday emergencies, to delivering the largest home defence exercise in recent history next year, and investing over £1 billion in pandemic security – our work on resilience goes further than successive governments have ever gone before.

“However, we know there is still more work to do to make the UK the most resilient country we can be, including working with and learning from our allies.

“This was top of the Security Minister’s agenda when he met some of the UK’s closest allies aboard HMS Prince of Wales in Oslo last week.”

News.title: Kevin Pietersen fires up England squad ahead of ODI decider in Hobart
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Kevin Pietersen has fired England up for their ODI series decider against Australia, telling Harry Brook’s side that beating the old enemy on their own turf is the best feeling in cricket.

Pietersen was a key part in the last England side to win the Ashes Down Under in 2010/11 and recently rejoined the backroom team in a mentoring role ahead of next year’s World Cup in South Africa.

He has left the squad with the scores tied at 1-1 – improbably, to address a YouTube conference in India through his second career as a content creator – but his parting message stressed the importance of finishing the job in Hobart on Wednesday.

England had a false start in Perth where they were rolled over for 131 but hit back in emphatic fashion at the Adelaide Oval, to win by a crushing margin of 135.

open image in gallery Gus Atkinson featured in England’s Ashes misadventure (Nigel French/PA) ( PA Wire )

By the time their bowlers finished the hosts off a crowd of almost 32,000 had dwindled drastically as disappointed locals made their way to the exits.

“KP said that winning in Australia is the best thing you can have an an England cricketer,” said Gus Atkinson, whose previous experience in this part of the world was last winter’s Ashes misadventure.

“It was nice (to see their supporters leaving). I said to Harry Brook at mid-off ‘listen…it’s so quiet now’. It was really nice.

“We copped it a bit during the Ashes so come here and win was great. The first game didn’t go to plan but to come back and have the series on the line in Hobart is very exciting. If we can come away with it that would be fantastic.”

Atkinson and Jofra Archer will both be hoping to feature, with Jamie Overton vying for a recall after being rested for Sonny Baker, but the most pressing selection issue is the growing uncertainty over Adil Rashid’s role.

The leg-spinner is the second highest-wicket taker in England’s one-day history – sitting 25 shy of Sir James Anderson on 244 – and sits seventh on the list of all-time appearances with 165.

But his status as the team’s undisputed number one spinner is under threat. He has played just one of the last six games, overlooked for left-arm all-rounder Liam Dawson.

England explained his peripheral role in Pakistan as a horses-for-courses measure but have now made the same decision on vastly different surfaces in Perth and Adelaide.

It is hard to escape the feeling that they are stress testing the possibility of going into the World Cup campaign without him as a guaranteed pick, but former England captain Michael Vaughan believes there is a less drastic explanation.

“It looks to me like they are trying to get a lot of experience into Liam Dawson,” he told BBC’s Test Match Special.

“If you look at Australia there’s no Starc, no Cummins, no Hazlewood. They’ve done it for the last couple of World Cups, they don’t play their main bowlers leading in and when they get to the World Cup they bring them all back.

“I wonder if England are doing that with Adil. He’s got the all the knowledge, all the experience, he doesn’t need to play every single game. I get a sense they’re just trying to make sure all of the bowling attack arrives at the World Cup with a certain number of caps.”

News.title: Malta travel guide: how to spend seven sun-soaked days exploring historic sites, local cuisine and stunning coastlines
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Sunshine seems to infuse every inch of Malta, from the harbours, bluffs and beaches that lace the coastline to the stepped streets of ancient towns. It bounces off Valletta’s apricot-honey buildings and bursts from every bite of the country’s cuisine, which marries North African, Sicilian and Mediterranean influences and flavours.

Basking in more than 300 days of sunshine a year, the island is a year-round holiday destination. Once there, it’s easy to get around and explore the many landmarks and highlights, thanks to an extensive bus network and regular ferries connecting major towns.

And, when you travel with Jet2holidays, you can book your trip with a low deposit of just £60 per person*, with the option of settling the balance in three interest-free payments via PayPal**. Other benefits include 22kg baggage and 10kg hand luggage included, Free Child Places† and return transfers‡. You also have the flexibility to choose your holiday dates and duration and select from a range of two to five-star properties.

That just leaves what to do, see and taste while exploring this extraordinary destination. Here are just some of our expert recommendations of how to spend a week in Malta, day by day.

Day 1: Malta's best areas and towns to stay

Mellieħa hill top offers extensive views of of Malta's stunning coastline ( VisitMalta )

The island caters for every type of traveller and the airport transfer is quick and fuss-free no matter where you might choose to rest your head. Families might like to base themselves in Mellieħa, a charming hilltop village with Malta’s longest sandy beach or nearby St Paul’s Bay with its long promenade and easy access to attractions.

For couples, Sliema’s seafront promenade, idyllic swimming spots and regular boat cruises are a great option (families will love it, too), as is the wonderfully atmospheric 16th-century fortress city of Valletta, which offers fabulous shopping, restaurants and bars along its limestone-paved streets. Day one, after checking in, is all about taking some time to explore your surroundings.

Day 2: Valletta’s historic attractions and dining

No trip to Malta is complete without a visit to the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Valletta ( VisitMalta )

Wherever you’re based, carve out some time to explore the the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Valletta, whose buildings and walls wear a uniform buttery limestone. Don’t miss the magnificent St John’s Co-Cathedral, or the intricately patterned city gate, designed by Renzo Piano, stroll down Triq Santa Luċija, browsing stores with lace-like filigree jewellery and pausing for lunch of pizza and burrata at San Paolo Naufrago, with tables spilling on to the street’s broad steps.

Take a short ferry across Grand Harbour to the Three Cities: the fortified towns of Birgu, Isla and Bormla. Walk to the watchtower, carved with eyes and ears, in Gardjola Gardens and take in sweeping harbour views from 16th-century Fort St Angelo.

Back in Valletta, feast on seasonal Maltese dishes at cosy Legligin Restaurant, or savour the farm-to-fork tasting menu at Michelin-starred ION Harbour.

Day 3: Mdina and Rabat – a history and landmarks guide

Explore Mdina's impressive architecture and history-filled narrow streets ( Shutterstock )

Malta’s ancient capital, Mdina, is easily accessed from Valletta and other locations by bus or taxi. Enter through one of two grand stone gates, visit 18th-century St Paul’s Cathedral and delve into Maltese history at Palazzo Falson, a 15th-century townhouse turned museum.

Just outside Mdina’s walls, Rabat’s narrow lanes are lined with traditional limestone houses. Explore St. Paul’s Catacombs (dating back to the third or fourth Century BC) and Domus Romana, a museum around a Roman villa, before stopping at Is-Serkin for pastizzi – crisp puff pastry parcels stuffed with mushy peas or ricotta.

Day 4: Malta outdoors –hiking and nature parks

From hiking and biking to water sports, Malta is a great place for outdoor enthusiasts ( VisitMalta )

Take time to relax at your hotel before heading on an outdoor adventure. Hike up to Malta’s highest natural point, Dingli Cliffs, trace the rugged shoreline in Il-Majjistral park or follow an ancient Roman road past tombs and a 1,000-year-old carob tree on Xemxija Hill in St Paul’s Bay.

Or head inland to Ta’ Qali National Park for walking loops around the formal Maltese-cross gardens, then to the serenely beautiful San Anton Gardens. Not up for that much time on your feet? Much of Malta’s landscapes can also be explored on horseback, quad bikes, through Jeep tours or by cycling.

Day 5: Sliema’s coastal promenade and restaurants

Indulge in Malta's varied cuisine in Sliema and beyond ( VisitMalta )

Spend the day pottering around Sliema, whose long, flat promenade is lined with street stalls and cafes serving falafel, fresh seafood and specialities like hobż biż-żejt, crunchy Maltese bread rubbed with tomatoes and drizzled with olive oil. Nearby, Fond Għadir is a Blue Flag swimming spot with rock-carved bathing pools and ladders descending into the turquoise water.

Staying for the evening? Dine at Trattoria del Mare for Sicilian-inspired seafood and sunset views of Valletta’s elegant skyline, or join a catamaran cruise around the harbour.

Day 6: Malta’s coast for swimming spots and Gozo day trip

Head to Golden Bay for a Blue Flag beach with fine orange sand and shallow turquoise waters ( VisitMalta )

Malta’s coastline ranges from serene sandy coves to limestone cliffs and sea caves. Swim and snorkel in the natural pools of Qawra Point, accessed from the promenade in St Paul’s Bay, then learn more about Maltese marine life at nearby Malta National Aquarium.

Craving soft sand? Mellieħa Bay, on the north coast, is a powdery beach leading to gentle, shallow waters, making it ideal for families. Nearby, and close to the village of Manikata, Golden Bay’s soft, reddish sand pops against the blue-green water.

Want to venture further? See more of the coastline from the sea on a boat trip, or take a short ferry ride to Gozo to explore the smaller island’s bays, beaches and Neolithic Ġgantija Temples.

Day 7: More Malta – visit Marsaxlokk and the Neolithic temples

Experience one of the oldest sites in the world at the Neolithic Mnajdra Temples in Zurrieq ( VisitMalta )

Be whisked back in time by five millennia at the Neolithic temples of Haġar Qim and Mnajdra, believed to be among the world’s oldest religious sites. Visiting on a Sunday? Head southeast to the fishing village of Marsaxlokk, whose weekly market has stalls laden with honey, leather goods and souvenirs emblazoned with the Maltese cross.

Dine on fresh seafood by the harbour, watching crews haul in their daily catch in luzzus, the traditional wooden fishing boats. Painted blue, red, yellow and green, with the island’s ubiquitous ‘Eye of Horus’ motif, they add extra colour to the sun-soaked scenery.
