“I want to ask leaders in the Opposition, be careful. Don't listen to overzealous supporters and influencers; they will lead you astray. Remain focused,” he warned.

On the question of selecting a joint presidential candidate, Gachagua revealed that differences remained over the appropriate timing, with Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka proposing that the flagbearer be identified before December, while Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna favoured February and Narc Kenya leader Martha Karua suggested May.

Gachagua, however, argued that selecting a candidate too early could expose the individual to political pressure and possible frustration from the government.

He proposed April next year as a more suitable time, maintaining that the coalition was united on the principle of having one candidate even if its leaders differed on the timing.

The DCP leader also dismissed arguments that academic qualifications, experience or political credentials should determine who becomes the coalition's presidential candidate, insisting that electoral numbers and the support of ordinary Kenyans would ultimately decide.

“As others say they have experience and an agenda in the Opposition, the deciding factor is the numbers. I'm with the people. You say you have capacity, but the person to decide is the voter,” he said.

He added: “Akili nyingi ni nzuri, but bila kura unaweza kaa nayo nyumbani.”

World.title: Trump sank the GOP in 2026. He could do it again in 2028
World.content:
Judging by their choices since this month’s Democratic sweep, both the White House and congressional Republicans are vastly underestimating the party’s risk in 2028 if President Donald Trump remains as unpopular as he is now.

Dazed Republicans picking through the wreckage of their losses may console themselves with the thought that Trump’s dire approval ratings won’t pose as large a threat to the GOP in 2028, since he will be leaving the White House. But history strongly suggests that confidence is misplaced.

Outgoing presidents have cast a larger shadow than even many political professionals assume in the election to succeed them — especially when that retiring president faces widespread public discontent, as Trump does now. While popular outgoing presidents haven’t always ensured victory for their designated successors, the inverse has almost always been true: When the outgoing president is unpopular, his party has rarely won the election to replace him.

This month’s election underscored the danger looming for Republicans if Trump remains this weak. In House, Senate and gubernatorial elections across the country, the vast majority of voters who disapproved of Trump’s job performance — usually at least 80% of them — voted against Republican candidates, according to the most recently updated numbers as of November 12 from the Voter Polls conducted for CNN and other media organizations by SRSS.

“This massive repudiation of Republican candidates is totally and completely about Donald Trump,” said longtime GOP pollster Whit Ayres.

Even big losses in a midterm don’t guarantee defeat for the party holding the White House in the next presidential election. But presidents who have recovered from a bad midterm have usually changed direction in response to the rebuke (like Harry Truman after 1946 or Bill Clinton after 1994) or benefited from changing circumstances (as Ronald Reagan did when the economy recovered after his party’s poor 1982 midterm).

Trump, by contrast, remains caught in a grinding war against Iran with no clear exit. And far from adjusting his course, he has reaffirmed it with the appointment of Stephen Miller, his most ideologically extreme senior adviser, as White House chief of staff. House Republicans have responded to their losses in a similar way by choosing pugnacious Rep. Jim Jordan as their new leader.

Rep. Jim Jordan speaks with reporters after leaving the office of Senate Majority Leader John Thune at the US Capitol on November 11. Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters White House chief of staff Stephen Miller is seen in the Presidential limousine at Palm Beach International Airport in West Palm Beach, Florida on November 6. Alex Wroblewski/AFP/AFP via Getty Images

“Donald Trump is going to double down and triple down” on the policies and style that alienated voters this year, said Steve Schmidt, a longtime GOP strategist who has become a staunch Trump critic. “Any person with any attachment to real life would look at this election and say, ‘Well, they certainly should have gotten the message and they’ll be chastened,’ but that doesn’t appreciate the physics of politics, which is that as an extreme party gets smaller, it becomes more fanatical.”

History is clear on the consequences

Novelist Leo Tolstoy famously wrote that every happy family is alike, while every unhappy family is different. The relationship of outgoing presidents to the election to succeed them inverts that maxim: The impact of every unsuccessful president has been largely the same, while the role of successful presidents has diverged.

Good feelings toward popular retiring presidents Theodore Roosevelt in 1908 and Ronald Reagan in 1988 helped each man’s designated successor win election. But despite very strong job approval ratings, both Dwight Eisenhower in 1960 and Bill Clinton in 2000 saw their vice-presidents lose nail biters (although Al Gore, Clinton’s No. 2, did win the popular vote). Barack Obama in 2016 wasn’t as popular as Eisenhower or Clinton, but he also left office with majority approval — only to see his party’s designated heir, Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, lose another tight race to Trump (despite, like Gore, winning the popular vote).

But when an outgoing president has lost the public’s support, the record is far more consistent. Since the turn of the 20th century, each time an outgoing president has been broadly unpopular, his party has lost the race to succeed him. That was true for Democrats Woodrow Wilson in 1920, Harry Truman in 1952, Lyndon Johnson in 1968 and Biden in 2024, as well as for Republican George W. Bush in 2008.

According to the exit polls conducted for CNN and other media organizations, 88% of the voters who disapproved of Reagan in 1988 and Clinton in 2000 voted for the other party’s presidential candidate. In 2016, 89% of voters who disapproved of Obama voted for Trump; in 2024, 82% of voters who disapproved of Biden voted for Trump over Vice President Kamala Harris.

Trump’s two victories help explain why a popular outgoing president is no guarantee of success for his party — while an unpopular retiring president has been a more reliable kiss of death.

In 2016, according to the exit polls, Obama’s approval remained at or just above 50% in each of six swing states he had won in 2012. But Trump still flipped all of them — Iowa, Ohio, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Florida. The reason is that Trump captured a significantly larger share among the minority of voters who disapproved of Obama than Clinton won among the majority who approved. Trump harnessed virtually all the discontent about Obama, while Clinton’s own vulnerabilities prevented her from capturing as much of his support.

In 2024, the equation for Harris proved much more straightforward — and treacherous. Between 56% to 60% of voters in the seven major swing states disapproved of Biden’s performance and between 81% to 87% of those disapprovers backed Trump, powering him to victory in all of them, the exit polls found. Harris made missteps as a candidate, but her biggest problem was that pervasive discontent with the administration in which she served.

A poster cutout of Vice President Kamala Harris sits on the ground after a demonstrators protested the administration’s stance on aid to Israel on August 19, 2024, while the Democratic National Convention was being held in Chicago. Martha Irvine/AP

In recent times, the presidential nominee who had the most success separating from an unpopular outgoing president of his own party was Republican Sen. John McCain in 2008. Running against Obama, McCain won 30% of voters nationwide who disapproved of George W. Bush, the exit polls found.

As a senator who had occasionally clashed with Bush — and ran a bitter race against him for the GOP nomination in 2000 — McCain wasn’t intrinsically tied to his predecessor as closely as Harris, Gore and George H.W. Bush (who all served as vice presidents to the retiring president) or Hillary Clinton, who worked as Obama’s secretary of state. “There were famously enmities there,” between McCain and Bush, noted Schmidt, McCain’s chief strategist in the 2008 race.

Yet Schmidt said the campaign recognized it would take dramatic, even unprecedented, actions to overcome the public’s disapproval of Bush — which reached a stunning 71% in the 2008 exit poll amid fatigue with the Iraq War and fear and anger over that year’s financial crisis.

“It drove everything as a political consideration because you knew that there was a day of reckoning where you had to disrupt that headwind and fly out of it,” Schmidt said. That impulse, he said, drove McCain’s attempt to name Democrat-turned independent Sen. Joe Lieberman as his running mate. “It was going to take something like that to arrest the trajectory,” Schmidt recalled. (When Republicans rebelled over Lieberman, McCain abruptly pivoted to choosing Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin instead.)

In the end, even McCain could not paddle nearly fast enough to escape the undertow of Bush’s capsizing presidency. Obama that year won a higher share of the popular vote than any Democratic nominee since Johnson in 1964 and flipped nine states that had voted for Bush in 2004. In all of them, at least two-thirds of voters disapproved of Bush’s performance — and at least two-thirds of those disapprovers backed Obama.

The GOP’s 2028 conundrum

Through 2026, the one discordant sign for Democrats was polling consistently showing they were not winning nearly as many voters who disapproved of Trump as during his first term.

Democrats this year didn’t fully match the benchmarks they hit among Trump disapprovers in his first term. But ultimately Democrats carried about the same share of voters who disapproved of Trump as the opposition party did among voters who disapproved of Obama in 2010, Bush in 2006 and Bill Clinton in 1994. In the 2026 CNN Voter Poll measuring preferences in the national House popular vote, 86% of voters who disapproved of Trump backed Democrats; the party also won 85% to 89% of voters who disapproved of Trump in almost all the major Senate contests.

Democratic Sens.-elect Annie Andrews, James Talarico and Troy Jackson walk toward an orientation meeting for newly elected lawmakers inside the US Capitol on November 9. Win McNamee/Getty Images

That was plenty to power a Democratic landslide. Disapproval of Trump in this election was not only deep (at 63%, his national disapproval rating was considerably higher than those other presidents in their worst midterm elections), but also broad. Across the 45 states where Voter Poll data is available, most voters approved of Trump’s job performance in only five sparsely populated deep-red states — Arkansas, Idaho, South Dakota, West Virginia, and Wyoming.

In every state where Democrats flipped a governorship, a Senate seat, or both, a substantial majority of voters disapproved of Trump’s job performance — and those disenchanted voters provided the core of the winning Democratic coalition. In Texas, for instance, 96% of the votes for Democratic Senate victor James Talarico came from people who disapproved of Trump.

One reason Republicans could not surmount the Trump discontent in 2028 was that so few displayed any independence from him. As Ayres noted, Republicans concluded that if they clashed with Trump, he would either hound them out of the party or defeat them in primaries. Yet binding themselves to Trump to avoid primary challenges created insurmountable problems in the general election where “Trump and Trumpism have become toxic,” Ayres said.

That same conundrum looms over the potential 2028 Republican presidential field, particularly Vice President JD Vance. Trump is likely to fire social media thunderbolts against any attempt from Vance or other candidates to meaningfully distance from him, and no one seeking the nomination can afford too much conflict with the president, given his durable popularity with the MAGA base. Yet if Trump remains anywhere near as unpopular with the broad public as he is today, failing to separate from him could prove fatal for the eventual GOP nominee in the general election.

Vance himself seems to be aware of this catch-22; CNN reported last week that the vice president has given serious consideration to not running for president in 2028 in the wake of the GOP’s disastrous midterm performance.

There’s little sign Republicans will change course

All this underscores the GOP’s stake in Trump mounting at least some recovery by 2028. A decisive conclusion to the Iran War that lowered gas and diesel prices might lift him somewhat.

But Democratic pollster Anna Greenberg said it will be extremely difficult for Trump to regain much of the allegiance he lost over the past two years among the new voters who moved toward him in 2024 — particularly Hispanic Americans, Black men and younger men. Most of those voters, she said, feel not only disappointed but angry at Trump for failing to alleviate their economic squeeze as he promised — while focusing so much on his own priorities, like building monuments and padding his fortune.

“Especially for the people who are less ideologically committed to him… the betrayal and the broken promises make it very hard to come back from,” Greenberg said. “It’s not just the bad job performance.”

As problematic, Trump and congressional Republicans show no sign of rethinking the course that ran the party into this electoral ditch. Instead, through the elevation of the belligerent hard-liners Miller and Jordan, the GOP has not only ignored but actively rejected the voters’ roar of discontent.

President Donald Trump takes question from the media on the South Lawn of the White House on October 21. Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images

Add the prospect of extensive congressional hearings exposing corruption and self-dealing in the administration and many analysts believe Trump’s approval rating could fall even lower by 2028. “He may not be at his lowest point,” saud Emory University political scientist Alan Abramowitz, who has extensively studied the relationship between election outcomes and presidential approval. “He is going to have a hard time clawing his way back up to anything higher than he is now, given what is likely to be happening” with investigations and the economy.

If Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio wins the GOP nomination in 2028, they might find it especially difficult to escape negative feelings about Trump, since they served so closely with him. But, as Abramowitz said, “every prominent Republican has tied themselves closely to Trump over the past two years.”

Though voters still harbor many doubts about Democrats, if Trump can’t repair his public standing, those Democratic vulnerabilities may not matter as much as Republicans hope — just as they did little to stop the massive blue tide earlier this month.

World.title: Democrats look to what’s next after Trump. But first, an actual party
World.content:
Denver — The Democrats here were told: The big midterm win wasn’t about you.

But the vibes among the hundreds of party operatives, strategists and would-be 2028 presidential candidates who gathered to ask what’s next after nearly a decade of living in President Donald Trump’s shadow?

Party on, Wayne! Party on, Garth!

Democrats arguably haven’t had such a wide-open presidential field since the “Wayne’s World” era, when a preternaturally talented Southern state governor named Bill Clinton came almost out of nowhere to win the White House in 1992.

Now, Democrats have exploded out of a Trump-imposed political wilderness to their most sweeping midterm win since Watergate. And they were ready to take a beat before they begin what’s sure to be a frenzied season of presidential campaign announcements, hiring, fundraising and knife-fighting among a dozen or more White House hopefuls.

Even the would-be candidates could barely hide their elation during donor dinners, at hotel rooftop receptions, and over drinks at the bar at the Ritz-Carlton in downtown Denver, where many mingled late into the night.

Attendees listen to speeches during the What’s Next summit at Mission Ballroom in Denver on November 13. Mark Makela/Getty Images

But on the main stage, on the first day, those gathered here were warned: Voters still aren’t all that into them.

“These voters that we lost and that we have turned away are still out there and they have not become Democrats yet,” influential Democratic data guru David Shor said as the two-day gathering kicked off. “They will be here in two years, and if we have not persuaded them by then, we might not be happy with how things turn out.”

There was no agreement about how to do that. The prescriptions coming from the stage previewed the struggle that’s beginning to emerge: Did Tuesday’s wins signal an uncompromising fighter from the party’s left wing can dominate the nominating contest and go on to win a national election?

Or is the message that to win everywhere, the party should choose someone who can appeal to the voters who rejected the woke culture-war politics of the Covid era?

“The American people cannot wait two years for change. So we must work with President Trump,” said Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico.

“The only way we’re going to fix that is by fixing it together. We can’t do it with the same warfare that brought us here,” said Rob Sand, the incoming Democratic governor of Iowa.

US Representative Ro Khanna, D-CA, speaks during the “What’s Next” post-midterm election conference by the Democratic Party in Denver, on November 13. Kevin Mohatt/Reuters

Contrast those two millennial red-state newcomers with Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna, who hails from deep-blue California, co-chaired Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaign in 2020, and is widely expected to run for president in 2028 as an unapologetic progressive.

“This is not the 1990s. We cannot cobble together a fleeting big tent through perpetual triangulating, straddling, and calculating,” Khanna said onstage. The reference to “triangulating” was an unmistakable jab at a buzzword of the Clinton era.

The gathering offered a few reminders of the anger emanating from the party’s base. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen spoke after announcing he would challenge Chuck Schumer to be the next Senate majority leader.

Likely incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries was heckled by the audience, with one person yelling Jeffries was “a f**king liar!” before being escorted from the hall.

And protesters gathered outside the security perimeter, holding signs that read, “Abolish billionaires,” “No Schumer coronation,” and “No more do-nothing Democrats.” A Denver SWAT vehicle was parked between them and the rideshare dropoff line.

Protesters demonstrate outside before the second day of programming at the What’s Next summit outside Mission Ballroom in Denver, on November 13. Mark Makela/Getty Images

A protester gestures while being escorted outside by staff members during a talk with US House of Representatives Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-NY, at the “What’s Next” post-midterm election conference by the Democratic Party in Denver, Colorado, US November 13. Kevin Mohatt/Reuters House Democratic Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-NY, watches protesters screaming at him while participating in a question and answer event during the What’s Next summit at Mission Ballroom in Denver on November 13.. Mark Makela/Getty Images

But inside that perimeter and off the stage, all the divisions evaporated into an atmosphere of celebration bordering on elation. There were food trucks parked outside the brewery serving local craft beers on draft. There were musical acts performing in the outdoor plaza in between speeches. Both days were about 65 degrees and sunny, with the weather clear enough to see the mountains.

And it was very cozy and comfortable after hours at at the Ritz bar. The drinks started flowing Thursday night, with Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, who’s considering a presidential run, holding court. Pete Buttigieg was also spotted there Thursday night, as was Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro.

And Friday evening, the nationwide FAA ground stop stranded everyone in Denver at least for a few hours. Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin sat with Govs. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia and Mikie Sherill of New Jersey until the stop was lifted. Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock huddled off the record with reporters. Buttigieg was back too, spotted snapping a selfie or two. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker couldn’t attend the conference, but his team was at the Ritz bar too. So were operatives with ties to Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and a handful of others.

David Axelrod, senior political commentator at CNN and former senior advisor to former US President Barack Obama, from left, Mikie Sherrill, governor of New Jersey, Philip Weiser, Colorado attorney general, Abigail Spanberger, governor of Virginia, and former State Representative Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat from Alaska, during the What’s Next conference in Denver, on Friday, November 13. Chet Strange/Bloomberg/Getty Images

This was where the conference’s real business unfolded. A top priority was recruiting staff and making connections for presidential campaigns that are set to start kicking off as soon as January, if not earlier, according to conversations with over a dozen strategists and operatives with ties to presidential hopefuls.

Much of the chatter and speculation focused on possible candidates who weren’t in the room, Kamala Harris and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez chief among them. Their decisions to run or not to run for president in 2028 will fundamentally shape the rest of the field.

Wins across the South underscore the power of Black voters, already perhaps the most important single constituency in any Democratic primary, and Harris starts with an enormous advantage there, especially among Black women.

And then there’s the progressive wing, energized by victories from working-class candidates and people like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

“People are thinking there’s more room for someone on the left, and wondering if it means AOC is going to run,” said one top operative with close ties to a likely 2028 Democratic presidential candidate.

There was also widespread speculation about Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, whose been widely considered a top-tier likely 2028 contender. At the heart of his appeal had been the argument he can win big in one of the most important swing states on the map. Now, he’s got a lot of competition from newer faces in the party.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro speaks to the media outside after taking the stage during the “What’s Next” post-midterm election conference by the Democratic Party in Denver, on November 13. Kevin Mohatt/Reuters

“I’m proud to be the governor of what I think is the swingiest state in America, but we got a lot of company now,” Shapiro told me in an interview. “Look at Texas, look at South Carolina, Iowa, and a whole lot more. But I think that presents an opportunity for Democrats not to be thinking about how to get to 270 on an electoral map, but get to 370 back how Obama won and Clinton won.”

Other potential contenders, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, also didn’t appear here. Newsom, who had occupied something of frontrunner status in the invisible primary as he jabbed at Trump over the past year, seemed to have faded somewhat from the main conversation, at least in these halls.

(Newsom hasn’t faded, apparently, for Trump, who spent part of his weekend attacking Newsom for commuting the death sentences of all California inmates on death row and changing them to life without parole.)

As the hundreds of Democrats who gathered here struggled to find a way out of Denver, the airport chaos almost presaged what could be a massive post-Trump hangover for a party that’s elated but set for a bruising internal struggle over what’s next.

“If you ask the American people, there is no question about who we oppose,” said Massachusetts Rep. Jake Auchincloss. “But also no sense of what we believe. That is the question we have to answer right now.”

World.title: Rubio says more work to do and downplays election losses amid speculation about political future
World.content:
Amid speculation about his political future, Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared that there is more work to be done as he downplayed Republicans’ losses in the midterm elections.

“We have much more to do over the next two, the next six, the next 20 years. Great things that last are built in decades, not election cycles,” Rubio said in an address to the conservative Federalist Society’s National Lawyers Convention in Washington, DC, on Friday evening.

Rubio has faced mounting questions about whether he will seek the presidency in 2028, particularly in the wake of last week’s midterm elections. His speech, for which he was introduced by his daughter Daniella, could further fuel speculation.

“Though we are prepared for the twists and turns and the ups and downs of the road ahead, of this I believe with all my heart that we in this generation will leave for our children and our grandchildren what Americans always leave for their children and their grandchildren: the single greatest nation in the history of the world,” Rubio said to conclude his lengthy remarks, which were met with a standing ovation.

Rubio made direct references to his party’s defeats at the ballot boxes. He also joked to the packed ballroom of lawyers and law students at the Mayflower Hotel that “on election night there was a congressman that said we all needed to lawyer up, so here we are.” He was referencing a statement from Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia — the incoming House Oversight Committee chairman.

However, Rubio downplayed the absolute power of elections, saying, “politics requires more than simply winning elections, because the government is not the only source of political power.”

“Elections (decide) who holds office for a season. Elections … they do not decide by themselves what our institutions teach or what our lawyers believe, which ideas are treated as respectable, normal, and which are deemed beyond the pale,” he said.

The top US diplomat also cited setbacks suffered during the American Revolution, suggesting that “those who believe that one setback, one defeat, one bad election spells the end of the Republic” should look to the founding fathers.

“There will be more victories, and there will be more defeats. There will be more triumphs, and there will be more disappointments. This is the nature of all undertakings of this weight and of this magnitude. There are no great men or great causes in the pages of history that did not suffer the same,” he said.

Rubio lashed out against the “weaponization of international law” and “activist courts who seek to govern by injunction” in the US. He specifically targeted the International Criminal Court, which the Trump administration is working to dismantle.

In a question-and-answer session after the speech, Rubio reiterated, “America is exceptional, but it’s not self-perpetuating.”

“It has always required those in charge to do what it takes to keep it moving forward, and that that’s what we’re called to do, and then have confidence that we can do it. It’s an enormous undertaking, and it’s like I said in my speech, it’s something that happens over you know, years and decades, not election cycle to election cycle,” he said.

World.title: Jensen Huang resigned in disgrace from Nvidia. Many in Silicon Valley are still showering him with support
World.content:
Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia was marked by corporate scandal, but many of his own former employees and colleagues across Silicon Valley are coming out in droves to express support for the man they believe to be a legend.

Huang resigned on Thursday after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with at least one subordinate. He had already been under scrutiny after reports of an affair with another woman, who was described by US officials as a potential Chinese intelligence asset.

Huang was so integral to Nvidia’s brand that his image — with signature black leather jacket — was often turned into marketing material, including an AI-powered hologram at the company’s annual conference, known as GTC. Known for its low turnover and flat corporate structure, with Huang managing over 50 direct reports and responding to messages at all hours, Nvidia fostered deep employee loyalty.

Following his departure, current and former staff responded with tributes on social media. Edward Liu, a director and distinguished scientist who started as an intern at the company, called it “a heartbreaking day,” in a post on X, praising Huang as an inspiring leader who taught them to “reason from first principles.” Engineer Fei Peng went even further, writing that Huang’s departure “has killed NVIDIA’s soul.”

Others, like senior research scientist Gavin Woolery, openly suggested ulterior motives and suspicions about his ousting. Woolery posted on X that he felt Huang’s ousting came too quickly before all the information emerged.

“Everyone deserves a fair trial. It’s possible he has made mistakes, I’m not sure they were ill-intentioned ones, but in either case we should know the whole truth before we judge,” Woolery said.

Other employees expressed support for Nvidia’s interim leader, CFO Colette Kress.

“I am grief-stricken that Jensen is no longer with NVIDIA,” posted Bryan Catanzaro, Nvidia’s vice president of applied deep learning research. “At the same time, I fully support NVIDIA’s board and have confidence in their decisions. I’ve worked with Colette for years and know her as an extraordinary leader. She has my full support.”

Beyond Nvidia’s walls, Huang’s influence was felt across the broader tech ecosystem. Often called the “central bank” of the booming AI industry, Nvidia not only supplied the hardware powering the technology but also financed much of the sector through investments and partnerships, with Huang serving as its biggest cheerleader. That has led to criticism and fears of “circular financing,” in which Nvidia invests in companies that fuel its own growth when those businesses turn around and use Nvidia capital to purchase Nvidia products.

Exolabs founder Alex Cheema wrote about cold emailing Huang in June about an idea to make local AI much faster on Nvidia hardware. Huang responded in seven minutes and “approved a war room for us to work on this at NVIDIA HQ,” Cheema wrote.

Cheema pointed to Huang’s long-time support and promotion of open-source technology — software or hardware built on publicly accessible source code that anyone can freely inspect, modify and distribute. Most of the major AI models, like ChatGPT and Claude, run on closed-source systems.

“I don’t believe Jensen is replaceable, he’s a 1 of 1 human, but I hope NVIDIA will continue to aggressively support Open Source AI and Local AI, and continue to take bets on small startups with crazy ideas,” Cheema said.

Huang also found support among his peers — some of the biggest names in Silicon Valley and venture capital, including his longtime friend and business partner, Elon Musk. Even before Huang was ousted, Musk posted that it would be “an honor” to hire Huang after another user on X implored him to do so.

“A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too,” Musk later posted on Friday after Huang’s resignation.

“Dark, dark day. Horrible decision for the U.S. and the western world,” Andreessen Horowitz general partner Martin Casado posted on X. The firm’s account also posted a clip from a movie about Michael Jordan, along with the quote: “ You’re gonna be remembered forever because some things are eternal.”

Even those who have criticized his actions, like Sequoia Capital’s Shaun MaGuire, who called Huang’s actions a “dumb mistake” and “bad for America,” often come with a dose of praise. “He made huge mistakes with his infidelity, which is tragic for his family and NVDA. But simultaneously he will leave a huge void, with the loss of a: technical, aggressive, founder-CEO,” MaGuire wrote on X.

World.title: Court sentences husband of ‘Monufia Bride’ murder case to death
World.content:
The Wadi al-Natrun Appellate Criminal Court on Saturday sentenced the killer of Karima Awad to death by hanging in the “Monufia Bride” case.

Karima was murdered just four months after her wedding, having endured severe abuse at the hands of her husband.

A marriage filled with brutality, oppression, and humiliation

In its remarks accompanying the verdict, the court detailed the suffering endured by Karima Awad.

It affirmed that, throughout her brief marriage, she was subjected to “brutality, oppression, humiliation, mistreatment, and a complete deprivation of the most basic human dignity” at the hands of the defendant.

The court emphasized the severity of the crimes committed against a young woman who had only been married for a few months.

The court’s focus on the mistreatment and cruelty she faced brings back the details of the incident that took place in the village of Mit Barra, in Quesna District of Monufia Governorate.

Fatal beating

Investigations into the case revealed that the victim had been subjected to physical assaults, which resulted in severe injuries that ultimately claimed her life in December 2025.

According to the lawyer representing Karima’s family, the defendant assaulted his wife twice on the day of the incident. The first assault caused her to lose consciousness, after which he attacked her again, striking her in the chest and head.

The family’s lawyer explained that the victim’s injuries included internal bleeding and a fracture to her sternum (breastbone)—details he cited while calling for the maximum possible sentence for the defendant.

Court’s message

The court’s statement underscored the oppression, humiliation, and mistreatment endured by Karima.

These points echoed the arguments presented by the Public Prosecution during the trial, as it sought the maximum penalty for the defendant, emphasizing a husband’s duty to protect his wife and highlighting how such a crime constitutes a profound breach of the covenant of safety upon which the marital relationship is founded.

Background of the verdict

The court of first instance had initially sentenced the defendant to 15 years in prison.

However, the Public Prosecution appealed the ruling, bringing the case before the appellate criminal court.

During the previous hearing, the court decided to refer the defendant’s case files to the Grand Mufti of Egypt to seek a religious legal opinion (Fatwa) regarding the imposition of the death penalty.

In Saturday’s session, the defendant appeared in the dock, dressed in white prison attire, amid tight security measures, before the court handed down the death sentence.

With this verdict, the case has reached a new judicial milestone following months of investigations, hearings, and legal arguments.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Four people burn to death after two-vehicle collision in Aswan
World.content:
Four people were burned to death on Saturday evening following a collision between two vehicles on al-Abbasiya road in the Kom Ombo district of Aswan Governorate.

The impact caused both vehicles to catch fire, resulting in the charring of four individuals who were inside as one of the trucks was carrying petroleum products.

The Aswan ambulance dispatch center received a report of a collision between two vehicles on al-Abbasiya road in Kom Ombo district of Aswan.

The relevant authorities and civil defense teams rushed to the scene once receiving report on the accident, which involved a collision between two pickup trucks.

A formal report of the incident has been filed, and the Public Prosecution has been notified for investigations.

World.title: MP slams Finance Ministry’s move to allocate Egyptian state lands to reduce public debt
World.content:
A member of the Egyptian Parliament’s Economic Affairs Committee and economist Mohamed Fouad on Saturday criticized the practice of allocating state-owned land for the purpose of reducing public debt.

Speaking with TV host Amr Adib on the “al-Hekaya,” (The Story) show, the MP remarked: “The issue isn’t just whether the land is being sold or not; the economic implications are what matter most. Are we actually solving the problem, or are we merely postponing it?”

Fouad said that the recent allocation of 112 million square meters of land in the Red Sea region to the Finance Ministry mirrors the earlier case of the Ras Shuqair land, which he noted implies a lack of clarity regarding the outcomes of that previous initiative.

Fouad explained that a presidential decree issued on June 4, 2025, had allocated 174 million square meters in Ras Shuqair area to the Finance Ministry, with the stated objective of reducing public debt and facilitating the issuance of sovereign “Sukuk” (Islamic bonds).

He said that 17 months have passed without the development of an operational plan, or even a preliminary framework, which raises questions about the ultimate fate of these lands and the mechanisms through which they are to be utilized.

The newly allocated area in the Red Sea spans 112 million square meters, he noted, which is equivalent to approximately 60 percent of the size of the land at Ras Shuqair.

What became of Ras Shuqair?

Fouad explained that he has submitted a formal inquiry to uncover the details surrounding the allocation of the 112 million square meters of land in the Red Sea region.

He is also seeking clarification on the status of the previously allocated land at Ras Shuqair, the nature of the arrangements made for it, the plans for its utilization, and what has actually been achieved since its initial allocation.

Fouad further demanded an accounting of the funds generated and the sources intended for settling existing obligations.

He emphasized that the House of Representatives has the authority to hold the government—and the relevant minister—accountable regarding how these lands are being managed, plans for their development, and the expected economic returns.

Funds for Repaying Sukuk

Fouad raised questions regarding the mechanism for paying returns on sovereign “Sukuk” (Islamic bonds) once they are issued.

He inquired about the source of the profits and financial flows that would be used to meet these obligations—particularly in scenarios where the land in question has not yet reached the operational stage and is not yet generating revenue.

He further questioned whether such repayments would rely on returns from investment activities linked to the land, or on the state’s general public resources.

He called for clarification on the financial engineering of the process, the entity receiving the funding, the returns generated, and how financial flows are distributed among the various parties involved.

Fouad emphasized that his objection does not concern the use of state assets or the nature of the financial and investment transactions themselves, but rather the necessity of understanding the economic returns generated thereafter—pointing specifically to the Ras el-Hekma and Alam al-Roum deals, as well as other arrangements along the Red Sea coast.

The MP underscored the importance of shifting away from financing deals aimed solely at debt repayment.

Instead he advocated for the operationalization of assets and the establishment of projects that generate sustainable revenue, thereby helping to alleviate the state’s financial burdens in the long term.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: SCZONE Chief meets high-level Indian business delegation
World.content:
Head of the Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZONE) Mostafa Sheikhoon met with a high-level Indian business delegation comprising representatives of major Indian companies, coordinated by the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), at the authority’s headquarters in Ain Sokhna.

The meeting took place on the sidelines of the Indian Minister of Commerce and Industry’s visit to Egypt, as part of SCZONE’s efforts to strengthen international economic cooperation and attract global investment.

In a statement issued on Saturday, November 14, 2026, Sheikhoon said the fruitful cooperation and strong strategic relations between Egypt and India were increasingly translating into successful and promising investment partnerships for numerous Indian companies operating within SCZONE’s industrial and logistics zones.

He noted that these companies invest in a variety of sectors, foremost among them metal industries, chemicals and petrochemicals.

“The authority offers a comprehensive and competitive package of customs and tax incentives, supported by international free trade agreements (FTAs) that facilitate access to major global markets,” he added.

Sheikhoon also highlighted the authority’s focus on specialized technical workforce training centers as a targeted sector under its strategy, given their role in meeting investors’ demand for qualified personnel trained according to the latest scientific methods and in strengthening the integrated business environment.

The delegation attended a comprehensive presentation on SCZONE, its capabilities, key investment incentives and digital services. It also watched a documentary highlighting the authority’s network of ports and integrated industrial zones, major infrastructure and utilities projects, and other competitive advantages.

For his part, the CEO of industrial developer Orascom Industrial Parks highlighted the authority’s strong network of world-class industrial developers as a key pillar of SCZONE’s success, helping turn its vision into tangible achievements.

He underscored the industrial developer’s vital role in creating an integrated business environment and providing investors with extensive facilities under SCZONE’s umbrella. He also stressed the complementary roles of the authority and the developer under their longstanding strategic partnership, aimed at attracting new high-value investments and localizing a range of targeted industrial sectors.

The meeting also featured success stories of several Indian companies operating within SCZONE under Orascom Industrial Parks, highlighting the institutional support and distinctive competitive advantages they enjoy, including reliable energy supplies, world-class infrastructure and effective integration between ports and industrial zones.

This integration provides a wide range of export options to regional and international markets, the statement noted.

At the conclusion of the visit, the Indian delegation conducted an extensive tour of the Sokhna Integrated Industrial Zone to learn firsthand about its capabilities, infrastructure readiness, industrial developers and successful Indian companies operating in the manufacturing and heavy industries sectors and assess its potential to attract further investment.

World.title: Liberia: LACC Launches Digital Dashboard to Boost Transparency, Public Accountability
World.content:
Monrovia—The Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission (LACC) has launched the Liberia Anti-Corruption Dashboard System (LADS), a digital platform designed to strengthen institutional accountability, promote transparency, and enhance public oversight of the country’s anti-corruption efforts.

By Yawah Y. Jaivey

The Dashboard was developed under the Governance Reform and Accountability Transformation (GREAT) Project, with funding from the World Bank.



The platform will initially cover four key accountability institutions, including the LACC, Public Procurement and Concessions Commission (PPCC), General Auditing Commission (GAC), and the Public Accounts Committee (PAC).

It is expected to expand to other government institutions over the five-year project period.

Speaking at the launch, LACC Executive Chairperson Cllr. Alexandra K. Zoe said the Dashboard would support institutional performance monitoring, identify gaps, and promote evidence-based decision-making.

She noted that the platform provides an opportunity to strengthen accountability by making relevant information accessible to the public while improving the monitoring of institutional performance.

“The Dashboard provides citizens with access to information on corruption investigations and prosecutions, audit findings, procurement compliance, and other accountability actions, allowing the public to monitor institutional commitments, progress, and performance,” Cllr. Zoe stated.

She added that through the initiative, the LACC and its partner institutions seek to strengthen coordination, expand public oversight, and build citizens’ confidence in Liberia’s fight against corruption.

For her part, World Bank Country Manager Georgia Wallen commended the LACC and the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning (MFDP) for their roles in making the initiative a reality.

She explained that the platform brings together information from the LACC and other key integrity institutions, including the GAC, PAC, and PPCC, to make anti-corruption and accountability information more accessible and useful to government, citizens, civil society organizations, and development partners.

“The Anti-Corruption Dashboard started as an idea. Today, the idea has become a reality. I’d like to highlight three key aspects that determine the difference the Dashboard can make for Liberia—information access, quality, and use,” Wallen said.

The World Bank Country Manager emphasized that effective anti-corruption systems depend not only on strong laws and institutions but also on credible information about the performance of key accountability institutions.

According to her, the Dashboard makes an important contribution by consolidating information that was traditionally scattered across various institutions and systems into a more accessible and structured platform.

However, she cautioned that the credibility of the Dashboard would depend largely on the quality and reliability of the information it provides.

“The Dashboard is only as credible as the information behind it. As the system moves into public use, continued attention will be needed on (i) the quality, completeness and timeliness of the data; (ii) validation of information before publication; and (iii) clear institutional responsibility for keeping the Dashboard current. These will ultimately determine public confidence in the platform,” she stated.

Wallen further noted that while transparency is essential for accountability, it represents only part of the equation.

She stressed that the true value of the Dashboard would not be determined by the number of indicators it displays or website visitors it attracts, but by how the information is utilized to improve institutional performance and strengthen public accountability.

She explained that the platform could make a meaningful difference when institutions use its information to improve their performance, policymakers rely on it to identify and address governance challenges, and citizens and civil society organizations use it to engage government constructively.

Continuing, Wallen stated, “We hope this Dashboard will become a tool to strengthen opportunities for two-way engagement, allowing citizens—including civil society organizations, journalists, researchers, businesses and young people—to provide feedback and institutions to demonstrate how that feedback has been considered.”

She also described the launch as another important step toward strengthening Liberia’s integrity architecture in line with the country’s Vision 2030 and the ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development (AAID).

She noted that the agenda is central to the World Bank Group’s partnership with Liberia, which focuses on building the foundations for more and better-paid jobs.

Through the GREAT Project, she explained, the World Bank is supporting the LACC not only in developing the Dashboard but also in digitizing asset declaration and verification processes alongside other measures intended to strengthen corruption prevention, detection and institutional capacity.

She reaffirmed the World Bank’s commitment to supporting Liberia’s efforts to translate improved access to information into stronger institutions, greater accountability, and meaningful development outcomes.

The one-day launch ceremony brought together several local and international dignitaries, including Irish Ambassador to Liberia Gerard Considine, German Ambassador Carsten Hölscher, Integrity Watch Liberia Executive Director Harold Marvin Aidoo, PPCC Executive Director, Bodger Scott Johnson and GAC Deputy Auditor General for Administration, Foday G. Kiazolu.

In separate remarks, the dignitaries applauded the LACC for the initiative and recognized the Commission’s ongoing efforts to strengthen accountability and combat corruption in Liberia.

World.title: Liberia: Gov’t Officially Launches Seed Development and Certification Agency
World.content:
SDCA Director General , Mr. Jobson A. Momo

GANTA, Nimba County — The Government of Liberia has officially launched the Seed Development and Certification Agency (SDCA), describing the new institution as a major step toward building a reliable, transparent and sustainable national seed system.

By Franklin Doloquee

The launch ceremony was held in Ganta City, Nimba County on Saturday, November 14, bringing together government officials, development partners, agricultural institutions, private-sector actors, seed producers, agro-dealers, farmers’ organizations and members of the media.



The event marked what officials described as a significant milestone in Liberia’s effort to improve agricultural productivity, strengthen food and nutrition security and grow the rural economy.

The SDCA is Liberia’s principal authority for seed regulation, certification and sector development. It was established under the Liberia Seed Development and Certification Agency Act of 2019 and operates under the Ministry of Agriculture, with oversight from the National Seed Board.

The Act empowers the agency to coordinate, regulate and administer seed certification and control, while also leading seed-development activities for the benefit of Liberia’s seed industry.

Its creation comes after years of concerns over limited farmer access to quality planting materials, weak enforcement of seed standards, inadequate production and processing infrastructure and insufficient private-sector participation.

Earlier assessments had noted that the full implementation of the Seed Act was hindered by resource constraints and the absence of a fully functional seed-testing system.

Farmers urged to demand certified seed

Speaking at the ceremony, SDCA Director General, Jobson A. Momo, an Agronomist and Seed Specialist, urged Liberian farmers to insist on quality-assured and certified seeds rather than relying on uncertified or informal planting materials.

“Quality seed is a critical investment in improved productivity and better livelihoods,” Momo said. “To our farmers, we encourage you to demand quality-assured and certified seeds.”

He said certified seed gives farmers greater confidence that what they plant has met national quality standards and is suited to Liberia’s farming conditions.

According to the SDCA, improved certified seeds can help raise yields, reduce crop failure, increase household incomes and support national food security.

Momo described the launch as “more than the inauguration of a government institution,” calling it the beginning of a stronger national seed industry.

He said a functional seed system is essential if Liberia is to achieve food security, improve agricultural competitiveness and transform its farming sector. “Today, we are not simply launching an Agency; we are laying the foundation for a stronger national seed industry, a more productive agricultural sector and a more food-secure Liberia,” he said.

SDCA’s mandate

The Agency’s mandate covers the entire seed value chain, from research and variety release to production, inspection, testing, certification, marketing and trade.

Under the 2019 Act, the SDCA is responsible for seed quality control at all stages of production, certification, enforcement of seed regulations and the development of policies and programs for the seed industry.

Its responsibilities include regulating seed imports and exports to protect local agriculture and ensure imported seeds meet national and phytosanitary standards.

Registering and releasing crop varieties suitable for Liberia’s agroecological conditions. Conducting field inspections, seed sampling, laboratory testing and quality assurance.

Certifying seed producers, processors, importers, sellers and seed companies.

Monitoring seed markets and taking administrative or legal action against violations of seed laws.

Supporting community seed banks, local seed enterprises and farmer-based seed production, especially in rural communities and among women and young people.

Promoting research, innovation, private-sector investment and public-private partnerships in the seed industry.

Working with regional and international partners, including ECOWAS, FAO, USAID, Africa Rice, IITA and the Central Agricultural Research Institute (CARI), to harmonize standards and improve seed trade.

The law also requires that seed marketed in Liberia be listed in the national seed catalogue or the West African Catalogue of Plant Species and Varieties, while commercial producers, processors and seed companies must be registered with the SDCA.

Momo said the Agency will also work to ensure that farmers have access to improved, climate-resilient planting materials.

He said the SDCA will serve as a bridge between scientific research and farming communities, helping ensure that improved varieties developed by research institutions reach farmers in usable and affordable form.

Building a national seed industry

The Director General said Liberia has long faced challenges in its seed sector, including limited access to quality seed, weak enforcement, inadequate production and processing infrastructure, limited technical capacity and insufficient private-sector participation.

He said the SDCA was created to address those weaknesses by establishing a coordinated national system for seed quality control, certification and development.

The Agency is expected to help reduce dependence on uncertified seed and imported planting materials while creating opportunities for Liberian seed businesses.

The SDCA has already begun building its institutional structures and training seed inspectors, technicians and seed companies.

It has also supported the certification of local seed enterprises and worked with partners to strengthen seed production, quality assurance and farmer awareness.

Recent efforts to operationalize the agency have included the appointment of key staff, activation of the National Seed Board, validation of certification tools and inspector guidelines and the designation of the CARI Seed Laboratory as Liberia’s national seed-testing unit.

In January 2026, the SDCA also certified a new group of local seed specialists following a training program intended to strengthen the capacity of Liberia’s emerging seed companies.

Call for partnership

Momo said the SDCA cannot succeed alone and called on government institutions, research bodies, development partners, seed companies, farmers’ organizations, universities and financial institutions to treat the Agency as a shared national platform.

He urged research institutions, particularly CARI, AfricaRice and IITA, to deepen collaboration on early-generation seed, variety evaluation, research and technology transfer.

He also encouraged seed companies and private investors to see Liberia’s seed industry as a viable business opportunity.

The SDCA Director General pledged that the Agency would operate with professionalism, transparency, accountability and institutional integrity.

He acknowledged that building a strong seed sector would require sustained investment, technical expertise and cooperation among all stakeholders.

He thanked the Ministry of Agriculture, the Government of Liberia, development partners, research institutions and other stakeholders for their support in establishing and operationalizing the Agency.

A step toward food security

The launch comes as Liberia continues efforts to strengthen its agricultural value chains and reduce vulnerability in food production. Seed quality is widely regarded as one of the most important starting points for improved productivity because poor-quality seed can limit yields even when farmers use good land, fertilizer and sound management practices.

With the SDCA now formally launched, the government says it hopes farmers across Liberia will increasingly recognize certified seed as an investment in higher production, better incomes and improved livelihoods.

Our Nimba County correspondent at the event reported that farmers and agricultural produce sellers were in a happy mood as they marched through the principal street of Ganta to express their thanks and appreciation to the Director General of the Seed Development and Certification Agency, Mr. Jobson A. Momo.

The farmers also urged the Government of President Joseph Boakai and Vice President Jeremiah Koung, as well as the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, to help increase the budgetary allocation for the agency.

According to the farmers, the establishment of the SDCA will help them access quality seeds and other improved agricultural inputs for their farming activities.

They made the remarks during the launch of the agency over the weekend in Ganta, Nimba County.

They said reliable access to certified rice, vegetables, cassava and other crop seeds could reduce repeated planting losses, improve harvests and strengthen household food security across Nimba and other farming communities.

The farmers further called on the SDCA to expand farmer education, strengthen market monitoring and ensure that certified seeds remain affordable and available in rural areas before the start of each planting season.

World.title: Understanding COP31: Why Liberia’s Voice Matters
World.content:
Climate change threatens everyday life. Rising seas, extreme heat and changing rainfall put homes, farms, water and jobs at risk. Burning coal, oil and gas, and cutting down forests, release gases or pollution that trap heat around the Earth like a blanket of heat.

By Dr. Emmanuel K. Urey Yarkpawolo

Pollution crosses borders. Countries such as Liberia have contributed little to global warming but face serious harm with limited resources to respond. Countries must work together to reduce these gases and help those most affected. This is why the United Nations climate conference, known as COP, matters.



As COP31 continues in Antalya, Türkiye, what does it mean for ordinary Liberians?

What is COP?

COP means “Conference of the Parties.” The “Parties” are countries that joined the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, an agreement adopted in 1992.

The first COP took place in Berlin, Germany, in 1995. Countries meet to review progress and agree on action. Major achievements include the Kyoto Protocol in 1997 and the Paris Agreement in 2015. Under the Paris Agreement, countries agreed to limit global warming and prepare for its effects. COP31 is the thirty-first conference, running from November 9–20, 2026.

Why Liberia must participate

Imagine communities sharing a river. Pollution upstream can harm people downstream. Protecting the river requires everyone’s cooperation. Climate change works similarly: no country can solve it alone.

For Liberia, the sea is washing away coastal land, floods damage homes and roads, and changing rainfall affects farming. Attending COP allows Liberia to explain these problems, influence decisions and seek funding and practical help. This year’s discussions include more climate funding, stronger protection for communities and cleaner energy.

The Blue Zone and Green Zone at the COP

The Blue Zone is managed by the United Nations. Government representatives hold official negotiations here. Entry requires an approved conference pass. Journalists and other approved participants attend permitted activities. The area also hosts exhibitions, national pavilions and side events.

The Green Zone is managed by the host country and welcomes public engagement under its access rules. Businesses, community groups, young people and others share ideas, show practical solutions and learn about climate action.

Side events and personal contacts

Side events are discussions held alongside the formal talks. They allow people to share problems, experiences and possible solutions. A national pavilion is a country’s meeting and exhibition space. Liberia’s pavilion helps us explain our needs and meet potential partners.

Personal conversations also matter. A meeting with a funding organization can help us understand how to apply for support. Another country may share useful lessons on farming or coastal protection. Young people and researchers can make contacts that lead to training and joint work. These conversations need follow-up to produce results.

Liberia’s delegation

I am heading Liberia’s delegation, which brings together government officials, technical experts, civil society, students, young people, journalists, superintendents, traditional leaders and religious leaders.

This broad participation matters because climate change affects everyone. Experts follow negotiations, while other delegates share community concerns, report developments and build partnerships.

Progress Liberia is making

Liberia has hosted discussions on farming, youth opportunities, preparing for climate threats and fair management of natural resources. We have also discussed protecting people forced to leave their homes by climate impacts, including through a proposed West African Climate Mobility and Resilience Program.

I was one of four leaders from the Least Developed Countries group chosen to meet UN Secretary-General António Guterres, alongside the group’s chair.

Least Developed Countries, or LDCs, are countries the UN recognizes as having low incomes, major development challenges and high exposure to economic and environmental or climate shocks. They need international support.

During the meeting, Liberia argued that protecting our rich forests and biodiversity which include the variety of plants, animals and other living things; must bring benefits to our country and communities. Our forests help the world by absorbing carbon dioxide, a gas that warms the planet. People protecting these forests deserve support and opportunities to earn a living.

What Liberia hopes to achieve

Liberia seeks funding that is easier to access, useful technology and partnerships to protect coastlines, support farmers, expand clean energy and safeguard forests. We also seek help for communities suffering climate-related losses.

These efforts should support the Government’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development and NDC 3.0. NDC means “Nationally Determined Contribution”, a country’s climate action plan. Liberia’s third plan links climate action with national development, helping us improve lives while protecting nature.

Meetings are only the beginning. Success must be measured by projects delivered, communities protected, livelihoods improved and money used openly and responsibly. Liberia’s participation gives our people a voice and a chance to turn international cooperation into benefits at home.

World.title: Samura Retains Liberia Marathon Title as Liberians Make History in Half-Marathon
World.content:
Samura’s victory further cemented his dominance in the annual competition after returning to Monrovia to retain the crown he won last year.

MONROVIA — Sierra Leonean long-distance runner Amadu Sajor Samura successfully defended his Liberia Marathon full-marathon title for the second consecutive year on Sunday, November 15, while Liberian athletes Lee Dennis and Williams Saaweyea made history with a first- and second-place finish in the half-marathon.

By Christopher C. Walker, [email protected]

Samura’s victory further cemented his dominance in the annual competition after returning to Monrovia to retain the crown he won last year.



The 42.2-kilometer race began at the Samuel Kanyon Doe (SKD) Sports Complex in Paynesville, taking runners through major corridors across Montserrado County, including 72nd Boulevard, Japan Freeway, and Mamba Point. The route continued along UN Drive before looping back through Sinkor to the SKD Sports Complex, where Samura crossed the finish line as the overall winner.

Liberians Make History in Half-Marathon

Meanwhile, Liberia’s athletics sector recorded a major milestone in the 21.1-kilometer half-marathon, with homegrown runners Lee Dennis and Williams Saaweyea finishing first and second, respectively.

Dennis emerged as the overall half-marathon champion, becoming the first Liberian to win the category since the event’s inception. Saaweyea followed in second place, securing a historic one-two finish for the host nation.

The dual podium finish demonstrates the growing competitiveness of local distance runners against regional and international contenders and is expected to inspire a new generation of Liberian track and field athletes.

A Milestone for Liberian Athletics

The contrasting outcomes in the two headline categories underscored the regional appeal of the Liberia Marathon, with Samura preserving Sierra Leone’s hold on the full marathon while Liberians claimed the top spots in the shorter distance.

While the performance of Dennis and Saaweyea has sparked renewed optimism around Liberia’s long-distance running potential, sports observers note that the achievement also highlights the need for sustained investment in athlete development, modern training facilities, and institutional support to help local runners compete on bigger international stages.

As the 2026 edition concludes, Samura departs Monrovia with back-to-back full-marathon titles, while Dennis and Saaweyea have written a landmark chapter in Liberian athletics.

World.title: LFA Suspends Bea Mountain FC-II Coach, Player for Six Months Over Referee Assault
World.content:
MONROVIA — The Liberia Football Association has suspended Bea Mountain FC-II head coach Stephen G. Tarr and player Oscar Fahnbulleh from all football activities for six months following an assault on a match official during a 2026/2027 LFA Second Division match against Professional Sports Academy (PSA).

By Christopher C. Walker, [email protected]

The sanctions, which took effect on November 12, follow the abandonment of the Wednesday, November 11 fixture at the C.H. Dewey Field in Tubmanburg, Bomi County.



According to the LFA, the incident erupted in the 89th minute after the referee awarded a penalty against Bea Mountain FC-II, prompting members of the visiting side to invade the pitch and halt play. The match officials’ report stated that Tarr and Fahnbulleh physically assaulted the referee, forcing state security personnel and spectators to intervene and escort the official to safety. The match was subsequently abandoned with PSA leading 2-1.

Following a review of the report, the LFA ruled that both men violated its 2026/2027 Rules and Regulations—specifically Chapter 4, Article 1.0, Sections 1(a) and (b), and Chapter 3, Article 12, Section 1, Counts (c) and (d).

Under the ruling, Tarr and Fahnbulleh are barred from all football activities under the jurisdiction of the LFA, the Confederation of African Football (CAF), and FIFA for six months. Both have also been referred to the LFA Disciplinary Committee for further investigation, which could result in stiffer penalties.

Additionally, Bea Mountain FC-II has forfeited the match to PSA and been fined L$100,000 for the disruption.

Bea Mountain Condemns Incident

In a statement issued after the ruling, Bea Mountain FC strongly condemned the attack, acknowledging that its Second Team coach physically assaulted the referee over a penalty decision the club deemed unfair.

“While refereeing decisions can be questioned, criticized, and challenged through the appropriate official channels, no decision on the football pitch can ever justify violence or physical aggression towards match officials,” the club stated.

Bea Mountain announced it has launched an internal investigation to determine further club-level disciplinary action.Reaffirming its commitment to discipline, integrity, and fair play, the management stressed that the incident did not reflect its institutional values and pledged its full support to the LFA’s efforts to enforce professionalism across Liberian football.

LIFOCA Suspends Coach Tarr

Meanwhile, the Liberia Football Coaches Association (LIFOCA) has handed Tarr an indefinite suspension from all association activities, effective immediately.

In a strongly worded statement, LIFOCA denounced Tarr’s actions as unprofessional and reiterated its zero-tolerance policy toward violence against match officials, noting that further sanctions could follow pending additional inquiries.

Coach Issues Public Apology

Amid the fallout, Tarr issued a public apology taking full responsibility for his behavior during the November 11 match. He admitted that he allowed his emotions to get the better of him after the late penalty call, leading him to storm the pitch.

“I fully acknowledge that my behavior was unacceptable and did not reflect the discipline, respect, and sportsmanship expected of someone involved in football,” Tarr said.

He extended apologies to the match officials, Bea Mountain FC management, technical staff, players, supporters, and the general public, pledging to demonstrate greater restraint and professionalism in the future.

The incident has reignited concerns over the safety of match officials in domestic competitions. In response, the LFA urged clubs, players, and fans to respect referees and utilize established protest and appeals mechanisms rather than resorting to violence as the 2026/2027 season progresses.

World.title: Liberia: PLP Criticizes Boakai’s Spending Plan for 2027, Says Budget Ignores World Bank’s Warnings
World.content:
Monrovia — The People’s Liberation Party has criticized the Boakai administration’s proposed 2027 national budget, arguing that its spending priorities fail to address growing poverty concerns highlighted in the World Bank’s 2026 Economic Update on Liberia.

Tonzeah N. Zarwolo, the party’s Acting National Secretary General and National Vice Chairman for Political Affairs, said the government was not paying sufficient attention to the World Bank’s warning that economic growth was not translating into better living conditions for many Liberians.

According to the World Bank, although Liberia’s economy is growing, more people are falling into poverty because much of that growth is concentrated in sectors that employ relatively few Liberians.

Zarwolo said the Bank’s findings should guide national policy decisions rather than be dismissed as a tool for political attacks.



He argued that the proposed budget does not give agriculture the priority needed to address poverty, while a significant share of government spending remains committed to recurrent expenditure, including the cost of running government institutions.

He also raised concerns about increased allocations for the Executive Mansion and national security, warning that the spending priorities could leave more Liberians struggling financially if the government fails to invest in sectors that directly support livelihoods.

However, Zarwolo acknowledged the increased allocation to education, commending the Boakai administration for directing more resources to the sector.

He called on the Legislature to go further by increasing funding for rural schools, investing in technical and vocational education institutions, and recruiting more teachers to address the shortage of qualified personnel in public schools.

Zarwolo, an education policy expert, said the teacher-to-student ratio remains a major challenge that is undermining the quality of public education.

Finance Ministry Defends Government’s Economic Record

But the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning has pushed back against the World Bank’s poverty assessment and defended the administration’s economic policies.

Deputy Finance Minister for Administration Benedict Harleyson questioned the reliability of the Bank’s poverty estimates, arguing that they are too uncertain to be presented as confirmed findings.

Harleyson said the World Bank’s assessment relies on a model built using data from the 2016 Household Income and Expenditure Survey rather than a more recent household survey.

He also questioned changes in the Bank’s poverty estimates across its publications. According to him, the Bank described poverty as declining in October 2025 before reporting an estimated poverty rate of 35.8 percent in April 2026 and 36.1 percent in October 2026, without the release of a new household survey.

Harleyson further argued that the assessment does not adequately account for public investments made under the Boakai administration, including expanded electricity connections, road construction and increased budget allocations for health and education.

PLP Calls for More Investment in Agriculture

Despite the government’s defense, Zarwolo maintained that the proposed budget should reflect the World Bank’s concerns about poverty and the need to make economic growth more beneficial to ordinary Liberians.

He called for a review of the Ministry of Agriculture’s programs and better-designed interventions to improve farmers’ productivity and increase agricultural output.

While acknowledging the government’s efforts to construct more farm-to-market roads, he criticized what he described as a lack of direct government support for smallholder farmers in rural communities.

Zarwolo urged the Boakai administration not to dismiss the World Bank’s warnings, drawing a comparison with earlier concerns about congestion at the Freeport of Monrovia.

He argued that the failure to adequately respond to those warnings contributed to the current port challenges and cautioned against allowing similar inaction on poverty to create a bigger national problem.
