World.title: Liberia: Grassroots Petition Urges Morlu’s Return To CDC
World.content:
Former chairman, who quit in 2024 after a long rift with Weah, is asked to help rebuild the party for 2029

MONROVIA – A group calling itself the “Concerned Partisans, Grassroots Mobilizers, and Supporters” of the Congress for Democratic Change (CDC) on Saturday sent a formal petition to former National Chairman Mulbah K. Morlu, Jr. It asks him to “reconsider your departure” and come back to the party he left more than two years ago.

By Rodney D. Sieh



The petition is dated November 14, 2026 and carries the theme “Experienced, Trusted, Vibrant, Capable, and No-Nonsense Leadership Ahead of the 2029 Elections.” It says its backers come from all 15 counties. No individual signs it.

“We want you back! Not tomorrow. Not someday. Now! Today!” the document says. It ends with the chant “Morlu Must Return!”

What the petitioners want

The petition makes five requests. Morlu should return to the CDC, reconnect with ordinary partisans, lead reconciliation between rival factions, help rebuild the party and work with others to restore its “electoral competitiveness.”

It does not say outright that he should get his old job back. But FrontPageAfrica reported last week that his supporters, organized across Bong, Margibi, Grand Bassa and Montserrado counties, want him back in the party’s top post. As that report noted, a supporters’ petition cannot hand anyone the chairmanship; any change has to go through the CDC’s constitutional and electoral procedures.

The petitioners point to the 2023 result to argue that the party can still win. In the presidential runoff, Joseph Nyuma Boakai of the Unity Party received 814,481 votes and George Manneh Weah received 793,914, a margin of 20,567. The CDC also won 25 of the 73 House seats, the largest bloc held by any single party.

The document lists Morlu’s posts since 2005. They include chairman of the CDC-aligned Progressive Action for Change, vice chairman for operations from 2012 to 2018, deputy campaign manager in 2017 and national chairman from 2018 to 2024. It credits him with leading the 2012 internal campaign that removed then-Standard Bearer Cllr. Winston Tubman and restored Weah as standard bearer. It also says that in 2013 he led 11 members of the Executive Committee in defending Weah’s Senate candidacy, at a time when Robert Sirleaf, son of then-President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, was being promoted as an alternative.

Without naming anyone, the petition says it is not trying to “reopen old wounds, assign blame, or revisit past disagreements.”

Those old wounds

Those disagreements were mostly with Weah himself.

Morlu took over the party when Weah became president in 2018, and even that was disputed. Then-chairman Nathaniel McGill said that after consulting party leaders he would step aside and let Morlu, the vice chair for operations, act as chair until the convention. But a statement signed by then-Secretary General Janga A. Kowo denied that the national chairman had been replaced. Kowo now leads the party.

Morlu went on to win the chairmanship on a white ballot at the CDC’s 7th national convention, and he also chaired the wider Coalition for Democratic Change until he resigned.

The relationship with Weah broke down in December 2019, when an audio recording leaked in which Morlu made disparaging remarks about the president’s personal life. Morlu told this newspaper the remarks were “mere liquor talk,” said out of frustration and anger during the party’s internal crisis. Weah played it down in public: “everyone can get angry and talk,” he said. He saved his anger for whoever made the recording. By then Morlu had been publicly pressing the government to reshuffle the cabinet and dismiss officials who were not performing.

The two sides announced a reconciliation, but it did not last. As the 2023 elections approached, Morlu spoke less and less, mostly through written statements, and he was barely seen or heard during the campaign.

After the defeat, Morlu tried to take charge of the rebuilding. He announced a “CDC Comeback Retreat” to plan the road to 2029. Weah stopped it. He suspended all of Morlu’s plans for a retreat in Grand Bassa County, saying he had not been informed.

Morlu resigned as chairman on February 27, 2024. He blamed the shrinking room for him to do the job effectively and wrote: “I hold no resentment towards anyone for these difficulties, and I do not desire conflict.” FrontPageAfrica learned at the time that Weah had been marginalizing him since the leaked audio. In the letter, Morlu said his disagreements with Weah were “driven solely by my principles and love for the party.”

He promised to remain a lifelong member, but within months he had gone. He left the party and gave up his membership, saying he had been chosen as chairman and lead advocate of Solidarity and Trust for a New Day (STAND).

After that, he attacked Weah openly. In mid-2024 he accused the former president of failing to prosecute Sirleaf-era officials over alleged looting, which he called a criminal conspiracy, and he described it as the “biggest economic crime conspiracy against Liberia”. In August 2025, when Senator Saah Joseph quit the CDC, he claimed party insiders had targeted Morlu and that Morlu had been drugged and beaten. Morlu flatly denied it.

From party boss to street leader

As head of STAND, Morlu has become one of the loudest critics of the Boakai government. He has accused it of police brutality, presiding over a worsening economy, widespread corruption and “political witch hunts” against opposition figures. After the December 17, 2025 “Lead or Leave” protest, police charged Morlu and his deputy, Rev. Festus R. B. Logan, and sent the case to court. The Independent National Commission on Human Rights said a follow-up demonstration on July 17, 2026 drew more than 1,500 people and was largely peaceful.

The movement has also caused friction in the opposition. The Liberian People’s Party distanced itself, accusing STAND of political opportunism and of links to the CDC.

Where the CDC stands now

Kowo has led the party since Morlu left, first as acting chairman. In May, the party said it would begin preparing for an extraordinary national convention to reposition itself. Meanwhile, allies have already started mobilizing for a Weah comeback in 2029.

As of November 8, Morlu had not confirmed any response to the campaign. The CDC leadership has not said in public whether it would welcome him back.

The petitioners say they are ready. “Come back and help rebuild the house you helped construct,” the petition says.

World.title: Liberia: Mulbah Morlu Announces Return to CDC, Says He Is Not Seeking Party Leadership
World.content:
CONGO TOWN– Congress for Democratic Change (CDC) Former National Chairman Mulbah K. Morlu Jr. has announced his return to the opposition party, accepting a petition from grassroots supporters calling for the restoration of his membership.

By Jaheim T. Tumu- [email protected]

Morlu made the announcement on Saturday while responding to a group of CDC supporters who presented a petition urging him to rejoin the party, following his resignation as national chairman in June 2024.



In his response, Morlu made it clear that his return would be as an ordinary member and should not be interpreted as an attempt to reclaim the party’s chairmanship or compete for another leadership position.

Said Morlu, “In response to your petition, my statement makes today represent those who have felt lukewarm about the party and will return. “I hereby restore my membership in the CDC.”

“I am not coming because I desire office,” Morlu said, recalling that he resigned from the chairmanship with six years remaining in his tenure.

He explained that his resignation was motivated by his desire to prevent internal divisions from plunging the CDC into a prolonged political crisis following its defeat in the 2023 presidential election.

According to Morlu, he stepped aside because he believed the party’s survival was more important than holding on to leadership.

He said he was proud that his resignation helped create a period of peace and stability within the CDC.

Morlu also warned that the party must overcome internal disagreements and unite ahead of the 2029 general and presidential elections.

“If I should come back, I can be very relevant even as a full member of the party. I don’t need a title to be effective. I don’t need a title to serve,” he declared.

He further challenged the party’s future leadership to embrace inclusiveness, arguing that a chairman must be capable of bringing together supporters of different factions, including those who may disagree with his leadership.

A successful leader is one that brings people together to form a team, even those that don’t support his leadership,” Morlu said.

Beyond his return to the CDC, Morlu used the occasion to launch a strong criticism of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s administration, accusing it of targeting opposition figures through what he described as politically motivated prosecutions and selective justice.

He also called on the CDC to abandon what he termed its policy of constructive engagement with the government and adopt a more confrontational political approach.

Morlu while in the civil society community did not abandon his principles or political independence, maintained that his return would not mean exempt him from being Chairman of the Solidarity Trust for a New Day (STAND)

“I am an accomplished revolutionary. I cannot be bought. I cannot be compromised,” he declared.

He also acknowledged that his decision to return could affect some personal relationships, particularly with individuals who may disagree with his political position.

Despite those concerns, Morlu insisted that political differences should not destroy personal friendships, throwing jabs and alleging that House of Representatives Deputy Speaker, Thomas Fallah refused to allow him entrance to his house after news that he was returning to the CDC as chairman.

He described the CDC as one of Liberia’s most significant political institutions and said its survival must go beyond the ambitions and interests of individual leaders.

“CDC, whether I accept your petition or not, is the future, and CDC must survive or outlive all of us,” he said.

His return comes at a critical moment for the opposition party as it seeks to rebuild its political strength and position itself for the 2029 elections.

World.title: Imboela Says Grow Zambia Agenda Good On Paper But Failing In Practice
World.content:
NDC Says Grow Zambia Is Not Delivering As Government Tells Opposition To Write In For Talks With Hichilema

National Democratic Congress (NDC) president Ms Saboi Imboela has accused the United Party for National Development (UPND) administration of failing to turn the Grow Zambia Agenda into tangible results. She said the 2027 national budget does not reflect the promises made to Zambians.

The challenge comes as Government sets out how the opposition can take such concerns to the top. Chief Government Spokesperson Elvis Nkandu said President Hakainde Hichilema is open to meeting opposition parties, provided they formally state their intention to discuss matters of national interest.

Ms Imboela did not dismiss the agenda itself. She described the ruling party’s development plan as good on paper, but said Government had failed to match its promises with action.

She pointed to two budget measures she said were hurting citizens: the removal of maize export restrictions and higher mobile money transaction fees. Ms Imboela said ordinary Zambians were bearing the burden of some of the measures in the budget.

Her sharpest question was about maize. Ms Imboela asked how Government intends to reach its target of 10 million metric tonnes of maize a year, when the small-scale farmers who produce much of the country’s crop continue to face a range of challenges.

She urged Government to put citizens’ interests first in agriculture and in the management of mineral resources.

Mr Nkandu, who is also Minister of Information and Media, set out the route for opposition leaders who want a hearing. He said parties wishing to meet the President should formally express their intention, and state that they want to discuss national issues and ways of promoting economic development.

He said President Hichilema is open to engaging all citizens, including opposition political parties, on matters that advance economic growth and national development.

Mr Nkandu said the Head of State remains focused on the development agenda and the targets set out under the Grow Zambia Agenda. He said the President has continued to engage citizens across society, including students, marketeers, footballers and members of the media.

The maize target Ms Imboela questioned received a confident assessment elsewhere. Corteva Agriscience managing director Mr Samson Nyendwa, whose company is behind the Pannar and Pioneer seed brands, said the 10 million tonne goal was not an ambitious target.

“That is not an ambitious target because we can always achieve that even with the current area planted,” Mr Nyendwa said during a courtesy call on Minister of Agriculture Moses Moyo.

Small-scale farmers’ costs, which Ms Imboela raised, have also reached the Minister. Mr Moyo urged seed companies to make improved seed varieties more affordable, warning that high prices could force smallholder farmers to recycle traditional seed and hurt their yields.

“Let’s ensure that the price should be affordable to our farmers to avoid them using traditional means,” Mr Moyo said.

He also asked seed producers to offer smaller, cheaper packs for smallholder farmers who cannot afford larger quantities.

On maize exports, the Ministry of Agriculture said Zambia is set to export 200,000 metric tonnes of maize to Malawi and 540 metric tonnes to Kenya. It said the exports show growing demand for Zambian produce in other countries.

The 2027 budget, totalling K284.8 billion, is now before Parliament. Ms Imboela’s complaints about maize and mobile money remain on record, and Government says the door to State House is open to any opposition party that puts its request in writing.

World.title: State House Says Gagging Term Limit Calls Would Be Dictatorial, Refuses To Drag Hichilema In
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema will not answer calls to rule out a third term, State House has said. It argues that any statement from him would be turned against him, and that silencing those pushing to remove term limits would be dictatorial.

The position came a day after former Minister of Justice Mr Given Lubinda challenged the President to publicly distance himself from any attempt to extend his stay beyond the two terms the Constitution allows.

“He must unequivocally distance himself from any third-term agenda, discourage attempts to undermine the existing constitutional term limits and reassure the nation that his priority is delivering on the mandate entrusted to him,” Mr Lubinda said.

State House Chief Communications Specialist Clayson Hamasaka made clear the President will not oblige. He said Mr Hichilema would not dignify the matter with a comment, despite pressure from some quarters.

Mr Hamasaka’s reasoning rests on what he presented as a trap. He questioned what those demanding a statement expect the President to say, and warned that any comment could be twisted into accusations that he was restricting democratic freedoms.

“When he speaks, they are the same people who will stand on the mountain and claim that he does not want people to speak out on national issues,” he said.

The other option, ordering an end to the calls, would be worse, in his view. Mr Hamasaka said it would be dictatorial for the President to unilaterally curtail citizens’ constitutionally guaranteed freedom to express themselves on matters of national interest.

He described demands for Mr Hichilema to halt a discussion he neither started nor influenced as unfair and malicious.

“This has nothing to do with the head of State, so why should he be dragged into it?” Mr Hamasaka said.

His defence leaves one point unsettled: where the calls are coming from. State House says they come from citizens satisfied with how the country is being run. The loudest voices have come from inside the ruling party’s own ranks.

Some United Party for National Development (UPND) supporters, including nominated Members of Parliament who entered the House under the mixed-member proportional representation system, have urged Parliament to begin removing the presidential term limit. They cite Mr Hichilema’s performance and economic vision. The Constitution currently limits a President to two five-year terms.

Mr Hamasaka said those trying to pull the President in were politically mischievous and wanted to distract him from implementing the Grow Zambia Agenda. He did not distinguish between the UPND voices behind the push and the opposition voices demanding that it be stopped.

Government’s own lawyer has taken a similar line before. Attorney-General Mulilo Kabesha has said the country should allow open discussion on whether presidential term limits should remain, and that time will tell whether removing the limit is necessary.

What State House has offered instead of a yes or no is a commitment to the existing law. Mr Hamasaka said President Hichilema would continue to uphold the Constitution and govern in accordance with the rule of law.

He listed the matters he said deserve the President’s time: the effects of El Niño, food and energy security, and the prevention of hunger-related deaths. He said Mr Hichilema was pursuing the 10-10-5-3-3-1-1-1 targets under the Grow Zambia Agenda, including 10 million tonnes of maize and 10,000 megawatts of electricity.

Mr Lubinda had pointed to history. He said Zambia’s rejection of a third-term bid in 2001 should remind the nation that presidential power has constitutional limits.

For now, the President’s position is silence. The two-term limit remains in the Constitution, and State House says Mr Hichilema will neither join the calls to remove it nor move to stop them.

World.title: Chilufya Warns Government Not To See Doctors Through A Political Lens After National Interest Retirements
World.content:
Former Minister of Health Dr Chitalu Chilufya has urged Government to exercise prudence and caution in managing doctors and other health workers. He warned that retiring medical staff in the national interest is no answer to problems in the health sector.

Dr Chilufya, who served as Health Minister under former President Edgar Lungu, described the retirement of some doctors in the national interest as regrettable. He said Government must carefully weigh what such decisions mean for the delivery of healthcare services.

He said doctors remain critical to advancing universal health coverage and the health-for-all agenda. In his view, the people who deliver that agenda cannot be treated as expendable.

Dr Chilufya said retiring doctors in the national interest should not be viewed as the ultimate solution. Any concerns about health sector personnel, he said, should instead be tabled and discussed until lasting solutions are found.

His sharpest warning was about how Government sees its own professionals. Dr Chilufya urged the administration not to view technocrats through a political lens.

He said they are trained civil servants whose expertise was built through investment of hard-earned public resources. On that reasoning, losing them means the public loses money it has already spent.

Dr Chilufya did not name the doctors he was referring to.

His remarks follow the retirement in the national interest of Dr Paul Kasalwe Chibwe, President of the Resident Doctors Association of Zambia (RDAZ). The decision was made by the Ministry of Health under Minister Dr Roma Chilengi.

Dr Chibwe is an orthopaedic and trauma registrar. He led the association through its long dispute with the Ministry over the employment of doctors and their conditions of service.

The use of national interest retirements across the public service has already reached Parliament. Vice-President Mutale Nalumango told the House that retirement in the national interest is part of public servants’ terms of service, and cited Section 39 of the Public Service Pensions Act.

State House has also distanced the Head of State from the practice. Chief Communications Specialist Clayson Hamasaka said the President has nothing to do with the retirement of civil servants in the national interest.

Dr Chilufya’s position is that the health sector cannot afford that approach. He said the potential impact on patients must come first, ahead of any administrative convenience.

His call is for dialogue rather than dismissal: concerns about health personnel should be put on the table and discussed. He said that path protects both the workforce and the services that depend on it.

The Ministry of Health has not publicly responded to Dr Chilufya’s remarks.

World.title: Kabesha Says Hichilema Is Not Bound To Nominate All 11 MPs, Or Any At All
World.content:
Attorney-General Mulilo Kabesha says President Hakainde Hichilema has constitutional discretion to nominate fewer than the maximum 11 Members of Parliament, or none at all. His ruling answers public questions over whether the Head of State must fill every nominated seat in the National Assembly.

Mr Kabesha said Article 68(1)(c) of the Constitution allows the President to nominate up to 11 MPs. He said the provision does not compel him to appoint the full number.

The Attorney-General said the clause works as a ceiling and nothing more. Because it prescribes a maximum number of nominated MPs but no minimum, he said, the President may nominate fewer than 11, or make no nominations at all if there is no need.

He found the same freedom in the question of timing. Mr Kabesha said the Constitution is silent on when nominations should be made, which leaves the President discretion over both the number and the timing of appointments.

He also addressed how long a nominee would sit in the House. Mr Kabesha said any MP nominated under the provision serves for the remainder of Parliament’s term, as provided for under Article 81.

The Attorney-General said he issued the clarification under the mandate of the Office of the Attorney-General in Article 177 of the Constitution. It followed public questions over whether the President was required to nominate all 11 MPs.

Mr Kabesha based his reading on the doctrine of literal interpretation. He cited the Supreme Court judgment in Akashambatwa Mbikusita-Lewanika and Others v Frederick Jacob Titus Chiluba (SCZ Judgment Number 14 of 1998), which held that clear legal provisions should be understood according to their ordinary meaning.

On that test, he said, Article 68(1)(c) means what it says: up to 11, and no more than that is required.

President Hichilema has filled the nominated seats in stages since the general election. In September, he nominated five MPs, who were sworn in by Speaker of the National Assembly Nelly Mutti.

In October, he nominated former Minister of Education Douglas Syakalima and former Minister of Technology and Science Felix Mutati. Neither round took the presidential nominations to the full complement of 11.

The presidential nominations are separate from the 40 seats filled under proportional representation. The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) validated those seats in September, with women, youths and persons with disabilities making up the list.

Mr Kabesha’s opinion now places the remaining seats entirely in the President’s hands. Under his reading, Mr Hichilema may fill them, leave them vacant, or nominate at a time of his choosing, and anyone he appoints will serve until Parliament dissolves.

World.title: MINERAL EXPLORATION YIELDED ENCOURAGING RESULTS IN KASAMA
World.content:
Barrick Zambia says mineral exploration activities in Kasama District have yielded encouraging results that could support future copper discoveries.

Barrick Zambia Exploration Manager, Robert Kaemba, says the results obtained so far have raised hopes for increased mining investment and economic growth in Northern Province.

Mr Kaemba disclosed that preliminary findings show that the geology in parts of Kasama shares similarities with areas of Zambia where copper mines already exist.

He, however, explained that this does not yet confirm the presence of a copper mine, as further investigations are required before any conclusions can be made.

Mr Kaemba said this during a meeting with Northern Province Acting Permanent Secretary, Beauty Undi-Phiri at the Provincial Administration in Kasama.

“The geology gives us confidence that something may be possible, but more work is needed before we can determine whether there is a viable mineral deposit,” he said.

He added that Barrick Zambia has adopted a long-term exploration strategy in Zambia and expects exploration activities to continue for the foreseeable future.

“We are committed to exploration in Zambia for a long term, Kasama is one of the areas attracting our attention and we are working closely with Government institutions to identify opportunities where we can expand exploration activities,” he said.

He added that his company is working closely with the Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development to identify additional areas with mining potential.

Mr Kaemba said Barrick is currently conducting exploration works in three project areas in Northern Province, namely Lubeshi Central, Milunga, and Menga.

Mr Kaemba, has disclosed that the company has already carried out drilling, mapping, soil sampling and other studies aimed at understanding the area’s mineral potential.

“What we have seen so far is encouraging because it confirms that the geological environment is similar to those found in other copper-producing areas. The next stage is to gather more evidence to determine whether there are deposits of economic value,” he said.

He added that Barrick plans to continue drilling, soil sampling and other studies to determine which areas show the greatest potential for future investment.

“The company is also preparing to conduct an airborne survey across its exploration licences to improve understanding of the geology and identify areas that may require further investigation,” Mr Kaemba further disclosed.

He said Barrick has established an active field camp in the area and is employing local people for general labour while specialist personnel provide technical support to the exploration programme.

“Our approach is to work with local communities wherever we operate. We have engaged local people in our activities and will continue building relationships as the programme advances,” he said.

And Northern Province Acting Permanent Secretary Beauty Undi-Phiri said Northern Province was looking to mineral exploration and possible mining investments in order to unlock its economic potential.

Ms Undi-Phiri noted that the province’s contribution to the country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) remains low and expressed optimism that projects such as Barrick’s exploration programme if successful could help stimulate economic activity, create jobs and attract investment in the province.

“Northern Province has enormous potential. For a long time, the province has largely depended on consumption rather than production, so investments in sectors such as mining can help change that narrative,” Ms Undi-Phiri said.

She said the province has largely remained a consumption-based economy with limited manufacturing and industrial activity, making mining investment an important opportunity for economic transformation.

“Mining companies are important development partners because their investments create opportunities for local businesses, provide employment and contribute to national development,” she said.

The Acting Permanent Secretary also emphasised the importance of continued engagement between government, mining companies, and the media to ensure the public receives accurate information about exploration activities and to help manage expectations.

“It’s important that people understand exactly where the company is in its exploration journey so that expectations are based on facts rather than assumptions,” she said.

“These engagements are valuable because they allow the government to provide the public with accurate information while also giving investors an opportunity to explain their plans and progress,” Mrs Undi-Phiri added.

She further commended Barrick for building strong relations with host communities and recruiting local people where possible.

Northern Province Acting Permanent Secretary also praised the company’s early community support initiatives, including assistance towards traditional ceremonies and the purchase of a new engine for the Chambeshi River pontoon, which serves local communities.

“The fact that Barrick is already supporting communities even before establishing a mine demonstrates goodwill and a commitment to partnership. That is something we appreciate as a province,” she said.

Ms Undi-Phiri expressed optimism about the province’s future, saying continued exploration and investment could help transform Northern Province’s economic outlook.

“The future is bright for the Northern Province. We are encouraged by the level of interest being shown by investors, and we hope that these exploration efforts will eventually translate into sustainable economic benefits for our people,” she said.

Northern Province is exploring investment opportunities in different sectors in order to broaden the base for contributing to the Grow Zambia Agenda.

World.title: PRESIDENT HICHILEMA CALLS FOR SUPPORT FOR THE GROW ZAMBIA AGENDA
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has cautioned citizens against circulating misleading information on social media.

President Hichilema implored the citizenry not to allow false narratives to distract them from participating in the Grow Zambia Agenda.

He stressed that national development requires collective responsibility, calling on communities in Macha and Mapanza Chiefdoms to channel their energies towards productive activities that contribute to economic growth.

The Head of State said this when he addressed hundreds of people who gathered to see him off at St Mark’s Secondary School grounds in Mapanza, shortly after attending a church service.

President Hichilema said the government remains committed to ensuring that rural communities benefit from various developmental projects and improved service delivery.

The President cited the planned construction of a dam at the confluence of Ngonga and Munyeke streams, which he said would be completed during his second term.

He said the project would support irrigation-led agriculture and strengthen food production in the area.

“Part of the Grow Zambia Agenda is to enhance agriculture, therefore the construction of irrigation facilities on the dam will ensure the agricultural sector in this community is sustained,” He said.

The Head of State urged residents to diversify into various agricultural activities as a way of improving household incomes and contributing to national economic development.

“We therefore implore communities here to ensure they diversify into various agricultural activities,” he added.

Meanwhile, President Hichilema thanked residents for electing United Party for National Development (UPND) officials at various levels of leadership.

“Thank you for trusting us to serve you. You put UPND officials in power at local government level, mayoral and constituency levels, and ensured you contribute to retaining my seat as President,” he said.

He assured the residents that the government would reciprocate their confidence through dedicated service delivery.

“We will ensure to serve you diligently,” President Hichilema said.

The President further pledged to ensure that developmental projects are rolled out in Macha and Mapanza, reaffirming the government’s commitment to extending development to rural communities.

He called on residents to work with the government in advancing the Grow Zambia Agenda, saying community participation remains important in achieving the country’s development aspirations.

World.title: ZRA Says Fake Export Claims Are Draining The Treasury As Gold Yields Just K64 Million From One Firm
World.content:
ZRA Says Fake Export Claims Are Draining The Treasury As Gold Yields Just K64 Million From One Firm

The Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) paid more than K25 billion in Value Added Tax (VAT) refunds to businesses last year, and Commissioner General Dingani Banda said the Treasury was losing substantial revenue to fraudulent refund claims built on fictitious exports, particularly on the Copperbelt.

Mr Banda said the authority had introduced measures to strengthen the refund system and curb fraudulent claims. He said ZRA remained committed to stopping the practice. He was speaking in Kitwe at the Zambia Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ZACCI) 2027 National Budget Copperbelt Symposium.

The VAT losses stand against a much larger contribution from the mines. Mr Banda said ZRA raised more than K13 billion in mineral royalty revenue from the mining sector last year. He said copper remained the major contributor to the national treasury, even though the country is endowed with vast mineral resources.

Gold tells a very different story. Mr Banda said the authority collected only K64 million from one gold company, despite the country’s extensive gold deposits.

He said ZRA was strengthening its monitoring of the mineral value chain to maximise revenue collection from the extractive industry. The authority, he said, was committed to ensuring that every kwacha collected went towards the country’s development.

The Commissioner General sees part of the answer to the gold gap in the 2027 National Budget. Mr Banda said that with the mineral royalty tax on gold cut from six to three per cent, those dealing in gold would now declare their dealings rather than trade outside the system.

Small-scale miners at the symposium welcomed the change. Small-Scale Miners Association of Zambia (SSMAZ) chairperson Mr Kelvin Tembo said the proposed 50 per cent reduction applies to miners who sell through Government-approved aggregators. He said it would encourage his members to move their gold through approved channels.

Mr Tembo said this would support Government’s efforts to maximise benefits from the country’s mineral resources. He also pointed to K450.7 million in the 2027 budget for training, certification and digitisation in the mining sector.

He did not think the budget had gone far enough for his members. Mr Tembo said more needed to be done to make local small-scale mining enterprises commercially productive.

Minister of Mines and Minerals Development Brenda Tambatamba said Government had been implementing measures since 2021 to formalise artisanal and small-scale mining. Ms Tambatamba said these included training programmes to equip miners with the skills they need, and that Government would continue supporting the initiative.

The minister also turned to the Copperbelt business community, urging local firms to tap into mining investment opportunities as Zambia targets three million tonnes of annual copper production by 2031. Ms Tambatamba said reaching that figure requires a strong domestic industrial base to supply the mining industry.

In a statement issued by the Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development public relations unit, Ms Tambatamba said mining remained a key driver of economic growth through foreign exchange earnings, job creation, investment attraction and Government revenue. She said Government’s ambition went beyond increasing copper output to creating wider economic opportunities for Zambians.

She then addressed the business leaders in the room directly.

“Colleagues, let us achieve this ambition together, which requires sustained investment in exploration, mine development, expansion of existing operations, infrastructure, technology and skills development,” Ms Tambatamba said.

She said Copperbelt businesses had the technical expertise and entrepreneurial capacity to support the next phase of mining growth. Ms Tambatamba urged local firms to position themselves for new investments, mine expansions, exploration activities and local content opportunities.

Finance and National Planning Permanent Secretary for Economic Management Mulele Mulele set out the wider economic picture. Mr Mulele said the country wanted to move from crisis management to stabilisation, and from there towards greater economic expansion and structural transformation under the Grow Zambia Agenda.

He said Zambia should move further towards a private sector-led, export-oriented economy, but warned that growth depended on holding the gains already made.

“We have to still maintain macroeconomic stability and debt sustainability. I think the environment is very important for us, so for businesses to drive this: sustained fiscal discipline, and for inflation, and also if we complete our debt restructuring, and strengthen debt management, and enhance domestic resource mobilisation and expenditure efficiency within the economy,” Mr Mulele said.

For now, the gold royalty cut remains a proposal in the K284.8 billion budget, which ministries are defending before parliamentary committees. ZRA’s tighter controls on refund claims are already in force on the Copperbelt.

World.title: Chitambala heroics send U23 through
World.content:
Zambia have advanced to the final qualifying round of the TotalEnergies CAF U-23 Africa Cup of Nations Egypt 2027 after eliminating Burkina Faso.

The Junior Chipolopolo overturned a 1-0 first-leg defeat in Lusaka on Sunday, winning 3-2 on penalties after the tie finished 1-1 on aggregate.

Substitute Caleb Musonda scored a late goal as Zambia beat Burkina Faso 1-0 at the National Heroes Stadium to send the tie to penalties.

Goalkeeper Christo Chitambala was the hero of the day, saving two penalties at the National Heroes Stadium to send Zambia through.

Government and the Football Association of Zambia have saluted the Under-23 side for reaching the final qualifying round.

Minister of Sports, Likando Mufalali, said the team has made the nation proud.

“I wish to commend our Under-23 national football team for their determination, commitment and fighting spirit as they continue to represent our country,” Mufalali said.

“Every match is an opportunity to build experience, strengthen teamwork and demonstrate the immense talent within our young players,” he said.

“I encourage the boys to remain focused, disciplined and united as they continue with their football journey. The future of Zambian football depends on the investment, belief and support we give to our young talent. Keep flying the Zambian flag high. The nation is behind you,” Mufalali added.

Zambia will know their next opponents this week when the penultimate round is concluded.

World.title: Super Strikers claim Dream Inn Top 8 Cup
World.content:
Super Strikers have been crowned the Dream Inn–GMI Central Region Division One Super 8 Cup champions after edging past Grain Tigers 2–1 in an absorbing final at Chahwanda Stadium this afternoon.

Goals from Gerald Nyoni and Tineyi Subhu proved decisive for the Gwanda based outfit, who weathered a late surge from their opponents after Tinomuda Dzviti pulled back a consolation goal for the Kwekwe side. The victory caps a memorable run for Strikers in a competition that brought together the top eight clubs from the Zifa Central Region Division One league.

World.title: Makoni fifty leads Zim A fightback against Ireland A
World.content:
TANUNURWA Makoni scored a half-century as Zimbabwe A reached 127 for three at stumps on Day 2 of the second four-day match against Ireland A at Harare Sports Club on Friday.

Ireland A had been bowled out for 551 earlier in the day, so Zimbabwe A trail by 424 runs.

Makoni made 52 off 66 balls, with seven fours.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Harare lawyer petitions Parliament over Scottland match-fixing allegations
World.content:
HARARE lawyer Lonias Rozvi Majoni has petitioned Parliament over reported integrity concerns in Zimbabwean football after the Zimbabwe Football Association (ZIFA) and Premier Soccer League (PSL) allegedly failed to acknowledge his formal complaints against Scottland FC’s alleged misconduct.

Majoni lodged a complaint with ZIFA and the PSL on November 2, 2026, but the two football governing bodies are yet to formally acknowledge receipt of his petition, despite the expiry of the seven-day ultimatum he had given them.

He has since approached Parliament, seeking legislative and oversight intervention on matters he argues fall within the State’s jurisdiction, while maintaining that football’s internal disciplinary and governance processes must remain independent.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: 11 bodies lie unclaimed at Parirenyatwa Hospital
World.content:
POLICE in Harare have appealed to the public to assist in identifying 11 bodies held at Parirenyatwa Group of Hospitals mortuary.

Some of the bodies were recovered from road and mine accident sites, while some were picked from public places.

In a statement, police said the bodies were stretching the mortuary’s carrying capacity.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Clergyman Batsirai Java’s cyber violation case referred back to police for further investigation
World.content:
CLERGYMAN Batsirai Java, arrested Wednesday for allegedly violating provisions of the Cyber and Data Act has had his case referred back to police for further investigation.

The State had alleged that Java communicated false information with the intention to undermine public confidence in the country’s law enforcement agencies

But the prosecution referred back the docket to the police station after noting that there was no cyber report to support the case.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: RBZ pushes responsible AI adoption as digitalisation reshapes insurance industry
World.content:
THE Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe (RBZ) is pushing for responsible adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and stronger digital infrastructure in the financial services sector, as technology increasingly reshapes the banking and insurance industries.

RBZ director of banking supervision Philip Madamombe said digital innovation presented opportunities for insurers to widen access to financial products, improve service delivery and reduce transaction costs, but warned that it must be accompanied by strong consumer protection and institutional resilience.

Madamombe was presenting on behalf of RBZ deputy governor Jesimen Chipika at the 2026 Southern Africa Insurance Indaba in Victoria Falls.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Former mine director loses reinstatement bid
World.content:
FORMER Botha Gold Mine managing director, Themba Hlongwani, has suffered a major High Court setback in his bid to reclaim his job at the Bindura-based mining operation.

In a 15-page judgment issued on November 11, Justice Samuel Deme struck Hlongwani and former board chairman Augustine Manyau’s urgent application from the urgent roll with costs, citing significant weaknesses in their case.

The two had challenged resolutions passed at the company’s extraordinary general meeting on October 20, which endorsed their expulsion and appointed Munyaradzi Nzarayapenga as interim board chairman.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 16, 2026
World.content:
Ebola Response Must Extend to Remote Communities to End Outbreak

The outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo has killed more than 5,400 people, and more than 11,000 cases have been reported since its inception. Children account for more than a quarter of confirmed infections and a third of deaths, with seven in 10 infected children under five dying from the disease. Transmission has slowed in several initial hotspots. There are still between 400 and 500 new cases being recorded every week across 67 health zones in eight provinces. The response has been strengthened by increased testing, more treatment facilities and community health efforts. The problems remain, however, with insecurity, attacks on health workers, funding delays, and poor contact tracing. Health agencies have appealed for continued international funding and better humanitarian access to help contain the outbreak. Nearly 3,000 people have recovered, while close to 90% of registered deaths are now being managed through safe and dignified burials.

Polls Open In Cape Verde Presidential Election



Polling stations have opened in Cape Verde for presidential elections, with incumbent President Jose Maria Neves seeking a second term against five other candidates, including the country's first female presidential contender, Joana Rosa Amado. Neves is the front-runner and the winner of the 2021 election. Amado is campaigning on greater representation for women and addressing citizens' concerns. The election takes place in a country widely regarded as one of Africa's most stable democracies, but voters face challenges including rising living costs, youth unemployment, social inequality and limited transport links between islands. Provisional results are expected overnight. Cape Verde operates a semi-presidential system in which the president serves mainly as head of state, while executive power rests largely with the prime minister.

No Fingerprint Match Found In Job Sikhala Pretoria Explosives Case

South African police fingerprint analysis has dealt a setback to the explosives case against Zimbabwean opposition leader Job Sikhala and his uncle, Alexander Thema. A report by the South African Police Service (SAPS) Local Criminal Record Centre found that neither man's fingerprints matched those recovered from the vehicle in which police allegedly discovered 26 blasting cartridges and 15 fuse connectors. In November 2025, they were arrested in Pretoria on charges relating to the possession of explosives, which they denied. Sikhala has maintained that the case was a setup involving Zimbabwean security agents and rogue South African police officers. He alleges that explosives were planted in the vehicle. Both men were released on R10,000 bail each. The fingerprint investigation remains pending.

Fela Kuti Makes History at Rock & Roll Hall of Fame

Nigerian Afrobeat pioneer Fela Kuti has become the first African artist to be honoured by the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, nearly 30 years after his death. He was posthumously inducted in the Early Influence category during a ceremony in Los Angeles, alongside international music figures including Queen Latifah and Celia Cruz. The recognition celebrates Kuti's revolutionary music, political activism and influence on generations of musicians worldwide. Fela’s music is a mixture of jazz, West African music and soul. His music was a weapon against political corruption and injustice. The honor follows a posthumous Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in February 2026. His influence continues to be felt in the work of contemporary African artists, including Burna Boy and Salif Keita.

South Sudan Postpones First Elections to February

South Sudan has postponed its first national elections from 22 December to 11 February, amid escalating political and ethnic tensions and fears of renewed conflict. The electoral commission announced the revised date on the day voter registration was due to begin, with results expected on 15 February. The elections have already been delayed several times as violence involving forces loyal to President Salva Kiir and supporters of detained former vice-president Riek Machar continues to threaten stability. The United Nations has warned that holding elections under the current conditions could trigger renewed conflict and further humanitarian crises in the world's youngest nation. South Sudan gained independence in 2011. However, a civil war between Kiir's and Machar's forces from 2013 to 2018 killed an estimated 400,000 people.

Close 

Over 2,300 Migrants Arrive in Spain's Canary Islands

Nearly 1,600 migrants arrived in Spain's Canary Islands in a single day, with most landing on the island of El Hierro aboard 15 wooden fishing boats. The majority came from West African countries, including Senegal, Gambia and Guinea, while more than 2,300 people arrived across the islands. Spanish authorities and humanitarian organisations are assisting as the arrivals place additional pressure on local communities. Despite the latest surge, overall migrant arrivals in the Canary Islands between January and October were down 5.5% compared with the same period last year. Spanish officials have pledged to manage the increased arrivals humanely while taking into account the needs of island residents.

World.title: South Africa: Over 77,000 Gauteng Pupils Await School Placements - South African News Briefs - November 16, 2026
World.content:
press review

Over 77,000 Gauteng Pupils Still Await 2027 School Placements

More than 77,000 pupils in Gauteng are still awaiting school placements for the 2027 academic year, despite over 267,000 learners already being placed, reports EWN . Education MEC Lebogang Maile said 278 schools have reached capacity, with space shortages affecting parts of Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni. Parents with outstanding documents have until 4 December to submit them. Late applications will open on 17 December. Meanwhile, the department has said that it will pay the second tranche of school funding in instalments until March next year, subject to available funds. It has confirmed that scholar transport disputes over outstanding payments have been resolved.

28 Injured as Bus Overturns on N3 in Pietermaritzburg



Twenty-eight passengers have been injured after a luxury bus overturned on the N3 near New England Road in Pietermaritzburg, KwaZulu-Natal, reports SABC News. The provincial Department of Transport said some passengers were taken to nearby hospitals for medical treatment. The accident resulted in the closure of the affected route, with motorists travelling towards Durban urged to use alternative routes via Hayfields or Ashburton. Emergency teams and traffic officials attended to the scene.

SANDF Official to Testify in Mapisa-Nqakula Corruption Trial

A South African National Defence Force finance official is set to testify in the corruption trial of former Defence Minister Nosiviwe Mapisa-Nqakula, reports EWN . She is accused of soliciting R4.5 million in bribes from defence contractor Nombasa Ntsondwa-Ndhlovu between 2016 and 2019, allegedly receiving R2.2 million. Mapisa-Nqakula has denied the allegations and completed her testimony. The finance official is among two witnesses subpoenaed after reportedly becoming reluctant to testify. The former minister is expected to call three witnesses in her defence.

World.title: West Africa: Nearly 1,600 Migrants Arrive on Spain's Canary Islands in One Day
World.content:
A map showing the Canary Islands and Spain in relation to Africa.

The majority of the migrants who arrived on the islands on Saturday came from Senegal, Gambia, and Guinea. The surge in arrivals to the Canaries comes after Spain's Ceuta recently faced a migration crisis.

Nearly 1,600 migrants arrived on the Spain's Canary Islands in one day, Spanish news agency EFE reported Sunday, using tallies from the Spanish government's Maritime Safety and Rescue Society.

What do we know so far about the migrant arrivals on the Canaries?

Most of the 1,580 migrants who came ashore on Saturday landed on the island of El Hierro. They arrived aboard 15 wooden fishing boats.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Most of the migrants came from West African countries such as Senegal, Gambia, and Guinea. Between Friday and Saturday, over 2,300 migrants in total arrived on the islands, according to the Spanish authorities.

The Canary Islands, whose shortest gap with Africa is around 100 kilometers (around 62 miles), faces a migration crisis.

Spanish Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres Perez visited the town of La Restinga on Sunday, which lies on the southernmost tip of El Hierro. She met with residents of the town and thanked them for "their solidarity and commitment" as the island witnesses a large number of migrant arrivals.

"The Government of Spain continues to work to ensure that this surge in migration is managed with humanity and with the island's residents in mind," she posted on X. El Hierro has a population of nearly 12,000 people.

Although the Canary Islands saw a large number of migrants arriving on its shores over the weekend, overall migration to the islands is down 5.5% between January and October 31 from the same period last year.

Arrivals surge come after recent Ceuta crisis

The surge in latest arrivals to the Canary Islands comes after another Spanish territory, Ceuta, faced a migration crisis in late July.

An estimated 80,000 people, mostly young Moroccan men, crossed into Ceuta from neighboring Morocco. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, a member of the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE), has faced criticism from the opposition over his handling of the crisis.

Migration, along with housing, are expected to be major topics for voters as they head for snap elections in Spain later this month.

World.title: Zimbabwe: South African Police's Own Report Clears Job Sikhala and His Uncle in Explosives Case
World.content:
A SOUTH African Police Service (SAPS) fingerprint analysis has dealt a major blow to the State's explosives case against Zimbabwean opposition leader Job Sikhala and his uncle Alexander Thema.

The duo is facing criminal charges related to possession of explosive devices.

In a major twist, the SAPS Local Criminal Record Centre in Pretoria has concluded that neither Sikhala (54) nor Thema (78) left any prints on evidence recovered from the vehicle they were arrested in.

A report dated July 16, 2026, signed by the centre commander and a senior fingerprint expert, SAPS compared palm and fingerprint samples from both men against lifts taken at the scene, and did not find any match.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"The fingerprints of the following persons regarding the above-mentioned case have been compared with the prints found on the scene of the crime; 1. Alexander Thema 2. Job Sikhala. The result of the comparison is NEGATIVE," reads part of the report.

The fingerprint file remains pending.

Sikhala and Thema were picked up on November 6, 2025 along Kgosi Mampuru Street, Pretoria, after police acted on a tip-off about a suspicious vehicle.

Officers say they recovered 26 blasting cartridges and 15 fuse connectors from the car belonging to Thema.

Both men were released on R10,000 bail each. The State did not oppose bail. Sikhala and his uncle deny any link to the explosives.

Sikhala, head of the National Democratic Working Group, has from day one claimed a set-up, alleging Zimbabwean State security, working with rogue SAPS elements, orchestrated the arrest to keep him locked up in South Africa.

His defence team told court their client was lured to a Pretoria meeting. During the meeting, they allege, someone took the car keys and that is when the explosives were allegedly planted in the vehicle.

Sikhala, who has remained in South Africa since the arrest more than a year ago, is being represented by lawyer Bongani Dee of Mabuza Attorneys.

World.title: Africa: Six Months On, Accessing Hard-to-Reach Communities Key to Halting Ebola Outbreak
World.content:
Since the start of the outbreak, more than 11 000 cases and 5400 deaths have been reported. Children account for more than a quarter of confirmed cases and one third of deaths. Seven in 10 children under five with confirmed Ebola have died. While the response has slowed transmission in the initial epicentres, 400 to 500 new cases continue to be reported each week, and the outbreak has expanded to 67 health zones in eight provinces.

Contact follow-up remains below target. The high number of deaths occurring in communities, which account for two-thirds of confirmed deaths, show that infections are still being identified too late. Recent imported cases in Kenya and Nigeria underscore the continuing risk of spread beyond national borders. Delays in paying frontline health workers and responders create tension and slow the response.

Six months of collective action

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The United Nations, Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, regional economic bodies and humanitarian partners are fully mobilized behind government leadership. WHO is directing the technical health response, and the wider humanitarian system is helping enable access, logistics, protection, and continuity of essential services. Nearly 100 health and humanitarian partners are present across the affected areas, providing essential health services, including treatment for acute malnutrition.

Africa CDC and WHO co-lead the joint continental Incident Management Support Team, which supports the technical health response and coordinates health and development partners across affected and at-risk countries in response, preparedness and readiness.

Most of the early epicentres of this outbreak have been successfully brought under control and rapid transmission has been halted, including Mongbwalu, Nyankunde, Nizi, Rwampara and Butembo. Even in Bunia, one of the larger, early epicentres, though there is still significant transmission, the number of new cases has halved, and treatment centres are reporting low occupancy.

Diagnostic capacity has grown from two laboratories to more than two dozen, while close to 2000 treatment beds are now available in 104 treatment and transit centres. Around 3000 people have recovered from Ebola, and a quarter of those have enrolled in the survivor programme.

Over 17,000 community health workers and 46 000 community actors have been trained and provided with supplies to safely do their jobs. Health teams are implementing targeted strategies to support women and children, including by keeping maternal health services running. Nearly one million hot meals across 59 treatment, isolation and transit facilities have been delivered to more than 180,000 people affected by the outbreak and to support containment efforts.

Surveillance, contact tracing, risk communication, community engagement and safe and dignified burials have also expanded. Almost 90% of registered deaths are now managed with a safe and dignified burial, an important step in stopping onward transmission to mourners. Cross-border collaboration has strengthened surveillance, information-sharing and coordination, while scientific research is advancing, including the evaluation of candidate treatments and vaccines.

These achievements would not have been possible without the dedication of Congolese health workers, community volunteers and frontline responders who continue to serve affected communities, often under extremely difficult and insecure conditions.

These successes remain fragile, however, and must be to be protected and scaled up across the affected and at-risk health zones and provinces.

Violence prevents communities from getting help

Insecurity remains one of the greatest obstacles to the response. Attacks and threats against response teams disrupt lifesaving operations, while ongoing conflict, displacement and movement restrictions continue to complicate response efforts. A recent armed attack in Cantine-Aloya locality led to 66 civilian deaths, including that of three health workers. Three health facilities were looted. More than 1000 contacts were lost to follow-up, and three confirmed cases remain unaccounted for. A second attack on the town was reported early on 11 November. There have been over 80 attacks on health care since the outbreak was declared.

A halt in hostilities is urgently needed to protect communities and health workers, and to safeguard the progress made over the past six months.

Close 

Sustaining the response

The response must put the knowledge, tools and resources needed to stop Ebola into the hands of affected communities. It must take the wider view, listening to communities who have asked for help in addressing challenges beyond Ebola, from violence to hunger to weaknesses in the health system.

International support has enabled the response to move from chasing the virus to controlling transmission in many areas. That progress must now be protected. Fast, flexible funding must be sustained through 2027, alongside political commitment, safe access, protection of health care and meaningful community participation. Wider humanitarian needs, including food security, water and sanitation, child protection, mental health and psychosocial support, maternal and newborn health care and support for women and girls, must also be addressed.

The next phase must build on six months of progress while moving faster to reach those communities still beyond the effective reach of the response. That is essential to save lives, interrupt transmission and bring the outbreak to an end.

World.title: Kenya: Ruto Hits Back At Opposition Over SGR Corruption Claims
World.content:
Nairobi — President William Ruto has challenged opposition leaders over their interpretation of a World Bank report that raises concerns about corruption and procurement weaknesses in the construction of the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR), arguing that the project was undertaken under a previous administration.

Speaking in Narok, Ruto accused opposition politicians of selectively quoting the report while questioning their own possible links to the procurement dealings surrounding the railway.

"I have heard some leaders saying that the World Bank report said there was some corruption in procurement in government. What they are not saying is that the SGR was built under a different regime," Ruto said.



"It could be that part of the money sponsoring your campaigns are proceeds of the SGR tenders. Don't read part of the report and give us a lecture. Read the whole report," he added.

The President's remarks come days after the World Bank released its November 2026 Kenya Economic Update, which identified governance weaknesses in public procurement and cited the SGR as an example of how non-competitive contracting and questionable land compensation practices can increase infrastructure costs.

The report estimates that Kenya could have saved up to US$900 million (Sh117 billion) in initial construction costs had the Mombasa-Nairobi railway been delivered at the same cost per kilometer as Tanzania's Dar es Salaam-Dodoma line.

It attributes at least 30 percent of the potential savings to governance challenges, including preference for direct contracting over competitive tendering, land speculation and alleged fraud involving land titling, valuation and compensation.

The World Bank estimates that Kenya's railway cost approximately Sh988 million per kilometer, compared with Sh741 million for Tanzania's electrified railway and Sh689 million for the Djibouti-Addis Ababa line.

The findings have also drawn criticism from opposition leaders, with Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna arguing that the report validates longstanding concerns over opaque government transactions and inadequate accountability in public spending.

Sifuna questioned the limited disclosure of government procurement information, noting that although public procurement accounts for approximately 10 percent of Kenya's Gross Domestic Product (GDP), only Sh410 billion had some procurement information published for the 2024/25 financial year.

He further argued that the country needed stronger institutions and accountability mechanisms rather than an exclusive focus on infrastructure development.

The World Bank report identifies procurement transparency as a major governance challenge, noting that more detailed information, including contract amounts and successful bidders, was available for only Sh186 billion during the same financial year.

Close 

The disclosure gap raises concerns about public oversight of government contracts, particularly as procurement remains a significant channel through which public resources are spent.

The findings come as the government pursues reforms, including the rollout of an electronic government procurement system intended to improve transparency, competition and oversight.

World.title: Nigeria: With Nigeria's Fela Kuti, African Music Enters the Rock &amp; Roll Hall of Fame
World.content:
For the first time in its history, the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame has honoured a major figure in African music. Nigeria's Fela Kuti was inducted on Saturday evening during a ceremony in Los Angeles, nearly thirty years after his death, consecrating the musical influence of the rebellious king of Afrobeat.

Fela Kuti was named beside Queen Latifah, Celia Cruz, MC Lyte, and Gram Parsons to receive an "Early influence" honour by the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame Foundation, at the ceremony held in Los Angeles's Peacock Theater.

The Cleveland-based Hall of Fame surveyed more than 1,000 musicians, historians and industry members to choose the final entrants for 2026.

Hip-hop transformers Wu-Tang Clan and punk rocker Billy Idol were among the music luminaries inducted at a star-studded concert gala, where artists like Megan Thee Stallion and Remy Ma.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Phil Collins, Joy Division/New Order, Sade, Iron Maiden, Oaisis and the velvet-voiced late Luther Vandross also joined the rock pantheon.

The evening was an occasion to put Africa on a pedestal, for the first time with recognition for Nigerian musician Fela Kuti.

"For the first time in forty years of existence, the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame honours an African artist, proof that rock and roll is not an exclusively American art, but a genre that has been nourished by influences from all over the world, and this well before its creation," producer Ian Brennan told RFI.

Nigeria's Fela Kuti first African to receive lifetime Grammy award

"Going back to the roots of American music, almost all roads lead to Africa, and more specifically to West Africa. Fela Kuti's influence has not only continued, but has even increased considerably over the decades since his passing," he says.

Brennan worked for more than ten years to ensure that the "Black President" received a posthumous Grammy Award - finally awarded in February 2026 for his entire career, making him also the first African artist in history to receive this award.

Fela Kuti's name had been put forward to enter the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Foundation several times over the years, without success.

Revolutionary message

His name was initially included on the list of 16 candidates announced for the 2021 class in the performers category, which sparked a major campaign in Nigeria, amplified by singers like Davido.

But the 1,200 members of the electoral college did not include him in the final selection. A second attempt in 2022 was no more successful.

Close 

Finally, Fela's entry into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame was made public last April in the "Early Influence" category, after review by a specific committee.

To be considered, artists must have released their first commercial recording at least 25 years before the year of their nomination and to be an artist "whose music and performances have directly influenced, inspired and evolved rock & roll".

Angélique Kidjo says Hollywood star is 'for Africa, but also for France'

Rock & Roll Hall of Fame said that nearly thirty years after his death, "Fela Kuti's innovative music, revolutionary message, and generational impact continue to represent the indomitable and evolving spirit of rock & roll."

The Nigerian star is also described as "a revolutionary voice that denounced injustice [...], provoking political change while fusing jazz, West African music, and soul."

To illustrate this point, the official Rock & Roll Hall of Fame page dedicated to Fela highlights his key position between the giants of African-American music and the artists he inspired around the world.

On one side: Miles Davis, James Brown, and Parliament-Funkadelic - from whom Kuti borrowed various elements, both musically and in terms of approach.

On the other hand, there are the influences he exerted, notably on Salif Keita, Burna Boy, and Ginger Baker, who saw him as a role model or learned from him - highlighting the crucial place of the African artist at the heart of the global musical landscape.

World.title: Cape Verde: Cape Verde Votes for President, With Incumbent Favoured to Win
World.content:
Polling stations have opened in Cape Verde for a presidential election with incumbent Jose Maria Neves favoured to win a second term as head of state of the west African archipelago renowned for its democratic stability. He is up against the country's first ever woman candidate Joana Rosa Amado, among other contenders.

Polls will remain open for 10 hours with provisional results expected overnight.

The island nation made world headlines this year when its national football team reached the knockout stages in its first ever World Cup, and when a cruise ship containing people with hantavirus docked off its shores.

Located in the middle of the Atlantic approximately 600 kilometres off the coast of Senegal, the Portuguese-speaking country comprising 10 volcanic islands is attracting more tourists every year.



Unlike several of its west African neighbours where presidential elections have been tense in recent years, Cape Verde is known for its political stability and good governance.

It is considered a model of democracy in Africa, with strong economic growth.

The country is known for its "morabeza" ("hospitality", in local creole), openness, and carnivals. It also has its own style of music.

According to the Mo Ibrahim Foundation 2026 index on global governance, Cape Verde ranks third out of 54 countries on the continent.

Six candidates

The archipelago has a semi-presidential system in which the executive is dominated by the prime minister.

The president does not govern but acts more as an arbiter, working to guarantee unity and uphold the constitution.

The head of state appoints the prime minister based on the results of legislative elections and represents the country abroad.

Among the six candidates in the running on Sunday, two are frontrunners: incumbent Neves, 66, and Amado, 61, a lawyer and former minister of justice.

Each is supported by one of the country's two main parties.

South Sudan postpones first national elections until February

Neves, a strong favourite, was first elected president in 2021. From 2001 to 2016 he also served as prime minister and the president of the African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde (PAICV). He has also been a mayor and a deputy.

Neves has the support of the PAICV, which won legislative elections in May.

"In these times of international uncertainty, it is essential that Cape Verde continues to have a patriotic, experienced president capable of inspiring Cape Verdeans", he said this week during a meeting.

Challenges ahead

His main challenger Amado is supported by the Movement for Democracy (MpD), the main opposition party.

Her slogan is "Listen to Cape Verde," which she says "does not mean promising everything, but rather, knowing the real concerns and expectations of the population."

"The election of a woman to the presidency would show many young women and young girls that no government job is barred from them," she told the press.

Among the other candidates are 45-year-old surgeon Gilson Alves, an authoritarian figure who is promising to fight corruption, allow gun ownership and reinstate the death penalty.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

In July, Cape Verde was officially classified as an upper-middle income country by the World Bank due to economic growth in the tourism sector and a 16.8 percent increase in gross national income per capita between 2023 and 2024.

Close 

However, the country faces many challenges, including persistent social inequality, geographic isolation and a lack of affordable options for travelling between islands.

If elected, the main candidates have promised to implement measures to improve air and sea travel between the islands and also to construct new accommodation for tourists.

Among the population's major concerns are the increased cost of living, fuel prices and youth unemployment.

Since the end of the Covid-19 pandemic many young Cape Verdeans, including graduates and those with professional training, have immigrated and continue to move abroad, causing a labour shortage.

(with AFP)

World.title: Mike Vrabel doesn't want Patriots to 'b---h and complain' but he b----es and complains about his players a lot
World.content:
After his New England Patriots were demolished by the Detroit Lions in Munich on Sunday, coach Mike Vrabel told reporters he doesn't want to hear anyone "b---h and complain" because that's what "losers" do.

Except that if you listen to Vrabel, especially after that 35-10 loss, he did a lot of what he doesn't want to hear others do — b---h and complain.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

DRAKE MAYE TELLS REPORTERS THEY DON'T KNOW 'WHAT THEY'RE TALKING ABOUT' DURING GERMANY PRESS CONFERENCE

In one news conference, Vrabel suggested losing quarterback Drake Maye to an ankle injury probably had no effect on the outcome of the game.

In other words, having his starting quarterback wouldn't have helped the Patriots much.

"I don't think Drake's being in there or not would have really helped," Vrabel said. "I mean, it may have. I would highly doubt it, until we start doing the little things better in all three phases, the fundamentals, being able to run the football, being able to get open and catch and protect our quarterback, tackle, get off the field on third down, create turnovers."

Vrabel complained the New England defense provides only "glimpses" of what it's supposed to deliver, particularly the last two weeks when it has given up 80 combined points to the Lions and Green Bay Packers.

"Give up too many plays, too many missed tackles, too many clean pockets for the quarterback, and don't affect them," Vrabel said.

Look, the Patriots got out-classed the last two weeks. So it is understandable Vrabel doesn't love the way his players are performing lately.

His frustration makes perfect sense.

But it seems Vrabel never complains about his coaching staff. He never laments bad play-calls or preparation. It's always on the players.

And it happens a lot.

DRAKE MAYE VOICES SUPPORT FOR PATRIOTS COACH MIKE VRABEL AS OFF-FIELD CONTROVERSY CONTINUES TO SWIRL

A couple of weeks ago, Vrabel complained about the play of cornerback Christian Gonzalez. It seemed fair because Gonzalez didn't perform, but did anyone hear any attention placed on the secondary coach? Or the defensive coordinator?

After the Super Bowl last season, a game in which the Patriots yielded six sacks, Vrabel never suggested his offensive coaches got out-coached. Never said rookie left tackle Will Campbell might have benefited from some help.

He instead talked about how the sacks were "on the quarterback" or "somebody got beat."

Oh, and by the way, last spring when running back TreVeyon Henderson publicly defended Bulls player Jaden Ivey over his opinions about LGBTQ issues, Vrabel's default position was not to defend Henderson.

Vrabel instead pushed back on Henderson's judgment by stressing the player needed to consider how he represents the team and whether he's fully educated on topics he comments about.

The irony, of course, is that days later, Vrabel's representation of the team would be very much in question when his relationship with Dianna Russini became public.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

To be fair, Vrabel, on Sunday, did shoulder some responsibility for how his team is playing. But he soon added others to the group.

"I'm not going to, again, we've gotten beat two weeks in a row," he said. "That starts with me, and again, we're professionals. We're grown men. We all have to recognize what it is, we need to do better and improve. That's what winners do.

"Winners figure out ways to help the team win. They don't b---h and complain. They try to find ways to help the team."

World.title: Pete Buttigieg breaks with Democrats on student loan handouts, admits party ‘overtorqued’ on issue

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg admitted Sunday that he broke ranks with the Democratic Party on student loans, saying the party "overtorqued" the issue and may have dissuaded voters.

During a "Pod Save America" interview, host Dan Pfeiffer remarked that many of the Democratic candidates who won in the midterm elections disagreed with the party on at least one issue, whether it be gun control or the role of oil and gas in energy.

He asked Buttigieg whether he held any beliefs that ran counter to the mainstream Democratic Party.

BERNIE SANDERS ADMITS DEMOCRATS FAILED WORKING-CLASS VOTERS ON ECONOMICS, DRIVING THEM TO DONALD TRUMP

"In the 2020 campaign, I definitely staked out some positions that I still believe in that weren't always kind of popular in the party," Buttigieg said. "One thing is, I think...we really overtorqued on the student loan thing. As a party, I have a very hard time explaining to my relatives in Michigan who did not go to college why they should be paying for people who do."

He added, "I believe there are ways to make sure that you come out of college debt-free. I believe college should be more affordable. I don't believe in like a magic wand to fix that for everybody who borrowed money."

PETE BUTTIGIEG DISTANCES HIMSELF FROM BIDEN AMID 2028 TALK, SUGGESTS 'BUILD BACK BETTER' DOESN'T WORK

Though Buttigieg told Pfeiffer that he doesn't believe in a "magic" fix for student loans, he previously served under President Joe Biden, who repeatedly attempted to cancel student loan debt, even after the Supreme Court ruled against his administration in 2023.

His husband, Chasten Buttigieg, was also among those frustrated at the prospect of paying student loans after COVID-19-era loan relief was set to expire in 2022.

Fox News Digital reached out to Buttigieg's organization, Win the Era, for comment.

Veteran Democratic strategist Julian Epstein called the student loan forgiveness a scam and congratulated Buttigieg for having enough self-awareness to acknowledge it.

JOE MANCHIN WARNS DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ARE GAINING GROUND AS DEMOCRATS REMAIN SILENT

"Buttigieg shows an all-too-rare self-awareness for a Democrat elite on this issue. The student loan giveaway, also known as loan forgiveness, is a scam," Epstein told Fox News Digital. "It's welfare for the most privileged and elite amongst us that the working class has to help fund. It's Robin Hood in reverse, and it stands against everything the Democratic Party should be standing for."

Another issue Buttigieg disagreed with the Democratic Party on was the two-party system itself.
