Felix Gallardo had been behind bars since 1989, according to The AP.

His death comes more than four decades after Camarena’s abduction and torture, a killing that sparked the largest homicide investigation in DEA history, according to the agency.

In 2017, a Mexican federal judge gave Felix Gallardo a 37-year prison term for the murders of Camarena and Mexican pilot Alfredo Zavala, Excélsior reported. The judge also ordered more than 20 million pesos in compensation for the victims’ families, roughly $1.18 million at the time.

Camarena was heading to meet his wife for lunch on Feb. 7, 1985, when five men abducted him as he left the U.S. Consulate in Guadalajara, according to the DEA. One of the attackers identified himself as a Mexican law enforcement official.

DRUG CARTEL KINGPIN AMONG TARGETS IN SWEEPING TRUMP CRACKDOWN ON ALLEGED MEXICAN CORRUPTION NETWORK

The 37-year-old agent was never seen alive again.

The DEA says Camarena was believed to have been tortured for two days before dying from a crushed skull. His body was discovered on March 5, 1985.

His killing triggered Operation Leyenda, which the agency describes as the largest homicide investigation it had ever undertaken. Felix Gallardo was among the major Mexican crime figures arrested in connection with Camarena’s torture and murder, according to the DEA.

ICE RENEWS HUNT FOR EL CHAPO'S LAST TWO FUGITIVE SONS WITH MASSIVE REWARD

The agent, a Marine Corps veteran who joined the DEA in 1974, left behind his wife and three children.

Felix Gallardo’s reach helped reshape organized crime in Mexico. A 2023 report released by Sen. Chuck Grassley’s office described the former police officer as having brought traffickers together into a large organization that became a blueprint for many of Mexico’s major criminal groups.

EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE TRUMP'S CARTEL CRACKDOWN AS WHITE HOUSE OFFICIAL DETAILS PRESIDENT'S PRIVATE BRIEFINGS

The Guadalajara cartel was among the first Mexican trafficking organizations to work with Colombian cocaine suppliers, according to a historical DEA publication. The agency said Felix Gallardo and Rafael Caro Quintero formed the cartel to ship heroin and marijuana into the United States before it prospered from the cocaine trade.

Camarena’s legacy, meanwhile, lives on through the red ribbons worn each October in his memory as part of drug prevention efforts, according to the DEA.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: U.S. attorney warns Sen. Elizabeth Warren against investigating Trump associates
World.content:
A Justice Department official on Sunday accused Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., of intending to target private individuals close to President Donald Trump with investigations. The allegation came in a letter similar to others sent to congressional Democrats.

U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas Aaron Reitz sent a letter to Warren — who is likely the incoming chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee — calling on her to preserve documents related to investigations of Trump allies. Reitz noted that Warren appears “eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump’s private associates.”

Reitz referenced a Nov. 11 letter in which Warren, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., asked Meredith O’Rourke, a National Park Foundation board member and top fundraiser for Trump, to retain documents related to funding for the White House ballroom and other projects.

Reitz accused the three lawmakers of “demanding sweeping information about her and other private citizens and entities who associate with President Trump.”

The letter to Warren signals an expansion of Reitz’s inquiry into congressional Democrats tasked with government oversight. When Democrats take control of Congress next year, Garcia is likely to take the gavel of the House Oversight Committee, while Blumenthal is expected to lead the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs’ Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

Last week, the White House issued a threat to congressional Democrats against probes into the administration. Since their midterm victories, Democrats have said Trump family businesses and immigration enforcement are some of their top targets for investigation.

Reitz’s letter referenced an op-ed from Warren earlier this month in Time magazine, in which the senator wrote, “With astonishing brazenness, Trump has attempted to reengineer the federal government into a corruption machine designed to rake in profits for himself, his family, and his cronies.”

Reitz also accused Warren of planning to target businesses that associate with Trump, referencing an appearance on CBS’ “Face the Nation” in which Warren said tech CEOs, Wall Street executives and giant corporations who have broken the law “better get ready for some investigations — serious ones.”

“The context sends a strong smoke signal: you intend to target private individuals close to President Trump,” Reitz said.

A spokesperson for Warren did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday night.

Reitz, a former chief of staff to Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has sent similar letters to Blumenthal and Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., warning them against investigating Trump associates and calling on them to preserve documents.

Reitz posted his letter to Warren on X, and Trump reposted it to Truth Social later Sunday.

The letter to Warren also contained numerous references to Native Americans, such as “scalps,” “war cries” and “tomahawk,” a dig at Warren over her past claims of Native American descent.

World.title: Two games, one day: Ground stop means unprecedented double duty for NFL refs
World.content:
It was 4:17 p.m. Sunday in downtown Indianapolis when the Colts wrapped up a home win over the Miami Dolphins. Fans departed Lucas Oil Stadium. The teams scattered for home.

For the four-man officiating crew that worked the game, the work day was only half over.

The quartet boarded a van 24 minutes later and drove east for Cincinnati, where their second assignment of the day awaited — an unusual case of double duty that was set in motion by the FAA ground stop Friday that halted flights nationwide.

Holding an electrolyte drink and a portable massage gun, referee Don Willard arrived inside Cincinnati’s Paycor Stadium at 6:37 p.m., about 90 minutes before the Bengals hosted the Pittsburgh Steelers, along with his crew of umpire Terry Killens, field judge Jabir Walker and side judge Justin Larrew.

“To best of our knowledge, no NFL official has worked two games in one day,” the NFL Referees Association told NBC News in a statement. “Officials have worked two games in a week before, but we can’t find an instance where one has worked a double header like this.”

Friday’s four-hour ground stop did not require the NFL to adjust the kickoff times of any of Sunday’s games because air travel resumed by Saturday, when road teams traditionally travel. The teams would arrive on time; to ensure the referees would, too, the NFL reassigned officials to games within driving distance of where they live.

In an extreme case, referee Clete Blakeman — who was supposed to officiate the game in Cincinnati — drove about eight hours from his home in Nebraska to Green Bay to work the Packers-Vikings game, ESPN reported.

“We appreciate the commitment and dedication of all the officials, numerous gameday personnel and our network partners who made adjustments due to nationwide travel issues,” an NFL spokesperson said.

Seventeen officiating crews work in the NFL, and each has a backup referee who trains throughout the year to step in if necessary, the spokesman said. Three of those backup referees were pressed into duty Sunday. One was Willard, who has typically been a side judge during his nine years in the NFL. Sunday marked both his debut as a referee (Colts-Dolphins) — and his second career game as a referee.

Willard had done a “phenomenal job,” longtime NFL officials and NBC Sports rules analyst Terry McAuley said during NBC’s “Sunday Night Football” broadcast.

Officials are paid per game worked, the referee union said.

“This is a unique and unprecedented situation that has required all of our officials to make adjustments, and in some cases, travel many miles by car to get to their game sites,” said Scott Green, the executive director of the NFLRA. “However, over the course of their careers, all officials have faced unpublicized travel and other assorted issues, meaning they have experience working in less- than-ideal situations, in many games across all levels of play. Our members will do what they have always done, which is work the games to the best of their ability, regardless of the situation.”

World.title: Here’s the biggest news you missed this weekend
World.content:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy declined to apologize for the nationwide ground stop on Friday that stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country following a router issue that derailed air traffic control communications.

Instead, the secretary blamed his predecessors for “30 years of a lack of investment,” telling NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that previous presidential administrations did not do enough to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system.

“It happened on my watch, but we have to be clear: I am moving at an incredible speed that no one has done at the FAA or in decades, and I’m proud of the work we’re doing, the attention we’re bringing to this issue,” Duffy said.

Federal Aviation Administration contractor L3Harris was working on replacing a copper line with a fiber line at a remote site when the work led a router to overwhelm the national FAA telecommunications network, Duffy said Saturday.

On “Meet the Press,” the transportation secretary reiterated a call he’s made all weekend for more funding from Congress to modernize the nationwide air traffic control system, which has long been outdated and faced problems.

Duffy expects airports and airlines to resume normal operations by the end of the day or early Monday morning.

Sen.-elect Scott Colom says investing in the South can help Democrats

Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., emphasized on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Democrats need to invest more in Southern states like Mississippi, where he flipped a seat blue for the first time in decades.

“What we need to do now as a Democratic Party is understand we can’t continue to allow that lack of investment to occur,” he said.

Colom’s projected win brings Democrats to a 55-seat majority in the Senate, with Alaska’s Senate race yet to be called. His victory over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican, marked a seismic political shift in a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate 44 years ago and has not had a Black senator since the Reconstruction period.

Mike Pence says GOP voters ‘didn’t turn left’ but were ‘turned off’ in midterms

Former Vice President Mike Pence said on “Meet the Press” he disagrees with Vice President JD Vance’s assessment of Republican midterm losses, saying that the problem Americans have with the Iran war is that the U.S. “stopped short.”

“We sunk their navy, we had complete air superiority, took down 15,000 military sites in Iran. And then, we paused and began to embrace the politics of appeasement,” Pence said.

Why Democrat Mary Peltola is likely to win Alaska’s Senate race

Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola speaks during an election night watch party in Anchorage. Justin Sullivan / Getty

As Alaska continues to count and report votes weeks after Election Day, it is increasingly unlikely that Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan will hang on to his job.

His Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola, is on track to win the still-unresolved Senate race under either possible scenario — with an outright majority, or if the race goes to ranked choice ballots, according to an NBC News Decision Desk analysis of outstanding and tabulated votes.

It’s possible that the final result won’t arrive until Nov. 18. Wednesday is Alaska’s deadline for election officials to receive final mail absentee ballots, one reason why this close race has lingered for so long.

Politics in brief

Widening the lead : Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has won the Alaska governor’s race , NBC News projects, flipping the office from Republican control and extending Democrats’ gains at the state level in this year’s elections.

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has won , NBC News projects, flipping the office from Republican control and extending Democrats’ gains at the state level in this year’s elections. Par for the course: The Trump administration cannot close East Potomac Park to the public for now, a federal judge in Washington ruled Saturday, dealing a blow to the president’s effort to renovate the park’s golf course.

Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as company conducts probe over Nvidia fallout

Jensen Huang and Alice Huang at a restaurant in Taipei in 2025. TVBS via AP

Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International said that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sparked U.S. national security concerns, left the company last year.

Megaspeed, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers.

Could a viral teen comedy be Netflix’s answer to YouTube?

Hyde Healy, Julia Dicesare, Grace Reiter, Ryan Micho, Tommy Armstrong and Aidan Micho in "Minimum Wage." Netflix

Inside a make-believe pizza shop overlooking Onondaga Lake, a team of digital creators, filmmakers and young actors spent months cooking up a show that they hope will serve Netflix something it craves: a fresh audience.

“Minimum Wage,” a mockumentary that follows teens who work at a pizza shop, has garnered more than 30 million views across YouTube, TikTok and Instagram since launching in May 2024.

The media company’s decision to acquire the show for its platform reflects a broader shift in Hollywood’s battle for younger viewers, as streamers increasingly turn to internet creators and their built-in fan bases to drive subscriptions and engagement.

More culture news

PSA for CEOs: Former “Saturday Night Live” repertory player and writer Bowen Yang returned to help open the show this weekend with his portrayal of Jensen Huang.

Former “Saturday Night Live” repertory player and writer Bowen Yang returned to help with his portrayal of Jensen Huang. Warm welcome: Johnny Depp is back at the top of the box office with “Ebenezer,” his first studio movie in eight years, and first since the fallout from a contentious court battle with ex-wife Amber Heard.

Women with autoimmune diseases often misdiagnosed for 4 years or more

Women with autoimmune diseases such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis are more likely to be misdiagnosed or get delayed treatment compared with men. BSIP / Universal Images Group via Getty

Women with autoimmune diseases such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis are more likely to be misdiagnosed or get delayed treatment compared with men, with their symptoms often dismissed as “psychological.”

An online survey by British researchers found that it took women with an autoimmune disorder about four years to get a diagnosis, while it took men around three months to less than a year.

“Women in particular felt not listened to or not heard or not believed by their medical professionals,” said Sydnae Taylor, a co-author of the study published recently in eClinicalMedicine.

Autoimmune conditions can affect anyone but are more common in women than in men, according to the federal Office on Women’s Health.

Notable quote

Can you believe it? Look at her! Baby, she’s back! SpaceX commentator Dan Huot

SpaceX’s Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier. It was the first ever capture of a Starship flying back from space.

World.title: Trump plans to take Qatari jet to Asia, but it’s unclear whether it’s been ‘maxed out’
World.content:
President Donald Trump is expected to take the Qatari-gifted Air Force One to Asia on Monday as questions linger about upgrades the White House said were needed after a security threat from Iran forced the president to fly home from Turkey on a secret military plane in July, according to two U.S. officials.

For months, Trump has said the jet from the Qataris would be “going away” to get “maxed out” so it could “go into any territory.” In September, he said those changes to the plane would “take about 60 days.” The president flew on the new Air Force One to Ireland that month without any issues. He then used the plane regularly during a midterm travel blitz in October, which meant it was not out of commission for an extended period.

Instead, the plane has received some improvements and periodic maintenance, but it is unclear whether it has been fully “maxed out,” per the officials. A longer upgrade period is expected in the future, according to one of the officials, but those upgrades will not take a full 60 days.

In recent months, the plane has received some “cosmetic” enhancements to the interior, the other U.S. official said, but that did not cover the larger work that the White House said would take place eventually.

“We don’t comment on specific upgrades or modifications to Air Force Once,” a senior administration official told NBC News in a statement. “We maintain a consistent posture that ensures a safe, secure, and reliable capability for the President of the United States and routinely evolve the capability as required to maintain that posture. It is the greatest Presidential plane ever built.”

In July, Trump said the plane “has a lot of capability.”

“But as I understand it, in about a month ​or so, they’re gonna send it to have it be maxed out,” he said. “It’ll take about a month.” Trump did not detail the nature of the work, and the White House has not explained why the original assessment of 30 days later doubled to 60 days.

At the time, then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said in a statement that the new Air Force One was “perfectly safe” for domestic and overseas travel but noted in July that the plane would “receive additional upgrades and enhancements in the fall which will take approximately one month to complete.”

World.title: Russell Brand says ‘I am not guilty’ in statement from prison read by his wife
World.content:
Russell Brand declared “I am not guilty” in a new statement read by his wife on his YouTube channel Sunday, days after a London court sentenced him to prison on rape and sexual assault charges.

The 51-year-old comedian and former actor was sentenced Nov. 9 to 10 1/2 years in prison after a London court found him guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He pleaded not guilty to all counts and denied all of the allegations.

In a new YouTube video, Brand’s wife, Laura Brand, read the statement on his behalf.

“So, Russell has asked me to read something to you today: ‘Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ, God bless you for your support. As you know, I am not guilty for the offenses I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening,’” she said.

“I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey. ... I’m in the biggest sex offenders prison in Europe. The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated,” she continued, reading his statement.

“And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone. I don’t know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me. Let us all love, pray for, and forgive one another as God forgave us,” the statement said.

Brand closed by asking the public to support his wife and family. “I feel your prayers,” the statement said.

Brand’s YouTube channel features Christian-themed content, including a “Sunday Service” series he hosts with his wife. At the start of the video, Laura Brand said she would continue the series. Sunday’s episode included prerecorded video of the couple discussing faith and morality.

“Even though it’s painful, and obviously will take some getting used to for me to even sit here and not have my my companion, my person, with me, but I want to continue,” she said.

Justice Joel Bennathan called Brand a “sexual predator” before delivering his sentence. At sentencing, Brand’s victims shared in-person and written statements about the trauma and its effects on their daily lives.

Brand was convicted of raping a female fan at his home in 2009 after she met him at one of his shows. He was also found guilty of sexually assaulting three other women: one whose breasts he grabbed at a party in 2004; one who said he kissed and groped her at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005; and one who said he pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an  in 2009.

He was found not guilty of two other counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

The sentence marked a stunning fall from grace for Brand, who rose to fame as a broadcaster and stand-up comedian and went on to a Hollywood career, starring in films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek.”

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at https://www.rainn.org/get-help.

World.title: The biggest move of the NFL trade deadline paid immediate dividends
World.content:
Making his first start for the Minnesota Vikings since 2023, quarterback Kirk Cousins picked up where he left off — almost literally.

Cousins led the Vikings to a 30-10 victory over the Green Bay Packers on Sunday, ending Minnesota’s two-game losing streak and improving the team’s record to 7-2.

Cousins’s most recent start for the Vikings prior to Sunday also came at Green Bay. It was in 2023, and he tore his Achilles during that game, and Minnesota moved on from him the following offseason.

The Vikings have been looking for an answer at quarterback since, and they eventually came back around to Cousins at this year’s trade deadline. Cousins got the start Sunday only five days after he was acquired from the Las Vegas Raiders, and he made some big throws as he led Minnesota to its highest scoring output since Week 1.

“I didn’t even know what my code was to get into the building on Wednesday,” Cousins said postgame. “It took a village. I’m just grateful for all the people that stepped up to help.”

Cousins finished the game completing 21 of 31 passes for 207 yards, with two touchdowns and one interception. While his stats weren’t spectacular, he made a meaningful impact on money downs, as the Vikings finished the game converting eight of 16 on third down. (Entering Sunday, Minnesota was ranked 30th in third-down conversion percentage at 33.3%.)

Minnesota’s first touchdown came on a third and 23, as Cousins made a beautiful, drop-in-the-bucket throw to Myles Price, who bounced off defenders en route to the end zone. Cousins described it as a “big-time” play by Price.

Cousins made another great throw on a third-and-long later in the game, connecting with Tai Felton on a wheel route on a third and 15 in the second quarter. The pass set up a one-yard touchdown run on the next play.

Later, after the Packers had cut the Vikings’ 20-0 lead to 20-10, Cousins picked up another massive first, checking into a screen pass on third and 12 and finding Justin Jefferson for a first down.

“It was fun, it felt like old times watching Justin do what he just did on that play,” Cousins said. “It was like, ‘I remember that guy. He’s pretty special.’”

Five plays later, Cousins threw his second touchdown of the game and effectively iced any chances of a Green Bay comeback.

“[He] just brought a certain amount of poise, leadership, execution,” head coach Kevin O’Connell said postgame. “Ran the show incredibly clean. Can’t say enough about him, I know everybody in the organization felt it this week.”

Jefferson, one of the game’s top receivers, was perhaps the biggest individual beneficiary of his old quarterback’s return. Jefferson’s nine receptions and 13 targets were both season highs.

Though Cousins didn’t exactly light the box score on fire, his presence Sunday made Minnesota’s championship formula incredibly clear: Play lights out defense, and do just enough on offense with above-average quarterback play.

With Cousins helping push the Vikings out to an early lead, Minnesota’s defense pinned its ears back and got after Jordan Love. The Vikings finished the game with eight sacks, and limited the Packers to only 56 yards rushing.

Love, one of the game’s great deep-ball throwers, finished the game with 220 yards, his fewest since Week 4. His 46.6 QBR was also his third-worst mark of the season.

“For one of the first times this year, I thought we played complementary football,” O’Connell said.

The win was an important one for Minnesota. The Vikings are now two games clear of Green Bay in loss column in the loaded NFC North, and now also own the tiebreaker between the two teams. Minnesota kept pace with the Detroit Lions and Chicago Bears, both of whom are also 7-2.

The Vikings’ offense didn’t necessarily look perfect Sunday. But their quarterback making big throws and providing a steady hand while the defensedefense continued to dominate showed exactly why Minnesota decided to bring Cousins back.

World.title: Flights normalizing after ground stop. Here's what to know
World.content:
Air travel resumed normal operations by Sunday night after a rare national ground stop lasted more than four hours on Friday, causing chaos in the nation's airports as thousands of flights were canceled and travelers were stranded.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CBS News' "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday that travelers should expect delays to continue but "we should be running at full capacity" heading into Monday.

"What happens with a ground stop, like on Friday, we have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time for the airlines to get back and choreographed and at full capacity and operations, but we're well on our way," he said.

More than 1,400 flights are canceled for Sunday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware, while around 2,200 others are delayed.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, arrives for a news conference at the U.S. Department of Transportation, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. Tom Brenner/ AP Photo

How did the FAA ground stop happen?

The ground stop began at 3:36 p.m. ET Friday when the FAA ordered the stoppage while approximately 3,500 flights were in the air.

"The FAA issued a ground stop out of an abundance of caution while 3,500+ planes were in the air," Duffy said. All airborne planes were able to land safely.

It was lifted around 8:20 p.m. ET Friday.

This marked the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that, the last national ground stop occurred after the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks.

Around 9,159 flights were canceled on Friday and 7,190 were delayed, according to FlightAware, stranding passengers at major airports across the country.

Officials attributed the ground stop to aging system infrastructure and legacy technology.

"It's just the FAA is still using this really old telecom network that has to be updated, upgraded, and I think built brand new," Duffy said on "Face the Nation" on Sunday.

Duffy told reporters on Saturday that a preliminary investigation found that an L3Harris contractor was working in a remote FAA location and switching old copper wire to fiber while replacing a router. The router that was being switched then started flooding other routers, overloading the system. There were 1,000 attempts to log on every four to five seconds, he said.

Visitors watch an airplane as it prepares to land at Washington Dulles International Airport after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted nationwide ground stops in Chantilly, Va., Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. Cliff Owen/ AP Photo

The transportation secretary said the FAA is working to determine if the issue was human error or if a faulty router was installed. Duffy said that many contractors "take our money and provide really poor service." He also said that L3Harris, a technology and defense company, owned the system.

L3Harris said Saturday that the company has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the company said in a statement, adding they take the nationwide ground stop and "its impact" seriously.

Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters on Saturday that updating the wires was a routine maintenance issue that the agency had been working on for years. About 70% of the system has been transferred from copper wires to fiber. After the router began flooding the system for 45 minutes, the FAA could not determine the cause of the instability. The instability then spread to 17 facilities, he said.

"Out of an abundance of caution," the FAA decided to issue a ground stop, Bedford said. He said he stands behind that call.

Bedford said there was zero evidence of anything nefarious or anything AI-related.

Senior government sources told CBS News on Friday that the issue was isolated to specific hardware: Cisco 600 series routers manufactured between 2001 and 2006.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a Friday briefing there were no indications the ground stop was the result of a cyberattack. Duffy said Saturday he doesn't believe it was a cyberattack, but that it was an FAA system that didn't "meet the moment."

Request for more FAA funding

Duffy said in a social media post on Friday that the FAA is working to modernize "this aging infrastructure thanks to a $12.5 billion down payment secured by President Trump, but that isn't ENOUGH."

"I've been talking about this for almost two years, and I've been asking the Congress for money. I've asked for a lot of money," he said Saturday. "Now, the Congress gave me a partial payment. They gave me 12 and a half billion dollars. And one of the problems that we had was they weren't quite sure that we would spend the money well and we'd build with the money."

The Trump administration boosted its request for air traffic control funding to $30 billion late Friday.

President Trump, who broke his silence Sunday on the ground stop, said in a new post on Truth Social that his administration has begun upgrading that system, but that the task should not be done in "drips and drabs."

"If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently," Trump wrote on social media Sunday. "It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS!"

In another post, he complained about how his Democratic predecessor had maintained the FAA and the air traffic control system, accusing the Biden administration of making an "old and broken system worse than when they began."

Rep. Rick Larsen, the ranking member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and Rep. Andre Carson, the ranking member of the Subcommittee on Aviation, said in a joint statement Saturday that FAA and DOT staff will brief the committees on Monday about the additional $30 billion requested by the Trump administration.

"This ground stop left the flying public and aviation workforce in disarray and seeking answers that the Trump administration waited hours to share," the two Democrats said. "The safe travel of the flying public must always be our top priority. Our committee, on behalf of the flying public, will hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again."

The pair said the Trump administration has only used $1 billion of the $12.5 billion approved by Congress.

"Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money," they said.

Can Americans still travel safely?

Several U.S. officials said it is completely safe for Americans to fly.

"Our top priority right now is making sure travelers get home safely to their families as quickly as possible," Duffy said Friday.

The FAA administrator said on Saturday there were 50,000 flights scheduled for Friday and by the time the ground stop happened, 30,000 flights had been completed. Due to the ground stop, about 12,000 flights were not able to be completed — around 3,000 of those were private flights, while the rest were commercial, Bedford said.

Delays remain possible at major airports nationwide, including those in Boston, Atlanta, Miami, Pittsburgh, New York City, Los Angeles and Baltimore.

An American Airlines flight takes off from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Va., after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. Tom Brenner/ AP Photo

Duffy said travelers should check with their airlines before heading to the airport. Delta said on Saturday it would offer customers flexible rebooking options. The airline said it was continuing to restore operations after a four-hour ground stop.

"Customers traveling today should expect delays and additional schedule adjustments as we work to reposition flight crews and aircraft, " Delta said.

American Airlines said on Saturday the airline has taken a number of steps toward recovery, but travelers should continue to monitor the situation as operations return to normal.

"While we are taking every step to limit the impact on our customers and team members, the lingering effects of this major disruption to the national airspace system will continue today, including additional delays and cancellations."

Southwest said Saturday the airline instituted a waiver to allow customers to cancel their flights or rebook them at a later date without penalty.

"We are working to get our Customers to their destinations as quickly as possible," Southwest said.

World.title: Siblings of man run over by ICE agent say incident was "intentional"
World.content:
Houston — The siblings of a Mexican construction worker run over last month by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in an unmarked SUV allege the incident that left their brother with severe injuries was "intentional."

"It was not an accident," Miguel Parra Hernandez's sister, Carmen Parra, told CBS News in an exclusive interview. "The videos show everything."

Rodolfo Parra said he cried when he saw videos depicting the Oct. 10 incident that left his brother with a broken leg and hip injuries.

"You can hear all my brother say, 'Ah, you broke my leg. Ah, you're breaking my leg,'" Rodolfo Parra said.

The siblings described 48-year-old Parra Hernandez as a "hardworking" family man who has lived in the U.S. for 34 years, since leaving Mexico in the 1990s as a teenager.

"My brother is not a criminal," Carmen Parra said.

Mario Alberto Morales, the ICE officer who struck Parra Hernandez with his vehicle, was indicted in late October by a Texas grand jury on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Morales' attorney has called the incident an "accident," while ICE has denounced the prosecution as a "political stunt."

"He says he's done"

While Parra Hernandez does not have a criminal history and was not the target of the ICE operation the day he was hit and detained, he remains in the agency's custody, recovering from his injuries. ICE has not disputed that Parra Hernandez lacks a criminal record, but says the Mexican national is in the U.S. illegally and subject to deportation.

Parra Hernandez's siblings claim their brother's mental and physical health has deteriorated while in ICE custody, so much so that he's suffered from suicidal ideation.

"He says he's done," Carmen Parra said. "He wants to just go to sleep and not wake up because he says, 'I'm done in this life.' But we love him."

In a letter to acting ICE Director David Venturella and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Friday, a group of Democratic lawmakers led by Rep. Lizzie Fletcher accused ICE of obstructing efforts from Parra Hernandez's family and counsel to talk to him and rejecting food brought by relatives.

"The treatment of a long-time community member is unacceptable and a violation of his constitutional rights," the lawmakers said, demanding Parra Hernandez's release.

Representatives for ICE did not respond to questions about Parra Hernandez's health and treatment, and the allegations in the lawmakers' letter.

Parra Hernandez's siblings said he was on his way to work on Oct. 10 when he and a co-worker were approached by ICE agents. Surveillance video shows the two men running out of a white truck and attempting to flee, before an ICE vehicle appears to strike Parra Hernandez from behind.

In a statement following the incident, ICE claims Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle. But Sean Teare, the Harris County district attorney, alleges the ICE agent "aggressively steered his vehicle into Parra Hernandez."

Houston limits cooperation with ICE

Parra Hernandez's hospitalization is one of several ICE-related controversies that Houston Mayor John Whitmire said have spread fear in the Houston area and prompted him to take action.

Following the stunning Republican losses in Texas and across the country on Election Day, Whitmire blocked Houston police officers from contacting ICE when they stop someone who may be in the U.S. without a valid immigration status.

"We do not collaborate unless the person is a really bad person. We're not concerned about someone that got pulled over for a traffic violation, or someone over a noise ordinance," Whitmire told CBS News. "We are going after the bad guys that have committed a new offense, a new danger to our community."

Whitmire said local officials can still work with ICE when someone in the U.S. illegally is booked in jail for criminal conduct.

He argued his executive order is designed to lower "fear and anxiety" in the community, referencing the fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican immigrant killed by an ICE agent over the summer during an attempted vehicle stop. The deadly shooting remains under investigation.

Since the policy change in Houston, officials in Austin and San Antonio have announced similar proposals.

Whitmire said he's taking a risk with his directive, citing the threat that Republican Gov. Greg Abbott's administration could sue Houston. But Abbott will soon be replaced by Gina Hinojosa, the first Democrat to be elected Texas governor in decades, and Whitmire said he can "guarantee" she will not force him to work with ICE.

He also acknowledged the move may prompt the Trump administration to withhold federal funds from Houston.

"Of course, I'm concerned about the Trump administration every day, but you have to use your good judgment," he said.

World.title: Billy Evans tells his side of "You Can See Everything," Elizabeth Holmes' portrayal
World.content:
Billy Evans may be the most-talked-about person in the most-talked-about film of the year, the documentary "You Can See Everything." He sat down with "CBS Sunday Morning" for his first-ever TV interview.

Why now? "You gotta learn really painful lessons sometimes in life," he said. "And with Elizabeth going through everything she did in the press, the lesson that was ingrained in us is, 'You can't lose your voice.'"

"You Can See Everything" is a film by Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder, who shot to fame as an absurdist comedian, and who (along with cameras) moved in with Evans and his partner Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before the disgraced Theranos founder reported to prison in 2023.

Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes in a scene from the documentary "You Can See Everything." A24

Evans, a 34-year-old MIT grad who'd also worked in high-tech, emerges as a shape-shifting central character. Asked if he is the person we saw in the film, or something else, Evans said, "I'm deeply passionate about my family and about the work that I do. But no, I am not some controlling monster who's leveraging his wife for insert-whatever-anybody-is-saying. No, I am not those things."

It's easy to understand why the genre-bending film has become a cultural phenomenon … harder to understand why Evans agreed to do it.

"I think sometimes I take too big of risks," he said. Such as? "Inviting Nathan Fielder into your home for 34 days and trusting somebody to have the right to portray you in any way, shape or form that they so choose."

In the film, Evans is portrayed as a villain – controlling and manipulative. Yet, Evans doesn't seem angry about that: "It's super-painful, but me being angry about it doesn't help change it. Look, I'm going to live my life with integrity and with who I am, and I hope people can see that over time. But if they don't, what I care about is the people that I know, people that love me."

Billy Evans talks about the documentary "You Can See Everything." CBS News

In fact, of the documentary that has gotten rave reviews, Evans says, "I love the film," despite the fact that he is made out to be a villain. "I would have preferred for that not to be the case, but it's entertainment, you know, and I didn't get to control that edit."

His goal, he said, was "to have people see Elizabeth. And when I watch that movie, I see the person that I love in exactly who she is."

In 2014 Forbes Magazine crowned Holmes the youngest self-made female billionaire. By 2017, the year she and Evans met, she was under investigation for defrauding investors for a diagnostic machine that she falsely claimed could test for hundreds of diseases with a single drop of blood.

Evans says when they first met, he did not know who she was. "I had been at her office earlier that week," he said. "I had, like, seen her the same week. But no, really, like, the first time I met her, I did not know."

Theranos co-founder and CEO Elizabeth Holmes leaves the Robert F. Peckham Federal Building with her partner Billy Evans, during her fraud trial on November 22, 2021, in San Jose, Calif. AMY OSBORNE/AFP via Getty Images

"You Can See Everything" leaves us questioning what the truth is. There are also moments that are cringe-worthy, as when Evans is filmed in the shower completely naked. [You really can see everything.]

"I did not give consent to do that," said Evans. "Now, did I know they were filming me in the shower? Yes. But we would film 16 hours a day. Like, all sorts of things were filmed with assurances made. I was just as surprised as the rest of the country to have my whole body on camera for the world to see, and it's been an awkward experience in having, like, your kids' teachers see that. It's really uncomfortable."

Billy Evans, Elizabeth Holmes and Nathan Fielder in "You Can See Everything." A24

Evans said there were "inappropriate" and "awkward" things that happened every single day, as well as requests to film things that, he said, "are not appropriate for television. All sorts of things that the details I'd rather spare the audience."

The film's production company, A24, said, "Everything that was filmed was filmed with their consent."

Some who see the film leave convinced the co-director, Nathan Fielder, had feelings for Holmes. "I think that there are bits that are played up to criticize his own bias," said Evans. "This is a film about, what can you trust? And at the end nothing is clear."

Evans says he has not spoken to Fielder since he's seen the film. "I think they're probably worried I'm gonna sue 'em," he said, adding he has no intention to do so. "Because maybe I'm a different person than most people think I am."

Evans lives with their two young children in Texas close to Holmes' prison, and carries a gun 24/7, he says, to keep his family safe. "We have threats of violence against us daily," he said. "I've got two kids. Threats of violence daily. And I would never forgive myself for having the tools, the skills, and the ability to protect my family and not doing it.

"I will give you an example: The other day, I was driving my kids to school. And a car came up behind us really, really quickly. And we stopped at the light. And the guy starts screaming next to me. And this isn't just road rage, okay? And his window is down. And he is screaming the most vile things you have ever heard about: 'I know where you live. I know who you are. I know where your kids sleep, and the things that I will do to you.' And it was terrifying."

Even given the fallout from the movie, he says he would do it all again: "With the same people, making the same film again, with everything that I know right now? 100%. Because I would also have a better understanding of what I was walking into."

Elizabeth Holmes could transfer to a halfway house next summer. Until then, Evans and their children visit her every week behind bars.

Having his children see their mother in prison, Evens said, has become "strangely normal. Like, I hate it. I absolutely hate that my daughter's first steps were in federal prison. I hate that. … But it doesn't mean that we can't find joy as we experience this. And our job, to them, is not to talk about how much it hurts and how painful it is, but to find the joy in seeing how many acorns we can collect in the prison yard and fit in a water bottle. It's finding, you know, the small, little games that we can play to make each time we go to the same place, every weekend, feel like you're going to Disneyland."

Evans said he used to count the days she was in prison, but that became too painful. "It's been since May 30th of 2023," he said. "I miss her so much. You know, I talked to her right before I came in here. And I told her, I said, 'I'm kinda nervous.' And she said, 'Just be zen. Enjoy it. Embody love. And I'll talk to you, when you're done.'"

World.title: Flight disruptions expected to last into Monday
World.content:
Flight disruptions expected to last into Monday

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/AP

Thousands of travelers are still waiting on airlines to reschedule cancelled flights after Friday's nationwide ground stop.

More than 2,300 flights have been cancelled and more than 8,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. are delayed as of Sunday evening, according to FlightAware.com . Airports in Dallas-Fort Worth and Atlanta were experiencing the largest number of delays, with more than 250 flights each.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that "by the end of today, end of tomorrow, I think we will be back to normal."

"What happens when you have a ground stop like what happened on Friday is we have airplanes and air crews that are out of position," Duffy said during an interview with NBC's Meet The Press . "It takes some time for the airlines to re-choreograph all of their crews and aircraft."

Sponsor Message

Duffy on Saturday blamed faulty maintenance by L3Harris Technologies Inc., a federal contractor, for the nationwide ground stop.

L3Harris was working on replacing two sections of old copper wire with new fiber-optic cables, Duffy said. At some point, the FAA's legacy equipment became overloaded and disrupted communications.

"The initial investigation indicates that two potential locations as the reason for the excessive data flooding the systems: a radar site in Amarillo, Texas and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas."

L3Harris on Saturday said it takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on the nation "seriously."

"With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3 Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system," the company said in a statement . "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel."

President Trump on Sunday called on Congress to approve more funding for air traffic control to update its aging systems.

"We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve," Trump said in a post on social media.

Sponsor Message

In 2025, under Trump, Congress approved $12.5 billion for air traffic control safety system upgrades. But on Friday, Duffy and the White House requested $50 billion in emergency funding.

"We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades," Duffy said on the Sunday news program. "We need to put money into it to make sure that it's still resilient for the future."

But two Democrats, Rep. André Carson of Indiana and Rep. Rick Larsen of Washington state, members of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, said billions have been appropriated but only a portion has been spent.

"Congress approved $12.5 billion for the Department of Transportation to make necessary safety upgrades to our air traffic control system," Larsen and Carson said in a statement on Saturday. "Fifteen months later, the administration's obligated $4.3 billion but only spent $1 billion, leaving $8 billion unobligated and $11 billion unspent. Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?"

Nick Daniels, president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, told NPR on Sunday that he encourages every effort to understand what led to Friday's ground stop, and ensure that policies, practices and mitigation plans were followed.

But the ultimate credit goes to the air traffic controllers, he said.

"It's one of those moments that nobody can be prepared for, nobody can plan for," Daniels told NPR. But it shows what air traffic controllers can do when an entire national airspace system is shut down while working on unreliable equipment, he said.

World.title: Far from home. Voyager 1 is now farther than anything man has sent into space
World.content:
Far from home. Voyager 1 is now farther than anything man has sent into space

toggle caption i AP/NASA

NASA's Voyager 1 has traveled farther than anything else that humans have launched into space. On Wednesday, it's set to reach a new milestone: reaching a distance that is one-light day away from Earth.

NASA is celebrating the occasion with the "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day . " Calling it a symbolic celebration, NASA is asking the public on Tuesday night to send Voyager's call sign V-G-R into the sky in morse code. Use a flashlight, phone light or anything that can blink a sequence.

If you want to take part:

V - Three quick flashes, one long flash

G - Two long flashes, one quick flash

R - One quick flash, one long flash, one quick flash

Sponsor Message

What exactly is a light-day?

A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, or more than 16 billion miles.

This NASA spacecraft has traveled for nearly 50 years, launching Sept. 5, 1977.

Over the course of its mission, Voyager 1 has conducted flybys of Jupiter and Saturn. In 1979, it discovered a faint ring system on Jupiter. In 1980, the spacecraft took detailed photos of Saturn's rings and moons.

While on its journey, on Feb. 17, 1998, Voyager 1 overtook the U.S. space probe, Pioneer 10, becoming the most distant human-made object in existence. It and its twin, Voyager 2, are the only spacecraft to have operated outside of the heliosphere, which acts like a protective shield of the solar system.

Voyager 1 reached the interstellar boundary in 2012. Its interstellar mission continues to chart and measure the magnetic fields, particles and plasma waves outside the sun's heliosphere and the atmosphere of other stars.

Earlier this year, NASA elected to shut off Voyager 1's Low-energy Charged Particles experiment, or LECP, which has helped scientists map the structure of space, in order to save power. Scientists said this could keep the probe alive longer..

Voyager 1 has two science instruments still running: one that measures magnetic fields and another that listens for plasma waves.

Sponsor Message

In addition, the Voyager spacecraft is carrying the Golden Record – an interstellar "time capsule" to communicate Earth's story to extraterrestrials.

toggle caption i NASA/JPL-Caltech/via AP

The gold-plated record contains 115 images, natural sounds such as surf, wind and animals, and spoken greetings in 35 different languages. Included are instructions, in symbols, on how to play the record and the origin of the probe.

Voyager 1 is estimated to reach "light-day status" at 5:16 a.m. ET on Wednesday, after 49 years, two months and 11 days of travel.

World.title: Who makes Sydney Sweeney's American Eagle jeans — and under what conditions?
World.content:
Who makes Sydney Sweeney's American Eagle jeans — and under what conditions?

toggle caption i Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/via Getty Images

KARACHI, Pakistan — In a slum dotted with shimmering pools of sewage, a garment worker nods in recognition as Sydney Sweeney slowly zips up her jeans in an American Eagle Outfitters  playing on a smartphone.

But it's not Sweeney she recognizes — it's the jeans and jacket. This woman, a single mother, has worked on American Eagle production lines and seen those denim styles and similar models. "I know how all of them are made, because I have worked on them," she says.

When Sweeney's  for American Eagle landed in July last year, with the tagline "Sydney Sweeney has great jeans," it triggered debate over whether it was a winking reference to eugenics because of Sweeney's va-va-voom beauty: thin, blonde, blue eyes, large breasts. Following the controversy, American Eagle said in a September 2025 statement that "'Sydney Sweeney Has Great Jeans' is and always was about the jeans." (Sweeney did not respond to NPR's request for comment.)

Sponsor Message

Missing from the debate over whether the  was about jeans or genes was any significant reflection on who actually made the American Eagle jeans that Sweeney was wearing — as in, the workers. The majority of garment factories operate out of Asia, so most Americans will never meet the workers making their clothes or see the conditions they're made under.

The workers who make Sydney Sweeney's jeans

Workers like that single mother. She asks that we refer to her as S., the initial of her first name, because she fears her bosses at the garment factory where she works will fire her if she's identified. "If you raise your voice, they'll push you out," she says. "We are helpless."

S., a young woman, works at a factory run by a company called Artistic Garment Industries, where she says she's paid about $144 a month, a sum that supports her son and her mother.

toggle caption i Betsy Joles for NPR

She says the factory is "oppressively hot." It was 106 F outside when we met her, and she says the factory inside is even hotter. She says it's hard to leave her workstation to drink water because she has to meet her production targets. She says she has to check the quality of 1,000 to 1,600 pieces of clothing a day — and she's fainted three times this year. "I feel faint, and I can barely stand. I have no energy in my hands and feet," S. says. "They don't even let us sit down." But S. says she has no other options.

Sponsor Message

Artistic Garment Industries confirmed it makes clothes for American Eagle but tells NPR that it does not push out workers who complain about their working conditions. The company says it has a robust complaints system that workers can use and says it frequently checks on temperatures inside different parts of its factories.

In response to questions NPR sent to American Eagle, the company says it's "committed to working directly with our suppliers to protect the health, safety, and rights of workers. We take the concerns raised by workers — and those whom NPR interviewed — very seriously."

S. is one of around 20 workers we interviewed over the spring and summer in Bangladesh and Pakistan, two of the world's biggest global garment production hubs outside of China. Those men and women worked in five different factories. All of those workers asked NPR not to use their full names and to use only the initial of their first name, worried they'd lose their jobs or be blacklisted from future jobs if they were identified.

Inside the world of fast fashion

Although we focused on the American Eagle jeans worn by Sweeney for the 2025 campaign, the reporting led to a bigger issue: how fast fashion is made, because garment factories make clothes for multiple brands at once. Workers we met told us they made clothes for Levi's, Massimo Dutti, The Gap, H&M and American Eagle. They said it's common knowledge at the factories which brands they are making clothes for, in part because some workers are stitching on the labels.

The garment workers we spoke to offered strikingly similar accounts. And they echoed worker testimonies in multiple reports by labor and climate rights groups. The workers told us they're paid low wages, even as they're expected to reach what they say are unreasonably high production targets, often laboring in sweltering factories.

Sponsor Message

These are production targets like stitching 200 sleeves an hour or checking the quality of a thousand pieces of clothing a day. The workers we interviewed say they are unable to hydrate or cool down properly, even as extreme heat caused by climate change makes their workplaces and homes even hotter.

It can be four to six degrees hotter inside a factory, says Jason Judd , executive director of the Global Labor Institute at Cornell University, which researched heat inside garment factories and worker homes . "You've got all those bodies, all that material, all that machinery putting off heat. You've got ventilation problems."

"We're starting to see fainting, heat illness, exacerbation of chronic disease, even death," says Cara Schulte, a re searcher at Climate Rights International. She authored two reports on the impacts of heat on garment workers.

Schulte says workers are put under that extreme pressure to reach production targets. A major reason is that brands demand their suppliers make enormous volumes of clothes on tight deadlines and on thin profit margins. And she says garment workers are vulnerable to the heat because they're clustered in countries like Bangladesh and Pakistan. She cites U.N. publications stating that t hose factories are "in areas that are warming faster than the global average, that are [already] incredibly hot and humid."

H&M, one of the brands that workers identified making, said it "put great effort" in ensuring fair payment to its suppliers and that labor costs are "excluded from the price negotiations of our product orders" to ensure that worker wages were not driven down.

Citing her own research, Schulte of Climate Rights International says garment workers are compelled to risk their health to survive. It's not a choice, she says. "Workers are not choosing to take these risks," she says. "They're being forced into them by poverty."

Sponsor Message

One worker's survival strategy

Like a woman who asks we call her R. When we met in February in the Bangladesh capital, Dhaka, R. said she was working six days a week, at least 12 hours a day, for $140 a month at a garment factory run by a company called MBM, which makes denim clothes, including for Levi's. Her job is to stitch 150 pieces of fabric per hour, which are assembled into jeans.

R. says she's considered old for a garment worker — around 40 — and says she's slowing down. She says she's berated by managers who tell her, "Why aren't you speeding up your work?" She says, "If you're short by even a single piece, you face a lot of harassment."

R. says she's managed to meet her targets so far. "Allah has kept me safe," she says. She says friends of hers who could not meet their targets were fired by the company. To reach her targets, R. says, she stays at her station throughout her shift. "Even going to the washroom has become extremely difficult."

So despite Dhaka reaching 98 F this summer, R. says she doesn't drink much water to avoid the need to take bathroom breaks. There's no AC on the factory floor, but R. says managers run ceiling fans and keep windows open.

R. says that if workers feel faint, their bosses will let them rest in a sick room for about 20 minutes. But, she says, management will terminate employment if workers say say they feel sick too often, so she pushes herself to keep going.

MBM did not respond to questions from NPR about worker allegations.

Despite the issues she raised, R. says she works in a good factory. She says the pay is higher than other garment factories. And if she's terminated, she says the company will pay the wages, including overtime, that she's owed. But she doesn't want to be let go.

Sponsor Message

Taking the heat

These garment factories are blazing hot in part because it's expensive to retrofit them with air conditioners. A manager for MBM, who asked that NPR not use their full name because they are not authorized to speak to media, says that the company needs a brand to commit to purchasing long term in order for retrofitting the factory to pay off. The manager says no brand had committed to that kind of long-term business.

Conditions in Bangladesh are still better than in other garment hubs, because of the scrutiny after a building collapse killed more than 1,100 garment workers in 2013. Just three weeks after that disaster, a legally binding commitment called the International Accord emerged between hundreds of brands, companies and trade unions in Bangladesh to protect worker health and safety. So far, 248 global brands and retailers have signed on, covering 2.8 million workers. A version of the International Accord was established in 2023 in Pakistan but has a smaller footprint.

toggle caption i Jeff Holt/Bloomberg/via Getty Images

toggle caption i Munir Uz Zaman/AFP/via Getty Images

There's meant to be more progress on protecting workers from extreme heat soon. Last December, the International Accord agreed to develop a protocol on heat stress. That means keeping workers cool will be an enforceable commitment for brands. For apparel companies in Bangladesh and Pakistan that have signed on to the accord, the International Accord staff will regularly inspect factories to ensure they're kept cool.

Judd, of the Global Labor Institute, says he believes there will be positive changes because the garment industry knows "they've got a problem — whether it's from a worker rights perspective, or from a business perspective, workers are slowing down, productivity is falling," he says. Either way, "you've got an interest in reducing the heat stress."

But for now, workers in Pakistan , in particular, described sweltering conditions, particularly in the port city of Karachi , one of the world's hottest garment hubs, according to the U.N.'s International Labor Organization.

toggle caption i Betsy Joles for NPR

In a dusty bazaar in Karachi, we met seven factory workers who mostly worked for two companies: Artistic Garment Industries — S.'s employer — and another called Artistic Milliners. Both produce clothes for big Western brands.

Sponsor Message

In their interviews with NPR, women who work, or worked, for Artistic Garment Industries described vomiting, fevers and fungal skin infections that they say were caused by the heat.

One young woman worker is I.

Her workday starts at 8:30 a.m. She says she is expected to work beyond her regular, nine-hour shift — often till 9 p.m. — and on Sundays as well, at some stretches. But she says she isn't paid all her overtime. I. also says supervisors on her floor berate workers if they leave their stations to drink water because it might cause them to miss their targets. So, I. says, "one person goes" to the water cooler and weathers the abuse, "fills a water bottle" and shares it with colleagues. I. says she gets about a glass full.

I. accuses the company of "eating" her money — and her health. "They exploit us," she says.

She says she suffers from dizziness and what she describes as a sense of fatigue and weakness. She pushes herself to work: "I can't lose my job — who else will support my family?"

Artistic Garment Industries contested these claims of unhealthful and exploitative working conditions. The company told NPR that it has a robust internal complaints system that workers could, and do, use. The company says it pays all overtime and does routine checks to ensure that the heat and humidity are not excessive on the factory floor. The company says it places water stations near workers to encourage them to hydrate and says it would not tolerate supervisors who pressure workers not to drink or use the bathroom.

Workers at Artistic Milliners described hot working conditions that badly impacted women and older male workers. One woman reported constantly feeling faint but said she pushed through. The workers said their supervisors let them drink water when they needed to, but they were pressured not to use the bathroom. Some workers said they were not paid for all the overtime they worked.

Sponsor Message

A 66-year-old former worker at Artistic Milliners, Sardar, said he was let go during the pandemic but had not been given compensation owed to him by the company. When NPR met him in June, he was homeless and relied on his children for meals. When we asked if he'd ever asked for charity, he began crying: "I'd feel ashamed if people thought I was begging."

Artistic Milliners did not respond to requests for comment about statements by Sardar and other workers. Parts of the company are certified through Fair Trade USA , a nonprofit organization that certifies companies that uphold high ethical standards for treatment of workers. NPR has sought comment from Fair Trade regarding allegations made by men and women who used to work for Artistic Milliners but has not received a response.

Answers from fast fashion brands

NPR also sent detailed questions to brands that workers said they made clothes for, alongside American Eagle.

Levi Strauss & Co. says it takes "allegations of worker rights violations seriously."

Inditex, the parent company of Zara and other labels, says Artistic Milliners , which makes clothes for one of its prominent brands, Massimo Dutti, was "subject to a corrective action plan." NPR contacted Inditex for clarification on what that corrective action plan entails but did not get a response.

Gap Inc. says it is "committed to supporting the rights and safety of workers."

H&M said in an emailed response that it has "required" AGI "to develop and implement corrective action plans to address the issues identified" by NPR: "Compliance with our requirements is a condition of our business relationship." H&M also said it recognized "the increasing risks associated with extreme heat" and is part of a pilot on heat stress in Pakistan conducted by the International Accord to develop "effective and sustainable solutions."

Sponsor Message

Those big brands partly ensure working conditions in factories are up to standard through regular audits. I. and other workers tell us they regularly saw auditors visiting their garment factory floors. They also tell NPR that supervisors give them advance warning. I. says that the supervisors "tell us to say that the working conditions are better than they actually are."

Anna Bryher is part of the workers' rights group Labor Behind the Labels, which published a report in July on the "clear mismatch" in the garment industry auditing system "between what the brands are saying and believing and hearing and what the workers report." Bryher says her findings suggest that the auditing system relied on by big brands is not working.

Artistic Garment Industries says workers may have confused regular updates informing workers of their rights with being told what to say at audits. The clothing brands that NPR reached out to did not comment on allegations regarding workers being told what to say during audits.

Some workers tell NPR that their supervisors warn them that if the workers were to criticize working conditions to auditors, the companies running the factories will lose business — and that they should paint a positive picture of their workplaces. "In other words," I. says, "they ask us to lie about everything."

With additional reporting by Hanan Biswas in Dhaka, Shahzaib Wahlah in Karachi and Abdul Sattar.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: New Orleans port sues owners of tanker involved in Mississippi crash
World.content:
New Orleans port sues owners of tanker involved in Mississippi crash

toggle caption i Gerald Herbert/AP

New Orleans port officials filed a lawsuit against the owner and operator of the tanker that crashed into a docked cruise ship in the Mississippi River on Friday.

The Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans is seeking at least $1 million in damages from people connected to the tanker, which is called Atlantic Asphalt. The lawsuit also names the tanker's owner, Nave Shipping SA and its management company Thome Ship Management as defendants.

The lawsuit states that at 12:30 p.m. Friday, the Atlantic Asphalt tanker crashed into the American Heritage river cruise paddleboat which was docked at the Thalia Street terminal for disembarkment of passengers.

Sponsor Message

There were almost 200 people on board the American Heritage at the time of the crash, which left the ship on its side and partially submerged. All passengers and crew survived, including more than 100 who were rescued from the river, leading New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno to dub the incident "the miracle on the Mississippi."

There were 32 people brought to the hospital, none with critical injuries.

The port commissioners said as a result of the collision, the Thalia Street terminal had significant damage.

"The extent of said damage remains under investigation, but physical damage is currently estimated to exceed [$1 million], with additional substantial direct, indirect and consequential damages anticipated," the lawsuit reads.

The lawsuit also states that the port expects to incur additional costs, including clean-up, surveys, repair, replacement and salvage costs.

On Friday, port officials requested the tanker be seized and sold to cover costs of the damage. A federal judge approved the seizure request.

Officials claimed that the collision occurred "as a result of the negligence, gross negligence, fault or carelessness" by Atlantic Asphalt, Nave Shipping SA and Thome Ship Management.

toggle caption i Gerald Herbert/AP

Clearing the Mississippi

As of Saturday, eight people remained in the hospital, two in serious condition.

Mayor Moreno said Saturday that the Atlantic Asphalt had been towed away from the site, but noted it could take weeks to fully remove the American Heritage.

Sponsor Message

Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said that operations were now focused on fully reopening the river and safe removal of hazardous material on board the American Heritage. Burnham said it is estimated there are 160,000 gallons of fuel on board the ship.

"We're going to have divers in the water so they can do a full assessment on what's the right path to be able to remove it," Burnham said. "We also have teams that have been deployed throughout the entire area, the river system to monitor the area for any pollution."

Burnham said there are restrictions in place for boat traffic along the Mississippi River.

The exact cause of the crash is unknown, though Burnham said the tanker appeared to have an issue with steering. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the crash.

John DeLeeuw, board member with the NTSB, said during a Saturday briefing that the tanker's voyage data recorder was recovered.

"The voyage data recorder essentially is going to provide the data," DeLeeuw said. "It's like a flight data recorder on an aircraft. We can look at speeds and all kinds of information. It's essentially covering speed all kinds of maneuverings that was done on the ship."

A preliminary report by the NTSB is expected within 30 days, with the final report on probable causes and safety recommendations coming in 18 to 24 months.

World.title: Laws limiting coal miners' exposure to toxic dust are in danger of being rolled back
World.content:
Laws limiting coal miners' exposure to toxic dust are in danger of being rolled back

Coal miners who are exposed to silica dust are at a higher risk of black lung disease. Despite decades of advocacy, new efforts to regulate the toxic dust are under threat.

Transcript

AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:

An epidemic of an incurable disease among coal miners in Appalachia got new attention this past Tuesday. Federal regulators propose major changes in the rules that are supposed to protect miners from black lung disease. Our former NPR colleague Howard Berkes has been reporting on this since 2011. His new "Frontline" PBS film, "Coal's Human Cost," also came out Tuesday. He joins me now to discuss the film and the difficulties in regulating the mining industry. Thank you so much for being here, Howard.

HOWARD BERKES: It's good to be with you, Ayesha.

RASCOE: For many people, black lung disease sounds like something out of the dark days of coal mining a hundred years ago. Why is there still an epidemic of black lung disease?

BERKES: Because the biggest coal seams in Appalachia were mined out in recent decades, and mining companies turned to much thinner strips of coal. And they're embedded in rock, and so the mining machines pulverize rock as they cut into coal. That results in very fine, easily inhaled particles of highly toxic silica, which cause severe scarring and stiffness in the lungs.

RASCOE: I mean, that just sounds horrible. Before we get to that human cost you focused on in the film, what rule changes did the federal Mine Safety and Health Administration propose Tuesday?

BERKES: You know, this goes back actually to 2024 when the Biden administration imposed strict limits on silica dust and, for the first time, direct enforcement. The changes proposed on Tuesday give mining companies more control over monitoring silica dust because, the agency says, mine operators have 40 years of experience. But, you know, that experience hasn't prevented thousands of cases of disease, and the rate of disease now among some miners is back to what it was in 1978. So the bottom line for mining advocates is that the proposed changes make enforcement weaker.

RASCOE: What does the failure of mining companies and federal regulators to keep miners safe look like on the ground?

BERKES: I met miner Tim Balthis in Virginia. He was diagnosed five years ago with the advanced stage of disease.

(SOUNDBITE OF DOCUMENTARY, "COAL'S HUMAN COST")

TIM BALTHIS: The death is real. That's going to happen. If the rest of my body stays in good shape and I don't get killed in a car accident or something like that, I'm going to die of black lung. I know that. With the diagnosis that I have, I'll probably be lucky to live into mid-60s.

BERKES: How old are you now?

BALTHIS: I will be 58 in November.

BERKES: Mid-60s isn't far off.

BALTHIS: No. No, it's not.

RASCOE: Your film also steps back in time a bit and revisits some scenes from another film of yours eight years ago. Why did you do that?

BERKES: We wanted to show how little has changed since then, so we talked to some of the same people we featured back then. That includes Ron Carson, the now-retired director of the Stone Mountain black lung clinics in Virginia.

(SOUNDBITE OF DOCUMENTARY, "COAL'S HUMAN COST")

RON CARSON: For us to be sitting here discussing what we are talking about over the past eight years and nothing's been done - it just - it's horrifying. It's just horrifying, 'cause we put the data out there. We put the facts out there. And something should have been done on a higher level to make sure that we wouldn't be here today talking about this.

RASCOE: Howard, like, is there no hope for minors with this disease, no treatment? Maybe lung transplants, for example - could that help them?

BERKES: There really is no cure, but one of the miners we featured in the film did have one of those double lung transplants five years ago. Greg Kelly described for us how difficult that surgery was.

(SOUNDBITE OF DOCUMENTARY, "COAL'S HUMAN COST")

GREG KELLY: The surgeon, when he talked to me - he said, I had to scrape your lungs out. He said, I couldn't even pick them up. He said, that's how bad they was. He said, you cold miners are extremely tough to do lung transplants on.

BERKES: That's how bad these miners' lungs get. Now, lung transplants for coal miners are rare, and recovery isn't easy. Greg Kelly is one serious infection away from losing his new life. He's thrilled that he's had five more years. But the median life expectancy for a minor with a lung transplant is just 6 1/2 years.

RASCOE: Yeah. That's really tough to go through. With this new proposed regulation, like, what's ahead for coal miners?

BERKES: Lawsuits are certain for the regulation. It'll likely be months, and maybe longer, before the new regulation is final. And in the meantime, the tougher regulation that the Biden administration put in place is on hold indefinitely. So miners today have the same protections that failed so many of them in the past.

RASCOE: Howard Berkes, thank you so much for joining us.

BERKES: Thank you, Ayesha.

RASCOE: The film "Coal's Human Cost" from the PBS program "Frontline" is now available for streaming on YouTube and at pbs.org.
