World.title: Costa Rica Bill Would Let Towns Cap Airbnb Rentals
World.content:
Costa Rica’s municipalities could limit how many short-term rentals operate in a neighborhood, a residential building or even on certain floors of a condominium tower under a bill filed in the Legislative Assembly by the opposition Frente Amplio party. The same bill would create a 10% tax on the commissions and service fees that platforms such as Airbnb earn from stays in Costa Rica.T

The bill, brought forward by Frente Amplio caucus leader José María Villalta, would overhaul Law 9742, the 2019 framework law that governs vacation rentals booked through digital platforms. It would also rename the law to emphasize coexistence between short-term rentals and the residents around them. The bill does not ban vacation rentals or set a national cap.

Under the proposal, local governments could limit the number, density, concentration and type of tourist lodging by district, neighborhood, zone or property. Any limits would have to rest on technical studies of housing, infrastructure, public services, the environment and mobility, with public participation and periodic review.

In mostly residential buildings, municipalities could restrict rentals to certain floors or sections if studies show they harm access to housing. The bill would also amend the Condominium Property Law so that building rules could not override those municipal limits, and it would recognize a right of residents not to be displaced by a disproportionate expansion of short-term rentals.

The 10% tax would apply to platform commissions, service fees and other income from stays in properties located in Costa Rica, regardless of where the platform is based. The bill as described in its filing does not say whether platforms could pass the cost on to hosts or guests.

Half the revenue would go to municipalities, in proportion to what each canton generates, for affordable housing and community infrastructure. Another 30% would go to the Banco Hipotecario de la Vivienda (Banhvi) for housing and affordable rental programs in cantons under housing pressure, and the remaining 20% would go to the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) for registry and oversight work.

Registration rules would also tighten. No property could be advertised without ICT registration, and each would receive a unique number that must appear in every listing. Hosts would have to prove ownership or authorization, comply with zoning and municipal licensing, be current on tax and social security payments, meet safety and sanitary standards, declare maximum capacity and provide an emergency contact. Platforms would have to register with the ICT, share information with state institutions and withhold and pay applicable taxes, with joint liability if they fail to do so.

Fines would be set in base salaries, the unit Costa Rica uses to calculate legal penalties. Hosts would face 1 to 3 base salaries for minor infractions, 4 to 10 for serious ones and 11 to 20 for very serious ones, along with possible suspension or cancellation of their registration. Platforms would face 20 to 100 base salaries for serious infractions and 50 to 200 for very serious ones. Publishing a listing without verifying its registration, leaving out the registration number or ignoring an order to remove a listing would all count as serious infractions.

The bill’s explanatory text argues that short-term rentals, especially those booked through platforms, have affected the housing market and the makeup of neighborhoods, and it cites a 2025 OECD study on housing pressure in coastal areas. It says the current law treats vacation rentals mainly as a tourism, commercial and tax matter without accounting for their effect on housing, and it states that the reform does not aim to restrict tourism.

Villalta has said the proposal seeks to balance tourism development with communities’ right to remain where they live and to find affordable housing. Law 9742 already requires owners of vacation rentals to register with the ICT and with the Finance Ministry’s tax administration, and stays booked through platforms are already subject to the 13% value-added tax. The ICT and the Finance Ministry would have nine months after the reform took effect to set up information-sharing protocols with municipalities.

The bill faces a long path. The Legislative Assembly is in extraordinary sessions through Jan. 31, a period in which lawmakers may only debate bills placed on the agenda by the executive branch, and the government’s latest agenda includes no bills from opposition parties, including the Frente Amplio.

To become law, the proposal would need to clear committee and pass two votes in the full Assembly.

World.title: Nearly Half of Costa Rica Driving Tests Failed in 2026, the Most Since 2015
World.content:
Nearly half of all practical driving tests for a standard car license in Costa Rica have ended in failure this year, the highest rate in more than a decade. Of 104,497 practical tests for the B1 license with a recorded result through Nov. 12, 51,050 ended in failure, a rate of 48.9%, according to the Road Safety Council (Cosevi).

That is the highest failure rate for the category since 2015, when it reached 52.5%. The rate fell to 28.4% in 2023 and 29% in 2024 before climbing to 37% in 2025. The figures count tests, not people, and leave out no-shows. A driver who failed twice is counted twice. Motorcycle tests were the next hardest to pass. The A1 category had a failure rate of 35.2% and A2 had 30.2%, while categories such as B2 and C2 came in near 18%.

Across all license categories, 74,946 of 202,714 practical tests ended in failure this year, or 37%. Cosevi’s records show one person has failed the practical exam 40 times, the most it has recorded, while the individual record on the regular written exam is 55 failures. The data released did not include reasons for the failures. If you are working through the licensing process, the numbers suggest planning for the possibility of a second attempt.

The figures come as Costa Rica marks the World Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims on Sunday. The National Insurance Institute (INS) counted 535 road deaths through its October cutoff, up 13.6% from 471 at the same point in 2025. Motorcyclists accounted for 268 of those deaths, roughly half. They also made up about two-thirds of the injured, 27,182 of the 41,388 people hurt in traffic crashes from January to September, according to the INS.

The INS recorded 37,392 crashes in those nine months, and the number of people injured rose 9% from 37,974 in the same period of 2025. The Costa Rican Red Cross says it responds to a traffic crash about every eight minutes. The cost is borne in part by mandatory vehicle insurance. The INS said the compulsory policy, known as the SOA, has spent 50,576 million colones (about $112 million) this year on medical care and compensation for crash victims, or more than 185 million colones (about $411,000) a day.

With two months left in the year, the road death toll on Costa Rica’s highways and streets is already 64 higher than it was at the same point in 2025.

World.title: Gasoline Could Drop in December as Cooking Gas Jumps
World.content:
Filling your tank in Costa Rica should get cheaper in December but cooking with gas will cost more. The Costa Rican Oil Refinery (Recope) has asked regulators to cut the price of regular gasoline by ₡103 a liter, while the standard 11.3-kilogram (25-pound) cylinder of cooking gas would rise by ₡912, according to preliminary figures Recope presented on Friday to the Public Services Regulatory Authority (Aresep).

Under the proposal, regular gasoline would fall from ₡807 to ₡704 a liter, a drop of about 13%. Super would fall ₡28, from ₡805 to ₡777, and diesel would ease by ₡9, from ₡807 to ₡798. The 25-pound gas cylinder, the best-selling size in the country, would climb from ₡7,721 to ₡8,633, an increase of about 12%. None of the new prices is final. Aresep must review Recope’s figures and approve them before they take effect.

For anyone driving, the cut on regular is by far the largest of the three. At the proposed price, a liter of regular would cost about $1.58, or roughly $5.97 per US gallon, at the current exchange rate. On a 45-liter (11.9-gallon) tank, the change would save about ₡4,635, or roughly $10, each time you fill up. It would also undo an unusual situation that began in October, when regular became more expensive than premium. In December, regular would again cost ₡73 less per liter than super.

Recope attributed the lower gasoline and diesel prices to falling international oil prices, easing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and greater availability of crude on world markets, according to Teletica. The gas increase has a different cause. Recope said cooking gas it bought on international markets at higher prices during October kept later price declines from showing up in this adjustment, Monumental reported.

The cylinder increase will be felt in a lot of kitchens. About half of Costa Rican households use liquefied petroleum gas, mostly for cooking, according to Aresep. At the proposed price, a 25-pound cylinder would cost about $19.35, up from about $17.31. If you are due to swap a tank, buying before the new price takes effect would save you the difference, and it is worth taking 30 seconds to check that the cylinder is safe before you carry it home.

The December adjustment follows a stretch of rising energy costs. Fuel and transport fares drove consumer prices higher for a second straight month in October, when diesel alone rose more than 17%, and Costa Rica has paid $701 million more for imported fuel this year. Aresep has not said when the new prices would take effect. Adjustments normally apply from the day after the regulator’s resolution is published in the official gazette, La Gaceta.

World.title: El Salvador’s Marcelo Arévalo Opens ATP Finals With a Win
World.content:
El Salvador’s Marcelo Arévalo and Croatian partner Mate Pavić began their ATP Finals campaign with a 7–6 (7), 6–4 victory over France’s Theo Arribagé and Albano Olivetti on Sunday. The fourth-seeded pair recovered from a 2–0 deficit in the second set to win their opening match in the Todd Woodbridge Group at Turin’s Inalpi Arena. The match lasted one hour and 27 minutes.

Arévalo and Pavić had to work through a tense first set before taking control. They missed five chances to win the set, including four in the tiebreaker, but eventually claimed it 9–7. The French pair responded by breaking early in the second set. Arévalo and Pavić fought back, winning six of the next eight games to finish the match in straight sets.

The final numbers showed how close it was. Arévalo and Pavić won just five more points than their opponents but converted two of their four break-point chances. The win gives the Salvadoran-Croatian team a strong start in a tournament where one loss does not mean elimination. The eight doubles teams are divided into two groups of four, and each pair plays the other three teams in its group.

The top two teams from each group advance to the semifinals. Also in their group are defending champions Harri Heliövaara of Finland and Henry Patten of Britain, and Brazil’s Orlando Luz and Rafael Matos. Heliövaara and Patten won their opening match Sunday, beating the Brazilians 6–3, 5–7, 10–4.

Arévalo and Pavić are seeking their first ATP Finals title together. They reached the final in 2024 and return to Turin as one of the more experienced teams in the field. This is Arévalo’s fifth appearance at the year-end event and Pavić’s ninth. Their opponents on Sunday were making their ATP Finals debut after winning six doubles titles during the season.

Arévalo and Pavić still have two group matches to play. The semifinals are scheduled for Nov. 21, with the doubles final on Nov. 22.

World.title: Costa Rica Free Zones Barely Grew and Jobs Disappeared
World.content:
Production in Costa Rica’s free zones, the export parks that host most of the country’s multinational employers, grew just 0.6% year-on-year in September, according to the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR). That is 13.6 percentage points slower than in September 2025, when the sector was riding a surge in medical-device exports.

Employment in the regime is also slipping. The Central Bank’s three-month moving average put free-zone jobs at 195,410 in August 2026, down from 197,101 a year earlier, a loss of 1,691 positions.

The Central Bank now projects free-zone output will expand about 3% in 2026, compared with a preliminary 12.7% in 2025. The rest of the economy, known as the definitive regime, grew 3.3% in September and accounted for 96% of national growth, according to the bank’s monthly economic activity index (IMAE).

The slowdown has revived a long-running dispute over the strong colón. The weighted average dollar price on the Monex exchange market fell from 503.02 colones on Nov. 6, 2025, to 449.58 colones on the same date this year, a drop of 10.6%. Exporters and multinationals earn in dollars but pay salaries and local costs in colones, so each dollar they bring in now covers less of their payroll. The dollar hit a record low of 446 colones this week.

According to minutes of the Central Bank board’s Oct. 23 session, Henry Vargas, the bank’s division manager for data and statistical analysis, told directors that the 2025 export spike had to normalize and that international uncertainty is the main drag on the sector. He cited a U.S. Commerce Department study of possible new tariffs. Vargas said the exchange rate did not rank among the leading factors that companies named in a regional business survey the bank conducted with other central banks in October and November 2025, in which about 70% of firms said international uncertainty affected them deeply, though he acknowledged that business chambers do raise it.

Board member Jorge Guardia questioned why the exchange rate did not appear among the factors, noting that outside reports frequently point to it, according to the minutes. Central Bank President Róger Madrigal said job reductions in the sector are tied mainly to decisions by parent companies rather than directly to the exchange rate, while allowing that profit margins may have narrowed even where output has not.

Vargas also told the board that the closures of operations by Intel and Qorvo had been fully completed by September. The bank has attributed part of the year-on-year slowdown to that base effect, along with the exceptional medical-implement exports of 2025. September did bring the first month-to-month acceleration in free-zone output after 12 consecutive months of deceleration.

Business groups dispute the bank’s reading and the free-zone association Azofras has said the colón’s appreciation pressures operations and could weigh on company decisions to stay, expand or keep staff. Sergio Capón, president of the Costa Rican Chamber of Industries, has said it is unreasonable to separate multinationals’ decisions from the exchange-rate trend.

The debate comes after free zones lost jobs for the first time in seven years, and as several companies have scaled back hiring plans, including a call center that cut its Costa Rica job pledge over competition from Asia. Analysts have also warned that office vacancy could climb as multinationals cut jobs.

The Central Bank has bought more than $1.2 billion on the exchange market this year to slow the colón’s rise, and Madrigal has said the market has an excess supply of dollars.vFree zones employ close to 200,000 people and are one of Costa Rica’s largest sources of dollars, so a sustained slowdown would reach well beyond the export parks themselves. Whether the sector’s first monthly uptick in a year marks a turning point or a pause will become clearer as the Central Bank releases its October and November figures.

World.title: Should You Buy Travel Insurance for Costa Rica After the US Ground Stop?
World.content:
The nationwide ground stop that froze US air travel on Friday lasted a little more than four hours, but it left a question that will outlast the backlog. If a failure inside the air traffic control system can strand thousands of people bound for Costa Rica, should you buy travel insurance for your trip?

The quick answer to this is that insurance would not change what you get back for your flight, but it could cover almost everything else. Ten flights were canceled at Juan Santamaría International Airport on Friday and 23 were affected in all, according to airport operator Aeris, as the US ground stop spilled over into Costa Rica.

In the United States, airlines canceled more than 5,000 flights on Saturday as planes and crews worked their way back into position, according to the flight-tracking service FlightAware. For visitors, that meant missed first nights at hotels, lost tours and unplanned nights at a gateway airport or in San José.

Airfare is the one part of your trip you do not need insurance for. Under US Department of Transportation rules, if your flight is canceled and you choose not to travel, you are owed a full refund, even on a nonrefundable ticket, and that holds no matter what caused the cancellation. Airlines also waived change fees after the ground stop.

What airlines do not owe you is the cost of being stranded. Their promises of meals and hotels cover only disruptions they cause, and federal rules treat air traffic control failures as outside their control. After an outage like Friday’s, you pay for your own hotel, meals and ground transport unless the airline chooses to help.

That gap is where a comprehensive policy comes in. This kind of plan insures the full prepaid cost of your airfare, hotels and tours and bundles several benefits together. Trip delay coverage pays for a hotel room, meals and transport when you are stuck, usually after a wait of 3 to 12 hours and up to a daily limit. Trip interruption coverage reimburses prepaid nights and tours you lose when you arrive late. Missed connection coverage helps with the cost of catching up, which matters if you are booked on a domestic flight to the coast or a boat transfer to a remote lodge.

The wording matters more than the brand. The strongest policies cover a delay by a common carrier for any reason. Others list specific causes, so check that air traffic control failures or government action are on that list. Coverage that comes with a credit card tends to be narrower. During last year’s US government shutdown, American Express said its card benefits, including trip delay and trip cancellation coverage, would not pay for cancellations or delays caused by the FAA’s emergency order.

There are other limits. Insurance pays only what you cannot recover from the airline, hotel or tour operator. Canceling your entire trip over a one-day delay is rarely covered. Cancel for any reason upgrades cost more, usually return only part of your trip cost, often up to 75% or 80%, and generally require you to cancel at least two days before departure. You also have to buy a policy before trouble starts, because once a disruption is in the news, new policies will not cover it.

Comprehensive policies are commonly priced at about 4% to 10% of the insured trip cost, depending mostly on your age and coverage limits. For a couple spending $6,000 (about ₡2.68 million) on a Costa Rica vacation, that works out to roughly $240 to $600 (about ₡107,000 to ₡268,000). The same policy usually includes medical and evacuation coverage, which many US health plans, including original Medicare, generally do not provide outside the United States.

Whether that is money well spent depends on how you book. If your hotels are refundable and you have a spare day at each end, you have little to lose beyond a night or two. If you have a prepaid week at a jungle lodge, a sportfishing charter and a tight connection home, you have far more at stake. With the high season only weeks away and no way to rule out a repeat, it is worth doing that math before you book.

If you decide to buy, you can compare quotes from multiple travel insurers side by side and filter by the coverage that matters most for your trip, such as trip delay and missed connections.

World.title: The Perfect Family Beach Day at Playa Carrillo, Costa Rica
World.content:
This is between me and you. Don’t tell anybody else. We don’t want too many people overcrowding the places I’m about to tell you about. Here’s how to spend a perfectly wonderful day at the beach in Guanacaste with your family. My little family and I have done this a bunch of times, so we’ve now got it down to a science. We’re going to spend the day at Playa Carrillo.

This works best if you’re staying along the coast in the general Tamarindo/Playas del Coco area in which case it can be a there and back again day trip. Here we go. First, you and your significant other have to plan on leaving at a decently early hour in the morning. For us it’s something like 9am. This will allow you plenty of time for driving, lunching, beaching, and returning. Of course, you’ll never hit this lofty goal. Anyone with kids knows that a series of things will inevitably happen that will push back your departure time, but that’s life.

Once everybody’s finally in the car with seatbelts in place the drive begins. The drive is actually part of the fun of this day trip. The most common route takes you through the historic city of Nicoya. When I say through it, I mean wiggling your way through the city’s narrow, sometimes one-way streets, past all of the little stories, people selling things on the sidewalks, and a mix of contemporary and historic-looking buildings. If you feel like it, you can pull over at the park with the neat old church and buy the kids some ice cream. Even if you don’t stop, driving through the buzz of human activity has a nice vibe.

The nice drive portion of the day continues after you make it out of Nicoya. As soon as the city ends you drive through a series of adorable little towns separated by hilly green cow pastures dotted with palm trees. For reasons that are unclear to me, the houses on this stretch of road are particularly well maintained, brightly painted with well-manicured gardens. ‘What a nice place to live’ comes to mind as you drive.

Right about now everybody in the car is starting to get antsy and that’s ok because I know exactly where you need to stop. Since you missed that departure time by about an hour, it’s time for lunch anyway. As you approach the coast, you need to wind your way steeply uphill before cresting the mountain and riding downhill to the coast. As you reach the highest point of this mountain (almost definitely driving 5 miles per hour behind an enormous truck that you can’t pass), there’s a restaurant called La Roca.

I have no affiliation with La Roca. This info is all coming from the love in my heart. My family has been going there for years. Originally, it was pretty rustic, but sometime over the last few years they completely remodeled it and now it’s modern and very nice. Either way, the magic of the restaurant was, and still is, the view. It sits atop the mountain with a stunning view of the countryside below. You can even see a waterfall in the distance.

There’s a clearly marked trailhead right next to the restaurant and you can hike to the waterfall that you can see from the balcony. We always say we’ll do the hike next time and never do. Waterfall hike or not, order anything on the menu, it’s all delicious. Enjoy the view, recharge your batteries, and then pack everybody back into the car and start driving downhill to the beach.

As you arrive at the coast, you’ll hit the small beach town of Samara, which is a fun place to explore, but you’ll have to save that for another day because you’re heading to Carrillo. After Samara you only have about ten minutes left in the car. After you cross a one-way bridge over a small river, you’ll want to pull over at the little store for snacks and drinks because it’s the last one before the beach.

Fully stocked with goodies from the store, you’ll drive five more minutes until you hit Playa Carrillo. You’ll know you’ve made it when you’re driving next to an enormous beach with calm waves, the entirety of which is lined with several rows of palm trees. You can pull over at any spot you please. Throughout the entire palm tree section of the beach there are benches, tables, and grills. The vibe is laidback and local, with lots of families enjoying the shade and waves.

After several hours of fun in the sun, it’s time to pack everybody and everything back into the car and start the drive home. If your family is anything like mine, the return trip is a lot quieter than initial drive as your kids will be slouched over sleeping like a pile of puppies. So, there you have it, the perfect family beach trip. Remember, this is between me and you. I don’t want the tables at La Roca and the shady spots at the beach to be full of other people.

About the Author

Vincent Losasso, founder of Guanacaste Wildlife Monitoring, is a biologist who works with camera traps throughout Costa Rica

World.title: Costa Rica Flights to the US Back on Track as Trump Blames Biden for Ground Stop
World.content:
If you’re flying between Costa Rica and the United States today, your flight should run close to schedule. The nationwide US ground stop that froze departures on Friday afternoon ended after about four hours, and airports in Costa Rica reported operations returning to normal on Saturday.

Check your flight in your airline’s app before you leave for the airport anyway. Aeris, which runs Juan Santamaría International Airport outside San José, has asked passengers to confirm their flight status directly with their airline, since itineraries can still change. Friday’s disruption hit both of the country’s main airports. At Juan Santamaría, Aeris said 12 departures and 11 arrivals were affected, and six departures and four arrivals were canceled. The rest were moved to overnight and early Saturday slots.

In Liberia, Guanacaste Airport representative Renata González said seven flights were canceled and that operations returned to normal over the course of Saturday. The outage was not an attack. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said it began during maintenance work to replace old copper wiring with fiber-optic cable, which disrupted communication with planes and radar feeds. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no evidence of hostile action.

Duffy said more than 9,000 US flights were canceled and nearly 25,000 were delayed. It was the longest nationwide ground stop in the United States in 25 years. On Sunday, President Donald Trump made his first public comments on the ground stop and blamed his predecessor. In posts on Truth Social, he called the Biden administration “an FAA disaster” and said “everything they touched turned bad.”

Trump said his administration has a plan for the flight control systems and urged Congress to approve the money quickly, saying much of the current air traffic control system is 50 years old. Efforts to modernize the FAA’s systems have spanned several administrations of both parties.

If your flight was canceled Friday and you have not rebooked, start with your airline’s website or app rather than the airport counter. If you decided not to travel at all, US rules entitle you to a refund for a canceled flight, even when the cause was out of the airline’s control. Whether a policy would have covered you is a separate question, covered in our guide to travel insurance after the ground stop.

Many US airlines fly a plane into Costa Rica and send the same jet straight back, so delays at a US hub can still ripple into a departure here, as Friday’s cancellations showed. Air traffic between the two countries has largely recovered, but the episode has renewed debate in Washington over how quickly, and at what cost, the US air traffic control system should be replaced.

World.title: Tru-Juice make it five straight with win over Racing United
World.content:
In this file photo, Tru-Juice FC striker Daniel Roberts celebrates after scoring the winning goal in the club’s 1-0 victory over Molynes United in the Jamaica Premier League at Stadium East. (Photo: JPL)

ST CATHERINE, Jamaica – Tru-Juice FC extended their winning run to five straight games on Sunday, beating Racing United 2-0 at Ferdie Neita Park in their Legend Jamaica Premier League first round game.

Tru-Juice took their points total to 23 from 10 games, four points more than Montego Bay United who snapped a four-game winless run by hammering Tivoli Gardens 4-0 at the Edward Seaga Sports Complex. Arnett Gardens, Cavalier FC, defending champions Portmore United and Dunbeholden FC also recorded wins.

Both goals at Ferdie Neita Park came late, a Marcovich Brown own goal in the 77th minute giving Tru-Juice the lead before substitute Rodave Murray made the points sure with a well taken goal in time added in the second half.

Montego Bay United had their first ‘clean sheet’ since early October with their win over Tivoli. Richardo Ramsey scored a double, in the 32nd and 44th minutes; Nashordo Gibbs, who got a rare start this season, scored in the 39th minute, and Devonte Campbell added a fourth in the 72nd minute. It was back-to-back losses for Tivoli and third in four games, resulting in them dropping to ninth place in the tables.

Arnett Gardens followed up their win over Waterhouse on Monday by beating last-placed Humble Lion 3-0 at Effortville. It was Arnett’s first time getting consecutive wins this season, bringing them to fifth place on 16 points, on goal-difference over Cavalier.

Giovanni Taylor scored an early double – in the 15th and 19th minutes – to lead Arnett and take over the scoring lead with nine goals, while Revaldo Mitchell scored the third goal in the 84th minute.

Cavalier were also back-to-back winners, getting past Treasure Beach 3-1 at Turners Oval; Adrian Reid sent them ahead from the penalty spot in the 17th minute but the visitors drew level in the 32nd minute through Jardel Williams.

Treasure Beach missed a chance to take the lead just before half time when Daniel Hardy missed a penalty kick in time added at the end of the first half.

Romarion Thomas restored Cavalier’s lead in the 48th minute before Dwayne Allen added a third in the 84th minute.

Javier Brown scored two penalty kicks to lead Portmore United to a 5-2 win over Molynes United to move to 13 points from eight games.

Jevaughn Grant gave Portmore the lead in the eighth minute but Molynes equalised a minute later through Tyrique Wilson.

Brown restored Portmore’s lead with his first goal of the game in the 12th minute but they had to wait until the 73rd minute to get a third goal when Peter McGregor scored.

Brown added his second and the team’s fourth in the 77th minute and Demario Dailey scored their fifth in the 80th minute while Ronaldo Barrett scored a second for Molynes in the 87th minute.

Dunbeholden created some space from the relegation zone teams after their 2-1 win over Chapelton Maroons at Dunbeholden Sports Complex.

Marlon Allen scored for Dunbeholden in the 21st minute to take the lead, Robino Gordon levelled for Chapelton in the 28th minute but Shakeen Powell scored the winner in the 39th minute.

Sunday’s Results

Cavalier FC-3, Treasure Beach-1

Humble Lion FC-0, Arnett Gardens FC-3

Tivoli Gardens FC-0, Montego Bay United-4

Dunbeholden FC-2, Chapelton Maroons-1

Racing United-0, Tru-Juice FC-2

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Holness urges labourites to push back against ‘lies and misinformation’
World.content:
Prime Minister Andrew Holness addresses Jamaica Labour Party supporters at a mass rally on Sunday, August 10, 2025. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Prime Minister and Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) Leader Dr Andrew Holness has implored party workers and supporters to push back aggressively at what he said are lies being spread about the Government, in particular as it relates to the distribution of hurricane relief.

Holness made the rallying cry Sunday, as he addressed the 83rd annual conference of the governing JLP at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James. This year’s scaled-back conference was a delegates-only affair.

The prime minister said there was a thought process around how information surrounding the distribution of hurricane relief should be disseminated.

“Should we publish a list reserving the private information of the beneficiaries or we could create a little database and if you want to go on the list and you want to look at what anybody get, then you have to put in your ID and a notification is sent to the person that got the benefit that you scrutinising them,” Holness said.

The reaction of the crowd suggested they were not in favour of such an approach but the prime minister said, “We’re at this point because we cannot allow the lies that they have told about our distribution to stand”. He said the Government was not afraid of criticism, declaring that he was first to be critical of himself when things were not happening fast enough.

“I’m the first to come out and say I’m not satisfied, I’m the first to say people haven’t gotten [aid],” said Holness.

The Government has for sometime been forced to push back at what it has deemed to be lies and misinformation in the public space, in particular on social media, about how hurricane relief has been distributed, and the pace at which it is distributed.

The Administration has been locked in a war of words with veteran entertainer Beenie Man since late last month following a controversial interview the dancehall artiste gave on a British broadcaster. During the interview on ITV News, Beenie Man questioned how millions of dollars in donations intended for Hurricane Melissa victims was distributed.

“This is nothing new that the Government get the money, the Government distribute the money the wrong way. The people who supposed to get the money haven’t been getting any,” Beenie Man claimed.

That was met with vigorous pushback from senior members of the Government including the prime minister. But, with no side backing down, and with several other entertainers throwing their support behind him, Beenie Man has since penned and released a song titled Weh di money deh. He has also reacted with colorful language to a senior Government minister who suggested that he was a washed-up entertainer seeking relevance.

Last Thursday the Minister of Justice and Constitutional Affairs Delroy Chuck admitted the Government had failed to adequately communicate to the Jamaican people how hurricane relief has been allocated.

On Sunday the prime minister warned that where substantial effort has been made, where changes are being made, “and we continue to portray this general view that there are no systems and there is no distribution taking place, then people look on at us will say ‘why should we give Jamaica?’”

“There is a level of thinking in the country that labourites must stand up against, don’t be afraid, challenge the lies, don’t be afraid to speak the truth, let your voices be heard,” Holness encouraged.

“We are not afraid of criticism and we will make our own criticism as well, that is a democracy,” he added.

He said: “They have been used to making lies and falsehood and we sit down and tek it and say a so it go but we cannot do that [anymore]”.

World.title: Which company is the best employer in Jamaica?
World.content:
JACKSON… chairman of the Award Selection Committee

Ten of Jamaica’s most worker-centric companies have been nominated for the inaugural Gordon “Butch” Stewart Business Leader Award.

The programme, which is being staged under the theme ‘Business Leader: Employer of Choice’, will highlight the success that many of the country’s forward-looking boardrooms have had in introducing global best practices culture to their workforce.

The Jamaica Observer Media Group, which promotes the award project will, within the next few days, begin publishing stories on the firms that made the final list of 10 nominees. These institutions were trimmed down from an initial group of 60, then 40 which were further culled to 25. From this list, the final 10 nominees ultimately floated to the top

— separated in part by the compelling responses they submitted to an exhaustive and multifaceted questionnaire that, in its totality, teased out the most telling aspects of their industrial relations ethos and practices.

“All the companies that participated in the survey dedicated valuable executive time to provide granular details of their industrial relations practices,” said Moses Jackson, chairman of the Award Selection Committee.

“This was an unusually competitive group that all deserve to be nominated and to have their stories shared with Jamaica,” Jackson noted. “Even though they didn’t make it to the nomination stage, they contributed to the invaluable insight that the committee gained into the global best practices trend that Jamaica must continue to embrace so as not to fall behind. But the 10 nominees in particular are at the forefront of a positive transformation now underway at our workplaces.”

These nominees represent a wide range of industries — though not the country’s full breadth. From BPOs to financial services, manufacturing, utilities and tourism, the group of 10, both individually and collectively, present a leading-edge profile of modern management practices within corporate Jamaica.

But there are notable absences — not the least of which is the zero representation of private security services, one of the largest employers of labour in the country.

According to Jackson, that’s in part because while employers in this sector tend to lean disproportionately into contract employment, the award programme has a strong bias towards companies that offer permanent, full-time engagement. The job security and clear pathway to upward mobility that are fundamental features of this latter business model is a central value of the award programme.

To qualify for nomination, companies must have a minimum permanent staff count of 300, Jackson added.

“The Business Leader Award is by design a big business programme,” he explains. “We are interested in critical mass and the ability of employees to climb up a well-defined corporate ladder and organisations that can offer meaningful careers at scale.”

The Observer will chronicle the industrial relations successes of the 10 nominees in both its printed and electronic platforms.

However, readers will have to wait until Sunday, December 13 to learn which company in Jamaica is deemed the Employer of Choice — at least in large measure by the evaluation of the six independent individuals who make up the Award Selection Committee.

Five of the six committee members are themselves past nominees for the award. They are:

Ambassador Audrey Marks, founder and principal of Paymaster Ja;

Audrey Hinchcliffe, founder, principal and chair of Manpower and Maintenance Services Ltd;

Gassan Azan, founder, principal and chairman of MegaMart and Bashco Ltd;

Charles Ross, principal and chairman of Sterling Asset Management Ltd; and

Fred Smith, principal and chairman of Tropical Tours Ltd.

Ian Neita, former managing director of Yellow (Pages) Ltd, stands as the sole committee member who was never nominated for the award.

Importantly, employee voices will also be heard in the voting process; they will be polled to render their own verdict of the quality of the work environment that their bosses provide for them.

The award presentation and dinner will take place at AC Hotel Kingston on Lady Musgrave Road. In this regal setting the Gordon “Butch” Business Leader for 2026 will be announced as one of the final acts of an event that will begin with cocktail reception at 4:30 pm followed at 6:00 pm by the formal presentation and dinner.

The Business Leader Award is celebrating its 30th year to the very month, since its first staging in December 1996. It was branded then and up until days ago as the Jamaica Observer Business Leader Award. Earlier this month the Stewarts — family members of Sandals/ATL/Observer late patriarch Gordon “Butch” Stewart — consented to have the award renamed as a permanent tribute to their father. The rebranding was announced at a press conference at the Jamaica Observer headquarters in St Andrew.

Butch Stewart, as he was affectionately called, was known to have revered the award programme, viewing it as a vital and effective platform for the encouragement of business growth in Jamaica, and the direct promotion of local entrepreneurs.

This is the first time that the award is recognising businesses specifically for the quality of the work environment they provide staff — a particular corporate feature for which Butch Stewart was famous within the enterprises he founded and chaired. In fact, this point was emphasised by his son Brian Jardim who spoke at the press conference to announce the rebranding.

Jardim recalled his father’s obsession with staff welfare, and noted the convergence of this philosophy with the theme of the award that bears his name: Gordon “Butch” Stewart Business Leader: Employer of Choice.

World.title: Bad roads hurting south coast tourism
World.content:
HENZELL...we have had to refund many guests based on the fact that our website is saying it takes between two to two and a half hours from Montego Bay and, in some cases, now it is taking three to three and a half hours Photo: Kasey Williams

TREASURE BEACH, St Elizabeth — Tourism stakeholders in Treasure Beach on Jamaica’s south coast are demanding urgent repairs to the main road linking the area to Montego Bay via eastern Hanover and southern St James, warning that its deplorable condition is already driving a spate of booking cancellations ahead of the crucial winter tourist season, which runs from mid-December to April.

The section of the main road badly scarred with potholes stretches from the Westmoreland/Hanover border through Ramble to Anchovy in St James.

Well-known hoteliers Jason Henzell and David Folb, as well as Transport Manager Darin James last Wednesday expressed frustration over the deplorable road.

Henzell, who operates highly acclaimed Jakes Hotel and Jack Sprat with 125 staff in Treasure Beach, said the situation is dire.

“We have had to refund many guests based on the fact that our website is saying it takes between two to two and a half hours from Montego Bay and, in some cases now, it is taking three to three and a half hours,” Henzell told the Jamaica Observer.

“It has been very costly to us. Guests who have written about the conditions of the road also deter potential guests from coming, so it has been an extremely costly situation for not only Jakes, but all of the operators along the south coast,” added Henzell.

Folb, owner of the popular high-value Lashings Boutique Hotel and Villas and Lashings Beach Club in Treasure Beach with 10 full-time staff and more than 20 linked leased businesses, shared a similar sentiment.

“The [bad] roads are causing a monumental problem. People don’t want to come. I literally spoke to a friend of mine today who is thinking about coming here in a group of six people for Christmas and they said oh, we have spoken to such and such, ‘if the roads are going to be that bad then we will go to Barbados’,” Folb told the Sunday Observer.

“It is affecting our business drastically. There are actually people who are cancelling, because of the roads… There was a famous cricketer a few weeks ago who had to leave very early because he didn’t want to chance going back on those roads on the day of his flight,” added Folb.

James, the transportation manager at Jakes hotel and Lashings Boutique Hotel, suggested that the road be patched until a permanent fix can be done.

“That road, especially out from Ramble to Montpelier, is a total disgrace. The road has been like that for almost three years. Even if they have plans to do a major reconstruction of the road, just patch the areas until then. These potholes are so wide and deep. I have the biggest vehicle in our fleet and I don’t want to drive through that bad road,” he said.

He said utilising Norman Manley International Airport in Kingston is not a viable option as that is more costly.

“It is more expensive to travel from Kingston to Treasure Beach than from Montego Bay, even though it might be quicker, but it is twice the distance in mileage, so you are burning more gas and paying tolls. With my class three vehicle, to and from Kingston with four tolls, is over $12,000,” said James.

The effect the bad road is having on the tourism industry was also highlighted by reports that last week visitors travelling to Negril from Sangster International Airport in Montego Bay had to endure a six-hour bus ride.

Last week, Opposition Member of Parliament for St James Southern Nekeisha Burchell, in whose constituency the Anchovy main road is located, posted on her Instagram account that drain cleaning and preparation for asphalt laying commenced there on Tuesday.

“After more than a year of representations work has finally begun on Anchovy main road. I’m grateful to the [National Works Agency] and contractors for getting started, and to the residents who stopped to share their appreciation. I understand the frustration with the traffic; I use this road too. Crews will continue clearing drains and preparing the road for asphalt over the coming weeks, so please take care around them. I’ll keep following up and sharing updates,” the post read.

On Thursday the National Works Agency said temporary repairs are being done to the corridors pending a major project to repair critical sections of the main roads now in the procurement phase.

Henzell said he is eagerly awaiting further updates regarding the completion date for the now under-construction Long Hill bypass, which is to be connected to the Montego Bay Perimeter Road.

“I have been trying to get onto people about the Montego Bay bypass, which apparently is going to open shortly, I don’t know if the bypass includes the exit to the south coast road,” he said.

“I am pleased that there was a meeting at Pier One and there seems to be some movement and solutions happening for Negril, but as it pertains to the south coast now, I really am interested when the ramp to the Long Hill bypass will be activated,” added Henzell.

The perimeter road is slated for completion in December. The perimeter road is complemented by the Long Hill Bypass, a 10.5-kilometre corridor upgraded from its original two lanes to four lanes with Jersey barriers. The Long Hill Bypass is slated for completion in 2027.

World.title: Crowning controversy
World.content:
Shenseea

In 2021, when Shenseea’s Trending Gyal freestyle sent social media into a frenzy and prompted many listeners to hail her as the next queen of dancehall, the entertainer was flattered by the recognition but made it clear that wearing the crown was not particularly high on her list of priorities.

At the time, the Sheng Yeng leader insisted that her focus was simply on making music, enjoying the creative process, and allowing her work to speak for itself rather than becoming consumed by the expectations that came with a coveted title.

“I’m honoured that they [the fans] see me as such [the next dancehall queen], but it wasn’t a title I’ve always wanted. I want to do music and enjoy it for the fun, not because it is expected of me to do so,” she told local media back then.

Five years later, however, the Grammy-nominated entertainer appears to have had a change of heart.

In a recent interview that has been gaining considerable traction across social media, Shenseea expressed confidence that her accomplishments have now earned her the right to claim the dancehall crown.

Pointing to current statistics as the basis for her position, the

Alpha artiste suggested that she has done enough to warrant recognition as the genre’s leading woman.

Her declaration has once again stirred the long-running conversation about dancehall’s royalty, particularly as veteran entertainer Spice remains widely regarded as Jamaica’s reigning queen of dancehall.

But while Shenseea’s international profile and commercial achievements have undoubtedly strengthened her standing in the global music industry, whether those accomplishments are enough to displace an artiste whose legacy has been built over decades is another matter.

For entertainment publicist and digital media consultant Toni-Ann Kelly, of Black Butterfly Media, Shenseea has not yet earned the crown. While acknowledging the entertainer’s commercial achievements and impressive streaming numbers, Kelly questioned whether such statistics were enough to justify her claiming the throne.

“Where she loses me is how we get from streaming and YouTube and figures like that to her being the queen of dancehall,” Kelly argued. “Beenie Man is a good example of why I say that. Sean Paul’s international reach deserves every bit of respect, and anybody can make a case for Vybz Kartel’s influence, but I still give Beenie Man the title of king because, to me, he lives and breathes dancehall… You feel how much he enjoys the music, how well he knows his audience and how much he cares about what happens to the culture. I get that same sense of commitment from Bounty Killer and Sean Paul. I hold a queen to that same standard.”

Drawing comparisons with some of the genre’s most recognisable female figures, Kelly argued that international reach must be complemented by an unmistakable musical identity and a genuine connection with the culture.

“Lady Saw was hard to miss and harder to mistake. So is Spice. With Shenseea, I find the opposite happens too often. Everybody knows her name, yet on too many records her personality gets lost in the mix,” she said.

For Kelly, being a contender for the crown requires the kind of individuality that allows audiences to immediately recognise an artiste through her delivery, writing, and stage presence.

“For somebody claiming to be the woman who captivates this space, she’s still a little too easy to miss in it,” she continued. “All the kings and queens of dancehall were captivating in every era and there was none that was or is missed.”

Entertainment publicist, media practitioner, and director of communications at Prism Marketing Consultants Raymond “Shadow” Small offers a somewhat different perspective.

He told the Jamaica Observer that he believes Shenseea has established herself as a legitimate contender, even if that does not automatically make her the rightful successor to Spice.

Small acknowledged her impressive catalogue, international collaborations, Grammy recognition, performances on major stages, and ability to reach audiences beyond traditional dancehall markets. However, he cautioned against confusing international popularity with cultural leadership.

“Being internationally successful does not automatically mean that an artiste has inherited the crown. Spice’s position was established through years of consistency, hit records, commanding performances, cultural influence and her contribution to creating opportunities and visibility for female dancehall artistes,” he said. “Shenseea has a strong argument based on her current commercial success, but Spice has an established legacy that cannot simply be displaced by streaming statistics.”

Still, Small believes the genre has enough room for both women to establish their own legacies without one having to surrender her position for the other to thrive.

“Shenseea should not have to wait for Spice to become inactive before establishing her own legacy. Both women can dominate different periods and represent different dimensions of the genre without one having to diminish the other,” he said.

World.title: ‘Fix our roads properly’
World.content:
Motorists manoeuvring the Shettlewood to Mackfield main road in the vicinity of Ramble in Hanover on Friday. Garfield Robinson

ANCHOVY, St James — Residents and business operators along the Anchovy to Shettlewood and Mackfield main roads spanning southern St James and eastern Hanover are cautiously optimistic about the longevity of road repairs now being done a few weeks ahead of the winter tourist season.

Last Thursday, the National Works Agency said temporary repairs are being done to the corridors pending a major project to restore critical sections of the main roads now in the procurement phase.

On Friday, the Jamaica Observer saw marl being utilised on sections of the thoroughfare at Chester Castle in Hanover. A few kilometres east in Anchovy, St James, residents and business operators there said they are eagerly awaiting the completion of the Long Hill bypass, but are also hoping for a permanent fix to their main road amid ongoing works there.

“When the bypass is done and I am going into Montego Bay I won’t be going down Long Hill. I will be using the bypass 24/7. You can a go down Long Hill and there is a sudden breakaway and you gone a gully and dead. I just want them to finish the work on the bypass. It would be the best thing for everybody, but for now we need a good fix to the main road, it is what we have now to use everyday,” said a welder in Anchovy who gave his name only as Massop.

The Long Hill and Anchovy to Savanna-La-Mar main road is one of the main corridors connecting the island’s north and south.

“This road is very important. There are people who use this road to get to the airport and even work in Montego Bay coming from as far as Mandeville. They are coasters from Mandeville to Montego Bay,” he added.

He pointed to the daily struggle commuters face with delays.

“Every morning there is traffic from the south-west heading into MoBay because of the road condition. A contractor is doing some scraping on the bad part of the road and I hope that they will properly fix the road. The little scraping makes a big difference with the traffic flow. The bad road goes all the way towards Savanna-La-Mar at Mackfield,” Massop told the Sunday Observer.

“Just recently people blocked the road at Ramble on the Hanover side. The bad roads go through Hanover at Chester Castle, Bethel Town, Montpelier, all of these roads are no good…The little scraping, I hope they will fix the roads properly with quality work,” he added.

He recalled the distress one motorist experienced in Ramble when his vehicle was stuck in a pothole.

“You see right at Burn Ground [Ramble], I remember the road was being fixed one morning with patching and in the afternoon rain came and washed out everything and ever since that has been a recurring problem in Burn Ground. The road patching was poor and rain just washed it out after. Hurricane Melissa came and made it worse,” Massop said.

Category 5 Melissa unleashed extensive damage to roads, buildings, infrastructure and lives on October 28, 2025.

“I saw a car on the Burn Ground road go into a pothole and people had to use another vehicle to pull it out,” he added.

Residents from Mount Carey are also hoping that the road works will last.

“From Montpeiler to Mount Carey is a good road, but the rest of the road is bad, so now that they are doing work on it, please do it properly. When the road work doesn’t last we as taxpayers lose,” said Mount Carey resident Denise.

Anchovy vendor Tadge Jones is also calling for quality work to be done.

“We want the work to be done quickly, because the traffic is terrible, but, at the same time, we want it to be done properly,” he said.

Granville Wright, a resident of Shettlewood in Hanover, complained that the bad roads are costly to motorists.

“Is the first time from the storm blow some work is being done. You see the problem is, when they are to put three inches of asphalt they put one and a half and then we the motorist suffer,” he claimed.

“Me nuh stop buy front-end parts and all sorts of rubbers in order to get my car to drive good,” he added.

World.title: MORE THAN A GAME
World.content:
Reggae Girlz team manager Crystal Walters.

For Crystal Walters, the journey from the football field to the administrative corridors of the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) has been defined by unexpected opportunities, quiet determination, self-respect, and an unwavering belief in women’s football.

It is a journey that, in some ways, mirrors the evolution of the women’s game in Jamaica — significant breakthroughs born out of perseverance and a continuing fight for recognition.

Today, as Reggae Girlz team manager and an emerging figure in safeguarding within Jamaican football, Walters occupies a position of considerable responsibility. But hers is more than a story of professional advancement. It is about a young woman, who has experienced the sport from almost every perspective and is determined to ensure others benefit from the opportunities afforded to her.

“I never imagined being actively involved administratively at the senior level, but there is always a saying that the youths just need an opportunity, and I got that and made use of the opportunity,” Walters told the Sunday Observer.

Like many aspiring Jamaican footballers, she developed her talents within the school system, moving from Jonathan Grant High to St Jago High, where she shared the field with a young Khadija “Bunny” Shaw.

Walters later represented Harbour View and The University of the West Indies in the Women’s Premier League before moving to Shortwood Teachers’ College, where her playing career blossomed.

There, she collected several accolades, including the Principal’s Award, became the institution’s first female footballer to score 10 or more goals in a season, and helped Shortwood capture the intercollegiate title in her first year.

It was also at Shortwood that she received her first national call-up, although an opportunity away from the field would ultimately reshape her future.

While still a player, Walters began assisting with administrative duties, including helping members of the national programme complete health insurance documentation. The late Jean Nelson recognised her potential and increasingly entrusted her with assignments involving the Reggae Girlz.

“She would oftentimes call me in to assist her with paperwork or even drive to Shortwood to drop off documentation for the Reggae Girlz for me to complete,” Walters recalled.

With Nelson’s assistance, another opportunity emerged, setting Walters on a path that would lead to the JFF.

She joined the federation as an intern during the historic 2019 Women’s World Cup qualification campaign, working her way through the programme as Jamaica prepared for its first appearance at the global showpiece.

Following that campaign, she continued working within the federation, assisting with marketing responsibilities, while developing the administrative skills that would eventually see her entrusted with managing the senior women’s national team.

Her progression through the various levels of Jamaican women’s football has been remarkable, but Walters admits it has been anything but straightforward.

“It has not been easy. It has been a rough journey in terms of just looking back on all that I have experienced in terms of pushback and challenges,” she acknowledged.

“It was important for me to stand firm as a woman and maintain my discipline. If it wasn’t for passion and discipline, I probably would have walked away already.”

Those experiences have strengthened her conviction that women deserve greater opportunities to contribute to football beyond their playing careers, while reinforcing the importance of maintaining her values.

“It’s never easy as a female, but it’s the respect that you put out there for yourself, you will get it back in return.”

For Walters, increasing female representation in football administration is essential to the sport’s development.

“I definitely think we need more women administrators,” she said, pointing to the increasing emphasis being placed on female involvement in women’s football programmes by international governing bodies.

“Beyond a few women that are behind the scenes, you don’t really have much involvement.”

She is particularly interested in creating pathways for former players to transition into administration, recognising that their experience and understanding of the game can be invaluable.

Plans are already being explored for workshops and consultations to strengthen women’s participation in the sport’s administrative structures.

“I am looking forward to mentoring a few women, whether past players who want to be a part of sport administration, especially football,” she shared.

“It is important for me after this campaign to see how best I can mentor, to see how I can share that wealth of knowledge to strengthen what we currently have.”

Walters is equally conscious of the responsibility attached to representing one of Jamaica’s most recognisable sporting brands.

“I represent a big brand — the Reggae Girlz, a pool of players that are elevated, educated, and are doing so much for themselves and their country,” she said.

“The onus is on me as the team manager to elevate myself. No one can do that for me except me.”

That commitment to personal development extends beyond her immediate responsibilities with the national team.

While helping Jamaica secure another World Cup appearance in 2027 remains her priority, Walters is also seeking to make a lasting contribution through safeguarding.

Having completed specialised training in Zurich, Switzerland, she has assumed a lead safeguarding role within the JFF, helping to promote safer and more respectful environments throughout the sport.

“Taking on the FIFA safeguarding lead for the JFF, it means helping to create a safer environment for our youth, administrators, everyone involved in the sport,” she explained. “How do we make it a safe space, a comfortable space for everyone to experience the love, camaraderie, but in a safe and respectful way?”

Her work addresses concerns ranging from bullying and intimidation to sexual misconduct and other threats to athlete welfare.

Walters has already led two internal safeguarding sessions involving JFF staff and conducted engagements with the St Catherine Football Association and club administrators. She has also engaged with the national Under-17 programme.

A formal safeguarding policy is being developed with FIFA’s support, subject to JFF approval.

For Walters, whose own career was transformed when someone recognised her potential and extended an opportunity, the ambition is now to help create a better environment for those following in her footsteps.

And perhaps that will ultimately prove to be one of her most meaningful contributions to Jamaican football; not simply helping the Reggae Girlz reach another World Cup, but ensuring that the next generation of women has a clearer, more welcoming and safer pathway to positions of influence.

World.title: How Brussels is learning to spot a spy
World.content:
When EU foreign ministers meet in Brussels today, the war in Ukraine will top the agenda, along with Gaza and Iran.

Ministers will assess Russia’s maximalist demands from last week’s talks in Abu Dhabi, which have cast further doubt on the prospects for future negotiations involving Europe. They’ll also discuss how to respond to the worsening humanitarian crisis in Gaza, where an estimated 400,000 displaced people are living in areas at extremely high risk of flooding — half of them children.

Next, EU countries are expected to announce a deal to set up a deportation hub in Rwanda — outside the bloc’s borders. Such hubs have become possible thanks to changes to EU migration rules agreed in June. Zoya and Nick explain how the plan would work and why rights groups are so concerned.

Finally, as tech giants in the U.S. fall for alleged intelligence operatives, Brussels bureaucrats are learning to think like spies.

World.title: Feijóo: “Haré una auditoría a las cuentas públicas de España. No me creo los datos”
World.content:
RESPUESTA. Lo que está pasando es que el Partido Socialista está haciendo una fusión por absorción a lo que se conocía como Sumar. Vox está subiendo. Y el PP está manteniendo el grueso. Nosotros hemos absorbido los 600.000 votantes del PSOE. Lo que estamos perdiendo con Vox lo estamos rellenando con el PSOE y con los abstencionistas.

P. En la configuración de las listas han cobrado relevancia perfiles diferentes. Por ejemplo, Borja Sémper o Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo tienen sensibilidades muy distintas. ¿Está tratando de equilibrar esas dos almas del PP?

R. Ya llevo cuatro años de presidente del partido y conozco más en detalle a las personas que conformamos el PP. El PP es un partido muy amplio, desde la derecha hasta un centro reformista liberal. Tenemos claras cuáles son nuestras coincidencias. A partir de ahí, las tonalidades de un mismo pentagrama son distintas. No es lo mismo una guitarra eléctrica tocada por un solista o por otro. No es lo mismo una sinfonía tocada por una orquesta o por otra.

Cayetana ha cumplido un excelente papel de marcador de Bolañosy ha denunciado todos los atropellos al Estado de derecho. Y Borja Sémper es una persona que proviene de una política muy dura en el País Vasco, que ha pasado también por una experiencia personal impactante, y siempre me entendí con él. De hecho, conseguí que dejase una consultora con el doble o el triple de sueldo y se viniese conmigo de portavoz del partido.

P. ¿No teme que el mensaje del PP quede desdibujado con perfiles que intentan abarcar un espectro tan amplio?

R. No somos un partido de influencers ni somos un partido de modas. Nosotros somos un partido de Estado. Nos hemos quedado solos defendiendo la Transición, la Constitución, el Estado de derecho. Y no va mal porque gobernamos para el 70% de la población y somos el partido con mayor porcentaje de voto dentro del Partido Popular Europeo.

World.title: Warum Merz jetzt auf Söder setzt
World.content:
Friedrich Merz reist schon wieder zu Markus Söder nach München.

Es geht um Stromsteuer, kalte Progression und politische Glaubwürdigkeit. Während die Union um Milliarden für die Mütterrente pokert, brodelt es in der SPD-Spitze. Manuela Schwesig könnte in Schwerin erklären, dass sie als SPD-Co-Chefin zur Verfügung steht. Hubertus Heil hat sich schon für eine Kampfkandidatur in Stellung gebracht. Rixa Fürsen und Rasmus Buchsteiner besprechen, was all das für Lars Klingbeil und seine Wahrnehmung in der Regierung bedeutet. Die beiden diskutieren aber auch: was hieße eine SPD-Chefin oder ein SPD-Chef ohne Regierungsamt für den Kanzler?!

Fünf europäische Staaten, darunter Deutschland und Österreich, treiben in Wien einen Plan voran: Abgelehnte Asylbewerber sollen in Return Hubs nach Ruanda gebracht werden. Doch das Vorhaben stößt auf rechtliche Hürden. Wie realistisch ist das Modell, an dem bereits Großbritannien gescheitert ist? Darum geht’s im Gespräch mit Ricarda Breyton von WELT.

Im 200-Sekunden-Interview äußert der innenpolitische Sprecher der SPD-Fraktion, Sebastian Fiedler, Zweifel an den Ruanda-Plänen. Er warnt vor ungeklärten Fragen und kritisiert die Kosten, bei gleichzeitig geringen Fallzahlen. Stattdessen fordert er eine echte Perspektive im Bleiberecht für integrierte Arbeitskräfte.

World.title: Accelerating the EU’s electric heavy-duty vehicle transition
World.content:
The EU’s transition to electric trucks, buses and coaches depends on many enabling conditions, from affordable vehicles and electricity to sufficient grid capacity and accessible charging infrastructure. But when it comes to charging, the EU needs to think beyond public stations along motorways.

Raluca Marian, general delegate of the permanent delegation to the EU, IRU

For transport operators investing in electrification, charging is an integral part of the business case. Having control over where, when and at what cost vehicles recharge is essential to managing operations and making electric vehicles economically viable.

This is why depot charging deserves much greater attention in the EU’s infrastructure strategy — and why enabling operators to share charging facilities could help make every investment go further.

World.title: Brewing up Europe’s competitiveness
World.content:
As Europe steps up the implementation of its One Europe, One Market agenda, attention is turning to how its competitiveness ambitions can translate into investment and growth. Founded in Amsterdam in 1864, Heineken has become Europe’s leading brewer, supporting a value chain stretching from farmers and bottle makers to local pubs and restaurants. Following the November 4 Beyond the Glass: Brewing Local Competitiveness event in Brussels, Heineken’s president of Europe, Glenn Caton, reflects on how policymakers and businesses can work together to sustain investment, and why the practical experience of suppliers, hospitality entrepreneurs and other partners should help shape European policymaking.

Glenn Caton, President of Europe, Heineken

Heineken has been brewing in Europe for more than 160 years. What has made it such a good place to do business?

”Europe has an enormous amount going for it. We’ve got fantastic talent, world-class universities, strong institutions and an industrial base built up over generations. And of course, there’s the single market, which is a tremendous advantage for businesses operating across Europe.

Heineken started brewing here when beer was still delivered by horse-drawn carts, and Europe has been our home ever since. We still brew close to our consumers and work with local customers and suppliers, some through relationships going back generations. They know our business, we know theirs, and that helps us keep improving and innovating together.”

You’ve mentioned innovation. Brewing is one of Europe’s oldest industries. What does innovation look like at Heineken today?

“As you said, beer has been part of European life for a very long time. But that doesn’t mean the way we make it has stood still. There’s an enormous amount of science and technology behind brewing today, from developing new products to making production more efficient and reducing our environmental footprint.

One of our key areas of innovation is alcohol-free beer. We’ve invested a great deal in improving the taste and quality of 0.0 beer, as well as finding new ways for people to enjoy it. We know that when Heineken® 0.0 is available on draught in bars, significantly more consumers choose it as a natural part of their out-of-home experience. That’s why we’re delighted that it’s now available on draught in 10,000 outlets across Europe.

Heineken started brewing here when beer was still delivered by horse-drawn carts, and Europe has been our home ever since.

We’ve also invested €45 million in our global R&D center in the Netherlands, which opened in 2025. It brings together specialists from 12 countries, combining their expertize to develop the next generation of brewing innovations. The center is close to Delft University of Technology, where we have a dedicated Heineken laboratory and collaborate on biotechnology and fermentation research.

We’re pioneering new technologies to lessen our usage of natural gas as we decarbonize our operations, whether that is solar thermal and biogas solutions in our Spanish breweries, which now run on 100% renewable energy, or our heat battery project in Portugal, which will go live in 2027. This innovation doesn’t happen in isolation. We work with equipment manufacturers, technology companies and researchers to turn new ideas into products and experiences people enjoy every day. For me, that’s one of Europe’s great strengths: bringing together industrial expertize, research and talent to make innovation happen.”

And how does Heineken contribute to the wider European economy?

“Just look at what goes into a glass of beer: farmers growing barley, businesses making bottles and equipment, transport companies delivering the beer, and the cafés, pubs and restaurants serving our products. It’s a huge eco-system, much of it made up of family businesses rooted in their communities.

Source: Heineken

Our activity supports close to 430,000 jobs across the value chain and around €34 billion in GDP contributions. In 2025, we purchased around €9 billion in goods and services from European suppliers. And because 98% of the inputs used by our European operating companies are sourced within Europe, much of that value stays within the European economy.”

Recent FoodDrinkEurope research suggests that Europe’s attractiveness as an investment destination is under pressure. What will it take to keep businesses investing here?

“We spend a lot of time talking about which new industries Europe needs to attract, and rightly so. But we should pay just as much attention to what it takes for established businesses to keep investing here.

I’m a farmer’s son from Yorkshire, so I grew up understanding long-term investment. Farming families think in generations, and I see that same long-term mindset at Heineken. In 2025 alone, we invested more than €500 million in our European production sites. Investments like these depend on access to talent, competitive costs and clear, predictable rules.

For me, that’s one of Europe’s great strengths: bringing together industrial expertize, research and talent to make innovation happen.

Packaging is a good example. We’ve invested for years in reusable systems, from beer kegs to returnable bottles and crates. We absolutely support Europe’s ambition to make packaging more sustainable. But when businesses are making long-term investments, clarity matters. We need realistic timelines, clear guidance and rules that recognize systems that are already working well.

The same applies to proposals on territorial supply constraints. We understand the objective, but any new rules need to work for businesses like ours that are decentralized and produce close to local consumers. We should be removing barriers to growth and investment across the single market, not inadvertently creating new ones.

And the same is true of the energy transition. Decarbonizing an industrial business requires significant long-term investment. Projects like those we’re pioneering in Spain and Portugal show what’s possible, but scaling these technologies will require businesses, governments and energy partners to work together. The investment conditions have to support that.”

Beyond its economic contribution, what role does the brewing industry play in European communities?

“One of the things I love about Europe is its hospitality and bar culture. Whether you’re in a Dutch brown café, a Spanish taverna, a French café or here in Brussels on Place Luxembourg, these are places where people meet, talk and spend time together. They are third spaces. In a world where so much happens through screens, I think that role matters more than ever.

And their economic contribution matters too. Across Europe, our activities support 186,400 jobs in hotels, restaurants and cafés, contributing €6.4 billion to the region’s GDP. Hospitality is also closely linked to tourism. Tourists spend close to €2.5 billion on Heineken beers in Europe each year, much of it through hospitality venues. So when we talk about keeping Europe’s hospitality sector vibrant, we’re talking about local jobs, tourism and the social fabric of communities as well.”

What would you like European policymakers to take away from this conversation?

“Europe has some fantastic businesses, and we shouldn’t take for granted what they can continue to contribute to our economy. We need new industries and technologies, absolutely. But we also need the right conditions for established businesses and their partners across the value chain to keep investing and growing.

The Brussels event reinforced something quite simple for me: policymaking works better when there’s an open dialogue. At Heineken, we want to be a constructive partner, bringing not just our own experience but what we hear from farmers, suppliers and hospitality entrepreneurs across our value chain. Ultimately, we share the same ambition: a Europe that is competitive, sustainable and remains a place where businesses want to make their next investment.”
