World.title: Europe’s moment to lead: Backing research in a global race
World.content:
Europe’s population is aging, with an increased burden of chronic diseases: more than half of adults in the European Union are now overweight and one in six is obese.1 In parallel, we are exposed to new threats from biosecurity, the malicious use of artificial intelligence, climate-related health threats and drug-resistant superbugs.

We are not passive bystanders. European teachers, biologists, nurses and manufacturers have all played a role in developing innovations that protect our populations and help them thrive. Now is not the time to step back. We believe health research and innovation are economic drivers of Europe’s future, not discretionary costs. Backing research in health as a pillar of our future in a global race is the right choice. It enables Europe to lead and support sustainable growth, as a pillar of the new architecture of global health.

We believe health research and innovation are economic drivers of Europe’s future, not discretionary costs.

The evidence is all around us. A vaccine developed against tuberculosis has been a frontline bladder cancer treatment for over 40 years,2 technology first developed for a malaria vaccine now helps protect millions against shingles,3 and mRNA research, developed over decades, enabled Europe’s fastest-ever vaccine response to Covid-19.4 Scientific progress rarely remains confined to the place or problem where it begins.

World.title: French presidential election: Meet the contenders you didn’t see coming
World.content:
Some prominent figures are trying to stop the race from turning into a showdown between two populists.

The French presidential race is getting more colorful.

With political moderates struggling, people from all walks of life are wading into the race, believing they have what it takes to stop the contest from hurtling toward a showdown between the far left and far right.

They include the head of the European Central Bank, an Olympic legend, a politician notorious for being a thorn in Elon Musk’s side, someone crisscrossing France on bicycle, plenty of talkative Uber drivers, several opinionated flâneurs chatting over coffee and cigarettes and one busker not too far from POLITICO’s office. (Some have better odds than others.)





“What’s clear right now is that the French are not satisfied with the current political offer,” said a senator from center-right candidate Edouard Philippe’s party Horizons, who was granted anonymity to discuss Philippe’s struggles on the campaign trail.

They may not all be formal candidates (yet), but here are some of the names you should watch over the coming months as challengers emerge to far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen and far-left hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who is surging in the polls.

The safe asset

ECB President Christine Lagarde has long been rumored to be considering a run, and the signals have been there for months.

She’s got an autobiography in the works and raised eyebrows in September with an unusual stop at a political rally in her home region, Normandy, eating morning oysters and chatting with apple liquor producers as any serious French presidential candidate would do.

Speculation reached fever pitch when she announced last month that she would leave her job at the ECB on Feb. 7 to regain the freedom to speak publicly about politics and not just on monetary policy.

“I can no longer stay neutral,” she told reporters in Frankfurt.





Asked by POLITICO whether she was still ruling out running during a panel at the Paris Peace Forum on Wednesday, Lagarde stuck to her guns: “I said I want to recover my freedom to speak, my freedom to engage in matters that are not monetary policy, and that’s what I want to do.”

Many in the centrist and conservative camp, including former economy and finance minister Bruno Le Maire, think she would be a great fit. And a recent poll commissioned by POLITICO showed the head of the European Central Bank polling on a par with Philippe.

Her financial pedigree at the ECB and as chief of the International Monetary Fund during the Euro sovereign debt crisis could prove useful in a country struggling to get its fiscal affairs in order.

But not everyone’s a fan.

“She’s out of touch,” dismissed a former centrist minister, who, like others quoted here, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Can you imagine her having a sense of ordinary people’s concerns?”

The Olympian

If French voters want a leader who could beat the crap out of Vladimir Putin in his preferred martial art, they may consider Teddy Riner.

Riner, a judoka with five Olympic gold medals to his name, stunned the country by announcing last week that he was running for president. In an interview with the daily Le Parisien announcing the bid, he said he’s neither on the political left nor right.

Though Riner, 37, is one of France’s most popular public figures, he has no political experience, no party and only six months to pitch voters on his candidacy.

His platform is short on specifics as well. So far, he’s pledged to adjust France’s costly pension system, ditch France’s 35-hour working week and boost wages by cutting employers’ social security contributions.





At his first campaign stop in a hospital in one of France’s poorest areas, the Parisian suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis, Riner said Friday “health is the number one priority” as he towered over the swarm of journalists following him.

Riner, who was born in the overseas French Caribbean territory of Guadeloupe and grew up in Paris, enters a crowded field. A recent poll from Cluster17 puts him at 2% in the first round of the presidential election — though it was conducted right after his announcement, giving respondents little time to consider his bid.

But the former minister previously quoted said Riner “ticks all the boxes” of a successful candidate: He’s new, he’s not from President Emmanuel Macron’s political family and can appeal to younger voters.

And size matters. Standing more than 2 meters tall and weighing 140 kilograms, Riner will impress world leaders even if he “makes mistakes,” said the former minister.

“It’s the reality of power dynamics,” said the official.

Putin might want to up his judo training.

The bulldozer

Former European Commissioner Thierry Breton has had some epic clashes with Ursula von der Leyen and Elon Musk, but that might not be enough to conquer the French presidency.

While he left Brussels two years ago amid tensions with the Commission chief, Breton never left the French media landscape, becoming a regular on French TV to discuss global and French politics.

The unstoppable former tech executive and science-fiction author, who has just published his 12th book, announced that last week he was not ruling out running for president and that he was waiting to see whether a strong candidate would emerge in the central bloc.





Breton, who was also economy and finance minister under conservative President Jacques Chirac, wants to make Europe less dependent on the United States and rein in France’s massive debt by adding strict rules about debt accrual to the French constitution.

As one of the architects of EU platform regulation, he has become the nemesis of X’s owner Musk. The Trump administration even sanctioned him last year, accusing Breton of being behind a new wave of digital censorship. Breton has the backing of former centrist Prime Minister François Bayrou — but Bayrou isn’t too popular right now.

The writer

Former Economy Minister Bruno Le Maire hasn’t declared he’s running, but he’s certainly behaving like a candidate. On Thursday, conservative Le Maire didn’t rule out joining the presidential race as he presented his manifesto “for another France,” which very much looked like a presidential platform.

He’s currently teaching at the University of Lausanne and writing books. His latest one focuses on his political legacy, and it doesn’t have any sex scenes. He is also a member of Mario Draghi’s exclusive Rhine Club.

If Le Maire were to run, he’d likely tout his economic credentials after serving for seven years as economy minister.

But his calling card is also a liability, given how Le Maire’s political opponents hold him responsible for France’s skyrocketing debt, and see him as a member of France’s distant chattering classes.

The humanist

Dominique de Villepin, 72, offers an unusual mix of leftism and Old World panache he hopes will seduce French voters.

The former prime minister under Chirac is not officially a candidate, but he has launched his own party, A Humanist France, has started collecting endorsements and is canvassing voters. In an interview this week, De Villepin said he “wants to be ready” in case he runs.





De Villepin is best remembered for his momentous speech at the U.N. Security Council in 2003, when as France’s foreign minister he issued a prescient warning against the United States as it prepared to invade Iraq. In recent years, the former diplomat’s popularity surged due to his fierce opposition to Israel’s war in Gaza.

But with poll ratings hovering around 1%, many expect De Villepin to throw in the towel sooner rather than later.

The socialist revenant

Pierre Moscovici might not be the rock-star candidate the French might be looking for. Still, the socialist veteran caught everyone by surprise when he announced last month that he would leave the European Court of Auditors after serving less than 10 months of his six-year mandate to come back to Paris.

Just like Lagarde, socialist Moscovici said he wanted to regain the freedom to speak freely “in the difficult, even tragic, times ahead.”

Moscovici — who also served as a European economy commissioner, a finance minister under President François Hollande and the chief of France’s top audit body — pledged to bring his experience to the French political debate.

The sequel

Former President François Hollande left office in 2017 with record-low popularity ratings. But he thinks he might just have one more shot at winning the French presidency.

Hollande, who is now a Socialist MP, is hitting the campaign trail hard.

But he is waiting until the end of the year to decide whether to run in the 2027 election. His decision will likely depend on the prospects of Raphaël Glucksmann, who won a center-left primary but has been unable to catch up to the far left’s Mélenchon in the polls.

“It’s like Celebrity Survivor,” said a Macron ally. “He thinks if he hangs in there long enough, he might have a chance.”

World.title: Estonia has a plan for Russian occupation: Run its government from the cloud
World.content:
Now, Tallinn is preparing to move its public services to the cloud “either when data centers are destroyed or there’s boots on the ground and we cannot operate,” said Tõnu Grünberg, an architect of the new strategy and former deputy secretary general for digital infrastructure and cybersecurity at Estonia's Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs.

Estonia already has a data backup in its “digital embassy” in Luxembourg, effectively a copy of the country's blueprint that includes everything from citizen registries to land registries and its legal code.

“Now we want to really be online, whatever happens,” Grünberg said. "All critical services stay online … Everything needs to stay operational.”

The Estonian government is building secure applications on cloud providers including Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services as well as its own state cloud platform. The country is shipping the system to its data embassy and other places in Europe, said Grünberg, who started a job as CEO of tech infrastructure provider Levira this month.

Allan Allmere, an adviser for IT architecture and infrastructure at the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs, said in comments to POLITICO that Estonia wants to minimize the impact of the worst-case scenario.

“Ideally, we would like to build systems that can withstand every possible crisis, but in reality no country can predict or eliminate every risk," he said. "In the most severe scenarios, we also need to preserve a trusted foundation from which Estonia’s digital state can be rebuilt."

World.title: Zelenskyy urges US and Musk to restore Starlink access after wave of Russian strikes
World.content:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged the United States and Elon Musk to lift restrictions on Ukraine's access to the Starlink network, saying "It is important to be on the right side of history."

 

"Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161 kilometers per hour and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds,'" Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X.

"We are counting on these restrictions being lifted."

Kyiv relies on the network for its frontline communications and operating drones, including interceptors that shoot down incoming Russian drones.

Last week, Zelenskyy said that Ukraine's military was facing "systematic" restrictions on the service, operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, with connections only working when devices were moving slower than 161 kilometres per hour.

"We still have no clear explanations," Zelensky said on Friday, confirming the restrictions were still in place "along the entire front line" and over territory occupied by Russia.

Ukraine relies on Starlink for battlefield communications and access to the military-grade Starshield to intercept drones and missiles in its territory.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks to the media at the airport in Dublin, 12 November, 2026 AP Photo

Ukraine first reported problems using Starshield last month following a row between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump over a US-Russia diesel deal, before access was eventually restored.

Kyiv says the restrictions effectively make it impossible for them to intercept Russia's jet-powered drones, which can travel at up to 1,000 km/h.

Wave of drones

Meanwhile, Russia said on Monday it had intercepted more than 1,300 Ukrainian drones overnight, including hundreds targeting Moscow, one of Kyiv's largest attacks of the nearly five-year war.

Air defences intercepted around 600 drones flying towards the Moscow region overnight and into Monday morning, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said on Telegram.

"Most were destroyed by the defence ministry's air defence system on distant approaches," he said, adding that 191 drones were "neutralised on their approach to Moscow".

There was no immediate information on damage and casualties.

Russia's defence ministry later said air defences had intercepted and destroyed 1,336 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight across multiple regions, including the Moscow area, as well as over the Black Sea and Sea of Azov.

The interceptions came hours after Ukrainian forces struck a major Russian petrochemical plant, an oil refinery and a military production site as part of Kyiv's campaign of attacks deep inside Russia.

The barrage came days before a summit in Shenzhen between President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Beijing confirmed on Monday that Xi would hold talks with Trump and Putin in Shenzhen on November 19 on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

The Kremlin and White House had previously confirmed the meeting.

Beijing provided no details about the agenda, while Trump has said he intends to discuss denuclearisation and the Iran war.

He is not expected to discuss Russia's war against Ukraine in the trilateral talks, according to US officials.

A residential building is seen damaged in a Russian strike on Zaporizhzhia, 13 November, 2026 Ukrainian Emergency Service/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

Washington is pursuing separate negotiations involving Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the conflict, with US negotiators meeting both Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last week.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said Xi recently showed "irritation" at suggestions that Ukraine could be discussed in the trilateral format.

"He explicitly pointed out that this is a European conflict, in which the Europeans must also be at the table," Steinmeier told the public broadcaster ARD.

Zelenskyy has warned that the Shenzhen meeting risks becoming a 21st-century version of the 1945 Yalta conference, where major powers could attempt to redraw spheres of influence without smaller countries at the table.

World.title: Europe Today: Sweden pushes for more support for Ukraine as Europe seeks a seat at the negotiating table
World.content:
On today's show:

We speak with Maria Malmer Stenergard, Sweden's Foreign Affairs minister, as her country pushes for more military assistance, particularly air defence, tougher sanctions against Moscow and the use of frozen Russian assets to help finance Ukraine.

 

Shona Murray interviewed Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs during the Informal European Summit held in Dublin last week as he said Vladimir Putin is playing tactical games and that Europe needs to show greater strength and confidence.

We debrief the escalating wave of cyberattacks Europe is facing with Juhan Lepassaar, Executive Director of the EU Agency for Cybersecurity, ENISA. Behind many of these incidents are increasingly sophisticated criminal and state-backed hackers, with Russia and other hostile actors exploiting Europe's digital vulnerabilities.

And as Ukraine is facing a new political test, we speak with Czech MEP Danuše Nerudová of the European People’s Party Europe's over who is prepared to pay for Kyiv's defence and how far the EU should go in confronting Moscow.

When and where to watch Europe Today?

You can join Euronews’ Stefan Grobe live on TV and Euronews' website as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram), every weekday at 8 am, 9 am and 10 am Brussels time.

In just 28 minutes, our new format brings you the day's key events plus crucial analysis of all the stories shaping the EU and beyond. It's also available as a newsletter and podcast.

World.title: Australian MP Helen Haines leaves hospital after losing both legs in alleged car attack
World.content:
An Australian lawmaker said she was "full of gratitude" as she was discharged from hospital on Monday following an alleged attack in October that resulted in her losing both legs.

 

Independent politician Helen Haines was struck outside her office in rural Australia, suffering serious injuries that eventually led to the amputation of her legs.

The attack has sparked much soul-searching in a country where political violence is rare but where police have documented a steady rise in threats towards elected officials.

The Alfred Hospital in Melbourne said the 65-year-old had been discharged four weeks after she was airlifted in for emergency treatment.

"I am very pleased to confirm that I have moved into the rehabilitation stage of my recovery, which will continue in Melbourne for the immediate future," she said in a statement.

"This is a really positive moment and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage."

Tributes and flowers are placed outside the electoral office for independent member of parliament Helen Haines in Wangaratta, 20 October, 2026 AP Photo

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he was in regular contact with Haines and her family and wished her the best for her recovery.

"We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation," he said in a statement.

Haines was standing near her car in the rural Australian town of Wangaratta when she was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser on 19 October.

Police have charged 43-year-old Brendan Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury and intentionally causing serious injury, as well as the federal crime of harming a public official.

Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as cracking down on corruption and stronger climate action.

World.title: Heavyweights deliver a spectacular finale at the Zagreb Grand Prix 2026
World.content:
It’s the third and final day of the Zagreb Grand Prix. Fans were treated to more incredible action as the heavyweights took to the tatami.

 

At -90Kg Brazil’s Guilherme SCHIMIDT was up against Theodoros TSELIDIS of Greece. In the final, with just 10 seconds to go, a perfectly timed ashi-waza gave SCHMIDT his third Grand Prix gold.

World Champion & Double Olympic Medallist, Mr Neil ADAMS awarded the medals.

Julie HOELTERHOFF of Germany and Austria’s Elena DENGG were both competing their first Grand Prix final at -78Kg. It was HOELTERHOFF who would dictate the result producing some fantastic counters to claim the title.

A couple of weeks ago I really wasn't sure if I’m going to win a medal again because I wasn’t too sure about my capability and I’m so happy that my family and friends supported me so much so this day was unbelievable. Julie HOELTERHOFF German judoka

IJF Head Sport Director, Mr Vladimir BARTA awarded the medals.

At -100Kg, Ukraine’s Anton SAVYTSKIY met Zsombor VEG of Hungary in the final. SAVYTSKIY took gold here in 2024 and a stunning switch from o soto to ko soto gari secured him another Zagreb title.

Beautiful place, beautiful country, city. It’s my second gold from Zagreb. Beautiful people, a good opportunity and I always love to come here. Anton SAVYTSKIY Ukrainian judoka

Mrs Louisa AGIUS GALEA, Logistics Director of the International Judo Federation awarded the medals.

Current olympic champion Beatriz SOUZA of Brazil was up against New Zealand’s Sydnee ANDREWS in the +78KG final. A huge Ashi-garuma from SOUZA showed just why she’s the one to beat.

An incredible 23rd world tour medal for SOUZA!

Dr Sanda CORAK, President of the Croatian Judo Federation awarded the medals.

At +100Kg Losseni KONE of Germany met Azerbijan’s Kanan NASIBOV in the final. Fresh from his World Bronze medal, a Waza-ari score gave NASIBOV his 2nd consecutive Zagreb gold medal.

Mr Mathieu BATAILLE, Referee Supervisor of the International Judo Federation awarded the medals.

It’s been an incredible tournament, thank you Croatia.

World.title: Nuremberg streets in Germany fill with sheep heading for winter quarters
World.content:
Around 600 sheep made their way through the centre of Nuremberg, Germany, on Sunday, 15 November, as they headed towards their winter quarters.

 

Watched by curious onlookers, the animals crossed the city's historic old town, turning its busy streets into the setting for an unusual annual spectacle.

The 10-kilometre route is the shortest way to reach their winter home, west of the city. The yearly procession also highlights the region's shepherding tradition and the role sheep play in preserving the landscape.

Grazing helps keep open areas from becoming overgrown, making the animals an important part of local conservation efforts.

World.title: Scientists uncover new sleep secret: how the body burns fat and builds muscle at night
World.content:
Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have identified the neural circuit that regulates the release of growth hormone during sleep, in a study published in the scientific journal "Cell". Their findings show that the relationship between sleep and growth hormone is not, as commonly assumed, a one-way street: sleep promotes the secretion of this hormone, while growth hormone in turn helps regulate when we wake up.

 

Scientists have long known that a significant amount of growth hormone is released during sleep. Beyond its central role in height gain in children and adolescents, this hormone continues in adulthood to help preserve muscle tissue, keep bones healthy, regulate the use of stored fat and control blood sugar levels.

Until now, however, it was unclear exactly how the brain regulates the release of this hormone across different sleep stages, and how neural activity, growth hormone levels and the timing of awakening are connected.

Xinlu Ding, a postdoctoral researcher in neuroscience at Berkeley and the study’s lead author, explains that scientists previously examined the link between sleep and growth hormone mainly by measuring hormone levels in the blood. In the new research, by contrast, they directly recorded the activity of nerve cells in the brains of mice.

According to Ding, this approach enabled the team to pinpoint a specific neural circuit that could serve as a basis for investigating future treatments.

How does the brain control growth hormone release during sleep?

To find the answer, the researchers focused on a part of the brain called the hypothalamus – a small but vital region involved in regulating hunger, body temperature, hormone production and the sleep–wake cycle.

In this area of the brain, one group of nerve cells produces growth hormone–releasing hormone, or GHRH, which stimulates the secretion of growth hormone. Another group produces somatostatin, which has an inhibitory effect. The interplay between these two chemical messengers fine-tunes the amount of growth hormone released by the pituitary gland into the bloodstream.

The scientists found that the activity of these cells is not the same across different stages of sleep.

During non-REM sleep – the phase that makes up much of the body’s deep, restorative sleep – the activity of somatostatin-producing cells drops, weakening their inhibitory effect. At the same time, the cells linked to GHRH become somewhat more active, creating favourable conditions for increased growth hormone release.

In REM sleep, the stage usually associated with vivid dreaming, the pattern shifts again. Activity related to both messengers rises and, despite their seemingly opposite roles, the precise coordination of neural activity in this phase further boosts growth hormone secretion.

In other words, the researchers have shown that the brain can draw on different neural pathways in different sleep stages to regulate the release of a single essential hormone.

How does growth hormone influence waking up?

Perhaps the most striking result of the study is that growth hormone is not simply a by-product of what the brain does during sleep; it also feeds back on the neural circuits that govern wakefulness.

The team discovered that as growth hormone levels rise during sleep, they stimulate the activity of nerve cells in an area of the brainstem known as the "locus coeruleus". This region plays a key role in alertness, attention, concentration and preparing the brain to respond to its surroundings.

Put simply, sleep increases growth hormone secretion, and the rise in growth hormone then signals to the brain that it is time to move towards wakefulness. The scientists describe this as a feedback loop that helps maintain balance between sleep, hormone release and alertness.

Daniel Silverman, a co-author of the study and postdoctoral researcher at Berkeley, says the findings show that sleep and growth hormone form part of a highly delicate regulatory system: inadequate sleep can reduce growth hormone secretion, while rising hormone levels in turn nudge the brain towards waking.

Maintaining this balance, he adds, is crucial for growth, tissue repair and healthy metabolism.

The researchers also highlight an unexpected observation. Although increased activity in the locus coeruleus usually makes us more alert, overstimulating the nerve cells in this region can have the opposite effect and lead to drowsiness rather than wakefulness.

This suggests that healthy brain function does not simply depend on ramping up or shutting down a single group of neurons, but on a finely tuned equilibrium between multiple signals.

Linking poor sleep to obesity, diabetes and brain disorders

The study’s findings may shed new light on the connection between insufficient sleep and certain metabolic disorders.

Growth hormone helps regulate fat use and blood sugar levels, and chronic sleep disruption can upset the balance of its secretion. Lack of sleep may therefore be one factor that increases the risk of obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular disease, even though these conditions also have many other causes.

The researchers also suspect that the link between growth hormone and brain regions responsible for alertness and concentration could have consequences beyond physical health.

Xinlu Ding notes that, in addition to supporting the building and maintenance of muscles and bones and regulating fat tissue, growth hormone may have a positive effect on cognitive performance, improving a person’s level of alertness after waking.

According to the team, identifying this neural circuit could eventually pave the way for new treatments for sleep disorders associated with metabolic diseases and neurological conditions such as Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s.

Even so, the scientists stress that their experiments were carried out on mice, and it is not yet clear whether the mechanism works in exactly the same way in humans. Further research will be needed to assess whether these insights can be translated into therapies.

The results therefore do not prove that a new sleeping technique can help people lose weight or build muscle. Instead, they represent a step towards understanding the mechanisms that tie these processes to sleep.

Ultimately, the Berkeley team’s work is a reminder that sleep, despite its calm outward appearance, is a period of intense, finely choreographed activity in the brain and body – a time when nerve cells and hormones constantly communicate to keep growth, repair, metabolism and wakefulness in balance.

World.title: Estonia to close Russia border after 'sabotage' bid on drone maker, foreign minister says
World.content:
Estonia said on Sunday it would close its border with Russia after stopping what it called an attempted arson attack by Russia's GRU military intelligence on a drone factory.

 

The move marked a sharp escalation in tensions between Estonia and Russia, which Tallinn sees as part of a broader campaign of hostile activity linked to Moscow's war against Ukraine.

"Estonia will close all Estonian-Russian border crossing points as of 1 December," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna wrote in a post on X, citing "clear evidence" that the GRU had ordered the attack.

Moscow said it would verify whether Estonia was indeed planning to shut all crossings.

"We will verify all this to see if it's true," Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told the TASS news agency.

"But if these are their (Estonia's) real plans, then it will be seen as yet another bout of aggressive and unbridled Russophobia," she added.

Earlier on Sunday, Prime Minister Kristen Michal wrote on X that the GRU had ordered a "sabotage attempt" at the Estonian defence company Threod Systems on Saturday night.

"Extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security measures and a swift reaction by law enforcement. The attackers have been detained," he added.

The foiled attack happened in Viimsi, north of the capital Tallinn.

Tsahkna, in his later post, said: "Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences.

"Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered."

He also said he had informed his Finnish, Latvian, and Lithuanian counterparts of the decision.

Security forces arrested eight individuals who live in Latvia, chief prosecutor Astrid Asi told journalists.

Michal called the incident "part of Russia's broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia".

"We will not be intimidated," he added.

Threod Systems manufactures reconnaissance and attack drones.

Estonia's Prime Minister Kristen Michal speaks to the media during the European Political Community Summit in Dublin, 12 November, 2026 AP Photo

In August, the defence subcontractor Milrem Robotics, based in Tallinn, was targeted in an attempted arson attack and Latvian nationals were arrested.

Estonia, a member of the European Union and NATO, currently has three crossing points with Russia at Narva in the north and the southern Luhamaa and Koidula crossing, that allow the movement of people and goods between the two countries.

Russia suspended vehicle traffic through Narva in February 2024, although pedestrians were still allowed to pass.

The crossings are among the few remaining overland links between Russia and the European Union still operating since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

World.title: ‘Stop fiddling and do what works’: How heat pumps could cut a quarter of EU energy emissions
World.content:
Heat pumps can cut a quarter of the European Union’s energy emissions, as leaders are urged to “stop fiddling while the world burns and do what works”.

 

New analysis from the European Heat Pump Association (EHPA) found that fitting heat pumps in every building and “compatible industrial process” – powered by renewables like solar and wind – would avoid around 600 million tonnes (Mt) of CO2.

This is more than the annual emissions of Germany, the bloc’s biggest economy, or the 17 smallest EU countries combined.

What are heat pumps and how do they lower emissions?

Depending on the type, heat pumps work by capturing energy from air, water or the ground and turning it into heat or cold air – rather than burning fossil fuels on-site.

They work in a similar way to a refrigerator but in reverse, using a liquid chemical that turns into a hot gas through compression.

This hot gas releases its heat to your central heating, warming your home. The gas then cools down, turning back into liquid form, ready to start all over again.

For every one kilowatt-hour (kWh) of electricity they consume, they typically deliver three to four kWh of heat.

According to EHPA, each residential heat pump installed displaces around 1,100 m3 of gas and two tonnes of CO2 per year on average, if the small amount of electricity it uses to run is from renewable sources.

There are already around 30 million residential heat pumps installed in Europe, with around three million added in 2025. This is one million fewer installations than the four million target set out by the European Commission.

Heat pump technology has become enmeshed in a “wave of misinformation” surrounding their ability to work in cold temperatures, their noise, and whether they can be installed in old buildings.

Euronews Earth has already debunked these myths here.

‘Climate change does not wait’

“Leaders need to stop fiddling while the world burns and do what works,” says Paul Kenny, director general of EHPA. “Heat pumps are already delivering emissions cuts and protection from fossil fuel prices.”

Kenny urged nations to make it easier to install heat pumps in every building and low temperature industry by ensuring upfront support, affordable, clean electricity and a “smooth” grid connection.

“Climate change does not wait and nor should we,” he adds.

World.title: Turkey talks green at COP31 while cracking down on activists
World.content:
As the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya co-hosts the COP31 climate conference with Australia, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is using the global spotlight to promote his country’s climate ambitions. But his green image is being challenged at home by environmentalists, who say they face an intensifying government crackdown.

Advertising

The summit opened with a cinematic video highlighting the growing threat of global warming. “When did you decide to look at nature as if it’s not your nature?” a narrator asked during the opening presentation.

Addressing world leaders, Erdogan stressed Turkey’s determination to tackle climate change and presented Antalya’s ancient, multicultural history as fitting for its role as host.

Three-quarters of world's displaced people 'on frontlines of climate crisis'

“At the centre of our civilisations lies respect for nature,” he said. “The earth is a sacred trust that must be protected and guarded. We are a nation that considers even harming an ant a violation of rights, and that embraces the principle of planting the last sapling in your hand even if you know the apocalypse will come tomorrow.”

A different reality

The COP31 summit gives Erdogan a prominent international stage, but human rights campaigners warn of a very different reality outside the conference halls.

Last month, the US-based Human Rights Watch raised the alarm over a widening campaign against Turkey’s environmental movement. The report’s author, Deniz Bayram, said activists face a growing wave of arrests, fines and intimidation.

“People told us that when they protested, they faced police violence and abusive tactics by security officers, as well as legal harassment through unfair criminal investigations with no criminal evidence,” Bayram said.

She said the authorities had also put pressure on demonstrators through their families. In the eastern Black Sea region, security officers contacted the adult sons of women protesters who lived in other cities and told them to stop their mothers attending further rallies, according to Bayram.

“Women told us that they are not really afraid of facing such violence from the authorities, but they are having a hard time with these family matters with their own relatives,” she said. “So these abusive tactics create a chilling effect, preventing people from attending further demonstrations.”

Tear gas and court cases

Police intervention at environmental protests has become routine across Turkey, where local demonstrations have surged since the government relaxed restrictions on gold and coal mining.

Suheyla Dogan, a retired civil engineer who has become a leading voice in protests against gold mines, has repeatedly rallied villagers against mining projects. She said the personal cost of activism was rising sharply.

“If we take any direct action, we are punished; they open court cases against us,” said Dogan, who faces four separate legal cases. “At the demonstrations, we have faced a lot of tear gas, water cannon, beatings and so on.”

Ahead of a planned demonstration in Antalya during the climate summit, Dogan said, several organisers were detained by police and released a day later. She believes the move was intended to deter people from turning up, even though the rally had not been banned.

African push to triple climate adaptation finance left off Cop31 agenda

Legal experts warn that a climate of fear is deepening as pre-trial detention becomes standard practice, leaving activists in jail for weeks before their cases are heard, often only to be released later. The government maintains that the right to protest remains protected, but environmental lawyer Ismail Hakki Atal said lawyers defending activists were increasingly being targeted too.

Atal represented villagers fighting to protect the Akbelen Forest near the south-western town of Milas, where he alleges that the government-backed conglomerate Limak breached Turkey’s Olive Law by cutting down olive trees and dumping rubble on olive groves.

“Because I exposed this in a live news broadcast, police detained me twice within five days, even though I was acting as the villagers’ lawyer,” Atal said. “The ruling AKP has effectively established a judiciary in Turkey capable of having anyone it wishes arrested. The judicial system currently hangs over us like the Sword of Damocles and is used as a stick when necessary.”

Retirees on the front line

Dogan acknowledged that the mounting pressure was beginning to sap the movement’s strength, particularly among younger people.

“People are now more afraid to join us. Villagers are more afraid because if they protest and are taken to prison, they stay there for a long time,” she said. “When we call people on to the streets, they ask: ‘How are you going to protect us if something happens to us?’ Young people who have jobs and children are especially afraid.”

World set to breach 1.5C warming limit as UN warns time is running out

With fewer people of working age willing to risk their jobs and their freedom, the burden of frontline protest is increasingly falling on retirees such as Dogan.

“I am retired, I have my pension, and I don’t have a job to lose,” she said. “Maybe retired people are now more willing to be on the streets than young working people. I see it as my duty; I have to do it.”

For now, Turkish environmentalists say they refuse to be silenced. They have vowed to make their voices heard on the sidelines of COP31, as an older generation steps forward to keep the movement alive.

World.title: India news: Modi heads to ASEAN meet in Manila
World.content:
11/16/2026 November 16, 2026 Indian PM Modi to attend ASEAN summit in Manila today

Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to leave for Manila, in the Philippines, to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)-India summit and the 21st East Asia Summit.

The ASEAN meeting will focus on three main issues: maritime security, economic cooperation and development partnership.

According to the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), the Prime Minister will attend a dinner hosted by Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on November 16 before participating in the India-ASEAN Summit and the East Asia Summit process on November 17.

During his two-day visit to Manila, Modi is also likely to meet US President Donald Trump, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese as the leaders of the Quad group meet on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had indicated last month that the Quad meeting was planned alongside the wider meetings in the Philippines.

Announcing his visit to Manila, PM Modi said in a post on X, "Will be in Manila, Philippines later today and tomorrow to attend the following programmes: 23rd ASEAN-India Summit. 21st East Asia Summit."

World.title: Mexican drug lord Felix Gallardo dies at 80
World.content:
Felix Gallardo was considered to be the architect of Mexico's modern drug-trafficking trade. He died of multiple organ failure at the age of 80.

Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo — known as the "godfather" of Mexico's modern drug trade and a notorious trafficker himself — died in a hospital on Sunday. He was 80.

"After remaining under observation with a guarded prognosis, he died on November 15 at the medical facility" after "he suffered multiple organ failure," said a statement from the security ministry of the state of Jalisco, where he was being held.

An inmate's death

Having founded the Guadalajara cartel, one of Mexico's first major drug syndicate which would later birth the Sinaloa cartel, Gallardo had been imprisoned since 1989 and was transferred to a private hospital two days ago.

He was arrested and sentenced to 40 years in prison on drug-trafficking and weapons charges tied to the cartel. While already behind bars, he faced a seperate prosecution for the kidnapping and murder of a US drug-enforcement agent. This earned him an addition 37-year prison sentence and his reputation as Mexico's most notorious trafficker.

Felix Gallardo had been an inmate in a maximum-security prison in western Jalisco state even after his lawyers repeatedly sought house arrest on the grounds of his deteriorating health.

We met a cartel killer — who really runs Mexico? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The life of Felix Gallardo

Gallardo was born in 1946 in the Northwestern state of Sinaloa, which would later become synonymous with narco-trafficking.

He initially worked as a police officer and bodyguard for a local governer but soon transformed into a power criminal, known as the "boss of bosses."

Gallardo, along with others, set up the Guadalajara cartel becoming the first to move cocaine to the US on a massive scale. He was also the first to forge an alliance with Colombian drug cartels including Pablo Escobar's Medellin cartel.

In the 1970s, Gallardo rose to prominance as his narcotics empire expanded on the back of bribed law enforcers and the use of light aircrafts to move drugs across the continent.

His rise and fall as a Mexican drug lord was ortrayed on screen by Mexican actor Diego Luna in the 2018 Netflix hit series 'Narcos: Mexico.'

In his final years, Gallardo suffered poor health and was blind in one eye, practically deaf and unable to walk on his own. He maintained that he was innocent.

World.title: Rocket from Boeing-Lockheed firm fails mid-flight, destroys payload of Amazon satellites
World.content:
A Vulcan rocket suffered an anomaly about 10 minutes after liftoff from Florida, failing to deliver 40 Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. It was the first total mission failure in the company's history.

A Vulcan rocket operated by United Launch Alliance, a joint venture of Boeing and Lockheed Martin, failed about 10 minutes after liftoff from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Sunday. The incident resulted in the loss of all 40 AmazonLeo internet satellites aboard, marking the company's first mission failure.

"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in a ​statement.

The exact cause was not immediately clear.

"Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don't have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today," ULA added.

The failed launch marks ‌a major setback for ULA's new flagship rocket. The two-decade-old ⁠company was set to begin a regular cadence of launches for Amazon's burgeoning satellite internet program.

The Vulcan rocket was launched from the Cape Canaveral launch site in Florida Image: Manuel Mazzanti/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Mission failure raises fresh concerns over US launch capacity

The failure is expected to trigger a lengthy technical investigation, potentially grounding the Vulcan rocket for months.

US companies could face reduced launch capacity amid other rocket failures, industry challenges and uncertainty over the future availability of SpaceX's Falcon 9, the world's most active rocket. SpaceX is no longer accepting bookings for the rocket.

"There is risk with any launch, and that's especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01," Amazon said in a statement, referring to Sunday's mission. "ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they'll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan."

Is ULA in trouble?

ULA was formed in 2006 through the merger of Boeing's Delta rocket program and Lockheed Martin's Atlas rocket program. The incident marked the first total mission failure in the company's history, ending its record of successful mission deliveries since its formation.

Sunday's launch was Vulcan's fifth since its debut in 2024 and its first in nine months. The gap followed separate technical investigations into its solid rocket boosters and core BE-4 engines, which are supplied by Blue Origin, the space company founded by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.

The solid rocket boosters had come under scrutiny after anomalies on Vulcan's previous two flights, including a February 2026 mission for the US Space Force. Both missions successfully delivered their payloads into orbit despite the booster problems.

US national security clearance for Vulcan under scrutiny

The Space Force paused Vulcan's national security launches pending the outcome of an investigation and the implementation of corrective measures. Sunday's Amazon mission was expected to provide further data before the military decided whether to clear the rocket for those launches.

An investigation traced the problem to the engine's main oxygen valve. Blue Origin subsequently developed modifications for the BE-4 engines supplied to ULA, and the engines installed on Vulcan were retrofitted, ULA officials said.

It remains unclear whether the BE-4 engines played any role in Sunday's failure.

Nearly 400 satellites launched as Amazon challenges Starlink

Amazon relies on third-party launch providers to deploy satellites for its Leo internet network. Other launch providers have also faced technical problems and delays.

Blue Origin's New Glenn explosion in May occurred during a ground test, just days before the rocket was scheduled to launch Amazon Leo satellites.

Repeated launch setbacks have complicated Amazon's efforts to compete with SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet network, which has more than 11,000 satellites and millions of customers worldwide.

Amazon previously used ULA's Atlas V rockets for its launches (File Photo) Image: Joe Marino/UPI Photo/IMAGO

SpaceX's advantage over satellite internet rivals is partly due to its ability to use its own rockets to deploy satellites. Other companies rely on external launch providers, adding to the cost and complexity of building their constellations.

Before Sunday's failed mission, Amazon had launched 398 Leo satellites across 14 missions since 2025, according to Reuters. That represented about 12% of the 3,236 satellites the company needs for global coverage. Amazon had hoped to begin initial internet services this year.

World.title: Yemen: Anti-Houthi forces pull back as rebels advance
World.content:
Forces aligned with the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia are seeking to strengthen control over the interim capital Aden as the Iran-backed Houthis approach.

The Southern Armed Forces group allied with Yemen's UN-recognized government and backed by Saudi Arabia said Sunday they had repositioned themselves away from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Why are troops moving away from Bab el-Mandeb?

The Southern Armed Forces said the repositioning is intended to secure the southern city of Aden, "and the neighboring governorates, as well as strengthening the frontlines and addressing existing threats."

Aden, which has a population of over a million people, is the interim seat of the Yemeni government, formally known as the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC).

The Southern Armed Forces also intend to end the Houthi siege over the strategic southwestern city of Taiz.

Nearly two million people live in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city.

The siege is raising fears of famine for residents, as well as a possible medical crisis as hospitals face restricted supplies.

Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Houthis advancing towards Aden

The Houthis control much of northwest Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.

The rebels are a Shiite militant group backed by Iran. The US, Canada and several other countries regard them as a terror organization.

The Houthis in September launched a rapid offensive against the PLC, seizing much of the coastline along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.

It is also a key corridor for maritime trade and energy shipments.

The Houthis have taken control of the major port town of Mocha in September, firming their grip over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The latest redeployment of the Southern Armed Forces is likely to give the rebels even more control over the strategic area.

Sources told AFP news agency that Houthi forces are now just 60 kilometers (less than 40 miles) from Aden.

The conflict between the Yemeni government and the Houthis has lasted for over 10 years.

The fighting in Yemen, the poorest country in the Arab world, has been fueled by the wider rivalry between Iran and Saudi Arabia.

More fighting between Yemen's Houthis, Saudi Arabia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In recent weeks, the Houthis have been launching frequent attacks on Saudi Arabia. On Sunday, the rebels claimed that they targeted the King Khalid International Airport and financial district of the Saudi capital, Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the alleged Houthi attack.

World.title: Goodbye, overtourism? Sustainable travel gains ground
World.content:
As tourism booms across Latin America, alternative forms of travel are gaining ground. Making your holiday more sustainable means rethinking who calls the shots, who invests and who benefits.

Latin America is currently one of the world's most dynamic tourism regions. According to UN Tourism, the United Nations agency responsible for promoting responsible tourism, international arrivals in South America grew by 7% last year, while Central America saw a 5% increase, both above the global average.

But the boom comes at a price: overtourism. In some destinations, the sheer number of visitors is creating environmental and social problems, fueling tensions and raising questions about who really benefits from the business.

One famous example is Machu Picchu, the Inca citadel in Peru, which lures up to 5,600 visitors a day. In 2025, Peru's official watchdog warned that more tickets were being sold than permitted, potentially putting the site at risk of being added to UNESCO's List of World Heritage in Danger . The UNESCO World Heritage Committee has already expressed its concern.

People are flocking to Machu Picchu, the Inca citadel in Peru Image: Michalakis Ppalis/Zoonar/picture alliance

In a bid to protect the Galapagos Islands and its bountiful ecosystems that inspired Charles Darwin, Ecuador doubled the entrance fee for foreign visitors to $200 in 2024. Even so, pressure is mounting to construct new hotels and tourist apartments. And in Mexico City, the influx of tourists and digital nomads into neighborhoods such as Roma and Condesa has fueled protests over rising rents.

The Galapagos Islands introduced an entrance fee for foreign visitors to $200 in 2024 Image: Alie Skowronski/AP Photo/picture alliance

What can be done to make tourism more inclusive and sustainable? That's one of the industry's biggest questions. At ITB Americas, an international travel trade fair in Guadalajara, Mexico, DW spoke with three experts.

Sustainable travel moving from niche to mainstream

Richard Bazan is a regional manager for the Americas at Planeterra, a nonprofit organization that promotes and supports community-based tourism. He said several trends are emerging: group sizes are shrinking and travelers are seeking more intimate experiences.

"Where groups of 20 used to travel together, now it's four or five," he told DW.

So-called "nature-positive" tourism is also gaining traction, with travel programs that help fund, for example, reforestation projects. Bazan said even all-inclusive resorts are realizing that they can no longer shut themselves off from their surroundings. Instead, they need to offer authentic experiences that connect visitors with the destination.

"Community-based tourism is no longer a niche," he said.

Mexico has been trying to contain a record surge of foul-smelling sargassum seaweed, fueled by a mix of nutrient-rich runoff and shifting ocean conditions Image: Alfredo Estrella/AFP

Pressure for change is also coming from travelers themselves. According to Booking.com's 2025 annual survey, which polled 32,000 people in 34 countries, 93% said they wanted to make more sustainable travel choices. For the first time, more than half (53%) were aware of tourism's impact on local communities, not just the environment.

Communities know what's best for their land

Sarah Payne, director of the Reset Tourism Fund at the UnTours Foundation, pointed to the underlying problem. In the traditional tourism business model, most of the money generated never reaches local communities, the people who actually live with the influx of visitors.

"Access to financing is key, yet extremely difficult for communities," she explained. The financial products on the market tend to be expensive and inflexible, as tourism is considered a high-risk sector. Her foundation's fund offers low-interest loans with flexible repayment terms. Its guiding principle is that communities generally know what's best for their own land.

Sebastian Munoz, co-founder of Rutopia, a platform specializing in ecotourism and community-based tourism, has brought his experience from the nonprofit sector into social enterprise. His believes tours must be designed in partnership with communities so they feel a sense of ownership, rather than seeing them as something imposed from outside.

Saving Ladakh: Locals lead sustainable tourism drive To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bazan, meanwhile, thinks community-based tourism should not be approached as a humanitarian project, but through a market-driven lens: understanding what visitors are looking for and then planning hand-in-hand with the local community. In other words, building bridges between these two distinct worlds.

"It's not sustainable to create a product if no one comes to experience it," he said.

The challenge: Rethinking growth

The big question is how to grow without sacrificing sustainability. For Bazan, that decision doesn't belong to the tourism industry. Communities themselves must decide how they want to grow, and outside players should not pressure them. Their role, he said, is to amplify local voices, not to bring solutions or investments. "We have to learn to listen," he said.

The impact of community-based tourism is difficult to measure, Munoz acknowledged, because it has social impacts that go beyond the numbers. He cited the example of the Indigenous Mixtec community in Mexico that receives tourists interested in learning the local language. Suddenly, children who today speak only Spanish began joining the classes and asking their grandparents to teach them the language, too.

For Munoz, community-based tourism can be a powerful tool for valuing cultural and regional diversity. It's about creating value over the long term — and that, he said, is where the real experience for visitors lies.

The experts agree that change is slow. But they argue it's worth the effort: If there is more respect for local people and environments, in the end, everyone goes home happier.

This article was originally written in Spanish.

World.title: Zelenskyy urges removal of Starshield limits on Ukraine
World.content:
Ukraine's government has said the throttling of satellite-based internet system prevents Kyiv from intercepting Russian attacks.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the US should remove any restrictions on the Starshield satellite internet system.

Kyiv is "counting" on the move due to severe damage to civilian infrastructure as a result of Russian attacks, Zelenskyy said, sharing photos from eight locations in his country.

"The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," Zelenskyy posted on his X account.

The satellite-based internet system was limited to slower speeds in October, with the limitations only being lifted due to criticism from Ukraine.

Zelenskyy said he had instructed several ministries, including the Ministry of Defense and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, to "work as closely as possible" with the US and Starshield owner Elon Musk's SpaceX. He added that the throttling of the system had helped Russian attacks.

A Russian drone strike in Chornomorsk over the weekend heavily damaged this apartment block Image: Nina Liashonok/REUTERS

According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine's interceptor drones are not effective due to losing connection with operators at the speed of 161 kilometers per hour. This results in the drones not being able to hit Russian drones or rockets.

Russian attacks continue

The past week, Russian attacks in Ukraine included more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 glide bombs and 15 missiles and cruise missiles, Zelenskyy said, calling Moscow's strikes "brutal" and saying they are "difficult to counter."

The US government and SpaceX gave in part contradictory answers to the question of who was responsible for the Starshield speed limit.

A Russian strike on the port city of Chornomorsk over the weekend resulted in six injuries and damaged energy infrastructure, local authorities said.

Zaporizhzhia has been attacked several times in recent days Image: Iwan Fedorow/Ratsverteidigung des Gebiets Saporischschja

According to the authorities, a facility operated by DTEK Odesa Electric Networks was hit, thus leaving some 41,000 customers without power on a temporary basis.

Six people were also injured after Russian attacks on the city of Zaporizhzhia, with one of those injured being a 2-year-old boy, according to Ukraine's emergency services.

Estonia said Russia was responsible for an attempted arson attack on a drone factory, with the border between the two countries to close, citing "clear evidence" Moscow is behind the attack.

World.title: Czechia: Scores protest against public media reform
World.content:
Hundreds of thousands of people gathered to protest against the government's plan to abolish broadcasting fees. Critics say the nationalist coalition would like to secure control over the media.

A protest against plans to abolish broadcasting fees in Czechiadrew between 350,000 and 450,000 people in Prague, organizers said.

The amount of protesters resulted in overcrowded public transport, with many people traveling from other cities by bus and train.

According to protesters, the plan could bring public broadcasters under the control of the country's right-wing government under billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis.

The government would like public broadcasters to be financed by the state budget rather than through fees, arguing that while the plan will not affect editorial independence, broadcasters need to cut costs.

Critics accused the Czech government of wanting to secure more influence through the decision.

The suggested media reform would result in public media's budget being cut down by 15 percent.

Government denies takeover attempt

Babis himself defended the plan last week, saying that his government is not interested in controlling or nationalizing public media.

"None of what the people are protesting against… is true," Babi said.

Foreign Minister Petr Macinka also replied to the criticism by accusing the protest's organizers of turning demonstrations into a business model.

Since its introduction in April, the plan resulted in several large-scale protests, with Czech TV and radio going on a one-day strike in protest against it.

Hundreds of thousands of people attended the demonstration in Prague Image: David W Cerny/REUTERS

International groups have criticized the plan, including the European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists and Reporters Without Borders.

International criticism

The current coalition in Czechia is made of Babis's ANO party, the far-right SPD and the Eurosceptic Motorists.

Prime Minister Andrej Babis rejected the protesters' criticism Image: Michaela Rihova/CTK Photo/IMAGO

While the protests also saw the current coalition being criticized, polls show ANO still enjoys some 30% of support.

Per the Reuters Institute Digital News Report for 2026, trust in the media in Czechia is low and stands between 30% and 33%, with public broadcasters still being considered "the most trusted brands."

World.title: Estonia closes border to Russia after suspected drone factory arson
World.content:
Tallinn has accused Russia of conducting hybrid warfare after a drone factory was set alight in Viimsi. Now it will close its border crossings at the start of December.

Estonia foiled an attempted Russian arson attack on a drone fractory, authorities said on Sunday, prompting the country to close all border crossings with its larger neighbor.

Prime Minister Karsten Michal said that Russia's GRU intelligence service had attempted to sabotage the Estonian defence company Threod Systems in Viimsi on Saturday night.

He said "extensive damage" had been averted after a response by law enforcement, who detained the suspected attackers.

"This is part of Russia's broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia," Michal said.

Estonia to close border crossings with Russia

Hours after the announcement, Estonia's Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said the country would close all border crossings with Russia by December 1.

"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered," he said on social media.

"Closing the border crossings will reduce Russia's ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia and strengthen our efforts to prevent sanctions circumvention."

How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Tsahkna said he informed his Finnish, Latvian, and Lithuanian counterparts of the decision.

Moscow said it would verify whether Estonia was planning to close all border crossings.

"If these are Estonia's actual plans, they will be seen as yet another bout of aggressive and unbridled Russophobia," Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told the TASS news agency.

Eight Latvia-based suspects arrested over alleged sabotage plot

Security forces arrested eight people living in Latvia, Chief Prosecutor Astrid Asi told journalists.

Threod Systems manufactures reconnaissance and attack drones. In August, Milrem, a Tallinn-based defence subcontractor, was targeted in an attempted arson attack. Latvian nationals were arrested in connection with the incident.

Estonia, a member of the European Union and NATO, has three border crossing points with Russia: Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula.

Russia suspended vehicle traffic through Narva in February 2024, although pedestrians were still allowed to cross.

The crossings are among the few remaining operational overland links between Russia and the European Union since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

World.title: El PSOE remonta pero no altera la mayoría de la derecha
World.content:
Después de tres días de campaña, el tracking de 40dB. para EL PAÍS y la Cadena SER sitúa al PSOE en su mejor resultado de toda la legislatura. Por primera vez desde las elecciones de 2023, el instituto demoscópico, que ha venido haciendo barómetros mensuales y ahora realiza una prospección diaria en plena campaña, sitúa a los socialistas por encima del 30%. Pero ese avance no tiene mayor repercusión con vistas a la formación de Gobierno, porque la derecha sigue sumando una confortable mayoría por encima de los 190 escaños.

El cuarto tracking de campaña muestra una recuperación de los socialistas sin que debilite esta vez a las opciones a su izquierda, ya que el Frente Amplio experimenta también un pequeño avance, el primero desde que empezó la campaña. En la derecha, se advierte un ligero repunte del PP mientras Vox no crece en los últimos días. Con todo, la formación de extrema derecha sigue siendo la que capta a más antiguos abstencionistas. El 13,7% de los encuestados que no votó en 2023 afirma ahora que depositará la papeleta del partido de Santiago Abascal, mientras PP y PSOE aparecen casi empatados en ese segmento de la población, ambos con algo más del 10%. Entre ese sector de los ciudadanos que no acudió a las urnas en las anteriores elecciones, sigue primando la indecisión, en la que se declara un 18% de los encuestados.
