World.title: Doha diary: A historian amid the Iran war
World.content:
(Renowned historian and author, Rila Mukherjee, was scheduled to fly from the USA to India by Qatar Airways [QA] on February 25, 2026. Her route—Shreveport–Dallas Fort Worth–Doha–Kolkata—was expected to bring her to Kolkata on the night of February 26 or in the early hours of February 27. However, as of March 8, she was still stranded in Doha. Qatar’s skies were closed due to the US-Israeli attack on Iran. QA’s commercial flights were suspended. At the time of writing, evacuation flights to India were scheduled to start soon. She reached home on 12 March.)

Today is 8 March. I am now camping out in Doha for the ninth day since 28 February. The Qatar airspace is shut and padlocked. The authorities have thrown away the key. Limited numbers of passengers are being flown to Europe and the Americas on evacuation flights (they are called ‘relief flights’) organised by QA, and relief flights to Africa and Asia will start from tomorrow. But for the time being, I am effectively marooned in Doha.

Doha is one of the largest airplane hubs in the world, and a cosmopolitan group of transit passengers has been put up by QA in the 4-star The Royal Riviera Hotel. The hotel is situated on Doha’s Corniche. It is an ageing hotel; not terribly posh, and the plumbing is a bit iffy. But it is well located, with comfortable rooms, and it is a clean and friendly hotel. I feel safe here. Its staff is composed of Asians (from Bangladesh, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Nepal), North Africans (Algerians and Moroccans mostly) and some West Asians. All of them are helpful despite the pressures they are facing. They deal gracefully with the diverse demands and complaints of the passengers.

My room faces the Corniche and I can see the Persian Gulf from my window. As a maritime historian, this makes me very happy.

This country and its national airline are looking after us very well and, really, I have no complaints. QA’s representatives visit the hotel twice daily. There is no information forthcoming on my evacuation to Kolkata, and the greater part of passenger bags are still to arrive at the hotel. My South African neighbour says one of their bags has not been delivered; perhaps it is lost.

We are largely dependent on the clothes we have on our backs and those we had in our carry-on. Most of us are washing and drying them overnight. We have to use the hair dryer if they are still not dry.

My bags came in today, i.e., 8 March.

There are some elderly travellers. Many of them say that their medicines are running out. Mine will last another week.

Will I be able to get out by then?

We are told that a limited air corridor may open today; alternatively, we may be evacuated by the land route through Saudi Arabia to Riyadh (this would take around seven hours), where a leased QA aircraft may take us to India. But we have to make our own arrangements for the Saudi e-visa and overland travel. This seems a risky enterprise. And whether this potential leased aircraft would fly me direct to Kolkata is not known. There is no clarity to date.

***

But if I was scheduled to arrive in Kolkata on 27 February (and the war broke out a day later, on 28 February), how is it that I am still in Doha

Ah, thereby hangs a tale!

It is a cautionary tale on buying air tickets with multiple connections, and what ensues when the first connection does not take off as per schedule.

***

I had spent nine weeks in Shreveport with my son and daughter-in-law and was scheduled to leave on 25 February. Unfortunately, my flight from Shreveport to Dallas Fort Worth (DFW) by QA’s codeshare partner American Airlines (AA) did not take off. We were told that the incoming flight had nose gear problems and therefore could not land. Ultimately it made an emergency landing. Fire engines, firefighters, EMTs and ambulances were standing by. Luckily, there was no fireball and there were no casualties. The vice-chair of my daughter-in-law’s department was on that flight; I bumped into him in the terminal as he deplaned, and he said that the landing had been really scary.

There were no more AA flights to DFW that day. Roo and Stephanie came back to the airport and took me home. I spent a restless night. I hate flying at the best of times.

I was put on the same AA flight the next day, on 26 February, but when I reached DFW I was told that my connection flight to Doha was full. Apparently, the AA staff at Shreveport Regional Airport knew there were no seats on that flight; nevertheless they sent me on to DFW hoping I would ‘sort out’ the matter with AA’s customer care there. The only ‘sorting out’ that AA did at DFW was to put me on a later QA flight to Doha on the same day, that is, late evening on 26 February. It was a smaller aircraft (not the Airbus 350 on which I was ticketed), the flight was cramped and some of my co-passengers were not very well behaved. One lady kept on drinking; she skipped the meal service and was quite abusive. Another one, African American, told me that as an ‘American’ she was superior to Asians. Right, I thought, we all know how you as a Black person got there!!!

In all my years of travelling I have never encountered such blatant racism.

When we reached Doha very late on the night of 27 February (almost 24 hours later due to the time difference with DFW), I had missed that evening’s flight to Kolkata!

No problem, QA’s customer care said, we’ll talk with AA as it is their problem. This took a while, so I went off to buy myself a snack at Brioche Dorée in the airport’s food court.

By then it was early morning on 28 February.

Readers, note the date!

***

AA agreed to comp me a room for the remainder of the night at The Royal Riviera Hotel. I was granted a 48-hour emergency visa by Qatar Immigration and I was shifted to the hotel on 28 February at 2 AM. QA’s ground staff helped me throughout. The room was comfortable, the bed looked inviting, and I went to sleep, confident that my Kolkata flight would take off as scheduled at 18.45 hours on that day itself (that is, 28 February). At that point, I was going to reach only 24 hours behind my original schedule.

I informed Kolkata and asked my driver to collect me from the airport accordingly.

***

On 28 February, I was woken around 8 AM by a strange sound from my cell phone. It was a very loud, continuous screech. I don’t have international roaming and I wondered who was calling me and what was happening. I saw a ‘Security Alert’ on my screen but the text was in Arabic. I started hearing thuds and bangs. Another alert, still in Arabic, came in.

What was going on? I was mystified.

I was now getting alerts in English. It said the US and Israel had jointly attacked Iran. US bases and embassies and consulates across the Gulf were vulnerable. Qatar was in this critical area. Sirens were going off. I started watching Al Jazeera and Richard Engel on NBC.

This was Day 1.

Smoke rises following an explosion, after Israel and the US launched strikes on Iran, in Tehran, Iran, February 28, 2026. PHOTO: REUTERS

By Day 2, the Gulf was not just lying in a war zone; it had been converted into a theatre of war. Doha was undergoing regular drone strikes and missile attacks.

Day 3 was relatively quiet. Apparently, Qatar and Iran had a phone conversation, and Qatar urged Iran to stop the strikes. But our temporary visas were extended by Qatar. This was an indication that the phone call was not conclusive. This war was not going to end anytime soon.

The Qatar–Iran conversation does not seem to have yielded the desired result. There is no relief from Iranian attacks. These now form the backdrop to our daily life at The Royal Riviera. Drone attacks and missile strikes re-started from Day 4. None of them target the downtown area; they target only the US base and industrial areas in Qatar. Most of the drones and missiles are successfully intercepted; the few that are not cause localised fires. The attacks usually happen around breakfast and lunch, and sometimes they occur very late at night or in the early morning hours. This means we are always in a state of extreme alert. It is jarring on the nerves. We can neither eat properly nor rest. We are getting stressed out.

But I must also mention that the attacks and interceptions sound more like Diwali patakas than the very loud explosions that one expects.

*** Days 4 till 9 (that is, till date) have seen this regional war extending from land to sea: from the Hormuz Strait to the Indian Ocean. This is now becoming very serious. Critical choke points like this strait have become a curse. Ports across the Gulf are lying idle; almost no cargo is getting through. But we have had no alerts today. Does this mean that Iran will not strike Qatar for the time being? Is this a temporary reprieve? Will relief flights be able to take off? ***

Some bags arrived at the hotel on Day 5. Mine were not among them.

By Days 6 and 7 we have more or less settled into what is turning out to be our semi-permanent home. The hotel is no longer very ‘royal’; it has taken on the character of a London bedsit. Or a council housing estate in one of the UK’s inner cities! Children play noisy games in the corridors, an oddly comforting sound among the explosions, security alerts and sirens that go on regularly.

I see an enormous solidarity among the travellers, both on my floor and when we meet up at meal times. I have a very nice South African couple next door who check on me each morning, always asking how I am faring (‘please don’t hesitate to knock if you face any difficulties’). They have even offered to take me out to buy clothes (this was before my bags arrived). Elegant MENA (Middle East North Africa) people greet me each day at breakfast, a young Pakistani financial analyst from Toronto shares his insights with me at the breakfast table, and a British couple advise me to carry my passport with me at all times (especially when I leave my room in case of an attack and subsequent fire). They kindly offered to buy me my medicines, although they are at least a decade older than me. A young school teacher from Geneva shares my table at dinner. I have not seen her lately; perhaps she has already been repatriated on one of the relief flights to Europe which started operating from Day 7. The British couple and the South Africans are still here; the Pakistani man left for Toronto early this morning. He was given only two hours’ notice and he phoned my room to say goodbye at 1.15 AM this morning.

***

What does my daily schedule look like?

It is like what I imagine a day at boarding school would be. Because it is Ramadan, the hotel starts the breakfast buffet from 3 AM, lunch is from 12 noon, and dinner is over by 7.30. The food served (although mild in taste and quasi-institutional as regards the daily menu, which does not rotate much in terms of items), is nevertheless amazingly varied as regards the cuisine: Arabic, Turkish, Italian, Spanish and South Asian (the last is not good at all). A lot of lemon is used in the preparations, but practically no onions. This may be due to the fact that there was an onion shortage; onions came in from India only on Day 5. There are loads of different kinds of salads, some bland European cheeses and diverse types of hummus. In addition, there is feta cheese, stuffed vine leaves, green and black olives, veg and non-veg samosas and spring rolls, koftas, and baba ghanoush or baingan bharta. Good cappuccinos and lattes. Flaky croissants and brioches, pastries and amazing Arabian/Persian/Yemeni sweets. A decadent baked (and often caramelised) bread pudding called Umm Ali is served at dinner. Obviously, the Qatari supermarkets are still well-stocked with FMCG. The Indian-origin Lulu supermarket chain has flown in a whole lot of perishable and non-perishable food items.

Strangely, no fresh fruit!

***

Gas prices have shot up.

I have given up watching the death and destruction on TV, and watch Looney Tunes, Anthony Bourdain, Fawlty Towers and Mr Bean instead. Priyam Paul, my editor at The Daily Star, has sent me some e-books which help to pass the time.

When I am not reading, or watching sitcoms, cartoons and travel and food documentaries, I reflect on what brought us to this war. I see the Persian Gulf from my room; it is still a brilliant blue. But it is also desolate since the Hormuz Strait was closed off. I see no cargo ships or container vessels; there are no cruise ships or tankers. For a maritime historian like me, this is not the Persian Gulf I know. After all, it has been a crossroads since recorded history! My India in the Indian Ocean World (2022) documents this history of two thousand years at the very least. Now, mobility is severely constrained.

Persian Gulf. Photo: Collected

We are living now in a world of fragmented geopolitics, of accelerated climate degradation, and of critical demographic shifts. The world is undergoing these changes along with increasingly disaffected groups of peoples, perhaps terrorists, some of them. We are seeing the rise of AI which, to my mind, is linked, along with the toxicity of social media, with the increasing authoritarianism that we see worldwide. It horrifies me when I see a young nation declare it will bring ‘civilisation’ to Iran. It disregards the fact that Iran-as-Persia predates Arab culture and is one of the world’s oldest culture areas. Not just the glory of Shi’ite Safavid Persia (1501–1736), which political theorists and analysts invoke when describing this civilisational space and whose heritage modern Iran draws on: think of the period from c. 550 BCE to 651 CE (Muslim conquest and start of Islamisation by the Rashidun Caliphate), when four mighty Persian empires ruled a large portion of the then-known world: Achaemenid, Seleucid, Parthian and Sassanian. Persia challenged Egypt, Greece and Rome, and then it faced up to the Ottoman and Russian empires. This memory of resistance of 2500 years will not be easily erased.

However, the total disregard of international law and the collapse of the rules-based order will usher in a new regional order in West Asia. This will impact on the Gulf states. Once-biblical Lebanon is almost destroyed by a rampant Israel. Syria has closed its borders. As a rogue USA intimidates Persia and trains its eye on the Caucasus and Azerbaijan, it also destabilises Iraq. Iranian Kurds based in Iraq have been reactivated. How will this impact on the Turkish Kurds? Turkey, a NATO country, is already feeling threatened.

The relatively young post-WW1 statelets in the Gulf will lose out in the violent reshuffle in the greater region. The Dubai story was already over. And Oman had lost its sheen even earlier. Financial and service centres will shift eastward—to Singapore or perhaps to KL. As will global airline hubs. The Gulf states will see their importance in location, business and finance diminish. They will have to reconsider their dependence on the USA which has now become a double-edged sword. Iran will endure, but perhaps in a new form. But it will not be erased from the map of the world.

World.title: André Béteille: A sociologist Bangladesh should read
World.content:
My first encounter with the ideas of Professor André Béteille was in July 1966 in an introductory sociology course at the University of Dhaka (at that time in East Pakistan) through Professor Tom Bottomore’s book, Sociology: A Guide to Problems and Literature (1962). The emphasis on general theory of social stratification for an explanation of the Indian caste system found its empirical reflection, as Bottomore refers to, in the work of Béteille, especially in Caste, Class and Power: Changing Patterns of Stratification in a Tanjore Village (1965).

My second encounter with him was in the Fall of 1975 at Dalhousie University, Halifax where I was writing my Master’s thesis under Professor Bottomore, and he referred to read me Béteille’s “Closed and open social stratification” (1966). Reading Béteille after nine years under the Maple tree, I began to admire his empirical depth, comparative methodology, and theoretical clarity, which reshaped my understanding of social hierarchies in India.

In the Christmas of 1976, I had an occasion to share some of my understanding of Béteille’s work. At that time, I was at York University, Toronto where I was doing my PhD. Professor K. Ishwaran, one of our faculty members, who wrote Tradition and Economy in Village India (1966), invited me for Christmas dinner-- Turkey with cranberry sauce, cooked by his Dutch wife. There we talked about the contribution of both Béteille and his supervisor M. N. Srinivas towards understanding the impact of social change on Indian social stratification.

In order to realistically understand contemporary caste hierarchy, Béteille emphasised the “other factors such as class and power” that “have to be considered as independent variables” (1966). It appeared to me highly useful for comparative empirical research. It creates a distance from traditional essentialist and ideological perspective of inequality.

Borrowed from Max Weber, he focused on multidimensionality of stratification and examined how status, economic resources, and political control interact to shape multifarious social order. This was a tremendous contribution in the field of stratification studies. Though he focused on rural stratification, the model is also applicable to the study of urban social stratification.

It is puzzling that in Bangladesh universities, both sociology and anthropology disciplines overlooked and neglected the Weberian model of multidimensional stratification system: anthropology remained spell-bound under the dichotomous model of rural “ashraf-atraf”; and sociology was locked in the iron cage of simplistic Marxist model of “land ownership” under the name of peasant studies. In spite of teaching Weber’s “Class, Status, Party” (1922/1946) in the universities, there is a marked absence of the application of Weberian model in the study of rural and urban complex social hierarchy. Probably in Bangladesh, this shows the intellectual bankruptcy of these disciplines, which are suffering from morbidity.

In fact, in order to understand contemporary social change in Bangladesh, especially its regime of accumulation under crony capitalism, it is essential to understand the nexus between power and class. The determining power of traditional property ownership in the formation of classes and consequent class consciousness has diminished in Bangladesh.

The notion of political capitalism advanced by Max Weber is also useful in understanding Bangladesh social stratification, especially class formation. The party consciousness along with ruling party affiliation, may give legitimate or illegitimate access to economic resources, thereby determining class position in terms of life opportunities and life style. This in turn, heavily influence commodification of prestige and honour; and becomes marker of status.

André Beteille (1934 - 2026). Photo: Collected

The rural and urban dispossession, which is an integral part of neoliberal and crony capitalism’s regime of accumulation, is also the progenitor of emergent lumpen bourgeoisie, whose class position do not correspond with their demeaning status position. Again, the traditional status group in Bangladesh, as Béteille found in his Tanjore village study with respect to traditional caste, suffer from status dislocation, having less access to power and economic resources. The ontology of inequality and hierarchy can best be understood by the Weberian epistemology.

I think study of this process of social change, and its impact on inequality in Bangladesh, is vital towards understanding Bangladesh society. The internationally acclaimed Indian empirical model provided by Béteille can be one of the best guides to study the intersectionality of class, status and power in both urban and rural Bangladesh. It is unfortunate that social sciences in Bangladesh have neglected such a significant social dynamic that affects all our lives.

In March 1989, Professor Abhijit Dasgupta, a colleague of Professor Béteille, facilitated my direct meeting with him. Professor Dasgupta was kind enough to arrange a seminar talk by me in the sociology department of Delhi School of Economics. After the seminar, I paid a visit to Professor Béteille’s office room. He was very warm and hospitable to offer tea to me and my wife. He spoke in Bangla and affirmed his Bangali origin. I felt very comfortable to have a vibe of Bengal. I mentioned to him how I came to know of his work à la Bottomore and Ishwaran. I was so surprised to experience his stock of knowledge mediated by modesty and simplicity. The meeting with professor Béteille during the short-lived spring of Delhi was one of the most memorable events of my life. I wish his conceptual and methodological clarity inspire the young Bangladeshi sociologists to break the chain of ignorance, myopic framework, and the hegemony of intellectual infantilism.

A.I. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed is a professor in the Department of Sociology at the University of Dhaka.

World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Push to electrify global economy stalls at U.N. climate talks
World.content:
A bid to accelerate global electrification is faltering at United Nations climate talks, highlighting the challenge of securing new emissions-cutting commitments.

Organizers of the summit in Antalya, Turkey, are seeking support for a voluntary pledge to raise electricity’s share of global final energy demand to 35% by 2035, from just over 20% currently. They also want the target included in the COP31 summit’s final declaration, giving it the backing of nearly 200 nations.

The campaign has won endorsement from companies including ABB Ltd. and Schneider Electric, as well as more than two dozen countries.

Yet securing the consensus needed to include the target in the final declaration is proving difficult as negotiators enter a second week of talks.

The Like-Minded Developing Countries bloc, which represents two dozen nations including China, India and Bangladesh, has made clear it will not support any recognition of the electrification pledge in the text, according to people familiar with the matter who asked for anonymity to detail private negotiations.

Representatives of the negotiating bloc did not respond to requests for comment.

While parties might still find a compromise, the opposition also effectively spikes efforts to specify that the goal should involve commitments to use clean electricity.

Options considered to reference the proposal in the final text include simply acknowledging the initiative — with or without repeating its 2035 goal — or a more generic recognition of efforts to boost electrification globally.

“What we are seeking to do is to capture some of that ambition that’s around electrification,” Chris Bowen, president of negotiations at COP31 and Australia’s climate change and energy minister, told reporters Saturday. “There’s more work to do there. I am very keen to see those conversations continue.”

The issue is materializing as a test of how far the COP31 summit will go to address the world’s expected overshoot of Paris Agreement commitments to limit global temperature rise as wars, inflation and energy supply disruptions challenge multilateral consensus.

Nations at the climate talks are debating how to galvanize more emission cuts, unlock additional finance for developing countries and ensure the transition away from fossil fuels doesn’t leave some communities behind.

At the heart of the electrification push is an expectation that a growing reliance on electricity to meet transportation, heating and industrial needs will help the world decarbonize — especially if that power is generated by emission-free renewable sources.

Turkey first announced the initiative earlier this year, and by Saturday, more than 30 governments and nearly 100 private-sector organizations had expressed support for the pledge, according to COP31 President Murat Kurum.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said at the talks Thursday that his country will endorse the goal.

Previous voluntary targets have produced only modest results — including efforts to boost renewable energy and to pare methane pollution.

Electricity can come from a range of sources, including fossil fuels, and the existing proposals don’t discriminate between clean or polluting sources of generation. While the European Union had considered pushing for the electrification target to be limited to cleaner power, it recognized that might alienate countries with energy systems that remain deeply dependent on fossil fuels.

“A certain degree of pragmatism is probably warranted because otherwise you might end up with a relatively small group of people,” Wopke Hoekstra, the EU’s climate chief, told reporters Friday. “The name of the game of the COP is multilateralism and making the tent as large as possible.”

World.title: Raising neurodivergent kids in Japan’s international homes
World.content:
In Japan, trains run on the second, lines form without protest and crowded streets flow without a shove.

On social media, videos from vacationing parents have cast the country and its orderly society, culture and infrastructure as an unexpected haven for neurodivergent children.

But traveling through the country is very different from building a life in it.

World.title: Main hall of Okinawa’s Shuri Castle unveiled to media
World.content:
The interior of the Seiden main hall of Shuri Castle in Naha was recently unveiled to the media following its restoration after a fire in 2019.

The hall will be open to the public from Nov. 23 after a completion ceremony hosted by the government.

The interior consists of three floors, with the Usasuka throne occupying the center of the first and second floors, where kings of the Ryukyu Kingdom conducted political affairs and ceremonial events.

The second floor features decorations influenced by Chinese culture, including golden dragon pillars and glossy black lacquered handrails.

A tablet measuring 1.4 meters high and 3.5 meters wide, bearing an inscription inspired by a letter bestowed by a Chinese emperor, is displayed on the upper wall.

Based on knowledge gained since the 1992 restoration, the tablet’s background color was changed from vermilion to yellow, while the gilded dragon motifs were recreated as sculptures instead of paintings.

The second floor of the main hall features decorations influenced by Chinese culture, including golden dragon pillars and glossy black lacquered handrails. | JIJI

On the first floor, the Usasuka throne is adorned with hanging decorations featuring dragons embroidered with a traditional technique and brightly colored ornamental beads.

Guide panels explaining decorative features and how the hall was used have also been installed ahead of its public opening.

Admission to the interior requires advance reservations. According to the Okinawa Churashima Foundation, which manages Shurijo Castle Park, tickets for the opening day have sold out, although reservations remain available for visits from Nov. 24 onward.

World.title: Peak Energy eyes South Korea green projects as war upends fuel flows
World.content:
Countries including South Korea and the Philippines are becoming increasingly attractive to renewables developers such as Singapore-based Peak Energy, as governments accelerate clean energy adoption to overcome fuel disruptions due to the U.S.-Iran war.

Seoul has “set targets to connect more power to the grid and push costs down,” said Gavin Adda, chief executive of the company backed by Stonepeak Partners, an alternative investment firm that manages about $98 billion in assets. “You’re seeing a big increase in the number of developers trying to work out how to operate there.”

The growing interest comes as conflict in the Middle East continues to choke flows of liquefied natural gas from Qatar — the world’s second producer last year — and keeps prices of the fuel at multi-year highs. That’s forced governments to turn to alternatives, including accelerating the adoption of solar and wind. South Korea depended on Qatar for about 15% of its LNG supplies last year, according to World Bank data.

South Korean authorities in September announced measures to ease restrictions on renewable energy projects connecting to the power grid, particularly in the southwestern Honam region. The grid-connection date for one of Peak Energy’s solar farms has been brought forward by five years to 2029, with other developers seeing similar improvements, Adda said.

The country’s power demand should also increase as the artificial intelligence boom drives a rapid buildout of data centers, and Peak Energy has received requests to supply electricity to hyperscalers, he added.

Peak Energy has $250 million in projects in South Korea and another $100 million’s worth getting underway in 2027. These account for a large share of the firm’s 300 megawatts of operating assets, which are spread across eight Asia-Pacific markets including the Philippines, Japan, Australia and Taiwan.

The Iran conflict has also pushed the Philippines to bring renewable projects online earlier. The Southeast Asian country already allows full foreign ownership of projects and has a green lane to speed up approvals for major investments.

“It’s the fastest country in Asia for developing renewable projects,” Adda said in an interview last week. “So I can shake hands with you as a landowner, and I can start construction one year to 18 months later.”

The Philippines is expected to add 5.6 gigawatts of new solar capacity this year, more than all of its Southeast Asian peers, according to BloombergNEF forecasts. While the pipeline remains robust, the Department of Energy earlier this year terminated agreements for nearly 18 GW of clean-power projects, as many prospective investors had no plans to build them and were waiting to sell the rights.

World.title: ‘Zero’ break time: Fukuoka union uncovers strain put on teachers’ work
World.content:
A teachers union in the city of Fukuoka has obtained time sheets showing that almost every public junior high school teacher there had taken “zero minutes of break time” despite Japan’s labor law requiring employers to provide breaks.

The records, obtained from the municipal board of education through a freedom-of-information request, covered time sheets of about 4,000 teachers and staff members at all 72 municipal junior high schools from April through June. The more than 48,000 pages of document blacked out teachers’ names but listed their schools, start and end times, and break periods.

After examining the records, the union found that only eight entries showed anything other than zero in the column labeled “total break time.”

World.title: Japan planning to build network to share disaster information across Asia
World.content:
The government plans to build a network to share natural disaster-related information across Asia, as well as knowledge accumulated in Southeast Asia, government sources said Monday.

The government hopes to use the network to encourage countries across Asia to introduce early-warning systems that analyze meteorological data and issue alerts before natural disasters strike.

The plan will be announced during the 31st Conference of the Parties to the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, or COP31, which is being held in Turkey.

Early warning systems analyze data collected by satellites and radar to alert those at risk of sustaining damage from disasters. Examples in Japan include the government’s heatstroke alert system and “Kikikuru” service visualizing the risk of landslides and flooding on a map.

Japan started a public-private project in 2023 to spread services using disaster early warning systems in the Asia-Pacific region. It has conducted research on market needs and feasibility in member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and supported companies hoping to start related businesses in such countries.

In Thailand, where flash flooding caused by sudden weather changes is a major problem, Japan’s Weathernews provides weather information such as forecasts and warnings of sudden localized downpours.

Through the envisioned network, the Japanese government aims to share knowledge and examples from six ASEAN countries and facilitate the introduction of disaster early warning systems throughout Asia to help minimize the loss and damage from climate change.

World.title: Congo Ebola outbreak defies control as conflict, hunger fuel crisis six months in
World.content:
Six months into the biggest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s history, containing the virus increasingly depends on solving problems far beyond Ebola — hunger, armed conflict, mistrust and a health system already buckling under the strain.

More than 11,000 people have been infected and 5,500 have died since the outbreak was declared May 15. For months, Ebola has been killing roughly 240 people a week, the equivalent of about one and a half Boeing Co. 737 passenger jets crashing every week.

“It’s a systems problem compounded by basically geography, insecurity, conflict, poor roads, mistrust,” said William Clemmer, a physician who has worked in Congo for three decades and is senior regional health adviser for Corus International based in Goma.

World.title: Fukuoka mayoral election with record 13 candidates ends without winner
World.content:
Sunday’s Fukuoka mayoral election ended without a winner and will have to be held again after none of the record-breaking 13 candidates reached the minimum legal threshold to declare victory.

The total vote count was 592,723 — 45.6% of eligible voters and 11.3 percentage points higher than the previous election in the Kyushu region’s largest city.

But the large number of rivals diluted the vote. Only former Lower House member Shuji Inatomi, 56, came close to the minimum 25% of the vote necessary to declare victory. He won 137,667 votes, or about 23%.

“I have to solemnly accept that I was not strong enough. Although I received the most votes, I wasn’t able to reach my goal,” the former Centrist Reform Alliance member told his supporters early Monday morning after it was announced nobody had secured the legally required minimum.

The record number of candidates came about after incumbent mayor Soichiro Takashima announced in August he would not seek a fifth term but did not indicate who he wanted to succeed him, while the major political parties did not jointly back a single candidate.

Following Inatomi, former independent Fukuoka city council member Yu Shinmura, 46, finished in second place, squeaking ahead of IT engineer Kentaro Mori, 48, a member of the Conservative Party of Japan, by just 618 votes.

Another former city council member, Takashi Shirabe, 48, was nominated by the Liberal Democratic Party’s Fukuoka city council group. But due to a bribery scandal involving LDP prefectural assembly members, the party did not formally endorse him. He ended up in fourth place, and the top four vote-getters collectively won about two-thirds of the total.

Mayoral reelections due to large numbers of candidates and no one receiving at least a quarter of the vote are extremely rare. In 2003, Sapporo was forced to hold another election after none of the seven candidates received the minimum percentage. In the reelection, four candidates competed, and the winner was Fumio Ueda, who had won the most votes in the initial election.

Candidates in Sunday’s Fukuoka election are allowed to file objections if the city’s election commission declares there was no winner. If no objections are filed, a reelection will be held by Jan. 19.

World.title: Hong Kong’s John Lee pledges stronger regional ties ahead of Apec summit trip
World.content:
Hong Kong’s leader will depart for the Apec conferences in Shenzhen on Tuesday, as he pledges to strengthen connectivity with other economies and contribute to regional prosperity and development.

A government spokesman said on Monday that Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu would attend the Apec CEO Summit on Tuesday and Wednesday, as well as the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting on Thursday.

Lee said that Apec member economies were important trading partners of the city, accounting for as much as 87 per cent of Hong Kong’s external trade.

World.title: Geopolitics a threat to shipping but Hong Kong can tap mainland China’s potential: experts
World.content:
Geopolitics will remain the biggest challenge to Hong Kong’s shipping industry as it seeks to stay competitive, although US President Donald Trump’s indication to hold off on further attacks on Iran is positive news amid the global fuel crisis, industry leaders have said.

They also highlighted the strategic importance of the city’s container terminal in Kwai Tsing as a link between mainland China and the world, saying it was a key piece of infrastructure for Hong Kong despite a sustained decline in trade volume in recent years.

In a recent interview with the South China Morning Post, Hing Chao, co-founder and executive chairman of the Hong Kong Chamber of Shipping, said the city was often left exposed in geopolitical conflicts.

World.title: 5,000 people linked to HKMU may have had personal data leaked in cyber breach
World.content:
About 5,000 people linked to a university in Hong Kong may have had their personal data compromised in a cybersecurity incident, with information allegedly being offered for sale on the dark web.

Data advertised by dark web sellers reportedly included the names of Hong Kong Metropolitan University (HKMU) students, Hong Kong identity card numbers, telephone numbers, addresses and grade point averages (GPAs).

In response to South China Morning Post queries, the university confirmed on Sunday that it had discovered an “information security incident” on November 4 and notified all staff and students by email the following day.

World.title: Hundreds attend mass for Tai Po fire victims as bishop dismisses talk of pressure
World.content:
Hundreds of Hongkongers have flocked to a Catholic mass offered for the victims of the deadly Tai Po fire ahead of its first anniversary, as a church leader dismissed speculation that the event had come under pressure from authorities.

The Immaculate Heart of Mary Church in Tai Po on Sunday celebrated a mass “in memory of lives lost over the whole year and the deceased of the Wang Fuk Court fire”.

World.title: Hong Kong police investigate theft of HK$810,000 in cash, gold jewellery from flat
World.content:
A public housing resident in Hong Kong has lost more than HK$800,000 (US$101,960) worth of cash and gold jewellery that disappeared from her flat in Ngau Tau Kok, prompting a police investigation.

Police said the 41-year-old woman filed a report at about 11.55am on Sunday after discovering the items were missing from her home in Kwai Fai House, Lower Ngau Tau Kok Estate.

The missing items included gold jewellery worth about HK$500,000 and HK$310,000 in cash, bringing the total loss to about HK$810,000, according to police.

World.title: Hongkongers face chilliest days of the season as cold front brings wind and rain
World.content:
Hongkongers will experience the chilliest days of autumn this coming week, with temperatures expected to drop to 16 degrees Celsius (61 Fahrenheit) as a cold front sweeps across the southern Chinese coast.

The expected drop to 16 degrees on Friday and Saturday may mark the coldest days of the month, falling below the previous low of 17.5 degrees recorded in the city on November 10, according to records on the Hong Kong Observatory’s website.

Temperatures earlier in the month remained above 17.5 degrees, with the daily minimum ranging from that low to a peak of 26.4 degrees on November 6.

World.title: Geopolitics won’t affect Interpol assembly in Hong Kong: police chief
World.content:
Hong Kong’s police chief has dismissed concerns that geopolitical tensions could affect attendance at the coming Interpol general assembly to be held in the city, saying transnational cooperation on policing is “inevitable”.

Speaking on a television programme on Sunday, Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming responded to questions about whether American and European countries would send representatives to the meeting, to be held from November 30 to December 3 in Hong Kong.

“Geopolitics is one thing, but collaboration on policing is another matter. In the end, every region or country hopes to serve its residents. Some cross-border cooperation is inevitable,” he said.

World.title: Hong Kong taxi driver arrested after 2 Britons hit by cab in Wan Chai
World.content:
Hong Kong police have arrested a taxi driver for alleged dangerous driving after his vehicle hit two British nationals who were crossing the road in Wan Chai.

Police said on Sunday that the incident happened at 1.39am, when the victims – a 65-year-old man and a 58-year-old woman – were crossing the road near Hay Wah Building in Wan Chai while the taxi was travelling west along Hennessy Road.

The victims sustained head injuries and were admitted to Queen Mary Hospital in Pok Fu Lam. The man was semi-conscious upon arrival at the hospital before recovering later, while the woman remained conscious throughout, police added.

World.title: What Made Jade So Valuable in Ancient China and the Americas?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019256/What Made Jade So Valuable in Ancient China and the Americas?
World.content:
Recent exhibitions at the Shanghai Museum and Beijing’s Capital Museum have introduced Chinese audiences to the civilizations of the ancient Americas. For Chinese visitors, the importance placed on jade may feel familiar. In both ancient China and Mesoamerica, finely worked jade adorned the powerful and accompanied them into the grave, a striking similarity that has long attracted scholarly interest.

How did jade come to carry such authority? One way to explore this question is to compare the jade traditions of Liangzhu and the Classic Maya lowlands, two societies from ancient China and the Americas. Liangzhu was an early regional state near present-day Hangzhou, capital of eastern China’s Zhejiang province, around 3300–2300 BC, with a walled capital, an extensive system of dams, and a pronounced social hierarchy. In the Classic Maya lowlands, spanning parts of present-day Mexico, Guatemala, and Belize, cities ruled by royal dynasties flourished around AD 300–900. Both Liangzhu and Maya cities hold UNESCO World Heritage status.

Thousands of years separated the two societies, and there is no evidence of direct contact between them. Yet both had complex social hierarchies in which powerful ritual authorities played important roles. By tracing jade from the selection of raw stone to its final resting place, we can see how control over labor, knowledge, and materials helped establish its authority in ways that were both similar and distinct.

Jade was valued in both ancient China and the Americas long before Liangzhu and the Classic Maya. The concept of jade encompasses several kinds of stone. Liangzhu’s finest ritual jades were made from nephrite, while Maya jade was principally jadeite. Both were prized for their appearance and could be polished to a lustrous finish. Craftspeople shaped jade using abrasives such as sand mixed with water. Working with different stones helped them recognize differences in hardness and toughness and determine which materials were best suited to particular objects.

In Liangzhu, material choice was closely tied to the form and status of the finished artifact. Other stones, such as serpentine, were generally used for small, less prestigious ornaments. Among the Maya, by contrast, the symbolic meanings of stones were more closely associated with their colors. Green and blue-green evoked water, cultivating maize, and renewed life. Jadeite remained highly prized, but a wider range of similarly colored stones could also be valued for their quality and craftsmanship.

Not everyone had equal access to these raw materials or the specialized skills needed to work them. This inequality helped establish jade’s association with power.

Workshops within and immediately outside Liangzhu city made prestigious ritual objects from nephrite. A short distance away, a large workshop complex specialized in small serpentine ornaments. Despite their proximity, the workshops used different materials and produced different types of objects. The fine finish of these serpentine ornaments, however, shows that their makers were skilled.

This contrast suggests that proximity and skill alone did not guarantee access to nephrite. Access appears to have depended on a workshop’s role and status within the production system.

Evidence from the Maya suggests broader access to raw jadeite, but tighter restrictions on the skills and knowledge required to produce elaborate royal artifacts. Near the jadeite sources in Guatemala’s Motagua Valley, in the country’s southeastern highlands, households of different social ranks shaped, sawed, and drilled the stone. At Cancuén, in the country’s center, much of the waste from the early stages of production was found in modest residences. Elaborately finished objects, however, were concentrated in elite buildings, alongside some tools used to polish ear ornaments.

While non-elite households carried out the early stages of jade production, finer carving, including sacred images and inscriptions that conveyed ritual and political meanings, appears to have been largely reserved for elites or specialist craftspeople working for them. Creating these details required skills and knowledge that were less widely shared. Access to raw jadeite did not necessarily mean access to the expertise needed to produce elaborate royal artifacts.

As jade artifacts took shape, their imagery became another critical means of expressing power. This is particularly evident in elite burials, where jade objects helped convey the status and ritual authority of those buried with them.

A jade cong, or ritual tube, from Fanshan, an elite cemetery within Liangzhu city, illustrates how craftsmanship and sacred imagery conveyed authority. Its surface bears an intricately carved human-and-animal-face motif known as the Sacred Insignia. The finest versions appeared on the most prestigious ritual jades, whose material and craftsmanship signaled status.

The cong also belonged to a prescribed set of burial goods. Within Liangzhu’s political center, elite burials followed established conventions that linked the types and placement of artifacts to rank and gender, leaving little scope for personal preference. Differences in the quantity and quality of objects expressed the deceased’s rank and ritual authority within this prescribed framework.

Maya rulers, by contrast, drew on shared beliefs but had greater freedom in how they arranged jade. One example comes from the tomb of Pakal the Great, ruler of the Maya city-state of Palenque, in what is now southern Mexico. His funerary mask is a mosaic of carefully fitted pieces of jade in different shades of green. Scholars interpret its youthful face as linking the ruler to the Maize God. A cube in one hand, a sphere in the other, a bead beside each foot, and a central belt figurine have been interpreted as forming a quincunx, a five-point arrangement representing the four directions and a center in Maya cosmology, with Pakal at its symbolic center.

Pakal’s jades derived meaning from their individual forms and their placement within his tomb. Shared beliefs could guide such arrangements without requiring the standardized sets found in Liangzhu elite graves. Maya sacred imagery also appeared on multicolored ceramic vessels, carved stone monuments, and buildings. Jade was one of several materials through which rulers expressed their place in the world.

The movement and final placement of jade objects also reflected their association with power in both societies.

In Liangzhu, the movement of prestigious jade objects appears to have reinforced relationships among elites. Similarities in carving between the political center and neighboring settlements suggest that these objects circulated primarily among elites, possibly through gift exchanges. Local production continued, but the most sophisticated carving techniques remained concentrated near the political center. When finished, Liangzhu jades were deliberately buried; prestigious ritual objects were typically placed in individual elite graves, while lower-ranking burials contained smaller, less elaborate ornaments.

Among the Maya, jade served purposes beyond elite ownership. Different forms of jade circulated in different ways. Some ornaments bore inscriptions linking them to particular people and events, while plain beads and axe-shaped objects known as celts circulated more freely and may have been used as payment by the Postclassic period (900–1521). Non-elite households acquired small jade beads that could express wealth and status. At Cancuén, jade-working households buried raw or partly worked jade during house construction, suggesting that even unfinished jade material held ritual value. At Copán, in western Honduras, jade and shell artifacts were buried together in a residential courtyard, showing how different materials could serve similar ritual purposes beyond royal burials.

These differences reveal how the two societies developed distinct ways of turning jade into a symbol of wealth and authority. In Liangzhu, the quality of the stone, specialized craftsmanship, sacred imagery, and rules governing its use were brought together in a tightly regulated system. Among the Maya, jade acquired authority through a wider range of materials and ritual settings, allowing for broader participation and more flexible exchange alongside restrictions imposed by elites.

Jade’s beauty may have made it desirable, but it was people who made it precious. Through craftsmanship, sacred rituals, and control over who could possess it, ancient societies transformed stone into a symbol of wealth and authority. The treasures displayed in museums today reveal a larger truth: The value of precious things lies not just in what they are, but in who gets to decide what they are worth.
