World.title: Defense lists 4 more witnesses in Sara Duterte trial
World.content:
TRIAL. Defense lead counsel Shiela Sison briefs her team during Day 43 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on November 12, 2026.

(1st UPDATE) One witness will testify on legal concepts related to the Anti-Money Laundering Council, while three others will take up issues related to Calle88 Foods Corp.

MANILA, Philippines – The defense counsel of Vice President Sara Duterte is expected to present four more witnesses in her ongoing impeachment trial this week.

In a manifestation dated November 13, the defense sought the issuance of subpoena ad testificandum and duces tecum to the following witnesses directing them to participate, give testimony, and provide relevant documents in the impeachment proceedings from Thursday, November 19 to Friday, November 20:

Lawyer Rainer Dela Fuente, who will testify on legal concepts related to the Anti-Money Laundering Act

Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo, who will testify on Calle88 Foods Corporation’s registration with the Board of Investments (BOI)

Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Director IV Pilar Marilyn Pagayunan, who will testify on Calle88 Foods’ product registration

Center for International Expositions and Missions (CITEM) Department Manager III Rowena Mendoza, who will testify on communications between the agency and Calle88



The defense also wants the witnesses to identify and submit relevant documents, including Calle88’s BOI registration and FDA product registration, as well as communications and invitations exchanged between the company and DTI-CITEM concerning food expositions.

“The foregoing witnesses will provide material testimony to controvert the allegations and factual assertions against Respondent-Accused under Article II of Articles of Impeachment, and other relevant matters, as well as identify the documents relevant thereto,” the manifestation read.

“We issued subpoenas to all those named by the defense as witnesses for November 19 and 20. The subpoenas were sent electronically,” Senate Secretary Renato Bantug Jr. said.

Duterte is facing impeachment proceedings under Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, which involves allegations of unexplained wealth, including undeclared assets and properties.

After the prosecution rested its case, the defense began with its presentation of evidence last week, presenting witnesses to explain allegations on a forensic financial analyst’s report that the Vice President allegedly accumulated P871 million undeclared wealth, from 2022 to 2025, including income from the Davao City government.

Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison previously said the defense would present eight to ten more witnesses in the trial. – Rappler.com

World.title: Jensen Huang discusses comeback as Nvidia CEO with allies – report
World.content:
An ally of Jensen Huang says they are putting together a 'war room' of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief's return

Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive, and has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, November 15, citing people familiar with the matter.

One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief’s return and would try to garner support from the White House.

“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang’s support.

The report comes days after the FT reported that Nvidia’s board had approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside regular business hours.

Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy that raised questions over exports of the company’s advanced AI chips to China. The scandal has plunged the chipmaker into crisis and sent shockwaves across an AI industry he helped bankroll. – Rappler.com

World.title: EXPLAINER: What is the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement?
World.content:
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. hands over the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA)—the world’s first region-wide digital economy agreement—to ASEAN leaders during the opening of the 49th Summit at the PICC on November 15, 2026.

'DEFA will facilitate paperless trading, cross-border e-commerce, and trusted cross-border data flows, and it will establish interoperable trade systems,' says ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn

MANILA, Philippines – Members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) have signed the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), the first region-wide agreement of its kind.

Signed by ASEAN’s 11 member-countries on Saturday, November 14, DEFA establishes common rules for digital trade in a market of nearly 680 million people. Negotiations began in 2023, with the agreement becoming a priority deliverable of the Philippines’ ASEAN chairmanship this year.

“DEFA is not simply about economic growth. It is establishing the rules, systems, and cooperation that will allow our people and businesses to participate more fully in that growth,” Trade Secretary Cristina Roque said during the signing ceremony on Saturday.

Roque also said DEFA could help ASEAN’s digital economy grow from an estimated $1 trillion to $2 trillion by 2030.

But what exactly will it do?

At a high level, DEFA hopes to establish an “interconnected ASEAN digital marketplace,” with a framework covering cross-border e-commerce, electronic payments, protection of source code, cybersecurity, online consumer protection, and cooperation on emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence. It’s another step in ASEAN’s long-held aspiration of economic integration, though critics say progress toward a single market and production base has been painfully slow.

“DEFA will facilitate paperless trading, cross-border e-commerce, and trusted cross-border data flows, and it will establish interoperable trade systems,” ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn said at the ASEAN Business and Investment Summit on Saturday.

In practical terms, that means lower transaction costs, simpler cross-border operations, and easier access to customers in the region, especially for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs). This includes cutting down on paperwork through the wider use of electronic trade documents, signatures, and invoices, as well as establishing clearer rules for cross-border data transfers.

According to Finance Secretary Frederick Go, more than half of enterprises trading in ASEAN still face paper requirements at the border, and two out of three in using digital payments also reported delays.

“DEFA is built to remove exactly those frictions,” Go said in a speech at the ASEAN Business and Investment Summit.

When will it take effect?

Though the agreement has been signed, its implementing rules have yet to be fully developed, meaning many of the specifics remain unclear, and its benefits could still take months, if not years, to be felt.

“We hope, after signing today, ASEAN will fast track the ratification process and while the ratification process is moving forward, we are working on the implementation plan so that this will be ready by May next year when DEFA goes into effect,” Hourn said.

ASEAN expects the agreement to enter into force in 2027, with May identified as a target for implementation. The full text of the ASEAN DEFA is also expected to be published on the ASEAN Secretariat website by early 2027.

Locally, the Department of Trade and Industry plans to conduct trade shows and information campaigns in 2027 to help entrepreneurs understand the agreement.

Another thing to watch would be whether the gains under DEFA would redound only to large businesses or would reach all the way to MSMEs. As ASEAN Business Advisory Council (ASEAN-BAC) chair Joey Concepcion III put it, MSMEs will be the acid test for the agreement.

“What works for the smallest businesses can also work for the largest companies. If we can make cross-border trade simple, efficient, and secure enough for MSMEs, we create a foundation that can benefit businesses of every size,” the Go Negosyo founder said in a statement. – Rappler.com

World.title: Sandiganbayan junks Jinggoy Estrada bid to lift second 90-day suspension
World.content:
Jinggoy Estrada File photo

MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Fifth Division has rejected Sen. Jinggoy Estrada’s appeal to lift his 90-day preventive suspension over a plunder case involving alleged P573 million kickbacks from government infrastructure projects.

In a resolution promulgated on Nov. 10, the antigraft court denied Estrada’s motion for reconsideration, ruling that it had no merit.

Estrada filed the motion on Oct. 19, a week after the Fifth Division ordered his suspension in a resolution dated Oct. 12.

Article continues after this 

The senator argued that he had already served a separate 90-day preventive suspension imposed by the Sandiganbayan Second Division in a graft case. That suspension ran from June 22 to Sept. 20.

READ: Sandiganbayan suspends Jinggoy Estrada for 90 days over plunder case

He also argued that imposing “a second, successive ninety (90) suspension imposed four (4) months after the first suspension would already resemble a punishment rather than a preventive measure.”

However, the Fifth Division explained that the “suspension imposed by the Second Division is an independent determination of the validity of information filed against the senator; the service of suspension by the Second Court in the graft case does not dispense with the present plunder case; both graft and plunder cases are independent from one another; and his service of suspension could not prevent the court from performing its ministerial duty to place him under preventive suspension.”

In its resolution, the Fifth Division stressed that “the cases pending in this division are distinct and independent from that pending in the Second Division” noting that it already gave Estrada the opportunity to challenge the information filed against him.

Article continues after this 

“Thus, he cannot now argue that his preventive suspension in these cases is more in the nature of a penalty when any such variance in the timing of its imposition was simply due to this court’s hearing and resolution of the various challenges to the validity of the informations and their amendment which accused Estrada himself raised,” it added.

It stressed that preventive suspension was a mandatory duty under the law and did not mean the senator would be barred from performing his duties indefinitely.

Article continues after this 

READ: Court orders Jinggoy Estrada suspended for 90 day

“The imposition of the suspension here is a ministerial duty of the court to impose upon an accused in fulfillment of the statutes under which he is presently being charged with,” it stressed.

Ombudsman’s response

Meanwhile, the Office of the Ombudsman welcomed the ruling, maintaining that the cases pending before the two divisions were independent of each other.

Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavao said in a statement that the preventive suspension is a procedural safeguard and does not immediately constitute a finding of guilt.

The Ombudsman filed plunder and two counts of graft against Estrada and former Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan on May 28 in connection with alleged irregularities in infrastructure projects.

The antigraft court’s Second Division issued arrest warrants against Estrada and Bonoan last May 29 over the first graft charge, and the two were released the same day after posting bail.

World.title: Bishop urges probe into reported abuses during Asean rallies
World.content:
San Carlos Bishop Gerardo Alminaza — CONTRIBUTED PHOTO

MANILA, Philippines — Bishop Gerardo Alminaza of San Carlos, Negros Occidental, has called for an investigation into the arrests and alleged abuses against protesters opposing the Pax Silica initiative and the anticipated visit of US President Donald Trump for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit.

In a statement on Monday, Alminaza cited arrests at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila, Barangay Sucat in Muntinlupa City, and a church property in Manila on Sunday, lamenting that the incidents coincided with the Church’s observance of the World Day of the Poor.

READ: Police arrest 300 protesters in Muntinlupa City

Article continues after this 

The bishop also raised concerns over reports that children were among those detained, saying they require urgent attention and proper protection.

He likewise cited a report by the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines that at least 22 media workers were harassed by police during Sunday’s demonstrations.

“I urge the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) and other competent, independent bodies to investigate the arrests and all reported abuses, including those involving journalists and Church property,” Alminaza said.

“Authorities must cooperate fully, preserve relevant evidence, and allow independent access to detainees. Those responsible for abuses must be held accountable,” he added.

According to Alminaza, authorities have a responsibility to protect public safety, but this “must be exercised with restraint and respect for human dignity.”

Article continues after this 

During protests surrounding the ASEAN Summit on Nov. 15, 2026, a police barricade led to an altercation between protesters and police officers, with both sides violently pushing and shoving each other. (Photo by Zacarian Sarao)

He likewise called for the immediate release of protesters “detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights, and for the withdrawal of charges based solely on such exercise.”

“Every person in custody must have prompt access to legal counsel, family members and necessary medical care. Children must receive appropriate care, protection and assistance, with their best interests given priority,” the bishop said.

Article continues after this 

Meanwhile, the CHR told the INQUIRER that it had already launched an investigation into the incidents.

Groups, including farmers and Indigenous Peoples, have traveled to Metro Manila to express their opposition to the US-led Pax Silica initiative, which they said would displace Indigenous communities and farmers in Central Luzon.

READ: Bayan condemns Marcos’ ‘biggest mass arrest in a single day’

Alminaza said Indigenous Peoples and farmers “must have a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their lives.”

“Their concerns about ancestral lands, livelihoods, and the environment belong at the heart of any discussion of development. International cooperation loses its moral credibility when the people who bear the costs of development are denied a hearing,” the bishop said.

“A government that serves its people must listen, especially to those pushed to the margins. No international gathering, however important, can justify violating the rights of the people whose welfare our leaders have sworn to protect,” he added. /mcm

World.title: P4.56M ‘smuggled’ cigarettes seized in Zamboanga Sibugay; 1 nabbed
World.content:
CONTRABAND HAUL. Law enforcers inventoried over P4.56 million worth of suspected smuggled cigarettes seized during an anti-smuggling operation in Malangas, Zamboanga Sibugay, on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. A suspect was also arrested. Photo by Zamboanga Sibugay Police Provincial Office

PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur – Authorities seized P4.56 million worth of alleged smuggled cigarettes and arrested a suspect during an anti-smuggling operation in Malangas town, Zamboanga Sibugay, on Sunday morning.

In a report, the Zamboanga Sibugay Police Provincial Office (ZSBPPO) said operatives from the Provincial Intelligence Unit (PIU), in coordination with the Bureau of Customs (BOC) in Pagadian City and other law enforcement units, confiscated 74 master cases and 284 reams of assorted illicit cigarettes at Sitio Tampat, Purok 4, Barangay Lipacan at around 7 a.m.

The seized contraband carries an estimated market value of P4,565,664.

Article continues after this 

READ: NBI: 13 face raps over alleged P13-B smuggled cigarettes

Police said the operation was launched after a confidential informant tipped off the PIU regarding the transport of suspected smuggled cigarettes by a motorized pump boat in the coastal village.

Responding operatives caught an unidentified male suspect in the act of piling master cases of the illicit goods, leading to his immediate arrest.

The suspect and the confiscated cigarettes were brought to the Malangas Municipal Police Station for temporary custody before being turned over to the BOC for proper disposition.

ZSBPPO provincial director Col. Barnard Dasugo lauded the successful inter-agency effort, stressing that police will continue to crack down on illicit trade in the province.

Article continues after this 

“We will not let pass any illegal activity that damages our economy and the welfare of our citizens,” Dasugo said.

The seizure of over P4.5 million worth of suspected smuggled cigarettes is proof of the provincial police’s continuing efforts to stamp out illegal trade, he said.

Article continues after this 

“We will continue to intensify our operations, strengthen coordination with our partner agencies, and heighten our vigilance to ensure that illegal activities have no place in Zamboanga Sibugay,” he added. /coa

World.title: Ombudsman orders charges vs ex-Laguna Mayor Alvarez
World.content:
Facade of the Office of the Ombudsman — File photo by Niño Jesus Orbeta | INQUIRER

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman on Monday said it ordered the filing of criminal charges against dismissed Luisiana, Laguna Mayor Jomapher Uy Alvarez over the alleged unlawful appointment of a municipal administrator and unjustified withholding of benefits for former municipal officials.

The Ombudsman said it found “sufficient grounds” to file one count each of violation of Sections 3(e) and 3(f) of Republic Act No. 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, and Article 244 of the Revised Penal Code.

READ: Ombudsman suspends Cavite town mayor over gambling allegation

Article continues after this 

The Ombudsman said Alvarez failed to perform his duties in withholding the benefits of former municipal officials, describing his inaction as unjustified and possibly driven by ill motive.

“Clearly, respondent failed to perform his duties under said laws and policies. His inaction is not only unjustified but smacks of ill motive,” the administrative decision said, referring to the alleged withholding of year-end bonuses and cash gifts for municipal officials.

The case stemmed from a complaint filed by former municipal officials Nestor Alcala Rondilla and Ness Rondilla, who alleged that Alvarez refused to release their bonuses despite their entitlement to them.

Alvarez denied the allegations, saying he never received letters requesting the release of the benefits. However, the Ombudsman said his denial was unsupported by evidence.

“His mere denial that he did not receive the said letters cannot overcome this presumption, said denial being self-serving and unsubstantiated,” it added.

Article continues after this 

In a separate case, the Ombudsman also ordered the filing of criminal information against Alvarez for violating Article 244 of the Revised Penal Code over the alleged appointment of an unqualified person to public office.

The complaint, filed by Nestor, concerned Alvarez’s appointment of Emmanuel Babaan Villamin as municipal administrator of Luisiana in 2022. The complainant said the position required a college degree, first-grade Civil Service Commission (CSC) eligibility, and at least three years of experience in management and administrative work.

Article continues after this 

The Ombudsman found that Alvarez approved Villamin’s appointment “despite the latter’s failure to meet the prescribed qualifications” less than a month after the vacancy was posted.

READ: Ombudsman to intensify lifestyle checks on BIR, BOC

Alvarez and Municipal Human Resource Management Officer I Liza Ludovice Oblenida argued that their participation in the appointment process was “merely recommendary,” since the CSC had the final say on the appointment. However, the CSC disapproved Villamin’s appointment in 2023.

The Ombudsman maintained that Alvarez, as municipal mayor, was obligated to ensure that appointments to municipal positions complied with the law.

“Under the LGC (Local Government Code), the power to appoint municipal officials rests exclusively with the Municipal Mayor as the appointing authority, which is neither symbolic nor ceremonial as it carries with it a corresponding legal obligation to ensure that any appointment complies strictly with statutory requirements, qualification standards and civil service regulations,” it said in its decision.

It added that Alvarez could not claim he was unaware of Villamin’s lack of qualifications, as the requirements for the position were specified in the LGC.

In a press release, the Ombudsman said that “should the suspension penalties no longer be enforceable due to the respondents’ separation from government service, these shall be converted into fines equivalent to their respective salaries for one month and one day.” /mcm

World.title: Legarda wants unnecessary spending in 2027 nat’l budget slashed
World.content:
Sen. Loren Legarda —Photo from Senator Legarda’s office

MANILA, Philippines — Ahead of the sponsorship of the 2027 national budget at the Senate, Sen. Loren Legarda urged the chamber to remove unnecessary allocations from the General Appropriations Bill (GAB).

Senate Resolution No. 777, filed by Legarda on Nov. 12, called on the Senate to “avoid the adoption of projects that may bloat the GAB” and instead allocate funding to initiatives that promote macroeconomic growth.

“With better planning and more disciplined spending, we can contain the deficit and reduce our borrowing requirements. Over time, that also eases the pressure to raise taxes just to finance avoidable expenses,” Legarda said in a statement on Monday.

Article continues after this 

“We don’t need to pressure the public to fund unnecessary expenses. Families should have more room in their budgets for their own priorities. When people can afford to spend, and feel confident enough to do so, local businesses benefit and economic activity grows,” she added.

READ: Watchdogs question transparency in House OK of 2027 budget bill

The senator cited the House GAB, which allowed a P42.7-billion increase in the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) budget for multipurpose buildings while reducing allocations for the Metro Manila Subway and North-South Commuter Railway.

These changes were flagged in the People’s Budget Coalition’s analysis of the House GAB.

“We should ask whether our budget choices make economic sense. Why increase funding for projects whose need or readiness has yet to be demonstrated while cutting proposed allocations for mass transit that can reduce travel time and improve productivity?” Legarda said.

Article continues after this 

She also highlighted the potential “stagflation” affecting the country, citing the 7.8 percent inflation rate in October and 5.4 percent unemployment rate in September this year.

Her resolution urged the Senate committee on finance to investigate the effects of stagnant economic growth, high inflation and elevated unemployment in the country.

Article continues after this 

The probe, with the help of economic and development leaders, would help craft policies to respond to or cushion the effects of an economic downturn.

“A slowing economy needs government spending that works. We should protect investments that create jobs, move people and goods efficiently, and strengthen production, while removing allocations that cannot be justified,” she added. /mcm

World.title: Kanlaon Volcano emits ash anew on Nov. 16; Alert Level 2 remains
World.content:
An ash emission was observed over the summit crater of Kanlaon Volcano on Negros Island on Monday morning, November 16, 2026. (Photo: Phivolcs)

MANILA, Philippines — Kanlaon Volcano on Negros Island emitted ash on Monday morning, the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (Phivolcs) reported.

According to Phivolcs, the ash emission was observed from 6:35 a.m. to 7:55 a.m.

“The event generated grayish plumes that rose up to 350 meters above the summit crater before drifting southwest, as captured by the Kanlaon Volcano Observatory – Canlaon City IP camera,” Phivolcs said.

Article continues after this 

On Sunday, state seismologists recorded four ash emissions over the volcano, triggering ashfall in parts of La Carlota City and La Castellana in Negros Occidental.

READ: Kanlaon emits ash 4 times, triggers ashfall in Negros Occidental

Kanlaon remains under Alert Level 2, indicating a “moderate level of volcanic unrest.”

Phivolcs reminded the public that entering the volcano’s permanent danger zone is prohibited. /mcm

World.title: South Cotabato town gives free rice for pork to save hog industry
World.content:
A butcher prepares to slice meat cuts at the Tampakan Community Meat Shop, where consumers can get one kilo of rice for every kilo of meat they purchase. Photo by Tampakan LGU

TAMPAKAN, South Cotabato – To save the local hog industry, the local government here regulated the farmgate floor price for live pigs alongside launching a meat-and-rice incentive that benefits both vendors and consumers.

Mayor Leonard Escobillo issued Executive Order (EO) No. 40, Series of 2026, establishing regulatory floor prices for live pigs amid concerns raised by backyard hog raisers about predatory low buying prices and hefty production costs.

In addition, consumers who buy from the Tampakan Community Meat Shop and other accredited local vendors get one kilogram (kg) of rice for every kilo of meat purchased as part of the stopgap measures to protect the local hog industry.

Article continues after this 

READ: DA bans pork imports for 2 months to shield hog raisers

“There is a compelling necessity to establish a municipal floor price to prevent local livestock traders from exploiting small backyard hog raisers through predatory undercutting (of buying prices),” Escobillo stated in the EO.

The LGU pegged the farmgate prices of backyard-farm raised hogs at P160 per kg for butcher-quality sizes (80 to 110 kg); P100 per kg for culled sow and boar; P210 for lechon size weighing 30 kg and below; P200 for lechon size from 31 to 60 kg; and piglets at P3,500 to P4,000 each head.

Escobillo also directed the creation of the Municipal Swine Trade Oversight Task Force to monitor livestock traders for compliance with pricing regulations and to review and adjust farmgate prices based on feed price indexes, Department of Agriculture price bulletins, and macroeconomic supply-demand situation.

In regulating the floor price of live hogs, Escobillo cited Republic Act No. 7581 or the Price Act, as amended by RA 10623, which mandates state protection against unfair trade practices and illegal price manipulation, among others.

Article continues after this 

READ: Cheap imports didn’t lower pork prices—Sinag

At P160 per kg for the live-weight price of hogs, their meat products fetch between P240 and P280 per kg for premium pork bones, meat (laman), and belly cuts, Lance Hambala, livestock coordinator of the Municipal Agriculture Office, said.

Article continues after this 

“By regulating the farmgate buying price of live hogs and offering rice incentives to consumers, the LGU is helping hog raisers, meat vendors and the meat buyers. The impact is good, and we hope to sustain this until livestock buying prices stabilize,” he told the Inquirer on the phone Sunday.

Hambala said the cost to raise a pig weighing between 80 and 100 kg is at least P11,500, with feeding costs making up the bulk of production costs.

A private meat shop in Tampakan, South Cotabato that is among the beneficiaries of the free rice for meat purchase program of the local government. Photo by Tampakan LGU

For say, a 90 kg live pig bought at P160 per kg, it would fetch P14,400, giving the grower a meager income margin, he said, noting that it is better than having losses.

Hambala said the proceeds of the meat sold at the LGU-run Tampakan Community Meat Shop are returned to the hog raiser without deductions, with consumers getting a kilo of rice for every meat product they buy.

READ: DA pushes for higher tariffs on pork imports

The LGU-accredited private meat vendors also give free rice, subsidized by the LGU, to their customers. These vendors have a rice allocation equivalent to the weight of the meat carcass butchered at the local slaughterhouse, to encourage consumers to buy from them.

Non-residents can buy meat and get the equivalent free rice at the town’s community meat shop or accredited meat vendors, but buy on a set schedule, Hambala said.

He also encouraged local hog raisers to bring their stocks weighing between 80 and 100 kg to the LGU-run meat shop, which would sell them and return proceeds to the owners.

Local hog raisers across South Cotabato earlier slammed the unviable farmgate buying prices of live hogs, which fell to as low as P110 per kg.

The situation allowed meat vendors to sell premium meat cuts at P180 per kg.

READ: Farmers question delay in 60-day pork import restriction

Arnel Barroso, president of Titans Hog Raisers’ Association in Tampakan, said dozens of their mostly small backyard farm members (owning 1 to 10 sows) have stopped piggery operations because of the high production costs while buying prices were low./coa

World.title: Laborer arrested over P680,000 ‘shabu’ in Pagadian buy-bust
World.content:
Anti-narcotics operatives arrest a 40-year-old laborer who yielded approximately 100 grams of suspected shabu, valued at P680,000, during a buy-bust operation in Pagadian City on Saturday, November 14. Photo courtesy of PDEA-9

PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur —Anti-narcotics operatives arrested a 40-year-old laborer in Pagadian City during a buy-bust operation on Saturday, netting around 100 grams of suspected shabu (crystal meth) worth P680,000.

Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency-9 (PDEA-9) director Bryan Babang, in a statement, identified the suspect only as alias “Ben,” a resident of Barangay Bus-bus in Jolo, Sulu.

Operatives from the PDEA Zamboanga del Sur Provincial Office apprehended the suspect after he allegedly sold two heat-sealed transparent plastic sachets containing suspected shabu to an undercover agent.

Article continues after this 

READ: Drug suspects yield P.34M shabu in Imus

The operation was conducted in a mall parking lot in Barangay San Pedro at 2:50 p.m.

Authorities also confiscated from the suspect a mobile phone, paper bags, transparent plastic, eco-bag, and the marked money used in the entrapment operation.

The joint operation was carried out in coordination with the PDEA-9 Regional Special Enforcement Team 2, the Police Regional Intelligence Unit 9, and the 90th Maneuver Company of the Regional Mobile Force Battalion 9.

The suspect is currently in police custody and faces charges for alleged violation of Section 5, Article II of Republic Act No. 9165, or the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002, which penalizes the sale and distribution of dangerous drugs. /ts

World.title: ASEAN Seeks ‘Calibrated Engagement’ With Myanmar: Statement
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines—Southeast Asian leaders agreed Sunday on pursuing a “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar’s post-coup government, according to a joint statement, as the regional bloc seeks a path towards normalization.

Myanmar is still a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), but it has been frozen out of high-level meetings since a military junta seized power in a coup in 2021.

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize relations with Myanmar since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Bangkok has called for a “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar in an effort to implement ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC) plan aimed at ending the war between the military and a coalition of pro-democracy rebels and ethnic minority armed groups.

ASEAN leaders meeting in Manila adopted that language in calling for the pursuit of “a calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased and progress-based approach, taking into account developments on the ground,” according to the joint statement.

“Subject to sustained and concrete progress in the implementation of the 5PC by Myanmar, ASEAN may consider the gradual restoration of Myanmar’s full political representation,” the statement said.

The five-point plan has yielded little in the half-decade since it was agreed to, with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos conceding at a May summit he had not seen “any progress in Myanmar.”

On Sunday, in opening remarks at an ASEAN leaders’ retreat in Manila, he repeated a question he had posed to the group six months earlier: “What more can we do for Myanmar?”

“I hope our session leads to practical and forward-looking discussions on how we can further advance the implementation of the Five-Point Consensus, make our efforts more responsive to the realities on the ground, and support a peaceful, inclusive, Myanmar-owned and Myanmar-led process,” he said.

The ASEAN bloc’s rotating chair will pass at the end of this year from the Philippines to Singapore, a city-state analysts say opposes normalizing ties with Myanmar.

In 2028, it will be the turn of Thailand, which shares a long border with Myanmar and is leading the charge for closer relations.

“We believe it’s crucial to have someone at the table who can really talk on policy issues because engagement requires that they have someone who can really convey to us the position of Myanmar,” Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told AFP in Singapore on November 5.

“This is not about… recognizing… upgrading their position. But I think in reality, what is important is that we need someone at the table who can speak on behalf of Myanmar.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Seeks Closer Ties With Russian-Led Economic Bloc
World.content:
A delegation from the Eurasian Economic Commission (EEC) visited Naypyitaw this week, as Myanmar’s heavily sanctioned military regime intensifies its geopolitical pivot toward Russian-led multilateral blocs.

During the delegation’s visit—its third to the Myanmar capital—EEC Minister in charge of Integration and Macroeconomics Daniyar Imanaliev held talks with junta Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe on Wednesday.

According to regime media, discussions centered on securing observer status for Myanmar within the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Myanmar’s participation in Eurasian integration forums and exhibitions jointly held by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the EEC.

The EEC minister also held talks with the regime’s commerce and investment ministers, focusing on boosting bilateral cooperation across various sectors including manufacturing, agriculture, e-commerce, energy, transport and digital transformation. The Myanmar side discussed boosting exports of Myanmar’s agricultural and fishery products to five post-Soviet states, and invited investment from the countries in the Dawei Special Economic Zone in southern Myanmar.

Simultaneously, an EEC sub-delegation led by Dmitry Fesenko, head of the industrial development monitoring and analysis department, met with Deputy Industry Minister Dr. Aung Zeya to discuss technical cooperation regarding micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and agro-based industries.

The EAEU—comprising Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia—represents a critical bloc of junta allies. Naypyitaw initiated multi-sector dialogue with the EAEU and EEC in 2022, signing memorandums of understanding for closer cooperation in 2023.

Trade between Myanmar and the EAEU member states more than tripled between 2019 and 2024, surpassing US$1.5 billion, according to EAEU data released last year. Myanmar’s primary exports to the bloc include rice, coffee, palm oil and cocoa beans, while it imports EAEU fertilizers, consumer goods, machinery, metals, cement and pharmaceuticals. The official trade figures exclude weapons and military equipment supplied to the regime by Russia and Belarus, both major arms suppliers.

Despite these figures, regional analysts argue the junta’s Eurasian pivot is driven more by diplomatic survival than viable economic strategy.

“Compared to neighbors like China and Thailand, trade and investment from these [EAEU] countries is worlds apart. Even under the previous governments of U Thein Sein and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, how much investment actually came from them?” an analyst pointed out.

“If the regime wants to do business, it has a massive ASEAN market to tap. The regime’s focus on those faraway markets suggests its motivations are far more geopolitical than economic. They desperately want to join the Russian-led geopolitical bloc.”

Regime chief Min Aung Hlaing, who has publicly condemned major powers for utilizing economic sanctions and political pressure as violations of global norms, personally attended the 4th Eurasian Economic Forum in Belarus last year. During the summit, he made an urgent appeal for Myanmar to be granted EAEU observer status—a demand his foreign minister aggressively reiterated during Imanaliev’s visit this week.

Naypyitaw’s push to integrate into Moscow’s economic architecture mirrors the generals’ broader strategy to embed an isolated regime in non-Western multilateral organizations; in May 2023, Myanmar was formally recognized as a dialogue partner of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), led by China, Russia and India.

World.title: Myanmar’s Dwindling Debt to China, Scammers Nabbed in Shan, and More
World.content:
China no longer Myanmar’s biggest creditor

China is no Myanmar’s principal creditor, even though the military regime is bound for life and beyond by the money and favors it owes its protector. On paper at least, Japan is now Myanmar’s largest foreign government lender, while Beijing’s focus has shifted from extending new loans to managing existing debts.

According to the World Bank’s International Debt Statistics, Myanmar’s public and publicly guaranteed external debt stood at US$10.34 billion last year, down from around US$13.5 billion in 2021. Country-to-country debt accounted for $5.68 billion, with Japan holding $3.86 billion. China was owed only around US$1.5 billion, according to the World Bank’s creditor-by-creditor breakdown.

Prior to the political opening in 2011, China was effectively Myanmar’s only major lender, at interest rates as high as 4.5 percent. But after reforms began, Myanmar regained access to financing from institutions and partners including the Asian Development Bank and the Japan International Cooperation Agency on far more favorable terms.

“Myanmar will not borrow money from China any more if interest rates remain high,” then-deputy finance minister Maung Maung Win pledged in June 2020.

An AidData assessment released in May shows that China committed $14.7 billion in development finance to Myanmar between 2000 and 2023 through 505 projects. Nearly 92 percent took the form of loans, mainly from the Export-Import Bank of China and China Development Bank.

But AidData estimates that Myanmar’s outstanding debt to Chinese creditors had fallen to around US$1.7 billion by the end of 2024 or just about 19 percent of its external public debt.

The loans from China simply stopped. AidData found that China Eximbank, historically the largest lender, has not issued a new loan since 2019. While it was the COVID-19 pandemic that initially slowed lending, the trend has continued throughout the post-coup period.

The reason seems to be that the operating environment in Myanmar is deteriorating. Many planned Chinese-backed projects under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) are in conflict areas or regions entirely beyond the putschist regime’s control. Key trade routes, resource projects and infrastructure investments increasingly depend on arrangements with ethnic armed groups rather than Naypyitaw alone.

Bangladesh ties Rohingya crisis to Beijing’s Indian Ocean ambition

Dhaka has confirmed it is holding discussions with the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) that rules most of Myanmar’s Rakhine State as it seeks a solution to the long-running Rohingya refugee crisis—and that could force China’s hand in dealing with the new reality there.

At stake for Bangladesh is the burden of hosting over 1 million Rohingya refugees, most of whom fled the military’s brutal 2017 clearance operations. And since the AA controls entire Bangladeshi border with Myanmar, including Paletwa Township in neighboring Shin State, Dhaka has opened pragmatic dual-track discussions, engaging both the AA and the military regime after Naypyitaw’s repeated failures to facilitate the repatriation.

China, meanwhile, remains focused on its multi-billion-dollar projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC). The key project—a deep-sea port and special economic zone in Kyaukphyu—is designed to solve Beijing’s “Malacca Dilemma” by giving it maritime access to the Indian Ocean. Kyaukphyu also serves as the terminus for the twin oil and gas pipelines currently pumping energy to Yunnan Province. Yet the port project remains stalled, with Kyaukphyu under AA siege.

Dhaka is increasingly looking to China for leverage. During Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to Beijing in June—which closely followed a trip by Myanmar regime chief Min Aung Hlaing—Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed a tripartite China–Myanmar–Bangladesh economic corridor. That would provide Beijing with an alternative overland route to the Indian Ocean while Kyaukphyu remains in limbo.

In July, China’s ambassador to Bangladesh explicitly tied this proposed corridor to resolving the refugee crisis, suggesting it could facilitate Rohingya repatriation.

International scrutiny of the western front is intensifying. UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar Kelley Currie is currently in Bangladesh to assess the armed conflict in Rakhine and the deteriorating situation in the refugee camps. Yet Beijing’s diplomatic shield of the military usurpers in Naypyitaw remains firmly in place. Addressing the UN General Assembly’s Third Committee in late October, China’s representative reiterated that the crisis must be resolved bilaterally between Myanmar and Bangladesh, free from Western interference, a process China insists it is facilitating.

The International Court of Justice will rule next week whether the Myanmar military’s crackdown against the Rohingya people constituted a genocide.

No end to arrests of Chinese scammers in Shan

Some 759 foreigners were arrested between Aug. 1 and Oct. 31 for alleged involvement in scam operations in Shan State, and 502 were Chinese, regime media report.

Another 15 Chinese scammers were arrested on Monday in rural parts of Kyethi Township, southern Shan State. The township lies in an area that is contested by two rival ethnic armed groups: the Restoration Council of Shan State (RCSS) and the Shan State Progress Party (SSPP), whose headquarters are in nearby Wan Hai.

After a Chinese-led crackdown on industrial-scale scam compounds in the Kokang region of northern Shan State in late 2023, operations scattered across at least 17 townships in southern and eastern Shan, including Tangyan, Laihka, Tachileik and Muse. Others famously relocated to Karen State’s Myawaddy Township on the Thai border.

In other words, the syndicates adapted, their units becoming smaller and more nimble across scattered locations and moving further inland from prying eyes on the international border. Now they settle in places like Kyethi, where they can exploit lawlessness and administrative vacuums or collaborate with junta-aligned militias and armed groups.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: ASEAN Should Accept Myanmar Back at Diplomat Level: Bangkok
World.content:
BANGKOK—Myanmar’s foreign minister should be allowed back into meetings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) regional bloc, Thailand’s top diplomat said on Thursday after a visit to the war-torn country.

Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said his meetings with regime leader Min Aung Hlaing and others had revealed “a desire on the part of Myanmar to engage, to return to ASEAN.” But he said there was no talk of specific steps.

Myanmar has been excluded from high-level meetings of the 11-nation ASEAN since a 2021 military coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and triggered an ongoing civil war.

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize ties since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president earlier this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

“For Thailand, we believe that the next step is to have the foreign minister of Myanmar participate in the ASEAN meetings at the level of foreign minister,” Sihasak told reporters.

His comments came ahead of a meeting of ASEAN leaders starting Sunday in the Philippines.

Sihasak said he had also raised the “very urgent problem” of water pollution among tributaries of the Mekong River, which straddles five Southeast Asian countries and China, saying a working group would meet later this month.

Last week, authorities in northern Thailand suspended tap water production after arsenic levels at the waterworks intake was found to be 30 times higher than the safety standard. More than a dozen villages were affected by the suspension.

A subsequent field sample from the nearby Sai River measured arsenic at 25 times the safety standard, the government said.

Thai officials previously pinned the toxic sediment on wastewater from mining activity upstream in Myanmar.

Sihasak said he also raised the issue of a spillover of violence into Thailand.

World.title: Myanmar Faces Year of Blackouts as Regime Admits 30% Power Shortfall
World.content:
Myanmar’s rotating power cuts will remain in place through 2027, with generation expected to meet only 70 percent of national demand, Deputy Energy Minister Aye Kyaw announced Wednesday.

Addressing the regime’s rubber-stamp parliament, he said next summer’s 24-hour electricity demand is forecast at 5,010 MW, while generation capacity is only 3,540 MW.

“That’s why we need to continue the load shedding measures,” he said.

Despite having the poorest electricity access in the region, Myanmar made significant progress in grid connectivity under the National League for Democracy’s 15-year National Electrification Plan in 2015. By 2020, more than half of households had electricity access, and the NLD’s World Bank-backed plan aimed to achieve nationwide electrification by 2030.

However, the plan was scrapped after the 2021 coup, and regime mismanagement has since triggered rolling power outages across the country.

The World Bank says reliable supply has dropped sharply since the military takeover, affecting nearly half of connected households — with 41.6 percent receiving only enough electricity for basic lighting and phone charging, and 9.1 percent getting no electricity at all.

It blames the deepening generation crisis on the suspension of LNG power plants, declining domestic gas production, hydropower stress, infrastructure damage, and stalled investment.

In response, the regime reintroduced nationwide rolling blackouts, leaving residents in even major cities struggling to manage households and livelihoods.

“We have to be ready to fill up the water, cook meals, and iron our clothes the moment the power comes back on,” Ko Thant Zin from Insein Township in the suburbs of Yangon told the Irrawaddy.

He said the electricity supply rotates between four hours on and four hours off.

“Under the civilian government, the roads were bright with lights. Now, I have to open my eyes wide to see the way ahead while driving at night,” he commented.

The deputy energy minister told citizens to install solar panels if they want a reliable supply. However, import curbs and surging prices have put solar options out of reach for most urban residents.

“Forget about solar panels, most people can’t even afford a portable power pack,” a resident of downtown Yangong’s Botahtaung Township told The Irrawaddy. “Prices have been skyrocketing because of import restrictions.”

He added that power cuts would cause major suffering during the El Niño heatwave forecast for November through January.

“I can’t imagine how we will get through next summer,” he said, reacting to the rationing announcement. “It will be especially tough for young children and the elderly.”

Demand driven by outages has seen the price of solar panels surge to a record high. Yangon residents said a household solar power system now costs at least 10 million kyats (around US $4,760), putting it beyond the reach of ordinary families.

Last month, Yangon City authorities mandated that all commercial projects and high-rise buildings must install solar power systems to operate elevators and emergency lighting, as part of a nationwide push for solar amid deepening power blackouts.

The World Bank says chronic power shortages remain one of the main constraints on Myanmar’s economy, limiting its recovery and keeping poverty persistently high.

The deputy energy minister also announced plans to develop two 55 MW small-modular-reactors in cooperation with Russia’s atomic agency, ROSATOM, starting in fiscal 2028-29. The project is slated for completion in fiscal 2035-36 but locations have yet to be announced.

World.title: Three Years After Operation 1027, Hopang Transformed Under Wa Rule
World.content:
Friday marks three years since Hopang in the Wa Self-Administered Zone experienced its first taste of the joint ethnic offensive known as Operation 1027, when drones deployed by the Brotherhood Alliance bombed a monastery sheltering retreating Myanmar military personnel from nearby Kunlong base.

For the Myanmar military, which had controlled Hopang for decades, the drone strike was an early warning that its grip on the town was nearing an end. For the United Wa State Army (UWSA), it presented an opportunity to gain one of the most important towns in Wa territory without firing a shot.

Less than two months after the Nov. 13 drone attack, forces of the Brotherhood Alliance—which grouped the Arakan Army, Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA)—and allied groups entered Hopang with little resistance. Rather than holding the town themselves, they quickly handed it over to their ally, the UWSA.

Operation 1027, which inflicted one of the most devastating military setbacks in the Myanmar military’s history, had begun on Oct. 27, 2023, in Chinshwehaw, a border town just 8 km from Hopang. Just 19 km away, Kunlong, a key town on a China-Myanmar trade route, also fell after sustained drone attacks by alliance forces.

As Kunlong collapsed, its commander, officers and wounded soldiers fled to Hopang.

“A battalion commander and a soldier entered the monastery building and pleaded for shelter,” recalled a witness who was in the compound. “They told the abbot they had been under drone attacks for four days, and had only managed to retreat after receiving supporting fire.”

That same night, drones struck the monastery.

For Hopang residents, who had watched the fighting around Kunlong from hilltop pagodas, the attack on the monastery signaled that war was coming closer. By the next morning, many were fleeing the town, leaving their homes and shops behind.

Some local drivers found themselves ferrying displaced families back and forth, while others stayed behind to guard their properties. Residents feared not only a potential urban battle similar to the fighting in Kunlong, but also the prospect of Myanmar military airstrikes.

One restaurant owner recalled watching looters load crates of beer from his shop onto vehicles through CCTV cameras while he was fleeing.

Among those who fled were a monk who was injured in the November 13 drone attack, as well as health workers from a public hospital in Hopang.

Hopang was home to a military battalion and a police station, but all the surrounding towns including Kunlong and Chinshwehaw were controlled by the Brotherhood Alliance. At this point, Hopang was effectively isolated.

When MNDAA troops entered Hopang in early January 2024, the remaining military and police units reportedly surrendered with little resistance. Under a prior arrangement between the MNDAA and the UWSA, control of the town was then transferred to the Wa army.

Unlike Lashio, Laukkai, Chinshwehaw or Kunlong, Hopang largely escaped major battle damage. Yet residents say the town has since undergone a different kind of transformation, one increasingly shaped by Chinese capital and Wa administration.

The ethnically diverse town, home to Shan, Wa, Bamar, Kachin, Ta’ang and other communities, was once known for its Buddhist, Christian and traditional ethnic festivals. Today, residents say casinos, bars, hotels, massage parlors and prostitution-related businesses funded by Chinese investors have proliferated.

Some residents also complain of heavy taxation and a justice system that includes public executions, practices rarely seen under previous administrations.

The yuan now dominates much of the local economy, with residents increasingly pricing goods in the Chinese currency rather than kyats. In the healthcare arena, expensive Chinese-run private hospitals have emerged alongside the only public hospital.

Over the past three years, rumors have repeatedly surfaced that the UWSA will return Hopang to the regime. Residents say they see no sign that this is imminent, however.

The town, which participated in the 2010, 2015 and 2020 elections, did not take part in the regime-organized 2025 poll and is absent from the list of constituencies scheduled to be put to a vote in additional elections scheduled for April 2027.

Recently, regime Defense Minister and peace negotiator Lieutenant General Yar Pyae visited Panghsang, the UWSA headquarters. There was no indication that Hopang’s status was discussed during his meetings with Wa leaders, however.

While the UWSA remained officially neutral during Operation 1027, it emerged among the campaign’s biggest beneficiaries. Without openly joining the offensive, it gained full control of Hopang and Panlong, while also securing partial control along with the Myanmar military over Tangyan, a strategically important town on the route to Lashio, the largest town in northern Shan.

Three years after the first drone bombs fell on Hopang, the town has changed beyond recognition for longtime residents.

During Operation 1027, the MNDAA and TNLA went on to seize almost the whole of northern Shan State including the capital Lashio and all vital trade routes with China.

However, under strong Chinese pressure, in 2025 the ethnic armies were forced to halt fighting the Myanmar military and hand back several liberated towns to the regime.

World.title: Myanmar’s Coup President Barred From Upcoming 49th ASEAN Summit
World.content:
The Philippines announced Wednesday that Myanmar regime leaders remain barred from joining the 49th ASEAN summit and high-level meetings in Manila from November 15 to 17, upholding a ban imposed after the 2021 military coup.

Myanmar will instead be represented by the Director-General of its ASEAN affairs department, according to a statement issued by Manila’s Department of Foreign Affairs.

“We welcome this official confirmation that there is no place [at the summit] for junta leader Min Aung Hlaing,” Khin Ohmar, a prominent Myanmar democracy activist and founder of the Progressive Voice human rights foundation, told The Irrawaddy.

“ASEAN made the right decision in line with its principles. We have been demanding that no junta member be permitted to join the summit.”

She added that ASEAN would have sacrificed its credibility and responsibility to the people of Myanmar by inviting the junta leader, who faces a genocide ruling at the international court later this month.

Confirmation that the ban remains in place came after domestic and international rights groups warned the regional bloc against legitimizing a regime that is intensifying violence against civilians.

On Monday, the Special Advisory Council for Myanmar (SAC-M) and ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights urged regional leaders “to immediately confirm” that Min Aung Hlaing and his junta cohorts would be excluded from the summit.

It also called on ASEAN leaders to adopt “measurable benchmarks for compliance” with the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC), along with “a series of escalating punitive steps” if the junta continues to defy the peace plan.

Regime leaders were barred from regional summits for failing to implement the April 2021 consensus, including an immediate end to violence and constructive dialogue with the opposition.

The regime largely ignored the 5PC before formally rejecting it in a July 2026 vote by its rubber-stamp parliament. However, it continues to pay lip service to the plan.

During his latest talks with ASEAN special envoy Theresa Lazaro in Naypyitaw in October, Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe claimed the regime was implementing the 5PC “without compromising its national interests and sovereignty in accordance with its own roadmaps and objectives.”

The UN reports that at least 8,384 civilians have been killed by regime forces since the coup, in an escalating military campaign that has also left over 4 million displaced. Meanwhile, nearly 23,000 political prisoners remain in detention, including deposed democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

However, ASEAN members began bilateral engagement with the regime after it rebranded in civilian clothing in April following elections widely condemned as a sham. Since then, coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing has been invited on official visits to bloc members Laos, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Malaysia.

Both Malaysia—once a vocal critic of the regime—and Thailand drew widespread condemnation from rights groups for hosting the junta leader.

Both nations defended the visits as pragmatic re-engagement in search of solutions to challenges they face, such as refugee repatriation for Malaysia and transborder issues for Thailand.

Critics have warned that bi-lateral engagement may sway a collective ASEAN decision to reintegrate the regime.

However, the move to uphold the summit ban marks a major setback for a junta desperate for legitimacy on the international stage.

“This is a huge blow to the junta. I am sure it has not expected this kind of decision,” Khin Ohmar commented. “It also signals that the junta’s election farce failed to confer legitimacy, since even those advocating its return to the international stage want to avoid being seen as complicit in its violence.”

World.title: Myanmar Junta Seeks Record Military Budget as Millions Struggle With Poverty
World.content:
The Myanmar regime plans to increase the military budget to a record high for the 2026-27 fiscal year, even as approximately one-third of the country’s population lives in poverty.

Since 2021, the regime has been waging war against several established ethnic armed organizations as well as newly emerged resistance forces, including the People’s Defense Force, across the country, spending a large portion of its budget on military expenses.

Last Thursday, the regime’s rubber-stamp Union Parliament (Pyidaungsu Hluttaw), where the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) and its allies hold a majority of seats, debated a supplementary budget allocation bill.

The proposed allocation would bring total defense spending to 10.53 trillion kyats (US$5.01 billion), combining the initial 2026-27 fiscal year estimate of 7.95 trillion kyats with a supplementary grant of 2.58 trillion kyats.

Chit Swe, an Upper House lawmaker representing Ayeyarwady Region’s Constituency No. 11 and first deputy chair of the Joint Public Accounts Committee, urged parliament on November 5 to approve the regime’s proposed budgets, including the record-high military budget.

He said the committee had only eight days to verify the budget, with some items requiring ground observation, and that at least two weeks would be needed for verification.

If the supplementary allocations are approved, the budget deficit is projected to surge from 8.98 trillion kyats to 11.41 trillion kyats, he stated.

The military budget has surged continuously since the coup.

Under the last civilian government, led by ousted democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi, defense expenditure for the 2020-21 fiscal year stood at just 3.4 trillion kyats.

In the 2023-24 fiscal year, it increased to over 5.6 trillion kyats. Although defense expenditures for the remaining years were not officially released, the current budget figures show that spending has nearly doubled compared to 2023-24.

Meanwhile, approximately 17.9 million people are “multidimensionally poor”, while two-thirds of the population are either poor or at risk, according to a UN Development Programme (UNDP) report published on October 8.

After five years of military regime rule, Myanmar people continue to suffer from soaring prices of basic goods and living costs amid the civil war, and face personal safety and security concerns.

Although the budget is still in draft form, the proposed military expenditure has drawn widespread criticism from the public.

“The budgets that should be spent on the country’s education, health, social welfare and nation-building are instead being used to kill the people,” said Naung Yoe, a military defector who now works with the Myanmar Defense & Security Institute (MDSI), a research institute.

According to the MDSI, the Directorate of Defense Industries, which manufactures ammunition and aerial bombs used in the regime’s indiscriminate attacks, has consumed the largest share of the military’s budget since the coup.

“It is deeply tragic and unfortunate,” he said.

World.title: Beyond Crypto: Will Tokenization Democratize Access to Investment Markets?
World.content:
ASTANA – A government bond and a shipment of grain may seem worlds apart. But both are among the assets Kazakhstan is looking to bring onto digital platforms as it tests whether tokenization can open new financing channels and make investment markets accessible to more people.

The idea is no longer confined to cryptocurrency circles. Tokenization turns rights linked to real-world assets into digital tokens recorded on a blockchain. Depending on the legal structure, a token may represent a share in an asset, a financial claim or an entitlement to delivery. The distinction matters: a digital record does not, by itself, create ownership or guarantee a return.

Kazakhstan has begun testing the concept in its own securities market. The Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE) registered its first digital financial asset issued by a private company, ALTA Telecom, this October. The asset was divided into 100,000 tokens, with trading beginning on Oct. 28, marking another step in the development of Kazakhstan’s tokenized financial market. On Nov. 9, the National Bank placed a 10 billion tenge (US$22.4 million) tranche of tokenized short-term notes through the KASE as part of a 50 billion tenge (US$112 million) offering, also made available in traditional form. The 91-day notes carried a weighted average annual yield of 15.72%. The parallel placement let the bank test the digital format alongside established market infrastructure under the same pricing conditions.

The next step is already on the calendar. National Bank Governor Timur Suleimenov said Kazakhstan plans to issue tokenized government bonds jointly with the Ministry of Finance in the first quarter of 2027. Authorities are also looking at real estate, precious metals and mineral resources as potential assets for tokenization.

The asset is only the beginning

For Rachel Lee, director of blockchain and digital assets at Hong Kong Cyberport, the central question is not how many assets can be tokenized, but whether investors have a reason to use them. Tokenization still accounts for a small part of the financial system, she said, and turning it into everyday infrastructure will take more than issuing digital versions of existing assets.

“If it’s just tokenization, and you just buy and hold, and you don’t do anything with it, then there’s not much incentive for people to do so,” Lee said in an interview with The Astana Times.

Its value grows when a tokenized asset can be used in other financial activities, such as collateralized lending or on-chain financing. According to her, that can keep money and assets moving instead of leaving them idle.

That is a more demanding test than simply putting an asset on a blockchain. A token needs a market, buyers and a reason to change hands. It also needs financial institutions and service providers willing to support the new model. Lee noted that faster settlement, for example, could disrupt intermediaries whose business depends on existing transaction cycles. The challenge is not just to build a more efficient system, but to bring established market participants along.

Hong Kong has been building its digital asset ecosystem through cooperation between the government, regulators, financial institutions and technology companies. Lee said cross-border adoption will take time because blockchain may allow transactions to move across borders, but regulation still determines who can issue, hold and trade an asset in each jurisdiction.

Regulation is in place; the market must follow

Kazakhstan is among the more advanced jurisdictions in Central Asia in regulating digital assets, Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA) said in a written response to The Astana Times. The Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) began developing its framework in 2018 through the FinTech Lab regulatory sandbox. Since 2024, it has had a dedicated regime for platforms that issue and trade tokenized assets backed by real-world holdings.

But a rulebook alone will not create a market.

“The primary bottlenecks today are not technological but infrastructural and commercial,” the regulator said.

Kazakhstan needs more high-quality assets that businesses are prepared to bring to market, clearer recognition of tokenized rights across the AIFC and national legal systems, and deeper liquidity so investors can trade assets at transparent prices.

The sectors that appear best suited to an early start are commodities and agriculture. According to AFSA’s press service, Kazakhstan already has established production and supply chains in both, as well as businesses that need financing. Real estate could offer opportunities through fractional ownership, while infrastructure projects may require more complex legal and financial arrangements.

Tokenization could allow an asset that once required a large investment to be divided into smaller units. That may bring retail investors into markets previously dominated by institutions and give companies another way to raise capital. But accessibility has to come with safeguards. The regulator pointed to independent valuation and verification, secure custody, clear legal rights, adequate disclosure and controls against money laundering and terrorist financing.

“Ultimately, democratization should mean giving investors access to new opportunities, not exposing them to risks they do not understand,” AFSA’s press service said.

What does a grain token actually buy?

The question becomes concrete in agriculture. Anvar Niyetkaliyev, founder and CEO of Commodity Chain Ltd., is preparing a pilot project built around tokenized grain. The company received an AFSA license in June 2026 to organize trading and clearing of investment tokens within the FinTech Lab. It is now completing technological and operational preparations and has not yet begun transactions.

Niyetkaliyev said the first pilot will use a limited volume of grain. The company plans to test each step, from verifying the underlying commodity and issuing tokens to carrying out trades and meeting contractual obligations. The first transactions will take place only after the remaining procedures are completed and the company receives authorization to commence operations. The volume will depend on partner readiness and the results of testing.

The model does not mean that every token holder automatically owns a portion of grain stored in a warehouse. The rights attached to a token will depend on the legal structure of each issuance and could include a claim, a delivery entitlement or another contractual right.

“The mere fact of owning a token does not automatically transfer ownership of the physical commodity,” Niyetkaliyev said.

This distinction is central to how the business model works. A blockchain can record who holds a token and how it changes hands. It cannot confirm on its own that the grain exists, meets the required quality or remains safely stored. Commodity Chain plans to rely on documents confirming the grain’s existence and characteristics, as well as contractual arrangements with grain warehouses, independent inspection companies and other market participants.

“Behind the token there should be not just a record on the blockchain, but a legally formalized and enforceable obligation,” Niyetkaliyev said.

In other words, the technology can make records easier to track; the physical asset and the legal promise still need to withstand scrutiny.

The company sees grain as a starting point, not a one-off product. Niyetkaliyev said it is considering other sectors and sees potential to expand into Central Asian markets, where businesses face similar financing constraints. Whether investors will want to buy and trade these instruments at scale, however, remains to be tested.

Beyond the pilot

Kazakhstan now has two parallel tracks: tokenized securities being tested through its established financial market infrastructure, and real-world assets such as grain being prepared for issuance through a regulated platform. They address different needs, but both will face the same test. Investors must understand what they are buying, issuers must deliver what the token promises, and a secondary market must give buyers a credible way out.

Tokenization may lower the cost of issuing and transferring some assets, and fractional ownership may widen the pool of potential investors. It will not make every asset liquid, every investment safe or every investor ready to participate. The technology becomes meaningful only when it solves a practical problem better than the system already in place.

For Kazakhstan, the next milestone is not another announcement about what can be tokenized. It is a transaction that works from end to end: with a real asset, clear rights, willing investors and a market where the token can be used or traded. That is when tokenization will begin to look less like a promise and more like part of the financial system.

World.title: Turkic Investment Fund Eyes Transport Projects Linking Central Asia and Caspian Region
World.content:
ASTANA – The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway and potential investment opportunities along the Caspian transport route are among the regional connectivity projects attracting the Turkic Investment Fund’s (TIF) interest, including possible cooperation with the Azerbaijan-Uzbekistan Investment Company (AUIC).

TIF CEO Ramil Babayev discussed the fund’s priorities in an exclusive interview with Trend. According to him, the fund is also prioritizing energy, industrial development and support for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) as it expands its activities in Uzbekistan. Particular attention is being given to projects that strengthen economic ties among member states of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS).

These priorities were discussed at the fund’s third annual meeting of the Board of Governors, held on Oct. 22 in Tashkent. Participants identified transport and logistics infrastructure, industrial cooperation, green energy and entrepreneurship as key areas for expanding financing.

Transport connectivity and energy transition

Uzbekistan’s geographic position makes transport connectivity projects particularly important. As a double-landlocked country, it relies on transit routes through neighboring states to access international markets. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, the Middle Corridor and developing southern routes are expected to reshape the country’s role in regional trade and logistics.

Babayev noted that energy is another major area of potential investment. Uzbekistan plans to increase its power generation capacity by approximately 22 gigawatts by 2030 and raise the share of renewable energy to more than 50%. Achieving these targets will require investment not only in electricity generation but also in transmission networks, energy storage systems and efficiency improvements.

According to Babayev, the fund also sees opportunities in manufacturing and entrepreneurship. Industrial and machinery products already account for nearly half of Uzbekistan’s exports to OTS countries, while small businesses contribute more than half of the country’s gross domestic product and approximately three-quarters of employment.

Other areas discussed during the fund delegation’s October visit to Tashkent included digital infrastructure, agribusiness, resource efficiency (particularly water management), and public services.

Building a project pipeline and partnerships

TIF is developing a pipeline of potential projects in Uzbekistan through cooperation with international financial institutions, national development institutions and private-sector representatives.

During a visit to Tashkent from Oct. 20 to 23, a delegation led by Babayev held meetings with representatives of the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the European Investment Bank (EIB), AUIC, Vision Invest, Highland Capital, the Agency for the Development of the Light Industry and the Entrepreneurship Development Company.

The discussions covered infrastructure, transport and logistics, energy, textiles, agriculture and public services. The meetings aimed to identify potential projects that meet the fund’s criteria for commercial viability, measurable development impact and contribution to regional integration.

The fund has already established its first co-financing framework with the Islamic Corporation for the Development of the Private Sector (ICD). It provides for the potential mobilization of up to $300 million to finance private-sector development projects in five TIF member states, including Uzbekistan.

TIF’s total commitments under financial operations with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the Netherlands Development Finance Company (FMO), the OPEC Fund for International Development and other development institutions and commercial banks have reached $50 million.

The fund expects its further activities in Uzbekistan to rely primarily on co-financing and syndicated transactions with leading international and national financial institutions. This approach is intended to expand financing while drawing on partners’ expertise and local networks.

Fund seeks to mobilize additional capital

TIF has an authorized capital of $600 million. However, its objective is to build a network of partnerships that will enable it to finance projects worth several times that amount.

Alongside co-financing and syndicated lending, the fund is considering risk-sharing instruments, including guarantees, first-loss mechanisms and portfolio-based arrangements. These tools could use development finance institutions’ capital to expand lending to projects that commercial banks might otherwise be reluctant to finance, particularly those involving smaller businesses.

TIF has discussed these mechanisms with the IFC and EIB. Cooperation in this area is also envisaged under a memorandum with the Uzbekistan-Kyrgyzstan Development Fund (UKDF).

Babayev also identified obtaining an international credit rating as a strategic priority. This would allow TIF to attract additional financing from international markets and domestic capital markets in its member states.

The fund also sees considerable potential for mobilizing private investment from within the region. In 2025, investors from OTS countries made investment commitments in Uzbekistan worth approximately $3.8 billion, creating opportunities to channel regional capital into structured investment projects.

According to Babayev, the fund’s performance should be assessed not only by the volume of its own financing in Uzbekistan but also by the additional investment it helps mobilize.

Cross-border projects to strengthen regional trade

Cross-border investment is one of TIF’s core priorities. The fund assesses projects based on their regional significance, including how investment in one country can benefit businesses and infrastructure in others.

Uzbekistan’s trade with OTS countries increased from approximately $4 billion in 2017 to $10.8 billion in 2025. Meanwhile, freight traffic along the Middle Corridor has grown nearly fivefold since 2021, reaching approximately 4.5 million tons, while transit times have decreased from 18 to 15 days.

The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, currently under construction, is another project expected to create new opportunities for regional connectivity.

According to Babayev, TIF aims to support not only major transport routes but also the infrastructure and services needed to make them commercially viable. These include logistics centers, industrial zones, customs infrastructure, digital trade systems and reliable energy supplies for businesses operating along transport corridors.

The fund is also exploring opportunities to support regional production and supply chains, including Uzbek cotton and yarn supplies to Turkish textile manufacturers, as well as cross-border transport of agricultural products and machinery components for further processing and assembly. Potential financing instruments include direct lending, credit lines for banks serving exporters and trade finance facilities.

Institutional partnerships are expected to play an important role. A memorandum signed with UKDF in July 2026 provides for joint project identification, risk-sharing and support for expanding cross-border business activities. TIF has also held discussions with AUIC on potential cooperation along the Caspian route.

The fund’s regional approach also extends to energy and digital infrastructure. Initiatives such as the Green Energy Corridor connecting Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan with Azerbaijan, as well as the Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable, demonstrate the growing importance of interconnected regional infrastructure projects.

Measuring the development impact of investments

TIF assesses the expected impact of each investment before financing approval. Each operation includes a results measurement framework that defines project objectives, performance indicators and baseline data for comparison.
