Waste from the capital began to be transported daily to a landfill in the village of Shashakuara, in Gali district, 72km away, resulting in significant costs and wear and tear on vehicles.

“The Sukhum landfill contains hundreds of thousands of cubic metres of waste. But most of that volume is air. Only 15% consists of solid and liquid waste, while 85% is air. So these trucks keep driving back and forth, transporting air and burning fuel,” Russian hydraulic engineer Alexander Tsekhovoy explained to specialists in Sukhum in 2019.

According to his calculations, rather than endlessly transporting waste between landfills, each district should establish special compaction stations capable of compressing waste four- to fivefold. This would reduce the number of trips to the central landfill to just four truckloads a day.

However, instead of introducing these technologies, the authorities have continued simply transporting waste from one district to another.

Costly and pointless landfill in Katsikyt

A new waste management complex in the village of Katsikyt, in Gulripshi district, was supposed to provide a breakthrough solution to the waste problem.

The 5.5-hectare site was equipped with a waste disposal pit featuring a multilayer insulating base, treatment facilities and a conveyor belt for sorting waste. Construction proved extremely challenging, both technically and financially, with the project costing more than 150m roubles [$1.81m].

However, by the time the facility was nearly complete, it turned out that nobody wanted it.

Sukhum refused to use the complex, while the authorities in Gulripshi district were also reluctant to take responsibility for it. Security personnel were soon withdrawn from the site, which has since been effectively abandoned and remains unused.

Waste processing complex in the village of Katsikyt

The landfill in the village of Katsikyt was intended to be a financially sustainable facility. During its construction, Timur Agrba, then head of the Capital Construction Department and now mayor of Sukhum, said the facility could become self-financing by sorting, compacting and selling recyclable materials, including plastic, paper and metal.

According to Agrba, if properly managed, the facility could not only cover its operating costs but also generate revenue for further development.

However, in practice, the main obstacle is the tariff for household waste disposal.

“The current tariff policy does not reflect the realities or the costs incurred by our companies. International practice shows that waste collection and transportation should be funded through payments made by the residents who generate that waste,” Beslan Eshba, then head of the Sukhum city administration, explained back in 2014.

He promised that city authorities would seek to introduce relevant amendments to a new housing code. However, 12 years later, the new code has still not been adopted.

The current waste collection fee in Abkhazia is 27 roubles [$0.33] per person per month, a relatively modest amount. Yet most urban residents do not even pay this, as there is no clearly established system for collecting utility payments.

To obtain an objective assessment of the situation, Abkhazia’s Public Chamber held a series of meetings with Russian specialists, local environmental experts and representatives of district administrations.

As a result, an expert report was drawn up, providing a comprehensive assessment of the entire household waste management system. The report has already been submitted to the president, parliament, executive authorities and the Institute of Ecology.

For now, however, it represents little more than another faint glimmer of hope on the horizon. No tangible progress has been made towards resolving the problem.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Проблема мусора в Абхази

World.title: Special forces officers convicted of assaulting protesters jailed for five years each
World.content:
Special forces officers jailed for assaults

A court has sentenced special forces officers convicted of physically assaulting journalist Guram Rogava and protester Zviad Maisashvili during demonstrations in November and December 2024 to five years in prison each.

The special forces officer convicted of assaulting Guram Rogava, a journalist with Formula TV, was also banned from professional duties for three years. Lasha Gamkrelidze, the new prosecutor in the case, informed the journalist of the verdict by telephone.

According to Formula, Rogava had expected to testify as a victim during the trial. However, the prosecutor explained that his testimony was unnecessary because the court and the defence had accepted the charges as undisputed. Rogava himself believes that the person who directly assaulted him remains at large.

Two other special forces officers arrested in connection with the assault on Zviad Maisashvili were each sentenced to five years in prison. Lawyer Dimitri Mchedlishvili confirmed the information to Tabula.

On 30 November 2024, at around 06:30, special forces officers kicked Zviad Maisashvili in the face during a protest on Rustaveli Avenue, causing him to lose consciousness. Footage of the assault circulated on social media.

On 7 May 2026, Georgia’s Prosecutor’s Office announced that it had identified and detained five people in connection with assaults on Rogava, Maisashvili and opposition politician Levan Khabeishvili.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, four of those detained were current or former special forces officers, while the fifth was a serving officer with the Interior Ministry’s Security Police Department. Two of the suspects were already serving prison sentences at the time of their arrest.

Prosecutors said that on 29 November 2024, during a protest on Rustaveli Avenue, an officer from the Interior Ministry’s Special Tasks Department assaulted Guram Rogava while the journalist was carrying out his professional duties.

The detainees were charged under Article 333(3) of the Criminal Code with abuse of official powers involving violence. The officer detained in connection with the assault on Rogava also faced an additional charge of unlawfully obstructing a journalist’s professional activities.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office’s initial statement, the charges carried prison sentences of five to eight years.

Maisashvili said both special forces officers detained over the assault on him had admitted their guilt and apologised to him.

Guram Rogava and Zviad Maisashvili

Background

The assaults on Guram Rogava and Zviad Maisashvili were among several high-profile incidents of police violence during pro-European protests in Tbilisi in November and December 2024.

The protests began on 28 November 2024, after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that the government would take the issue of opening EU accession talks off the agenda until the end of 2028.

In the following days, law enforcement officers used water cannon, tear gas and other crowd-control measures against protesters on Rustaveli Avenue and near the parliament building. Numerous incidents of physical violence against demonstrators, journalists and human rights defenders were documented.

Both protesters and members of the media sustained injuries during the demonstrations. The assault on journalist Guram Rogava attracted particular attention. On 29 November 2024, a special forces officer attacked Rogava while he was reporting live from Rustaveli Avenue, leaving him seriously injured.

Media representatives and human rights organisations called for investigations into these incidents. On 30 November 2024, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) said the police’s use of water cannon, pepper spray and batons, including against peaceful demonstrators and journalists, had been disproportionate.

According to Georgia’s Public Defender’s 2024 report, the ombudsman and his representatives visited 624 people who had been detained or injured during protests between 15 April 2024 and 1 March 2025. Of those, 360 reported ill-treatment.

The report also noted that no police officers had been held accountable for violence committed by law enforcement personnel during that period.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office statement of 7 May 2026, more than 550 witnesses were questioned and thousands of investigative and procedural actions were carried out as part of the investigations into the cases involving Zviad Maisashvili, Levan Khabeishvili and Guram Rogava.

The Prosecutor’s Office said the investigations would continue to identify other possible perpetrators and bring them to justice.

World.title: Uzbekistan, South Korea consider integrated green energy systems for airports
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. Uzbekistan and South Korea have discussed potential joint projects in smart grids, renewable energy and energy storage systems, including the development of integrated green energy infrastructure at airports at a meeting on November 14.

According to Uzbekistan's Academy of Sciences, the discussions took place during a meeting between representatives of the Institute of Energy Problems under the Academy of Sciences of Uzbekistan and a delegation from the Korea Institute for Climate Change (KICC).

The Uzbek side was represented by D.T. Yusupov, acting director of the institute, and laboratory heads Sh.V. Khamidov and B.N. Erkinov. The South Korean delegation included KICC team leaders Jaeyeon Na and Geunyoung Lee.

The talks focused on developing joint research and practical projects in smart grid technologies, renewable energy sources, battery energy storage systems (BESS), smart airport infrastructure and electric mobility.

One of the key proposals involved establishing a "Green Smart Energy and Mobility Center" at airports. The concept envisages integrating solar photovoltaic panels, battery storage systems and intelligent energy management technologies into airport infrastructure.

Additionally, the parties discussed developing smart charging infrastructure for electric vehicles and buses, as well as introducing innovative parking and logistics solutions in cooperation with South Korean companies AMANO Korea and Hanjin Logistics.

The sides further explored opportunities to expand successful technological solutions to other regions of Uzbekistan.

Following the discussions, the South Korean delegation visited the institute's research laboratories, where it was introduced to modern energy measurement equipment, laboratory facilities and the institution's research capabilities.

The meeting is part of broader efforts to strengthen scientific and technological cooperation between Uzbekistan and South Korea in smart electricity networks, renewable energy and innovative infrastructure. No specific investment commitments or project implementation timelines were disclosed.

World.title: Tokayev replaces head of Kazakhstan's National Security Committee
World.content:
Photo: Press Office of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. Marat Irmenov has been appointed Chairman of Kazakhstan's National Security Committee (NSC), according to the press service of the President of Kazakhstan.

The relevant decree was signed by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. Under a separate decree, Yermek Sagimbayev was relieved of his post as Chairman of the NSC.

From 1996 through 2000, Irmenov held operational positions in the national security agencies, followed by senior positions in these agencies from 2000 through 2025. In October 2025, he was appointed Deputy Chairman of the NSC.

Sagimbayev had served as Chairman of the National Security Committee since January 2022. He was reappointed to the post in November 2022 and again in August 2026.

Prior to his appointment as NSC Chairman, Sagimbayev served in the Soviet Armed Forces from 1985 through 1987 and held officer positions in the national security agencies from 1994 through 2006.

From 2006 through 2019, he held officer and senior positions in the Office of the State Security Service of Kazakhstan, as well as in operational support units.

In May 2019, Sagimbayev was appointed Deputy Head of the State Security Service of Kazakhstan and Head of the Presidential Security Service. In July 2021, he became Deputy Head of the State Security Service, and on August 25, 2021, he was appointed Head of the service.

World.title: Investor interest in ABB bonds remains strong: orders exceed AZN 22 million across two issuances
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. The latest subscription round for ABB bonds has been successfully completed. During this round, two bond issuances with a combined value of AZN 15 million were offered to investors, both of which were fully placed. The total value of orders received across the two issuances reached AZN 22,173,200, approximately 1.5 times the amount offered.

1-year bonds with an annual yield of 8.5%

The issuance, valued at AZN 5 million, attracted orders totaling AZN 8,421,500, approximately 1.7 times the amount offered. A total of 83 investors participated in the subscription, submitting 347 orders. Of these, 345 orders were executed, with allocations made to 81 investors.

2-year bonds with an annual yield of 9%

The issuance, valued at AZN 10 million, attracted orders totaling AZN 13,751,700, approximately 1.4 times the amount offered. A total of 94 investors participated in the subscription, submitting 223 orders. All orders were executed, with allocations made to all 94 investors.

The bonds, each with a nominal value of AZN 100, were issued in volumes of 50,000 units for the 1-year maturity and 100,000 units for the 2-year maturity. Both issuances comprise registered, interest-bearing, unsecured bonds issued in dematerialized form. Interest payments will be made to investors every 30 days. Interest income earned by individual investors from these bonds is exempt from taxation.

The ABB bonds were placed through a public offering (subscription) on the Baku Stock Exchange, with ABB-Invest Investment Company acting as the underwriter. The bonds have been admitted to the Standard Market listing segment of the Baku Stock Exchange, enabling investors to trade them on the secondary market.

In addition to offering investors an opportunity to earn stable and reliable returns, ABB bonds make a significant contribution to the development of Azerbaijan's capital market.

For more information about ABB's modern, convenient and comprehensive range of products and services, please visit the Bank's branches and service offices, its official website at https://abb-bank.az/, contact the 937 Contact Center, or follow ABB's official social media channels.

World.title: Turkmenistan, Kuwait discuss telecom and high-tech cooperation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. Turkmenistan and Kuwait have addressed prospects for expanding bilateral cooperation in telecommunications and digital technologies, the Turkmen Embassy in Qatar reported.

The issues were reviewed during a meeting between Turkmenistan’s Ambassador to Qatar Myratgeldi Seyitmammedov, Kuwait’s Permanent Representative to the UN Office and other international organizations in Geneva Nasser Alhayen, and Chairman of Kuwait’s Communication and Information Technology Regulatory Authority (CITRA) Khalid Alzamel. The meeting was held on the sidelines of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) Plenipotentiary Conference in Doha.

According to the embassy, the discussions focused on developing cooperation in telecommunications and digital technologies, as well as strengthening coordination and engagement within international organizations.

Notably, Turkmenistan and Kuwait established diplomatic relations on January 13, 1995. Their cooperation has developed across political, trade, economic and humanitarian areas, with both countries maintaining contacts bilaterally and through international organizations.

A major step in strengthening the bilateral framework was made during the official visit of then Turkmen President Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov to Kuwait in March 2018. The two countries signed a package of 10 documents covering trade, economic and technical cooperation, the establishment of a joint intergovernmental commission, cultural ties and political consultations. The package also included a memorandum between Turkmengaz State Concern and Kuwait Petroleum Corporation, as well as cooperation documents involving the Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Tajikistan sign declarations to strengthen ecosystem protection
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. Uzbekistan and Tajikistan have signed two joint declarations to enhance ecosystem resilience, promote sustainable landscape management and establish a regional early warning system for forest fires in Central Asia during a high-level event titled "Regional Cooperation for Enhancing Landscape Resilience in Central Asia," held on the sidelines of the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye on November 14.

According to Uzbekistan's National Committee on Ecology and Climate Change, the event brought together representatives of Central Asian countries, international organizations and development partners to discuss regional cooperation on ecosystem restoration, biodiversity conservation, land degradation prevention and climate resilience.

The first declaration focuses on applying nature-based solutions to improve sustainable landscape management and strengthen ecosystem resilience. The second provides for the establishment of a regional forest fire early warning system.

The signing of two additional joint declarations involving Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan and Kyrgyzstan is also envisaged.

Participants emphasized that environmental challenges in Central Asia, including land degradation, forest fires, the spread of invasive species, biodiversity loss and growing pressure on protected areas, require coordinated regional responses, joint monitoring and cross-border cooperation.

The discussions also highlighted the RESILAND CA+ Regional Program, supported by the World Bank. The initiative aims to restore degraded landscapes, promote sustainable natural resource management and strengthen climate resilience across Central Asia.

The regional component of the program is coordinated by the Regional Environmental Center for Central Asia (CAREC), which facilitates cross-border cooperation, knowledge exchange and the implementation of joint environmental initiatives.

Participants noted that the declarations could provide a basis for coordinated regional mechanisms to address environmental threats, expand the use of nature-based solutions and develop practical projects with the support of international partners and financial institutions.

The agreements reflect growing efforts by Central Asian countries to address shared environmental challenges through regional cooperation and coordinated climate action.

World.title: Kazakhstan, UNEP look to deepen partnership on Caspian Sea conservation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. Kazakhstan and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) have discussed expanding joint efforts to protect the Caspian Sea ecosystem, including through closer cooperation between littoral states and international organizations, according to the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources of Kazakhstan.

The issue was discussed during a meeting between Kazakhstan's Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources Alibek Kuantyrov and UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen on November 15 on the sidelines of the 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye.

The parties discussed priority areas of cooperation between Kazakhstan and UNEP, as well as prospects for strengthening their partnership in addressing current environmental and climate challenges.

Particular attention was paid to the international negotiations on a global agreement to combat plastic pollution. The sides exchanged views on the work of the Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee and emphasized the importance of continuing constructive dialogue to develop effective international solutions.

Cooperation on protecting the Caspian Sea ecosystem was another key topic. Kuantyrov stressed the need to intensify joint efforts, coordinate the efforts of interested countries and international organizations, and develop practical cooperation to protect the marine environment and preserve biodiversity in the Caspian region.

The meeting also addressed methane emission reduction. Kazakhstan shared its experience in implementing measures to cut methane emissions and highlighted the importance of further international cooperation and the exchange of best practices in this area.

The meeting also highlighted the importance of strengthening Kazakhstan's cooperation with UNEP through projects supported by the Global Environment Facility (GEF). The parties noted the need to ensure the timely and effective implementation of projects that have already been approved and to promote new joint initiatives.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Acwa explore carbon credits for renewable energy projects
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. Uzbekistan and Saudi Arabia's Acwa have signed a memorandum of understanding to explore opportunities for the company's renewable energy projects in Uzbekistan to participate in international carbon markets under the Paris Agreement on the sidelines of the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye on November 14.

According to Uzbekistan's National Committee on Ecology and Climate Change, the document was signed by Aziz Abdukhakimov, Adviser to the President of Uzbekistan and Chairman of the National Committee on Ecology and Climate Change, and Mohammad Abdullah Abunayyan, Founder and Chairman of the Board of Directors of Acwa.

The memorandum aims to strengthen cooperation on implementing mechanisms established under the Paris Agreement, including international efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, develop carbon markets and advance sustainable development goals.

Under the agreement, the parties will explore the potential participation of Acwa's projects in Uzbekistan in international carbon market mechanisms. These include the Bash, Jankeldy and Kungrad wind power projects, with the latter incorporating a battery energy storage system, as well as the Karatau project.

The sides will assess the projects' compliance with Paris Agreement requirements and examine approval and registration procedures, as well as opportunities to generate, transfer and use carbon credits and emission reduction outcomes.

The memorandum also envisages technical and regulatory cooperation, the exchange of expertise on carbon markets, improvements to monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) systems, and capacity-building activities.

Another area of cooperation will focus on strengthening the climate resilience of renewable energy facilities and related infrastructure. The parties plan to exchange information on climate risk assessments for wind farms and energy storage systems, particularly risks associated with extreme temperatures, dust and sandstorms. They will also explore the use of climate data and early warning systems.

The memorandum provides a framework for further cooperation between Uzbekistan and Acwa on carbon market participation and climate resilience.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Oman target 2–3-fold increase in food trade from 2027
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. Uzbekistan and Oman discussed plans at a meeting in Oman on November 15 to increase bilateral food trade by two to three times starting in 2027, expand agricultural exports, and launch joint investment projects in food processing, fisheries, and organic fertiliser production.

Uzbekistan's Ministry of Agriculture said the two sides discussed the issues during a meeting in Muscat between Uzbekistan's Minister of Agriculture Ibrokhim Abdurakhmonov and Oman's Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries Wealth and Water Resources Saud bin Hamoud bin Ahmed Al Habsi.

The sides focused on expanding cooperation in food security, trade and investment. They also examined opportunities to increase exports of higher value-added agricultural products and improve logistics between the two countries.

In particular, the parties discussed establishing air cargo transportation through direct Tashkent-Muscat flights and making greater use of the Middle Corridor and other alternative transport routes.

The discussions also covered expanding exports of Uzbek fruits, vegetables, dried fruits and nuts to Oman, while increasing imports of seafood and dates from the Gulf country.

The two sides explored potential joint investment projects in food processing and packaging, fisheries and organic fertilizer production. Omani representatives also expressed interest in Uzbekistan's agricultural cluster and cooperative models, as well as its systems for providing preferential agricultural loans, crop insurance and incentives to improve productivity.

To facilitate knowledge exchange, the parties proposed establishing a technical working group to study Uzbekistan's experience in these areas.

Additional areas identified for cooperation included grain production, seed farming, water-saving technologies, halal certification, food quality and safety, scientific research and workforce training.

The sides also discussed the participation of Uzbek companies in Oman's annual agricultural exhibition, held in December.

During the meeting, the Uzbek delegation presented its "7D" concept for food systems, based on seven principles: data, diversification, design, discipline, delivery, interconnectedness and mutual respect. The Omani side expressed interest in considering the approach as a framework for cooperation.

Following the talks, the parties agreed to formalize the arrangements in a memorandum of understanding and begin practical work in the identified areas.

World.title: Sexual misconduct inside the NSW Police Force exposed
World.content:
When Ashlee graduated from the NSW Police Academy in 2018, she was in it for the long haul.

"I was bright-eyed and bushy-tailed when I joined. I never thought that I would even have to contemplate a different career," she told 7.30.

Ashlee is still a NSW Police officer and is using a pseudonym to protect her identity.

She is currently on medical leave due to her mental health along with a physical injury and says returning to work is still "too terrifying" to contemplate.

Ashlee is one of the few police officers who reported a senior colleague for assaulting her and took her case to criminal court.

New data obtained by 7.30 under freedom of information laws shows there have been dozens of other sexual misconduct allegations made against NSW Police employees in the period between 2021 and 2025.

The workplace culture within the NSW Police Force has been under scrutiny. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

In that time there were 483 reports of sexual harassment against NSW Police employees.

In the same period, there were also 67 allegations of sexual touching against NSW Police employees and 10 allegations of indecent assault.

There were also 45 allegations of rape against NSW Police employees, 17 of which were allegedly committed against their colleagues, some of these involved multiple allegations against individual officers.

According to NSW Police, a total of 36 employees were accused of rape in the past five years and of those, six police officers have been prosecuted for sexual assault. Eight of the accused officers have lost their jobs.

In its 2025 annual report the NSW Police Force said it had 15,887 officers and 4,508 administrative officers.

Ashlee believes those numbers are likely the tip of the iceberg.

"I would say it's at least double what those numbers are … I wouldn't be surprised if it was three times that number," Ashlee said.

Ashlee's 'terrifying' experience

After graduating, Ashlee worked as a probationary constable in Sydney's northern suburbs in 2019.

In June, she attended a house party hosted by another officer in Sydney's Northern Beaches.

Among those in attendance was leading Constable Ryan Dare, who was a more experienced and higher-ranking officer from a neighbouring station.

In the past five years, there were almost 500 reports of sexual harassment against NSW Police employees. (ABC News: ABC News: Adriane Reardon)

After the house party, the group went to a bar in Manly, where Ashlee alleges Dare's behaviour escalated.

"He would stand behind me, playing with my hair, hands over my shoulders, putting his head next to me and people were noticing," she said.

" That's when he stood slightly to the side of me and used his right hand to go from the small of my back underneath my shirt, wrapped his hand around me and proceeded to move up to my chest. "

Other officers who were there witnessed the assault and immediately stepped in and removed Dare from the venue.

After the house party, the group went to a bar in Manly, where Constable Ryan Dare's behaviour escalated. (ABC News: Nicole Chettle)

"I was hysterical, I think I was just in such shock," Ashlee said.

She was then faced with the difficult decision of whether to proceed with criminal charges against Dare.

"To think that it was another police officer that did it to me, that is not something I thought even possible when I joined the police force," she said.

" As a probationary constable ... to make a claim against a senior officer was, still is, such a big deal. "

Given there was CCTV of the assault and several witnesses, Ashlee decided to pursue criminal charges.

Dare was initially charged with sexual touching and faced a local court hearing, where Ashlee was cross-examined for several hours.

While the trial was ongoing, Dare was allowed to continue working as an officer at a nearby station, where Ashlee encountered him on the job.

She says he also lived in the same area and that she saw him both at work and while doing her grocery shopping.

During the legal process, Dare was allowed to continue working at a neighbouring station. (ABC News: Floss Adams)

"If it was a normal person, they would get an AVO, but I wasn't even treated like a normal [person], wasn't even given that opportunity to do that."

Ashlee said she didn't feel like she could request an AVO to be put in place given Dare had been allowed to return to the workplace.

In a statement, NSW Police told 7.30" "The need for an AVO depends on the particular circumstances, and at the time there was no identified need for an AVO."

"AVOs are utilised where there are concerns regarding a complainant's safety or the management of ongoing risk, which had already been mitigated."

A guilty plea for the lesser charge of common assault was eventually accepted by the prosecutor and Dare was suspended with pay.

"We pushed to have it continue as a sexual touching case and ultimately that was taken away from me," Ashlee said.

Dare was sentenced to a nine-month good behaviour bond and had his conviction removed from his record after an appeal.

After his guilty plea, Dare was allowed to continue working as a police officer for another year.

NSW Police said Dare was "managed in the workplace" with restrictions in place to ensure both parties did not come into contact, which included "transferring the officer to another station and prohibiting the officer from undertaking duties in certain commands".

Ashlee said during the process that NSW Police Force leadership asked her if she would support a decision to allow Dare to keep his job, with a demotion.

"My response to that was you can have him reinstated and you can give him back his badge, but I will be giving you my badge in return," she said.

It took almost four years from the day of the assault before Dare was sacked from the police force by then-Commissioner Karen Webb, as a result of the guilty plea.

Karen Webb was the first female police commissioner in NSW and ordered an independent cultural review. (ABC News: Warwick Ford)

The following year, Ms Webb, the state's first female commissioner, launched an independent culture review of the NSW Police Force, triggered by an ABC News investigation.

The review, published in June, uncovered hundreds of reports of sexual harassment and dozens of allegations of sexual assault within the NSW Police Force, along with a longstanding culture of silence.

Power imbalances and a toxic culture

Ms Webb retired before the findings and recommendations were delivered but told 7.30 she always maintained the organisation had a problem with its treatment of women.

"I'd seen it over the years, and it hadn't really shifted from 38 years ago right to the end," Ms Webb told 7.30.

"It was time to do something that would actually lead to substantial change, hopefully ... for the women coming through and the women in the organisation now that have still got long careers ahead of them."

Ms Webb said she knew some senior officers were routinely preying on probationary constables.

Karen Webb retired from the top job before the final report was delivered. (ABC News: Craig Hansen)

"It was a power imbalance, which made it even harder for women to come forward," she said.

Ms Webb said the number of officers accused of sexual misconduct in the past five years was "appalling".

"The thing that worries me, though, is that I know from being a detective and investigating sexual assaults that we know in society only 1 in 10 or 1 in 20 women come forward to report their sexual assault," she said.

"If that's representative of the number of women that have come forward in the organisation to report their sexual assault, then that number is much higher in reality."

Findings from a landmark review

Former NSW Police Senior Sergeant Mel Cooper, whose story helped trigger the independent culture review in 2024, said she also believes the number of women on the force who have experienced sexual assault, sexual touching and sexual harassment is much higher than reported.

Retired senior sergeant Mel Cooper says she is not surprised by the number of sexual misconduct allegations in the force. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

"Every single one of them has happened to me … and the fact that every single one of them is still happening to serving police officers by serving police officers currently … that breaks my heart," Ms Cooper said.

Ms Cooper said she never reported any of the assaults or harassment during her time on the force.

"You get lulled into this false sense of security ... that you should trust because they're police," she said.

"Then things happen … and you're put in a position where you have a choice to make as to whether you do come forward and report things … or whether you just put it aside."

Mel Cooper says she experienced harassment, unwanted touching and even sexual assault throughout her career. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

According to the culture review's final report, "very few" survey respondents felt safe reporting harmful behaviour and most commonly dealt with incidents by avoiding the perpetrator.

"We heard some stories about the targeting of probationary officers, including by field training officers who were signing off on their training and performance," the report stated.

"Participants also described unwelcome sexual touching of varying degrees of seriousness, including instances where leaders misused their rank and position of power."

Many of the culture review's 29 recommendations were aimed at fostering a safer environment for officers to report misconduct.

NSW Police said all the recommendations have been accepted by Commissioner Mal Lanyon and are being rolled out.

NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

"The Independent Cultural Review also recognised that the NSWPF has made significant improvements in complaints handling and reporting," a statement said.

"The New South Wales Police Force takes all allegations of sexual harassment, misconduct and assault seriously … sexual assault and misconduct are never acceptable."

NSW Police says all 29 recommendations from the culture review have been accepted and are being rolled out. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Ashlee says the experience has left her with little faith in NSW Police and the justice system to protect victims and hold perpetrators accountable.

She says she is unlikely to return to the police force.

"It has traumatised me so greatly in so many aspects of my life and even the continuation of work, that it is just absolutely not worth it for the ongoing and lifelong issues that I'm going to have for him to literally just lose his job," she said.

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: 'They cut a bit different': Khawaja opens up on facing racism growing up
World.content:
Usman Khawaja has spoken about having to deal with racism at school and around cricket as a relative new arrival in Australia.

Coverage of Khawaja's new autobiography, Sabr, has focused largely on the chapter on Sandpapergate, the scandal over Australian cricketers using sandpaper to tamper with the ball in the third Test against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018.

However, speaking on the Imperfects podcast, Khawaja dealt with a number of other topics including where he felt he belonged in Australia as a child arrived from Pakistan, his treatment by Australians growing up and his struggles in dealing with performance and failure in cricket.

Renshaw concerned about Khawaja's wellbeing Matt Renshaw reveals his check-in with the under-fire Usman Khawaja after Pat Cummins went on the offence during his press conference.

Khawaja said the five members of his family lived in a two-bedroom apartment for the first few years in the country.

His family began life in Australia in Sydney's eastern suburbs, but moved around a lot before going to the western suburbs, which he described as "like a whole different ball game".

"I remember the first time I'd ever been called a curry muncher," he said. "I think I must have been like … seven or eight, around there."

Khawaja spoke no English initially, with Urdu his main language. He made friends through his love of sport, but even though he learned English quickly, he said it didn't make it easier to deal with people focusing on racial stereotypes.

"When I was younger, what it used to do to me was like, it used to make me feel embarrassed about being where I was from, because it felt like there was nothing cool about the subcontinent," he said.

"Like people used to make fun of the accents, used to make fun of curries, you know, the old, you go to [have a] curry, then you have to go to the toilet straight away.

"[The] call, you smell like curry, curry's disgusting, and as much as I love the Simpsons [animated TV show] and I loved Apu, even Apu as I grew older, I look at him like, geez, they took the piss out of Apu a lot.

"I was pretty resilient … but it was like I should be really embarrassed about being Pakistani."

Chappell urges cricketers to move on The ball-tampering scandal doesn't look like it's going away any time soon, with Greg Chappell fearing Australian cricket could "eat itself".

Khawaja said people mocking Pakistani accents really "irked" him. "I was like getting into fights with people about it and stuff too."

Khawaja spoke about his journey in cricket, and that as he got better and started dominating games, he could see "the frustration in the white parents, and then I could hear it too".

"The parents' insults always sounded like vindictive," he said.

"They cut a bit different because, like, you'd walk past them and someone would say it on purpose, and I know they would.

"They'd walk past me like, 'Oh, yeah, there's that other Paki scoring runs again', and they'd say like … there's that, you know, little black so-and-so … just so I'd hear it, like they knew I was around."

Asked if he spoke to his parents about these incidents, Khawaja said: "Not really, because I reckon my parents would have been going through the exact same thing, but in a different context with other people."

Asked where he felt he belonged as a teenager, Khawaja said "on the cricket field" because that was where he felt respected and equal amongst his teammates.

Khawaja said he firmly believed that sport broke down barriers, which was why he set up his Usman Khawaja Foundation, to give cricket experiences to young Australians from refugee, immigrant and Indigenous backgrounds.

Ultra-competitiveness led to early mental health struggles

Khawaja also spoke about the performance side of cricket, particularly batting, which he called frustrating and a "mind screw".

Batting failures are commonplace in cricket, but Usman Khawaja (right) says he struggled mentally to deal with them early in his career. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

"Like you can literally go out there first ball, get out, and you're just sitting down all day just thinking about what am I doing with my life?

"So much failure [in cricket] and I talk [in the book] about really struggling with that early on … I'm so competitive and I wanted it so much that, [I] literally had suicidal thoughts a couple of times in my life.

"I remember two distinct times.

"Not that it got to a point [where I did something] … but those thoughts like it was hurting so much because I was so competitive and I [wasn't doing well].

"That's how much importance I placed on cricket and getting out and doing well and when you're losing and you're not scoring runs, you're [feeling like you're] letting everyone else down."

Asked when these happened, he said that it was early on before he worked on "my mental wellbeing and everything", including having self-worth aside from cricket.

"So, when I talk about being a human, I probably didn't treat myself like a human back then," he said.

"I treated myself like a cricketer."

World.title: Small regional town fights back against proposed AI data centre
World.content:
The small regional town of Miners Rest, north of Ballarat, is home to just under 4,000 people.

Locals say their quiet country life might be about to change after developer Resi Ventures announced to the Australian Stock Exchange in June its intention to build an AI data centre at the town's old quarry.

Volunteer firefighter and First Nations man Jedd Willis said the proposal on a 67 hectare plot of land in his town had been overwhelming.

"There been a complete lack of care for country which disturbs me as a First Nations person," Mr Willis said.

"[The site] has a very valuable resource for water and for firefighting."

Jedd Willis (left) says he often uses water from the proposed site to fill firefighting tankers. (Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram)

Mr Willis, who is a CFA volunteer, said firefighters would often use the water at the proposed site for fighting bushfires.

"Without that [water] source, we'd be forced to rely more heavily on the treatment plant," he said.

"Along that, the concerns around the lack of water availability across the state as a whole, let alone just this region and with the upcoming fire season being forecasted to be quite treacherous is concerning."

Thousands across Victoria protest

On Saturday, dozens of Miners Rest locals joined thousands from across the state at the steps of the state library in Melbourne to protest against the rise of AI data centres in Victoria.

As of September this year, there were 50 data centres operating across Victoria with another 18 in the pipeline.

Protesters called for a statewide moratorium on their construction.

Chris Phillips says the data centre proposed for Miners Rest could be up to 350 metres long. (Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram)

Secretary for the No Data Centre Miners Rest group, Chris Phillips said the developer had not been open about its plans.

He said locals learned about this proposal through the media, rather than consultation with the community.

"It's been extremely difficult [to find information about it]," Mr Phillips said.

"The benefit to the community would be very little."

Mr Phillips said one of his concerns was whether the company would be making use of an aquifer at the site.

"There's an aquifer [at the site] that goes many hundreds of kilometres underground and people draw water out of that to grow food like, potato farmers," he said.

"We don't want that touched.

" We're scared that water could get contaminated and flow through to the rest of our agricultural industry and be a blight on our area. "

'Nervously watching' upcoming election

Miners Rest locals say they are concerned about the light and noise pollution the proposed data centre may emit. (Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram)

Mr Phillips said locals were also concerned about the noise pollution that could come from the centre.

"It's going to have a noise transmission of 63 to 65 decibels, which will be heard up to 1 kilometre away, over a constant 24 hours," he said.

He said he would be anxiously watching the upcoming election and hoped politicians were listening to the local community.

"I think if [politicians] don't listen to people they're going to get a very, very rude shock come this election," he said.

"We are very nervously watching and we've had commitments from various political parties but we are also very nervous as to what could happen once the party is elected we could be steam rolled."

Locals say there has been no consultation from the developer regarding the proposed data centre. (Supplied: 60_harvests_left/Instagram)

In a statement Ripon MP, Martha Haylett said Miners Rest families deserved to be consulted before decisions were made that could fundamentally change their local area.

"There has been no planning approval, no permits issued, and no meaningful consultation with the community," Ms Haylett said.

"That is simply not good enough.

"A project of this scale and significance cannot be imposed on a community without proper scrutiny, transparency, and engagement."

The City of Ballarat said in a statement it had not received any planning applications for the proposal.

"While Council officers have had early conversations with the developer, no formal applications have been lodged," it said.

"All planning applications are subject to a thorough assessment process."

The ABC has contacted Resi Ventures for comment.

World.title: Biddulph lashes Rockliff over Christmas social media pile-on
World.content:
A Tasmanian-based best-selling author of parenting books has called on Premier Jeremy Rockliff to offer an unreserved apology for an incorrect social media post about a primary school's end-of-year celebrations.

The post on October 14 claimed that "all references to Christmas" had been removed from Trevallyn Primary School's end-of-year event.

Correspondence tabled in parliament revealed Education Department secretary Ginna Webster wrote to Mr Rockliff on the day of his post, informing him that Christmas remained an important part of the school's event.

Mr Rockliff has said he did not receive the letter until the day after, but that it was clear changes were being made.

While Mr Rockliff did not identify the school, it was later identified in comments on other social media posts and in the media. The school brought in security in response to abuse stemming from a subsequent social media pile-on.

Tasmanian premier Jeremy Rockliff's Facebook post critical of a school renaming an end-of-year Christmas event. October 2026. (Facebook: Jeremy Rockliff)

Mr Rockliff offered an apology on Friday "for the outcome it has created" and "for the effect on individuals, teachers and schools", but said he stood by his "expectations".

His apology did not acknowledge that he had falsely claimed "there have been efforts made to remove all references to Christmas in end of year school celebrations".

Loading...

Author and psychologist Steve Biddulph told 936 ABC Hobart the apology was "vague" and did not feel genuine.

"What he did at the weekend was like lighting a bushfire and blaming the trees," he said.

"There are really just seven words that need to be heard: 'I deeply regret the harm I caused', and 'what I posted was not true'.

" It's not the Jeremy that I know; it's very uncharacteristic of him, and I just don't understand what has happened here. "

The premier's post was publicly supported by several conservative government ministers, including Treasurer Eric Abetz, who posted an AI-generated image about a nativity play being cancelled.

Tasmanian Treasurer Eric Abetz's AI-generated image he posted to Facebook on October 19, 2026. (Facebook: Eric Abetz)

Ban on visits to continue

Loading...

The Tasmanian branch of the Australian Education Union (AEU) banned all state MPs from end-of-year events unless the premier apologised.

It met again on Monday to hear feedback from the school, and unanimously voted to continue the ban.

AEU Tasmania president David Genford said the apology was not accepted.

"The premier: any time you issue an apology and follow it with the words but and then try and explain yourself out of it simply isn't good enough," he said.

"For the premier to not actually take ownership for what he did is not okay."

The Tasmanian Principals Association has said it was "outraged" by the premier's actions, and the school's acting principal took leave.

Mr Genford said the school was still "suffering".

"It is unfortunate that the politicians won't be attending assemblies, but schools should not be political footballs," he said.

"The premier was more than happy to make this school collateral damage for a political play.

We are not going to stand by and allow that to happen. We want our kids to feel safe. We want staff members to feel safe."

World.title: Labour hire syndicates have 'little fear of consequence', watchdog says
World.content:
The New South Wales anti-slavery commissioner says he has seen no sign of proactive, intelligence-led policing of labour hire syndicates accused of exploiting migrant workers in regional NSW.

James Cockayne made the comments in his formal response to a parliamentary inquiry into the modern slavery risks faced by temporary migrant workers, which handed down its final report in August.

His response, tabled in parliament today, includes allegations that labour hire syndicates in the Riverina and on the Mid North Coast have underpaid workers and been involved in identity theft, money laundering and tax fraud.

These cases have been referred to state and federal police.



In a statement, NSW Police directed the ABC to the Australian Federal Police, which has also been contacted for comment.



Dr Cockayne said the state government was not doing enough to combat issues in the labour hire industry, which supplied migrant workers to farms across the state.

"For years, we pretended not to see the elephant in the room. The Committee changed that. Now the task is to move that elephant out of our homes and communities, and out of our supply -chains," Dr Cockayne said in a statement.

" Dodgy labour hire syndicates are exploiting workers and undercutting honest businesses. Some appear to be forging ties with organised crime. And they operate with little fear of consequence. "

James Cockayne has released a report on modern slavery. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht )

Dr Cockayne said multiple sources told him workers were moved off farms just before surprise inspections.

He also reported unverified allegations that some had been moved out of the region involuntarily, for weeks or longer.

The report said policing remained reactive, with fewer than 10 per cent of trafficking and modern slavery reports to the AFP reaching prosecution, according to Australian Institute of Criminology figures cited in the report.

Only about 1 to 4 per cent end in a trial, guilty plea or conviction.

Under pressure

The labour hire industry has been under intense scrutiny from advocates and government agencies for many months.

In August, a Four Corners investigation highlighted how migrant workers had been exploited by labour hire firms, with some fruit pickers saying they were treated like "animals".

During the same week, the NSW Parliamentary Inquiry into Modern Slavery released its final report, detailing "harrowing stories of mistreatment" faced by workers and making 31 recommendations to the government.

The report highlighted exploitation in the Coffs Harbour and Nambucca Valley regions on the Mid North Coast, asking for an investigation into allegations of systemic labour exploitation.

In its response on November 9, the state government said it was working with state and federal agencies on a range of measures and had improved information sharing.

Meanwhile, agencies have worked together to carry out surprise inspections on farms, while unions and migrant support groups ramped up their presence in affected regions.

Gershom Isaac at a caravan park in the NSW Riverina. (Four Corners)

Dr Cockayne recommended police step up proactive investigations into labour hire syndicates and publish their national protocol for combating human trafficking and slavery.

He also called for a plan to move high-risk industries away from exploitative labour hire, including support for worker-run cooperatives.

He said major buyers need to do due diligence on supply chains to ensure they were not contributing to modern slavery.

"Until licensing is in place, responsibility falls squarely on business," Dr Cockayne said.

"The biggest players in these supply chains have the most weight with which to leverage the system.

"They can afford to use it — and probably should, given big business may soon face criminal penalties for failure to prevent modern slavery in its supply chain.

"This is not only about doing the right thing. Responsible businesses are being undercut by operators who cheat workers and dodge tax. Acting now protects workers, and fair competition too."

Not enough

The NSW government said it was developing labour hire licensing legislation, which would be introduced into parliament next year.

Dr Cockayne said effective enforcement would not be in effect until 2028, leaving migrant workers vulnerable to exploitation for some time.

He said until the labour hire licensing scheme was in place, syndicates would continue to exploit the gap.

"The public has made its view clear. Three in four people in NSW want labour hire licensing. Many will weigh this issue when they vote come March," Dr Cockayne said in a statement.

World.title: NSW real estate laws shelved day before coming into effect
World.content:
Laws designed to protect buyers from real estate underquoting in New South Wales have been shelved amid fears they could backfire in the current housing downturn.

The rules were due to take effect on Tuesday, but the ABC has learnt they will be paused for up to a year, following a last-minute intervention from NSW Premier Chris Minns.

On Monday morning, the premier said he was concerned about agents being banned from lowering the advertised price of a property even if it was not generating buyer interest.

"It's not the seller or the agent's fault if the price of real estate is dropping," he said.

"The legislation, at least intuitively, believed that the prices would always rise.

"Well, that may not be the case."

By Monday evening, the premier had decided the controversial change should not proceed, just hours before it was due to come into force.

The rules were due to take effect on Tuesday before a last-minute delay was flagged. (AAP: Darren England)

'Unforeseen' consequences

Underquoting occurs when a property is advertised below the actual price that a real estate agent expects it to sell for.

While advertising a lower price can generate market interest in a property, it frustrates potential buyers and is therefore already illegal.

Under the next tranche of Labor's underquoting laws, which were due to begin on Tuesday, agents could be banned from advertising a price that was lower than a written offer rejected by the seller.

The change was designed to protect buyers by preventing agents from advertising unrealistic prices that the seller would not be happy to accept.

However, the market has turned.

Cotality data shows Sydney house prices have fallen by close to 9.7 per cent since the end of January, with units falling 5.2 per cent.

The market is experiencing downward pressure. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

Under the now-scrapped rule, if a buyer believed their home was worth $1.5 million and rejected a written offer of $1.3 million, their agent could not advertise the property for anything less than $1.3 million.

Even if the seller later realised their expectations were too high and wished to adjust their asking price, the agent would not be able to change the advertised price.

Real Estate Institute of NSW CEO, Tim McKibbin, said the rule would mean buyers would not know that a property had become more affordable.

"It misleads and disadvantages those purchasers and it certainly disadvantages the vendor," he said.

He said real estate agents had been warning the government that the legislation could backfire.

"We made clear that this wouldn't work out in the market [and] we were ignored," he said.

Mr Minns has hit pause on the legislation. (ABC News)

The premier said he had received negative feedback from real estate agents in his own electorate.

"I do think it's unforeseen, but it is something we're going to have to deal with," Mr Minns said.

"A deteriorating real estate market may mean that you rejected an earlier offer, but in actual fact, you'll take it a month later.

"Particularly if it's a distressed sale."

Reform reversal

With just a few days of parliament left for the year, the government is not expected to make any legislative amendments to pause the controversial changes.

Instead, it is expected to issue a regulation that would have the same effect.

Also being put on hold will be the requirement for agents to advertise a selling price, or price range, for properties.

Fines of up to $110,000 for underquoting will also be delayed, while the government reassesses the full suite of changes.

The reversal of key reforms will be a significant blow to Fair Trading Minister Anoulack Chanthivong, who is facing a separate preselection battle in his seat of Macquarie Fields.

Mr Chanthivong was unavailable for an interview.

Shadow Fair Trading Minister Tim James said the government should have designed laws that could withstand a property downturn.

"Property prices move in cycles," he said.

"The law needs to be able to meet the dynamics of the market at any given point in time."

World.title: Hail as heavy as snow seen as severe thunderstorms hit southern Queensland
World.content:
Seven-centimetre hail and 91 kilometre an hour wind gusts have hit south-east Queensland, with a severe thunderstorm warning in place.

The Bureau of Meteorology has issued a warning for destructive winds, giant hailstones and heavy rainfall.

The warning includes parts of Ipswich, Somerset, Scenic Rim, Southern Downs, Toowoomba, Lockyer Valley, Gold Coast, Sunshine Coast, Brisbane City and Moreton Bay.

Large hail stones have hit Grantham and surrounding areas. (Supplied: Heidi Hitila)

Hail stones of up to seven centimetres have been reported at Gatton, Lilydale and Heildon, while a 91 km/h wind gust was observed at Wellcamp Airport, west of Toowoomba.

In Pittsworth near Toowoomba, residents have described seeing hail as heavy as snow as the thunderstorm rolled in.

The storms are mainly heading east.

Loading...

Residents have been urged to take the necessary safety precautions.

A broader storm warning takes in parts of the south-east coast, the Central Highlands and Coalfields, Capricornia, Wide Bay-Burnett and the Darling Downs and Granite Belt.

How can you prepare for a thunderstorm?

The SES has a checklist of things you can do when storms are forecast.

World.title: Alleged murderer had scoped out paediatrician's home, court told
World.content:
A man accused of murdering prominent paediatrician Michael Yung had scoped out his house 24 hours before the alleged crime, a court has heard.

Kerem Aydin, 25, is standing trial in South Australia's Supreme Court after he pleaded not guilty to the murder of Dr Yung at his Gilberton home in the early hours of December 11, 2023.

He also pleaded not guilty to an aggravated charge of serious criminal trespass in a place of residence.

Opening the trial today, prosecutor Jim Pearce KC said Mr Aydin had scoped out Dr Yung's house before the alleged murder.

"It's the prosecution case that he scoped his target [and] that in the 24 hours or so prior to this attack the accused had been walking the streets of Gilberton, Medindie, Walkerville, looking for houses to break into," he said.

Michael Yung died in the Royal Adelaide Hospital the day after he was allegedly struck with a metal bar. (Supplied: SA Health)

Mr Pearce told the court that about 10:10am on December 10, 2023, CCTV footage from the street captured Mr Aydin scoping out Dr Yung's home when nobody was there because he planned to break-in and steal from the home.

He said the prosecution alleged Mr Aydin was motivated to steal because "the accused, his partner and their young child lived in rental accommodation at Thebarton" and "they were behind in their rent".

"The crown case is that there was clearly a financial need that saw the accused go into Dr Yung's house that morning," Mr Pearce said.

" It's not alleged he went there intending to kill someone, he went there to steal. "

Mr Pearce said that at 4:16am on December 11, 2026, Mr Aydin gained entry to Dr Yung's home through an upstairs window.

The court heard he gained entry using a ladder he found lent against the back verandah.

Victim was hit with metal bar, court told

Mr Pearce told the court it was alleged Mr Aydin made his way downstairs where he was confronted by Dr Yung.

"In the moments that followed the accused struck Dr Yung to the head — struck him twice," Mr Pearce said.

"He also struck him to the left side of the torso.

"It's alleged he struck Dr Yung using a makeshift weapon that he had brought with him.

"The weapon was a metal bar about 30cm, maybe a bit more, that had a drill bit wedged into the end of the metal bar."

Police attended the Gilberton home on December 11, 2023. (ABC News: James Wakelin)

Mr Pearce told the court Dr Yung's 30-year-old son, who was upstairs in the home at the time of the alleged attack, came downstairs "upon hearing his father say something to the effect of, 'How was it that you got into the house?'," followed by a scream.

"He found his father lying on the dining room floor," he said.

The court heard Dr Yung was rushed to the Royal Adelaide Hospital where he died from "a non-survivable catastrophic brain injury" on December 12.

Mr Pearce said that Mr Aydin was arrested on December 12 and was found to have "some obvious injuries to his left eye" and an injury to his calf.

"It's the prosecution case, these were injuries sustained when he crashed through the French doors to make his escape from the house," he said.

DNA allegedly found on torches

Mr Pearce told the court that blood allegedly matching Mr Aydin's DNA was found at the scene — including on the band of a head torch.

He also said another torch with Mr Aydin's DNA was allegedly found on a bed in an upstairs bedroom.

Following his arrest, the court heard that Mr Aydin had made calls to several people from custody and allegedly told them he had broken into Dr Yung's home under the impression it was a deceased estate.

Mr Pearce said that in those phone calls Mr Aydin claimed Dr Yung had grabbed a knife and that it led him to "react".

"As soon as he's gone for a knife, I've just reacted," Mr Aydin allegedly said to his mother in one of the calls.

"After I reacted, I panicked and I've run straight through the glass sliding door and cut my whole head up."

No 'murderous intent', lawyer tells court

Mr Aydin's defence barrister, Jane Abbey KC, said it was not disputed her client had scoped out Dr Yung's house, nor that he "intended to break into that house and steal things to help pay for his overdue rent".

"What is in dispute is his knowledge and recklessness about someone being present," she said.

Defence lawyer Jane Abbey KC said it would be disputed her client killed Dr Yung. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

Ms Abbey also said it would not be disputed that the pair engaged in a confrontation and that Mr Aydin crashed through the door.

However, she said it was disputed that her client killed Dr Yung.

"Mr Aydin did not cause his death, and he certainly didn't at any stage, form a murderous intent," she said.

The trial, which is expected to run for two weeks, continues.

World.title: ‘Not a murderer’: Mum denies killing kids in house fire
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts ‘Not a murderer’: Mum denies killing kids in house fire Rex Martinich November 16, 2026 — 6:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A mother who lost five children and her partner in a house fire has denied setting the blaze herself, telling a coroner she is “determined” to get answers. Four-year-old twins Kyza and Koa Godinet, and Nicky (3), Zack (11) and Harry Stephenson (10) were killed when their house on Russell Island, south-east of Brisbane, caught fire on August 6, 2023. The blaze claimed six lives. Nine News The boys’ 43-year-old father Wayne Patrick Godinet died after running upstairs while flames and smoke poured out of the house in an attempt to save the children and an adult occupant. The children’s mother, Samantha Stephenson and her stepsister Connie Campbell escaped the fire that trapped the others upstairs in a “classic Queenslander” home elevated on stumps.



Stephenson was the first witness called at the start of a coroners inquest on Monday into the six deaths. She broke down in tears as she was asked to confirm her relationship to each of the deceased. “I’m more than determined to get to this answer,” Stephenson said. Fire crews battling the blaze that engulfed multiple homes on Russell Island in 2023. Nine News She was escorted to the witness stand by a corrective services officer and she told Coroner Donald MacKenzie she was on remand for alleged cannabis possession and public nuisance.



An investigation found the fire likely started on the ground floor but the precise location could not be determined and deliberate ignition could not be ruled out, counsel assisting Corinne Leach told the coroner. “Did you start the fire?” Leach said. “No,” Stephenson said. Loading Leach asked about Stephenson’s alleged statements and behaviour while living at a unit complex after the fire.



A neighbour overheard Stephenson say, ‘I’m terribly sorry, mummy is just a murderer,’ Leach suggested. “I never said it,” Stephenson said. She also denied saying to neighbours “I let the smoke kill my kids”, screaming “I’m a murderer” or nodding when someone asked if she was guilty. Godinet and Stephenson had fallen asleep together after sharing a cannabis bong on a couch in a “chill out area” underneath the house, MacKenzie heard. Stephenson said she was woken in the early hours by Godinet jumping across the couch.



“I realised everything was on fire,” she said. “Wayne definitely would have gone upstairs at some point.” Stephenson tried to follow the father up into the house but the flames had engulfed the staircase. “I opened the door and it literally exploded,” she said. A Rural Fire Brigade crew arrived at 6.35am.



But Queensland Fire and Rescue Services were nearly an hour away, requiring a barge to get to the island east of Brisbane. The coroner is examining several issues including the fire’s cause, whether the installation of compliant smoke alarms would have prevented the deaths and whether emergency service resources on Russell Island are sufficient. The inquest will hold hearings over the coming two weeks. AAP

World.title: ‘They mean everything to me’: Thieves steal three Melbourne Cups won by Makybe Diva
World.content:
Updated NationalVictoriaCrime ‘They mean everything to me’: Thieves steal three Melbourne Cups won by Makybe Diva Alexander Darling Updated November 16, 2026 — 6:13pm ,first published 4:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Thieves have stolen the three Melbourne Cup trophies won by Makybe Diva after breaking into Flemington Racecourse in an early morning raid. Victoria Police said an unknown number of offenders stole the trophies about 6.30am on Monday from a cabinet, where they were on display as part of an exhibition honouring the legendary racehorse. Loading By Monday afternoon, the entrance to the exhibition had been boarded up, but an image reportedly from inside taken this morning shows a display cabinet with smashed glass, and several empty ledges next to the famous blue, red and white silks worn by jockey Glen Boss. There are reports the thieves were disguised as construction workers or tradespeople, but neither police nor the Victoria Racing Club (VRC) has confirmed this.



“The circumstances are yet to be established and an investigation into the incident is ongoing,” police said in a statement on Monday afternoon. The VRC said it had reported the theft to police and that it was assisting with the investigation. Makybe Diva in 2005 with strapper Christine Mitchell and the three Melbourne Cups the racehorse won. The trophies were stolen on Monday. Sebastian Costanzo “We are devastated by the incident and are in direct contact with Tony Santic [Makybe Diva’s owner].” Santic told this masthead he was first been made aware of the theft at 10am on Monday.



“The VRC called me and said they’d had a break in and the three Melbourne Cups had been stolen,” he said. “They told me the alarm went off, and five minutes later security arrived, and they [the trophies] were gone.” Santic also said the VRC told him the thieves were believed to have been wearing high-visibility clothing. “They mean everything to me,” he told this masthead. “I’ve lived with them like Australia has lived with Makybe over the last 23 years. Many hundreds of people have had a drink out of the cup.” Later speaking on 3AW, Santic pleaded with the thieves to drop the cups off “in one piece”, saying they were irreplaceable.



He said that if the cups were returned, this episode would deter him from exhibiting them publicly again. “They belong to the people as well. She [Makybe Diva] gave me and the people a lot, and I want to share that.” Tony Santic won three Melbourne Cup’s with Makybe Diva Pat Scala Makybe Diva remains the only horse ever to have won the Melbourne Cup three times, which she did in consecutive years, from 2003 to 2005. The legendary mare died in February at the age of 27.



Crafted with 18-carat gold, a Melbourne Cup weighs nearly two kilograms and takes more than 10 days to make. Each cup is valued at more than $1 million. The three cups were on display at the Hill Stand at Flemington – between the Terrace and the Atrium – as part of an exhibition titled “Makybe Diva: Queen of the Cups”. The horse’s ashes are also on display. This is not the first time something like this has happened.



Related Article Flashback From the Archives, 1963: Melbourne Cup stolen from display window In 1963, that year’s Melbourne Cup trophy was stolen from a display window near the corner of Elizabeth and Collins streets in Melbourne’s CBD in broad daylight, also by a group of three thieves. It is understood the VRC has shared CCTV footage from the building with Victoria Police, and that the display area featured 24/7 surveillance and alarms. World.title: Perth MP throws weight behind controversial uni merger idea
World.content:
NationalWAUniversity Perth MP throws weight behind controversial uni merger idea Holly Thompson and Michael Philipps November 16, 2026 — 5:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
