Federal Member for Perth Patrick Gorman has declared there are too many universities in the state, and has welcomed the proposed merger between the University of Western Australia, and Curtin and Murdoch University. Speaking at a press conference on Monday morning, Gorman was asked whether he favoured a merger between the universities. Federal Perth MP Patrick Gorman. Holly Thompson The merger has proved to be a controversial topic, with the vice chancellors at both Murdoch and Curtin University claiming joining all three institutions would be disastrous for the state’s tertiary sector. Students have also largely been against the decision, hosting protests including on the steps of Parliament House.



But Gorman has confirmed he would support a merger. “Well, for 20-something years, I have thought we have had at least one too many universities in Western Australia, so I am really open to the conversation,” Gorman said. “I think you put the case that the students always want the best value degree they can get, and that is what this conversation should be about. “Edith Cowan University is in my electorate and is the one university which is not part of those discussions. “I have been clear with the state government for a long period of time that my priority when it comes to education in my electorate is getting another inner-city high school.”



In 2024, Gorman spoke with this masthead on the issue, claiming there had been a lack of forward-thinking when it came to education in Perth’s CBD – a position he maintained on Monday. “Currently, we don’t have a (public) high school in the City of Perth, and that is a priority as we continue to see, over time, more and more housing come into the inner city, so that is my priority,” he said. “When it comes to university mergers, these are really big, complex things that will take a period of time. I will note that even the premier said he’s got an open mind about it, I also have an open mind and indeed, I have had an open mind about these questions since 2005.” Gorman said he was on the Curtin University Council in 2005, and had “extensive conversations about Curtin and Murdoch merging” at the time. “And if you go back into the archives, you will find quotes from me supporting that merger, which was controversial at the time,” he said.



“But I also note that you want to make sure that students get a better value degree, and taxpayers get better value for money, and that is the work that’s being done now. “I am happy to see the case put forward, but we want to make sure that it is done right.” Curtin University Vice Chancellor Harlene Hayne said Curtin would “vigorously oppose” the merger. “Cost, waste, and loss of choice, jobs and legacy will be the hallmarks of the planned merger of universities proposed by the Western Australian government,” she said. And Murdoch University encouraged its staff to join a student protest of the government’s university merger plan at Parliament, with their Vice Chancellor Andrew Deeks also a staunch critic of the idea. UWA is the only university to offer tentative support of the merger.

World.title: PM’s own radiation watchdog shoots down his mobile phone health warning to Bowen
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership PM’s own radiation watchdog shoots down his mobile phone health warning to Bowen Rob Harris November 16, 2026 — 5:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Anthony Albanese’s own radiation safety experts have rejected his claims that carrying a mobile phone close to the heart can interfere with its rhythm, declaring there is no scientific evidence to support the prime minister’s unsolicited health advice to cabinet colleague Chris Bowen. The Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency, which advises the federal government on the health effects of electromagnetic radiation, has also dismissed concerns that keeping phones in trouser pockets could damage sperm or fertility. The prime minister and Chris Bowen in the moment when the conversation was captured by a TV microphone. Seven News The unusually blunt scientific clarification follows an embarrassing hot-mic exchange between Albanese and Bowen at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey, where the pair discussed the potential dangers of mobile phone radiation before joking about the relative importance of their hearts and genitals. “There is no substantiated evidence that [Radiofrequency Electromagnetic Energy] exposure at levels below the safety limits will have any impact on health including on heart function, sperm quality or fertility,” an ARPANSA spokesperson told this masthead.



“Precautionary measures to reduce EME exposure are not required, and there are no known safety concerns with carrying a mobile phone close to your body.” The intervention directly contradicts Albanese’s warning to Bowen during a private conversation inadvertently captured by television cameras as the pair prepared for a renewable energy investment roundtable in Antalya on Friday. After placing his phone in his jacket pocket, Albanese asked Bowen whether he was right-handed and where he usually carried his device. “Generally yeah,” Bowen replied, pointing to his jacket pocket. “It should be away from your heart,” Albanese warned. “It can interfere with your rhythm.” “A little bit radioactive?” Bowen asked. “Yeah. It makes absolute sense,” Albanese replied.



But Bowen was more concerned about another part of his anatomy. “Speaking personally, I’m more conscious of putting it in my pants pocket,” he said. “Because of your dick?” Albanese interjected. Related Article Political leadership ‘No one was hurt’: Albanese responds after his crude ‘hot mic’ incident “Because of my dick,” Bowen replied, laughing. “Arguably more important than the heart.”



The exchange, first broadcast by Seven News, prompted criticism from the Coalition, which accused the pair of engaging in inappropriate locker-room talk at an international summit. Chief Medical Officer Michael Kidd declined to comment on Albanese’s health advice, instead directing questions to ARPANSA. Albanese subsequently apologised, telling reporters in Manila on Sunday that the conversation had been intended as light-hearted banter between friends. “I, of course, regret that and I apologise,” he said, while stressing that nobody had been hurt or harmed. ARPANSA said its radiofrequency safety standard sets exposure limits many times below the levels at which known adverse health effects occur.



The agency, which continually reviews international scientific research on electromagnetic energy and health, said Australians did not need to take additional precautions when carrying their phones. The episode has echoes of another Labor prime minister whose fascination with the possible dangers of modern technology extended well beyond conventional medical advice. Paul Keating became so concerned about mobile phone radiation that his staff began wearing hands-free headsets during the 1996 election campaign, joking that the devices would stop them “frying your brain”. Paul Keating in 1997 with the Ozemail phone. Andrew Taylor As this masthead reported in 1997, virtually the entire prime ministerial office had adopted the headsets by the end of the campaign’s first week, although nobody could remember whether Keating or his chief political adviser, Don Russell, had first raised the alarm.



Keating’s suspicions went considerably further, according to former economic adviser John Edwards’ 1996 biography, Keating: The Inside Story. Edwards wrote that the former prime minister was deeply sceptical of conventional medicine, regularly consulted a Canberra herbalist and drank a daily glass of Chinese herbal medicine. He even installed a trampoline in the backyard of his rented Canberra home, believing the brief moment of weightlessness at the top of each jump could destroy cancer cells. Edwards described Keating as “inclined to fanciful cures for ailments”, while revealing he used an earpiece and small microphone to keep his mobile phone away from his head. The prime minister’s office was contacted for comment.

World.title: ‘They’re keeping an eye on us’: Details of plot to sell fighter jet parts revealed
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland courts ‘They’re keeping an eye on us’: Details of plot to sell fighter jet parts revealed Cloe Read and Nick McKenzie November 16, 2026 — 5:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australia’s national security could have been endangered by a plot to sell parts of a military fighter jet between Russia and China, a court has heard, as details of how two men worked with an alleged Chinese spy were revealed for the first time. Facts of the case against Brisbane-based Russian émigré Alexander Cher and Gold Coast businessman Kim Bowei Lee have remained secret until this week, as a suppression order was lifted over their court cases. The pair were charged in 2022, as revealed by this masthead, after having flown to Russia in 2018, where they held meetings to sell parts of an SU-35 fighter jet. One of the men spoke about the parts being restricted and needing Russian connections to “carry this out quietly”. Alexander Cher leaves the Brisbane District Court. AAPIMAGE The trip was allegedly paid for by Chinese national and former Melbourne businessman Brian Chen, a member of the Chinese Communist Party. An official source described Chen to this masthead in 2022 as a Chinese military intelligence operative “who travels the world as a spy”.



The prosecution said if the transaction for the jet parts had gone through, it would mean Australia had not enforced its international obligations to stop the acquisition of weapons. The arrests came as part of a broader ASIO investigation into an alleged Chinese Communist Party spy network operation in Australia, with ties to a relative of Chinese President Xi Jinping. There was no suggestion Lee and Cher were involved in espionage activity. Alleged Chinese intelligence operative Brian Chen. Australian Federal Police began investigating Chen’s activities and executed search warrants in December 2019 in Melbourne. On Monday, Cher pleaded guilty in the Brisbane District Court to brokering involving military goods, with his barrister Mark McCarthy submitting he should receive a lesser sentence than his co-accused, of 12 to 18 months.



Judge David Kent described the offending as serious, and difficult to detect, but found Lee was in a higher position to Cher, and acted as the conduit between him and Chen. He sentenced Cher to 18 months’ imprisonment, but to be released immediately on a recognisance order. Kent said a letter of apology by Cher showed he accepted responsibility, and referred to his offending as an inexcusable mistake. The spare parts were for an SU-35 fighter jet. AP At Lee’s sentence last year, the court heard he had worked as a broker with AMP Suncorp until 2015. He met Chen in 2015, with prosecution and defence both submitting Lee did not know who Chen was. He sat calmly in the dock and spoke quietly with his legal team during the proceeding. In an almost empty courtroom, he appeared to be accompanied by three supporters, including his wife.



Lee’s barrister, Jeffrey Hunter, KC, told the court his client first met Chen in Hong Kong, where he saw photographs of him with various foreign dignitaries. Lee assumed he had “good connections”. “He didn’t know that Chen was in fact ... a loyal member of the [Chinese Communist] Party, and someone who was overtly working on behalf of the Chinese government,” he said. The court heard Lee communicated with Chen about getting aviation parts from Russia, including jet fuel. The jet fuel was a legitimate transaction, the prosecution said, and was used as the official explanation to the Russian government during the negotiations. Jennifer Single SC, representing the Commonwealth, said Chen in January 2018 advised Lee that the “SU-35 engine I need now is an airborne-phased array radar. Make initial arrangements for 45 sets.”



Single said from the beginning, Lee knew the size of the transaction that was sought, and that it was about the SU-35 engine. Editor's pick Analysis

China relations Beijing gets ready to welcome Putin and ‘lame duck’ Trump She said from as early as February 2018, Lee knew the purchases were restricted, because Chen had advised him: “There is quite a large climate for spare parts for these. Normal military purposes are restricted from Russia. So those things will be sold through other channels.” Chen also explained there was no way to buy the whole machine back for training. “This is restricted. Therefore, we need an ... intermediary to seek connections and carry this out quietly. See whether connections can be made in Russia.”



Lee messaged Chen later in the year. “You, I and the company have all passed the Russian national security clearance. Now they have already given us level two. We can advance corporation with their highly sensitive departments! Remember, I said to you they would definitely do checks.” Single said before travelling to Russia, the pair communicated about the clearances, writing: “they’re keeping an eye on us”. Lee claimed upon reflecting on his offending: “I know what I did was wrong … If it had occurred, the security of Taiwan and Australia would’ve been impacted. I’m so sorry.” Single said these comments demonstrated that Lee knew if the transaction went ahead, the security of Taiwan and Australia would have been impacted. Hunter said his client had pleaded guilty and made admissions to police, and should receive less than 3½ years.



The court heard Chen, who was the subject of an Interpol red notice at the time of Cher and Lee’s arrest, was in Australia and in Hong Kong at some stages of the communications between the group. Chief Judge Brian Devereaux sentenced Lee to two years’ imprisonment, to serve six months upon entering a release order. “Even if this arrangement might never have succeeded, the risk of such offending is … the consequential impact on Australia’s national security and place among the community of like nations,” he said. World.title: Fifty years after Sir Douglas Nicholls, Ken Wyatt makes history as WA’s first Indigenous governor
World.content:
NationalWAWA Parliament Fifty years after Sir Douglas Nicholls, Ken Wyatt makes history as WA’s first Indigenous governor Hamish Hastie and Michael Philipps November 16, 2026 — 5:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

WA’s next governor Ken Wyatt says his focus in the new role will be on the future generations of Western Australians, while recognising the importance of his historic appointment. Premier Roger Cook made the announcement of Wyatt’s new position on Monday morning, calling the appointment of the first ever Indigenous WA governor a historic moment. Premier Roger Cook with former federal MP Ken Wyatt. Hamish Hastie It has been 50 years since Sir Douglas Nicholls was named the first Indigenous governor of an Australian state, when he took on the position for South Australia in 1976. Wyatt said he respected the trust that had been placed in him and hoped to repay that trust over the next four years in the role.



“As we approach the 2029 bicentenary of the establishment of the Swan River Colony, I will support a thoughtful and inclusive conversation,” he said. “We will approach the anniversary with an understanding that the history of this place reaches far beyond two centuries. “We must make room for the experience of Aboriginal people, acknowledge difficult chapters honestly, and recognise the contribution of all of the generations who have made Western Australia their home.” Wyatt said young people and regional WA will be a priority throughout his time in the role. “I will encourage meaningful community participation, a strong regional presence, and opportunities for young people to help shape the legacy of that occasion,” he said.



“My hope is that our participation will leave us with a deeper understanding of one another and stronger relationships in the future.” Related Article Exclusive

Indigenous ‘Sit down, talk with Indigenous Australians’: Wyatt’s message to Hanson after ‘primitive’ comments Wyatt said he recognised the difficult nature of working in a government based on the colonial history of European settlement in Australia while honouring his Aboriginal heritage. “Look, we’re based on a structure of government that emanated from out of the United Kingdom,” he said. “Those structures have served us well. So, in my consideration of both the colonial past, I also considered the way in which we’ve come forward as West Australians.



“That while we’ve had chapters in our history that people have not known of, my focus is on contemporary Western Australia, where we’ve come from and where we lead to for our grandchildren and future generations.” “Common sense has to provide as well, but I’ve been handed an incredible opportunity, and it’s a privileged position within the structure of this state. “In one sense, I look at the premier, and from a monarchy sense, I’m his boss. “But on the other hand, I have worked with the premier previously on many other issues when I was a federal member in the areas of aged care, and it didn’t matter who we were.” Wyatt was the federal member for Hasluck from 2010 until 2022 where he represented the Liberal party.



Wyatt said it was a profound privilege to be entrusted with the office of governor. “I thank His Majesty the King for the confidence placed in me, and the Premier for recommending me for this responsibility,” he said. “To the people of Western Australia, I make a clear commitment: I will serve you faithfully, impartially, and in the best of my ability. “Service above self will guide my conduct. The responsibilities this offers will have my full attention and dedication, with the support of my wife Anna. Wyatt said he understood the significance of the trust he had accepted by taking on the role.



“The governor’s constitutional responsibilities are fundamental to our parliamentary democracy,” he said. “I will discharge those duties with independence of judgment, respect for constitutional principle, and the care they require. “I will uphold the impartiality of the office and serve Western Australians of every background, belief, and circumstance.” Wyatt also thanked outgoing governor Chris Dawson, who will step down from the position at the end of the year. The 74-year-old will take over as the 35th representative of the monarchy after current governor Dawson’s term expires on December 31.

World.title: Forrestania grabs control of Zenith in WA gold power play
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Forrestania grabs control of Zenith in WA gold power play Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward November 16, 2026 — 5:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Forrestania Resources has put its foot on a controlling 72.56 per cent stake in Zenith Minerals after its off-market takeover offer officially closed late Friday evening. The move is a major chess piece in the company’s strategy to build a significant Western Australian gold business through regional consolidation. The offer, first announced in June, brings Zenith’s 675,000 ounces of gold into the fold and will likely prove to be a significant step in that process. Forrestania Resources is transitioning to producer status at its Edna May gold project in Western Australia. Forrestania’s play is anchored in a classic hub-and-spoke growth strategy, centred on two strategic processing hubs at its Edna May and Lake Johnston projects. The company is also aggressively building an inventory of additional ore sources via ore-purchase agreements within economic haulage distance to feed its hungry, soon-to-be operational, processing infrastructure. Last Friday, the company entered into another ore purchase agreement, adding to a raft of similar agreements announced over the last month. The fresh deal with ASX-listed Western Gold Resources (WGR) proposes supplying 1.1 million tonnes of ore from WGR’s Gold Duke project over up to 30 months. Notably, WGR is responsible for transport and delivery costs, reflecting Forrestania’s strategy of preserving its processing margins.



Forrestania is rapidly transitioning from explorer to producer at its Edna May gold project, where it says dry commissioning is now underway. The first ore processing from its Taipan deposit is targeted for next month, marking its arrival as Australia’s newest gold producer. While advancing a growing list of ore sources at Edna May, the company is also progressing refurbishment at its Lake Johnston operation as a second strategic hub designed to support future growth and further regional consolidation. Lake Johnson is slated for commissioning in early 2027, with ore from the company’s British Hill deposit already trucked to site and ready for processing. By moving to secure a controlling stake in fellow ASX-listed Zenith, Forrestania is signalling its ambitions extend well beyond developing its own assets, as it looks to play a much bigger game in Western Australia’s rapidly consolidating gold sector. Management says its focus is on growing its resource base and expanding production opportunities through disciplined exploration, targeted acquisitions and project development. Regional consolidation around central processing infrastructure is a well-trodden path to success in the WA goldfields, with some of the industry’s biggest names having been built on the back of similar strategies. By owning two processing hubs and then systematically acquiring surrounding deposits, companies can build critical mass, reduce processing costs and de-risk operations by reducing reliance on a single ore source. With the Zenith deal now locked in, another ore purchase agreement sealed and the Edna May plant just weeks away from its first gold pour, the company appears to be rounding a major corner into the home straight.



Forrestania has moved decisively to secure a significant regional footprint and is now on the cusp of generating cashflow. With two strategic hubs and a controlling stake in a significant regional peer, the company looks set to generate plenty of newsflow as it brings its production and consolidation strategy to life. World.title: Perth teenager shot by police laughed at Anzac Day ceremony, blew up toilet during descent into extremism
World.content:
Breaking NationalWACourts Perth teenager shot by police laughed at Anzac Day ceremony, blew up toilet during descent into extremism Hannah Murphy November 16, 2026 — 5:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A Perth teenager who stabbed a man before he was shot dead by police had been caught with graphic beheading videos at school, laughed during an Anzac Day ceremony and bragged he was being monitored by officials after becoming increasingly radicalised, an inquest has heard. The hearing into the death of 16-year-old Rossmoyne Senior High School student James Hollands opened in the WA Coroner’s Court on Monday, examining the lead-up to his death on May 4, 2024, and hearing how he had become the “most watched” child at his high school due to his fixation on explosives, firearms, military history, Marxism, Christianity and Islam. Loading The court heard James, who lived with autism and attention deficit disorder, phoned his dad for 30 minutes and had a conversation where he appeared in good spirits and had been making plans for his week before heading out to Islamic school Zakariya Academy later in the day. He stopped at home in Perth’s south to pick up his wallet before visiting an IGA, the academy again and petrol station, where he bought four dollars’ worth of fuel, and set a small fire at a nearby park.



The inquest heard James then sent a text message to about 33 people indicating he was “going on the path of jihad”, describing himself as a soldier and taking responsibility for that night’s events. Related Article Updated

Crime ‘Radicalised teen’ shot dead by police in Willetton after stabbing The teenager subsequently phoned triple-zero himself, and told police it was his intention to “kill all male civilians” in the area before hanging up. Minutes later, he was later seen on High Road in Riverton armed with a 35-centimetre knife, and ran at a member of the public who escaped and phoned police. The boy then approached another man from behind and stabbed him in the back, puncturing his lung. The police attended and spotted James walking in a Bunnings car park carrying the knife, and they approached him in their car. He repeatedly ran at them and officers attempted to maintain distance, but became concerned for a civilian driver who was also in the same car park.



The boy ran at the other car and opened the passenger door, before the car drove off. The officers got out of their car armed with Tasers and a gun, and repeatedly ordered James to drop his knife. Police at the scene of a knife attack in Willetton on Saturday night. Nine News Both officers discharged Tasers at him, however James continued to run at them, and said: “shoot me, I’ll f–king kill you and I’ll become a shahid. Allahu Akbar.” He charged the officer armed with a gun, who shot him in the chest.



James was later pronounced dead. An investigation by WA Police found the officer who shot the teenager had been “justified”, and the event was declared a terrorist attack. The man who was stabbed survived, but was significantly injured. The inquest is examining the lead up to James’ death, and the interactions he had with multiple authorities and programs who attempted to guide him away from extremism. The inquest heard James had converted to Islam when he was in year 9, and while his educators were not initially concerned about his religious beliefs, they noticed he had become fixated on “weapons, explosives, violent topics, religion, and extremism”. Rossmoyne Senior High School principal Alan Brown told the inquest he first become aware of the boy’s fixations when the boy downloaded extreme videos to the school computer.



Principal Alan Brown gave evidence at the inquest. Rossmoyne SHS Brown confirmed a beheading was pictured in one of the videos, and the school subsequently limited the boy’s internet access and ability to bring in his own device. Instead, the inquest heard, the boy started to use library computers to circumvent the rules, and was suspended for five days. However, Brown said it was only after one incident in a school toilet that he and others at the school became engaged with counterterrorism programs run by WA Police. Brown said in late 2022, James had put a lithium unit into a toilet, which caused a “minor explosion”. As a result, he was referred to a “multi-agency” group aimed at halting his descent into extremism. The school later reported James was allegedly telling his classmates he was a “high profile person” being looked at by WA police.



They started having ongoing meetings with psychologists, experts, and the boy’s family – who he had previously been violent with – and got him a religious mentor to guide him towards the positives of the Islamic religion and away from the extremist material he found online. The boy began to wear traditional Islamic dress to school. “[He was] the most watched child at Rossmoyne Senior High School,” a psychologist who had been engaged to help James told the inquest. Several other incidents were reported to the group managing James, including one where a Jewish student was attacked after making a remark about his Islamic faith, and another where he was again caught with graphic extremist videos on a USB. The Bunnings car park where the teenager was fatally shot. Rebecca Peppiatt



Brown told the inquest he had personally spoken with James following his “disrespectful” behaviour at an Anzac Day ceremony in 2024. He said James had been seen laughing, and he refused to stand during proceedings. “We had a conversation about respect and the right to have different beliefs and my respect of that - but with that, he needs to respect the rights of others,” Brown said. “He politely disagreed.” The inquest heard just 24 hours before he died in May 2024, a school librarian found pamphlets in James’ possession depicting a man with a gun on the front, containing an “inflammatory speech”. The school reported it to the relevant authorities, but the inquest was told the discovery had only been made at the end of the day, and as such, the email had likely not been read until later.



Brown said the school had been surprised to hear of the James’ final actions. Related Article Crime ‘It’s shocking’: Perth Ahmadiyya Muslim community concerned about Islamophobia after radicalised teen stabbing “While [the boy] was quite devout in his faith and his beliefs, we hadn’t seen any indication that he was wanting to [carry out] that kind of attack on other people,” he said. “He had not indicated that at all ... it was a surprising event from the school’s point of view, as we thought we were making a positive difference.” That view was echoed by psychologist Elizabeth Pinkerton, who had been involved in James’ care, and said it was her view he had begun to improve, as he had become more engaged in school and his work had improved.



However, she said he still refused to accept certain supports. “He didn’t want to be different,” Pinkerton said. Both Brown and Pinkerton told the inquest there had been no significant red flags prior to James’ death, but in retrospect, the death of his grandmother a week before had likely put his mental health at risk. The inquest is being attended by the boy’s family, and representatives from the Department of Education, Communities and WA Police.

World.title: ‘Not a murderer’: Mum denies killing kids in house fire
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts ‘Not a murderer’: Mum denies killing kids in house fire Rex Martinich November 16, 2026 — 6:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A mother who lost five children and her partner in a house fire has denied setting the blaze herself, telling a coroner she is “determined” to get answers. Four-year-old twins Kyza and Koa Godinet, and Nicky (3), Zack (11) and Harry Stephenson (10) were killed when their house on Russell Island, south-east of Brisbane, caught fire on August 6, 2023. The blaze claimed six lives. Nine News The boys’ 43-year-old father Wayne Patrick Godinet died after running upstairs while flames and smoke poured out of the house in an attempt to save the children and an adult occupant. The children’s mother, Samantha Stephenson and her stepsister Connie Campbell escaped the fire that trapped the others upstairs in a “classic Queenslander” home elevated on stumps.



Stephenson was the first witness called at the start of a coroners inquest on Monday into the six deaths. She broke down in tears as she was asked to confirm her relationship to each of the deceased. “I’m more than determined to get to this answer,” Stephenson said. Fire crews battling the blaze that engulfed multiple homes on Russell Island in 2023. Nine News She was escorted to the witness stand by a corrective services officer and she told Coroner Donald MacKenzie she was on remand for alleged cannabis possession and public nuisance.



An investigation found the fire likely started on the ground floor but the precise location could not be determined and deliberate ignition could not be ruled out, counsel assisting Corinne Leach told the coroner. “Did you start the fire?” Leach said. “No,” Stephenson said. Loading Leach asked about Stephenson’s alleged statements and behaviour while living at a unit complex after the fire.



A neighbour overheard Stephenson say, ‘I’m terribly sorry, mummy is just a murderer,’ Leach suggested. “I never said it,” Stephenson said. She also denied saying to neighbours “I let the smoke kill my kids”, screaming “I’m a murderer” or nodding when someone asked if she was guilty. Godinet and Stephenson had fallen asleep together after sharing a cannabis bong on a couch in a “chill out area” underneath the house, MacKenzie heard. Stephenson said she was woken in the early hours by Godinet jumping across the couch.



“I realised everything was on fire,” she said. “Wayne definitely would have gone upstairs at some point.” Stephenson tried to follow the father up into the house but the flames had engulfed the staircase. “I opened the door and it literally exploded,” she said. A Rural Fire Brigade crew arrived at 6.35am.



But Queensland Fire and Rescue Services were nearly an hour away, requiring a barge to get to the island east of Brisbane. The coroner is examining several issues including the fire’s cause, whether the installation of compliant smoke alarms would have prevented the deaths and whether emergency service resources on Russell Island are sufficient. The inquest will hold hearings over the coming two weeks. AAP

World.title: ‘They mean everything to me’: Thieves steal three Melbourne Cups won by Makybe Diva
World.content:
Updated NationalVictoriaCrime ‘They mean everything to me’: Thieves steal three Melbourne Cups won by Makybe Diva Alexander Darling Updated November 16, 2026 — 6:13pm ,first published 4:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Thieves have stolen the three Melbourne Cup trophies won by Makybe Diva after breaking into Flemington Racecourse in an early morning raid. Victoria Police said an unknown number of offenders stole the trophies about 6.30am on Monday from a cabinet, where they were on display as part of an exhibition honouring the legendary racehorse. Loading By Monday afternoon, the entrance to the exhibition had been boarded up, but an image reportedly from inside taken this morning shows a display cabinet with smashed glass, and several empty ledges next to the famous blue, red and white silks worn by jockey Glen Boss. There are reports the thieves were disguised as construction workers or tradespeople, but neither police nor the Victoria Racing Club (VRC) has confirmed this.



“The circumstances are yet to be established and an investigation into the incident is ongoing,” police said in a statement on Monday afternoon. The VRC said it had reported the theft to police and that it was assisting with the investigation. Makybe Diva in 2005 with strapper Christine Mitchell and the three Melbourne Cups the racehorse won. The trophies were stolen on Monday. Sebastian Costanzo “We are devastated by the incident and are in direct contact with Tony Santic [Makybe Diva’s owner].” Santic told this masthead he was first been made aware of the theft at 10am on Monday.



“The VRC called me and said they’d had a break in and the three Melbourne Cups had been stolen,” he said. “They told me the alarm went off, and five minutes later security arrived, and they [the trophies] were gone.” Santic also said the VRC told him the thieves were believed to have been wearing high-visibility clothing. “They mean everything to me,” he told this masthead. “I’ve lived with them like Australia has lived with Makybe over the last 23 years. Many hundreds of people have had a drink out of the cup.” Later speaking on 3AW, Santic pleaded with the thieves to drop the cups off “in one piece”, saying they were irreplaceable.



He said that if the cups were returned, this episode would deter him from exhibiting them publicly again. “They belong to the people as well. She [Makybe Diva] gave me and the people a lot, and I want to share that.” Tony Santic won three Melbourne Cup’s with Makybe Diva Pat Scala Makybe Diva remains the only horse ever to have won the Melbourne Cup three times, which she did in consecutive years, from 2003 to 2005. The legendary mare died in February at the age of 27.



Crafted with 18-carat gold, a Melbourne Cup weighs nearly two kilograms and takes more than 10 days to make. Each cup is valued at more than $1 million. The three cups were on display at the Hill Stand at Flemington – between the Terrace and the Atrium – as part of an exhibition titled “Makybe Diva: Queen of the Cups”. The horse’s ashes are also on display. This is not the first time something like this has happened.



Related Article Flashback From the Archives, 1963: Melbourne Cup stolen from display window In 1963, that year’s Melbourne Cup trophy was stolen from a display window near the corner of Elizabeth and Collins streets in Melbourne’s CBD in broad daylight, also by a group of three thieves. It is understood the VRC has shared CCTV footage from the building with Victoria Police, and that the display area featured 24/7 surveillance and alarms. World.title: Perth MP throws weight behind controversial uni merger idea
World.content:
NationalWAUniversity Perth MP throws weight behind controversial uni merger idea Holly Thompson and Michael Philipps November 16, 2026 — 5:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Federal Member for Perth Patrick Gorman has declared there are too many universities in the state, and has welcomed the proposed merger between the University of Western Australia, and Curtin and Murdoch University. Speaking at a press conference on Monday morning, Gorman was asked whether he favoured a merger between the universities. Federal Perth MP Patrick Gorman. Holly Thompson The merger has proved to be a controversial topic, with the vice chancellors at both Murdoch and Curtin University claiming joining all three institutions would be disastrous for the state’s tertiary sector. Students have also largely been against the decision, hosting protests including on the steps of Parliament House.



But Gorman has confirmed he would support a merger. “Well, for 20-something years, I have thought we have had at least one too many universities in Western Australia, so I am really open to the conversation,” Gorman said. “I think you put the case that the students always want the best value degree they can get, and that is what this conversation should be about. “Edith Cowan University is in my electorate and is the one university which is not part of those discussions. “I have been clear with the state government for a long period of time that my priority when it comes to education in my electorate is getting another inner-city high school.”



In 2024, Gorman spoke with this masthead on the issue, claiming there had been a lack of forward-thinking when it came to education in Perth’s CBD – a position he maintained on Monday. “Currently, we don’t have a (public) high school in the City of Perth, and that is a priority as we continue to see, over time, more and more housing come into the inner city, so that is my priority,” he said. “When it comes to university mergers, these are really big, complex things that will take a period of time. I will note that even the premier said he’s got an open mind about it, I also have an open mind and indeed, I have had an open mind about these questions since 2005.” Gorman said he was on the Curtin University Council in 2005, and had “extensive conversations about Curtin and Murdoch merging” at the time. “And if you go back into the archives, you will find quotes from me supporting that merger, which was controversial at the time,” he said.



“But I also note that you want to make sure that students get a better value degree, and taxpayers get better value for money, and that is the work that’s being done now. “I am happy to see the case put forward, but we want to make sure that it is done right.” Curtin University Vice Chancellor Harlene Hayne said Curtin would “vigorously oppose” the merger. “Cost, waste, and loss of choice, jobs and legacy will be the hallmarks of the planned merger of universities proposed by the Western Australian government,” she said. And Murdoch University encouraged its staff to join a student protest of the government’s university merger plan at Parliament, with their Vice Chancellor Andrew Deeks also a staunch critic of the idea. UWA is the only university to offer tentative support of the merger.

World.title: PM’s own radiation watchdog shoots down his mobile phone health warning to Bowen
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership PM’s own radiation watchdog shoots down his mobile phone health warning to Bowen Rob Harris November 16, 2026 — 5:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Anthony Albanese’s own radiation safety experts have rejected his claims that carrying a mobile phone close to the heart can interfere with its rhythm, declaring there is no scientific evidence to support the prime minister’s unsolicited health advice to cabinet colleague Chris Bowen. The Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency, which advises the federal government on the health effects of electromagnetic radiation, has also dismissed concerns that keeping phones in trouser pockets could damage sperm or fertility. The prime minister and Chris Bowen in the moment when the conversation was captured by a TV microphone. Seven News The unusually blunt scientific clarification follows an embarrassing hot-mic exchange between Albanese and Bowen at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey, where the pair discussed the potential dangers of mobile phone radiation before joking about the relative importance of their hearts and genitals. “There is no substantiated evidence that [Radiofrequency Electromagnetic Energy] exposure at levels below the safety limits will have any impact on health including on heart function, sperm quality or fertility,” an ARPANSA spokesperson told this masthead.



“Precautionary measures to reduce EME exposure are not required, and there are no known safety concerns with carrying a mobile phone close to your body.” The intervention directly contradicts Albanese’s warning to Bowen during a private conversation inadvertently captured by television cameras as the pair prepared for a renewable energy investment roundtable in Antalya on Friday. After placing his phone in his jacket pocket, Albanese asked Bowen whether he was right-handed and where he usually carried his device. “Generally yeah,” Bowen replied, pointing to his jacket pocket. “It should be away from your heart,” Albanese warned. “It can interfere with your rhythm.” “A little bit radioactive?” Bowen asked. “Yeah. It makes absolute sense,” Albanese replied.



But Bowen was more concerned about another part of his anatomy. “Speaking personally, I’m more conscious of putting it in my pants pocket,” he said. “Because of your dick?” Albanese interjected. Related Article Political leadership ‘No one was hurt’: Albanese responds after his crude ‘hot mic’ incident “Because of my dick,” Bowen replied, laughing. “Arguably more important than the heart.”



The exchange, first broadcast by Seven News, prompted criticism from the Coalition, which accused the pair of engaging in inappropriate locker-room talk at an international summit. Chief Medical Officer Michael Kidd declined to comment on Albanese’s health advice, instead directing questions to ARPANSA. Albanese subsequently apologised, telling reporters in Manila on Sunday that the conversation had been intended as light-hearted banter between friends. “I, of course, regret that and I apologise,” he said, while stressing that nobody had been hurt or harmed. ARPANSA said its radiofrequency safety standard sets exposure limits many times below the levels at which known adverse health effects occur.



The agency, which continually reviews international scientific research on electromagnetic energy and health, said Australians did not need to take additional precautions when carrying their phones. The episode has echoes of another Labor prime minister whose fascination with the possible dangers of modern technology extended well beyond conventional medical advice. Paul Keating became so concerned about mobile phone radiation that his staff began wearing hands-free headsets during the 1996 election campaign, joking that the devices would stop them “frying your brain”. Paul Keating in 1997 with the Ozemail phone. Andrew Taylor As this masthead reported in 1997, virtually the entire prime ministerial office had adopted the headsets by the end of the campaign’s first week, although nobody could remember whether Keating or his chief political adviser, Don Russell, had first raised the alarm.



Keating’s suspicions went considerably further, according to former economic adviser John Edwards’ 1996 biography, Keating: The Inside Story. Edwards wrote that the former prime minister was deeply sceptical of conventional medicine, regularly consulted a Canberra herbalist and drank a daily glass of Chinese herbal medicine. He even installed a trampoline in the backyard of his rented Canberra home, believing the brief moment of weightlessness at the top of each jump could destroy cancer cells. Edwards described Keating as “inclined to fanciful cures for ailments”, while revealing he used an earpiece and small microphone to keep his mobile phone away from his head. The prime minister’s office was contacted for comment.

World.title: ‘They’re keeping an eye on us’: Details of plot to sell fighter jet parts revealed
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland courts ‘They’re keeping an eye on us’: Details of plot to sell fighter jet parts revealed Cloe Read and Nick McKenzie November 16, 2026 — 5:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australia’s national security could have been endangered by a plot to sell parts of a military fighter jet between Russia and China, a court has heard, as details of how two men worked with an alleged Chinese spy were revealed for the first time. Facts of the case against Brisbane-based Russian émigré Alexander Cher and Gold Coast businessman Kim Bowei Lee have remained secret until this week, as a suppression order was lifted over their court cases. The pair were charged in 2022, as revealed by this masthead, after having flown to Russia in 2018, where they held meetings to sell parts of an SU-35 fighter jet. One of the men spoke about the parts being restricted and needing Russian connections to “carry this out quietly”. Alexander Cher leaves the Brisbane District Court. AAPIMAGE The trip was allegedly paid for by Chinese national and former Melbourne businessman Brian Chen, a member of the Chinese Communist Party. An official source described Chen to this masthead in 2022 as a Chinese military intelligence operative “who travels the world as a spy”.



The prosecution said if the transaction for the jet parts had gone through, it would mean Australia had not enforced its international obligations to stop the acquisition of weapons. The arrests came as part of a broader ASIO investigation into an alleged Chinese Communist Party spy network operation in Australia, with ties to a relative of Chinese President Xi Jinping. There was no suggestion Lee and Cher were involved in espionage activity. Alleged Chinese intelligence operative Brian Chen. Australian Federal Police began investigating Chen’s activities and executed search warrants in December 2019 in Melbourne. On Monday, Cher pleaded guilty in the Brisbane District Court to brokering involving military goods, with his barrister Mark McCarthy submitting he should receive a lesser sentence than his co-accused, of 12 to 18 months.



Judge David Kent described the offending as serious, and difficult to detect, but found Lee was in a higher position to Cher, and acted as the conduit between him and Chen. He sentenced Cher to 18 months’ imprisonment, but to be released immediately on a recognisance order. Kent said a letter of apology by Cher showed he accepted responsibility, and referred to his offending as an inexcusable mistake. The spare parts were for an SU-35 fighter jet. AP At Lee’s sentence last year, the court heard he had worked as a broker with AMP Suncorp until 2015. He met Chen in 2015, with prosecution and defence both submitting Lee did not know who Chen was. He sat calmly in the dock and spoke quietly with his legal team during the proceeding. In an almost empty courtroom, he appeared to be accompanied by three supporters, including his wife.



Lee’s barrister, Jeffrey Hunter, KC, told the court his client first met Chen in Hong Kong, where he saw photographs of him with various foreign dignitaries. Lee assumed he had “good connections”. “He didn’t know that Chen was in fact ... a loyal member of the [Chinese Communist] Party, and someone who was overtly working on behalf of the Chinese government,” he said. The court heard Lee communicated with Chen about getting aviation parts from Russia, including jet fuel. The jet fuel was a legitimate transaction, the prosecution said, and was used as the official explanation to the Russian government during the negotiations. Jennifer Single SC, representing the Commonwealth, said Chen in January 2018 advised Lee that the “SU-35 engine I need now is an airborne-phased array radar. Make initial arrangements for 45 sets.”



Single said from the beginning, Lee knew the size of the transaction that was sought, and that it was about the SU-35 engine. Editor's pick Analysis

China relations Beijing gets ready to welcome Putin and ‘lame duck’ Trump She said from as early as February 2018, Lee knew the purchases were restricted, because Chen had advised him: “There is quite a large climate for spare parts for these. Normal military purposes are restricted from Russia. So those things will be sold through other channels.” Chen also explained there was no way to buy the whole machine back for training. “This is restricted. Therefore, we need an ... intermediary to seek connections and carry this out quietly. See whether connections can be made in Russia.”



Lee messaged Chen later in the year. “You, I and the company have all passed the Russian national security clearance. Now they have already given us level two. We can advance corporation with their highly sensitive departments! Remember, I said to you they would definitely do checks.” Single said before travelling to Russia, the pair communicated about the clearances, writing: “they’re keeping an eye on us”. Lee claimed upon reflecting on his offending: “I know what I did was wrong … If it had occurred, the security of Taiwan and Australia would’ve been impacted. I’m so sorry.” Single said these comments demonstrated that Lee knew if the transaction went ahead, the security of Taiwan and Australia would have been impacted. Hunter said his client had pleaded guilty and made admissions to police, and should receive less than 3½ years.



The court heard Chen, who was the subject of an Interpol red notice at the time of Cher and Lee’s arrest, was in Australia and in Hong Kong at some stages of the communications between the group. Chief Judge Brian Devereaux sentenced Lee to two years’ imprisonment, to serve six months upon entering a release order. “Even if this arrangement might never have succeeded, the risk of such offending is … the consequential impact on Australia’s national security and place among the community of like nations,” he said. World.title: Fifty years after Sir Douglas Nicholls, Ken Wyatt makes history as WA’s first Indigenous governor
World.content:
NationalWAWA Parliament Fifty years after Sir Douglas Nicholls, Ken Wyatt makes history as WA’s first Indigenous governor Hamish Hastie and Michael Philipps November 16, 2026 — 5:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

WA’s next governor Ken Wyatt says his focus in the new role will be on the future generations of Western Australians, while recognising the importance of his historic appointment. Premier Roger Cook made the announcement of Wyatt’s new position on Monday morning, calling the appointment of the first ever Indigenous WA governor a historic moment. Premier Roger Cook with former federal MP Ken Wyatt. Hamish Hastie It has been 50 years since Sir Douglas Nicholls was named the first Indigenous governor of an Australian state, when he took on the position for South Australia in 1976. Wyatt said he respected the trust that had been placed in him and hoped to repay that trust over the next four years in the role.



“As we approach the 2029 bicentenary of the establishment of the Swan River Colony, I will support a thoughtful and inclusive conversation,” he said. “We will approach the anniversary with an understanding that the history of this place reaches far beyond two centuries. “We must make room for the experience of Aboriginal people, acknowledge difficult chapters honestly, and recognise the contribution of all of the generations who have made Western Australia their home.” Wyatt said young people and regional WA will be a priority throughout his time in the role. “I will encourage meaningful community participation, a strong regional presence, and opportunities for young people to help shape the legacy of that occasion,” he said.



“My hope is that our participation will leave us with a deeper understanding of one another and stronger relationships in the future.” Related Article Exclusive

Indigenous ‘Sit down, talk with Indigenous Australians’: Wyatt’s message to Hanson after ‘primitive’ comments Wyatt said he recognised the difficult nature of working in a government based on the colonial history of European settlement in Australia while honouring his Aboriginal heritage. “Look, we’re based on a structure of government that emanated from out of the United Kingdom,” he said. “Those structures have served us well. So, in my consideration of both the colonial past, I also considered the way in which we’ve come forward as West Australians.



“That while we’ve had chapters in our history that people have not known of, my focus is on contemporary Western Australia, where we’ve come from and where we lead to for our grandchildren and future generations.” “Common sense has to provide as well, but I’ve been handed an incredible opportunity, and it’s a privileged position within the structure of this state. “In one sense, I look at the premier, and from a monarchy sense, I’m his boss. “But on the other hand, I have worked with the premier previously on many other issues when I was a federal member in the areas of aged care, and it didn’t matter who we were.” Wyatt was the federal member for Hasluck from 2010 until 2022 where he represented the Liberal party.



Wyatt said it was a profound privilege to be entrusted with the office of governor. “I thank His Majesty the King for the confidence placed in me, and the Premier for recommending me for this responsibility,” he said. “To the people of Western Australia, I make a clear commitment: I will serve you faithfully, impartially, and in the best of my ability. “Service above self will guide my conduct. The responsibilities this offers will have my full attention and dedication, with the support of my wife Anna. Wyatt said he understood the significance of the trust he had accepted by taking on the role.



“The governor’s constitutional responsibilities are fundamental to our parliamentary democracy,” he said. “I will discharge those duties with independence of judgment, respect for constitutional principle, and the care they require. “I will uphold the impartiality of the office and serve Western Australians of every background, belief, and circumstance.” Wyatt also thanked outgoing governor Chris Dawson, who will step down from the position at the end of the year. The 74-year-old will take over as the 35th representative of the monarchy after current governor Dawson’s term expires on December 31.

World.title: Forrestania grabs control of Zenith in WA gold power play
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Forrestania grabs control of Zenith in WA gold power play Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward November 16, 2026 — 5:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Forrestania Resources has put its foot on a controlling 72.56 per cent stake in Zenith Minerals after its off-market takeover offer officially closed late Friday evening. The move is a major chess piece in the company’s strategy to build a significant Western Australian gold business through regional consolidation. The offer, first announced in June, brings Zenith’s 675,000 ounces of gold into the fold and will likely prove to be a significant step in that process. Forrestania Resources is transitioning to producer status at its Edna May gold project in Western Australia. Forrestania’s play is anchored in a classic hub-and-spoke growth strategy, centred on two strategic processing hubs at its Edna May and Lake Johnston projects. The company is also aggressively building an inventory of additional ore sources via ore-purchase agreements within economic haulage distance to feed its hungry, soon-to-be operational, processing infrastructure. Last Friday, the company entered into another ore purchase agreement, adding to a raft of similar agreements announced over the last month. The fresh deal with ASX-listed Western Gold Resources (WGR) proposes supplying 1.1 million tonnes of ore from WGR’s Gold Duke project over up to 30 months. Notably, WGR is responsible for transport and delivery costs, reflecting Forrestania’s strategy of preserving its processing margins.



Forrestania is rapidly transitioning from explorer to producer at its Edna May gold project, where it says dry commissioning is now underway. The first ore processing from its Taipan deposit is targeted for next month, marking its arrival as Australia’s newest gold producer. While advancing a growing list of ore sources at Edna May, the company is also progressing refurbishment at its Lake Johnston operation as a second strategic hub designed to support future growth and further regional consolidation. Lake Johnson is slated for commissioning in early 2027, with ore from the company’s British Hill deposit already trucked to site and ready for processing. By moving to secure a controlling stake in fellow ASX-listed Zenith, Forrestania is signalling its ambitions extend well beyond developing its own assets, as it looks to play a much bigger game in Western Australia’s rapidly consolidating gold sector. Management says its focus is on growing its resource base and expanding production opportunities through disciplined exploration, targeted acquisitions and project development. Regional consolidation around central processing infrastructure is a well-trodden path to success in the WA goldfields, with some of the industry’s biggest names having been built on the back of similar strategies. By owning two processing hubs and then systematically acquiring surrounding deposits, companies can build critical mass, reduce processing costs and de-risk operations by reducing reliance on a single ore source. With the Zenith deal now locked in, another ore purchase agreement sealed and the Edna May plant just weeks away from its first gold pour, the company appears to be rounding a major corner into the home straight.



Forrestania has moved decisively to secure a significant regional footprint and is now on the cusp of generating cashflow. With two strategic hubs and a controlling stake in a significant regional peer, the company looks set to generate plenty of newsflow as it brings its production and consolidation strategy to life. World.title: Perth teenager shot by police laughed at Anzac Day ceremony, blew up toilet during descent into extremism
World.content:
Breaking NationalWACourts Perth teenager shot by police laughed at Anzac Day ceremony, blew up toilet during descent into extremism Hannah Murphy November 16, 2026 — 5:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A Perth teenager who stabbed a man before he was shot dead by police had been caught with graphic beheading videos at school, laughed during an Anzac Day ceremony and bragged he was being monitored by officials after becoming increasingly radicalised, an inquest has heard. The hearing into the death of 16-year-old Rossmoyne Senior High School student James Hollands opened in the WA Coroner’s Court on Monday, examining the lead-up to his death on May 4, 2024, and hearing how he had become the “most watched” child at his high school due to his fixation on explosives, firearms, military history, Marxism, Christianity and Islam. Loading The court heard James, who lived with autism and attention deficit disorder, phoned his dad for 30 minutes and had a conversation where he appeared in good spirits and had been making plans for his week before heading out to Islamic school Zakariya Academy later in the day. He stopped at home in Perth’s south to pick up his wallet before visiting an IGA, the academy again and petrol station, where he bought four dollars’ worth of fuel, and set a small fire at a nearby park.



The inquest heard James then sent a text message to about 33 people indicating he was “going on the path of jihad”, describing himself as a soldier and taking responsibility for that night’s events. Related Article Updated

Crime ‘Radicalised teen’ shot dead by police in Willetton after stabbing The teenager subsequently phoned triple-zero himself, and told police it was his intention to “kill all male civilians” in the area before hanging up. Minutes later, he was later seen on High Road in Riverton armed with a 35-centimetre knife, and ran at a member of the public who escaped and phoned police. The boy then approached another man from behind and stabbed him in the back, puncturing his lung. The police attended and spotted James walking in a Bunnings car park carrying the knife, and they approached him in their car. He repeatedly ran at them and officers attempted to maintain distance, but became concerned for a civilian driver who was also in the same car park.



The boy ran at the other car and opened the passenger door, before the car drove off. The officers got out of their car armed with Tasers and a gun, and repeatedly ordered James to drop his knife. Police at the scene of a knife attack in Willetton on Saturday night. Nine News Both officers discharged Tasers at him, however James continued to run at them, and said: “shoot me, I’ll f–king kill you and I’ll become a shahid. Allahu Akbar.” He charged the officer armed with a gun, who shot him in the chest.



James was later pronounced dead. An investigation by WA Police found the officer who shot the teenager had been “justified”, and the event was declared a terrorist attack. The man who was stabbed survived, but was significantly injured. The inquest is examining the lead up to James’ death, and the interactions he had with multiple authorities and programs who attempted to guide him away from extremism. The inquest heard James had converted to Islam when he was in year 9, and while his educators were not initially concerned about his religious beliefs, they noticed he had become fixated on “weapons, explosives, violent topics, religion, and extremism”. Rossmoyne Senior High School principal Alan Brown told the inquest he first become aware of the boy’s fixations when the boy downloaded extreme videos to the school computer.



Principal Alan Brown gave evidence at the inquest. Rossmoyne SHS Brown confirmed a beheading was pictured in one of the videos, and the school subsequently limited the boy’s internet access and ability to bring in his own device. Instead, the inquest heard, the boy started to use library computers to circumvent the rules, and was suspended for five days. However, Brown said it was only after one incident in a school toilet that he and others at the school became engaged with counterterrorism programs run by WA Police. Brown said in late 2022, James had put a lithium unit into a toilet, which caused a “minor explosion”. As a result, he was referred to a “multi-agency” group aimed at halting his descent into extremism. The school later reported James was allegedly telling his classmates he was a “high profile person” being looked at by WA police.



They started having ongoing meetings with psychologists, experts, and the boy’s family – who he had previously been violent with – and got him a religious mentor to guide him towards the positives of the Islamic religion and away from the extremist material he found online. The boy began to wear traditional Islamic dress to school. “[He was] the most watched child at Rossmoyne Senior High School,” a psychologist who had been engaged to help James told the inquest. Several other incidents were reported to the group managing James, including one where a Jewish student was attacked after making a remark about his Islamic faith, and another where he was again caught with graphic extremist videos on a USB. The Bunnings car park where the teenager was fatally shot. Rebecca Peppiatt



Brown told the inquest he had personally spoken with James following his “disrespectful” behaviour at an Anzac Day ceremony in 2024. He said James had been seen laughing, and he refused to stand during proceedings. “We had a conversation about respect and the right to have different beliefs and my respect of that - but with that, he needs to respect the rights of others,” Brown said. “He politely disagreed.” The inquest heard just 24 hours before he died in May 2024, a school librarian found pamphlets in James’ possession depicting a man with a gun on the front, containing an “inflammatory speech”. The school reported it to the relevant authorities, but the inquest was told the discovery had only been made at the end of the day, and as such, the email had likely not been read until later.



Brown said the school had been surprised to hear of the James’ final actions. Related Article Crime ‘It’s shocking’: Perth Ahmadiyya Muslim community concerned about Islamophobia after radicalised teen stabbing “While [the boy] was quite devout in his faith and his beliefs, we hadn’t seen any indication that he was wanting to [carry out] that kind of attack on other people,” he said. “He had not indicated that at all ... it was a surprising event from the school’s point of view, as we thought we were making a positive difference.” That view was echoed by psychologist Elizabeth Pinkerton, who had been involved in James’ care, and said it was her view he had begun to improve, as he had become more engaged in school and his work had improved.



However, she said he still refused to accept certain supports. “He didn’t want to be different,” Pinkerton said. Both Brown and Pinkerton told the inquest there had been no significant red flags prior to James’ death, but in retrospect, the death of his grandmother a week before had likely put his mental health at risk. The inquest is being attended by the boy’s family, and representatives from the Department of Education, Communities and WA Police.

World.title: Staggered age of consent becomes 'difficult' with smaller age gaps - chief victims advisor
World.content:
It is worth having a conversation about a staggered age of consent for sex, says the chief victims advisor, but she also warns that there could be serious challenges in enforcing it.

The UK government is investigating a law change that could make sex between a much older adult and a teenager between 16 and 18 illegal - after recent cases where young women who legally were able to consent were allegedly groomed by much older men.

Media personality Russell Brand has been jailed for more than 10 years for serious sexual offences. A woman who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16 and he was 30, is now campaigning for a staggered age of consent.

British comedian and author David Walliams is also facing allegations he groomed teenagers as young as 15, but did not have sex with them until they were older.

Audio player for " Does NZ need to consider a staggered age of consent? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/crime-and-justice/2631607%2Fstaggered-age-of-consent-becomes-difficult-with-smaller-age-gaps-chief-victims-advisor

Does NZ need to consider a staggered age of consent? Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

In New Zealand, the National Party has promised it would review consent laws and chief victims advisor Ruth Money told Checkpoint that staggered age issues should be part of the conversation.

"It's a good conversation to have and it's certainly good timing when we do have a government to put it as part of that consent review that is going to happen."

But she said overseas experiences have shown there would be some operational challenges.

"If we look at Canada, for example, there is a five year difference, so they have criminalised sexual activity if your partner is five years or more older. I think it's difficult - is it five years, is it seven years? Obviously at the extremes, if I'm 13 and the person is 60, we could ask some questions about grooming and influence. But at the smaller margins it becomes quite difficult for the courts to operationalise, in terms of how can can you prove intent, was the age gap big enough, was there coercion, it becomes difficult."

She said it was such a complex issue and the important thing was to educate the public.

"So what does grooming and coercion look like, what does manipulation look like?"

Money said there were also major issues with NDAs being used to mask sexual misconduct, and there needed to be a wholesale review of consent laws in New Zealand.

"Yes, I will be working with the incoming government to do such a thing."
